rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act before adjusting Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against outstanding demands. The case arose in AY 2019-20 and concerned a refund/stay-of-demand dispute; the court specifically criticized the Department’s approach to treating its order as not covering matters dealt with by the ITAT on the ground that the Union of India was not a party, calling that justification unacceptable and inconsistent with the conduct expected of a model litigant.

From a compliance perspective, the key requirement reaffirmed is that before any refund is adjusted against a tax demand under section 245, the Department must follow the procedure mandated by that section rather than simply making an adjustment unilaterally. The judgment signals that authorities cannot rely on technical arguments to avoid the effect of a High Court order where the substance of the dispute requires compliance, and that departmental actions in refund adjustment matters are subject to judicial scrutiny. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines were stated in the excerpt, but the operative compliance point is that refund adjustments must be lawfully and transparently made in conformity with section 245 and the court’s direction, especially where related stay/refund proceedings are already pending or decided.

Mistri, Madhur Agrawal, Shyam Walve DATE: April 9, 2021 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: April 24, 2021 (Date of publication) AY: 2012-13 FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: Article 226/ s. 147: (i) A Writ Petition can be filed in the Bombay High Court against an order passed in Delhi if the assessee is based in Mumbai. The litigant has the right to go to ‘a Court’ where part of cause of action arises. The Bombay High Court held that a writ petition could be maintained in Bombay even though the challenged income-tax order had been passed by Delhi authorities, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. For compliance purposes, the more important ruling is that a notice under section 148 and a reassessment order under section 147 issued in the name of an amalgamated company that had already ceased to exist are **void and without jurisdiction**; this is not treated as a mere procedural defect.

The Court specifically rejected the argument that the defect could be cured under section 292B, and it also held that the assessee’s participation in the reassessment proceedings does **not** validate the proceedings or create any estoppel against law. In practical terms, if a company has been amalgamated before reassessment proceedings are initiated, tax notices and reassessment orders must be issued, if at all, in the name of the surviving entity; action taken against the non-existent predecessor entity is invalid.

The case concerned AY 2012–13, and the Court’s decision was pronounced on April 9, 2021 and published on April 24, 2021. The ruling reinforces a key compliance control point for corporate restructuring: once an amalgamation takes effect, the company should ensure tax records, PAN-related communications, and litigation notices are promptly aligned with the successor entity’s name so that any future assessment or reassessment proceedings are not directed at a dissolved legal person.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)**, which taxes a private company on **excess share premium received over fair market value**, does **not apply** where shares are issued to shareholders pursuant to a **scheme of amalgamation**. The case involved **AY 2013–14**, with the tribunal’s decision **pronounced on April 13, 2021** and published on **April 24, 2021**.  

On the facts, the assessee-company had filed its return for AY 2013–14, and during scrutiny the Assessing Officer found that **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** had amalgamated into the assessee under an approved amalgamation scheme. In that process, the assessee issued shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The tax department sought to treat the value arising from the amalgamation as **deemed income** under section 56(2)(viib), effectively characterizing the issuance as if there were an unjustified premium over face value.  

The tribunal rejected that approach, stating that the purpose of section 56(2)(viib) is to tax **unexplained or excessive premium received by private companies on issuance of shares where the shares do not carry corresponding underlying value**, not to cover share issuance mandated by an amalgamation scheme. It held that the **notional excess of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be treated as share premium** for this deeming provision. The decision also referred to **AS-14 issued by ICAI** and **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012** in support of the treatment of amalgamation accounting and share issuance as distinct from taxable premium.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where shares are issued **solely because of a bona fide amalgamation approved under a scheme**, the transaction should not ordinarily be exposed to **section 56(2)(viib)** tax on alleged excess fair market value. However, the ruling is limited to the facts of amalgamation-related issuance and does not change the general rule that **unjustified share premium in ordinary equity issuances** can still be scrutinized under section 56(2)(viib).

This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns **section 50C of the Income-tax Act**, which deems the **stamp duty valuation** of transferred property to be the sale consideration for **capital gains** purposes when the stated sale price is lower than the stamp valuation. The Tribunal stated that the **third proviso to section 50C**, inserted by the **Finance Act, 2018**, creates a tolerance band under which section 50C will **not apply if the difference between stamp duty value and actual consideration does not exceed 5%**; this tolerance was later **increased to 10% by the Finance Act, 2020**. Although those amendments were described as prospective, the Tribunal held them to be **curative in nature** and therefore applicable **retrospectively from 1 April 2003**, the date section 50C was originally introduced.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that where a property transfer’s **stamp duty value is up to 10% higher than the declared sale consideration**, the declared consideration should be accepted at face value and the **anti-avoidance substitution mechanism under section 50C should not be triggered**. The case was an appeal for **Assessment Year 2011–12** in the matter of **Maria Fernandes Cheryl vs. ITO (International Taxation 2(3)(1), Mumbai)**, with the Tribunal’s pronouncement dated **15 January 2021** and publication on **17 April 2021**. The ruling is relevant to taxpayers and tax teams handling **immovable property transfers**, especially where there is a small gap between contractual consideration and stamp duty value, because it supports using the statutory tolerance band rather than mechanically substituting stamp value for capital gains computation.

The Supreme Court held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 because Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable “as far as may be.” As a result, where a corporate debtor makes a written and signed acknowledgement of debt before expiry of the limitation period, that acknowledgement can extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application. The Court also clarified that an entry in the debtor’s books of account, including a balance sheet entry, can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18, provided it is read together with the notes annexed to or forming part of the balance sheet and the auditor’s report.

This decision specifically reverses the NCLAT Full Bench ruling in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund, which had taken a contrary view on balance-sheet acknowledgements. The Court reaffirmed the basic limitation principle that once time begins to run, it cannot be stopped except by a legally recognized process. For compliance purposes, this means companies facing potential debt enforcement or insolvency exposure should treat balance-sheet disclosures, related notes, and auditor commentary as potentially legally significant acknowledgements that may revive or extend limitation periods for creditors. The judgment was pronounced on April 15, 2021 and published on April 17, 2021.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** examined the **third proviso to section 254(2A)** of the Income-tax Act, which had provided for **automatic vacation of a stay granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) after 365 days**, regardless of who caused the delay in hearing the appeal. The Court held that this rule was **unconstitutional** because it was **discriminatory and manifestly arbitrary**: it could punish an assessee even when the ITAT could not hear the appeal in time for reasons beyond the assessee’s control, and it could also benefit the Revenue even when the Revenue itself was responsible for the delay.

As a result, the Court struck down the offending operation of the proviso and directed that the provision be **read down** by deleting the word **“even”** and the words **“is not”** after the phrase **“delay in disposing of the appeal”**. In practical compliance terms, a stay granted by the ITAT **does not automatically lapse merely because 365 days have passed**; the stay will stand vacated **only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. This means the focus shifts to **fault-based delay** rather than a strict time-based expiration.

For corporate taxpayers with pending appeals and stay orders before the ITAT, the decision materially affects **stay-of-demand management**: companies no longer face automatic loss of stay solely due to passage of time beyond 365 days if they are not at fault for the delay. At the same time, the ruling preserves the possibility of vacation of stay where the assessee’s conduct is responsible for delaying disposal. There is **no new filing deadline or compliance formality created by this judgment**, but it is important for legal and tax teams to document which party caused any adjournments or hearing delays so that stay protection can be defended if challenged.

This Delhi High Court ruling in **CIT v. D. K. Garg** concerns **Section 68 of the Income-tax Act** and the treatment of **accommodation entries**, **cash credits**, and the taxpayer’s attempt to claim the benefit of **peak credit**. The Court held that an accommodation entry provider who seeks peak-credit relief must make a **full and candid disclosure of all facts within his knowledge** about the credit entries in the relevant accounts; this includes explaining **the source of every deposit**, **the destination of every payment**, and the movement of funds through the account structure. In practical terms, the assessee must be able to show that money was moved **through banking channels** from the creditor’s bank account to the assessee’s bank account, that the **identity of the creditors** is established, and that the money later paid out from the assessee’s account returned to the creditors’ accounts; this is the **primary onus** on the assessee under Section 68.

The Court emphasized that a taxpayer cannot claim the benefit of peak credit merely by asserting that only the highest outstanding balance should be taxed; instead, the taxpayer must first produce a clear and credible explanation of the entire transaction flow and the linked accounts involved. Where the taxpayer fails to do this, the unexplained credits remain liable to be treated under Section 68. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court’s decision in **ADIT v. E-Funds IT Solution Inc.** addresses when a foreign company will be treated as having a **Permanent Establishment (PE) in India** under **Article 5 of the India–U.S. DTAA (1990)** for tax purposes. The tax authority had held that the U.S. companies had a **fixed place PE in Delhi** and were therefore taxable in India on income earned through that alleged PE; the CIT(A) also upheld the assessments, additionally reasoning that the companies had **service PE** and **agency PE** status under Article 5.

The Supreme Court explained the law on **fixed place PE, service PE, and agency PE**, and rejected the idea that mere **close association, dependence, or integrated business relationship** between the U.S. company and Indian group entities is enough to create a PE. It held that the correct test is whether the foreign enterprise itself has a sufficiently permanent **place of business in India through which its own business is carried on**, and that the **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** test is **not the proper test** for determining a location/fixed-place PE. The Court therefore clarified that a foreign company does not automatically become taxable in India just because related Indian entities perform support functions or because there is operational dependence between the entities.

For compliance purposes, the key practical takeaway is that **foreign enterprises using Indian affiliates or service providers are not automatically exposed to Indian PE risk solely because of group linkage or business dependence**. PE exposure must be assessed based on the actual facts showing whether the foreign company has a **fixed place**, **service presence**, or **agency relationship** in India within the meaning of the treaty, rather than relying on generalized notions of economic presence or business integration. The judgment is dated **October 24, 2017** (pronouncement), with publication on **October 25, 2017**.

rows.summary:
This circular explains how the GST return filings for July and August 2017 were to be handled during the initial rollout period, when the normal monthly return sequence under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 and rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017 was temporarily disrupted. Ordinarily, registered persons had to file outward supply details in FORM GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, inward supply details in FORM GSTR-2 by the 15th, and the monthly return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 20th; however, the GST Council extended the filing dates for GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 for July and August 2017 and allowed a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3B for those two months, to be filed by the notified due dates after payment of tax.  

The circular also notes that taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 of the CGST Act for their July 2017 liability had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017, and that this credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and could be used to discharge tax liability. Because FORM GSTR-3B was filed instead of the normal return sequence while the GSTR-1/GSTR-2 due dates were extended, the circular says the system would later reconcile the information furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 with the amounts reported in GSTR-3B once those returns were filed.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the simplified GSTR-3B filing did not replace the underlying reporting obligations permanently; it was an interim mechanism for the initial GST months, with reconciliation to follow once the regular statement/return data became available. The document is addressed to all Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax and all Principal Directors General/Directors General, indicating that field formations were expected to apply and oversee this reconciliation framework.

No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 27 August 2017 by the Ministry of Finance, clarifies how lottery tickets are to be classified and taxed under GST because assessees were encountering return-filing and tax-payment problems due to a coding mismatch. The circular states that, under the CGST Act, 2017, supply of lottery is treated as a **supply of goods**, even though the GST rate notifications had shown the classification entry for lottery as “-”. For compliance purposes, the government clarifies that this “-” should be read as **“Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975**, and that lottery must be taxed under the applicable GST rate notifications accordingly.

The circular specifically resolves the issue that the lottery description was appearing as goods while the code allotted in the system was under services, which had prevented some taxpayers from uploading returns or depositing tax on time. It emphasizes that return filing is linked to the rate of tax applicable to the supply, and that there is no ambiguity on the applicable lottery tax rate. The prescribed GST rate for lottery is confirmed as **12% or 28%, as the case may be**, depending on the relevant notified category.

This clarification applies to the GST framework under **CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST** rate notifications and is directed to all Central Tax field formations and systems officials. From a compliance standpoint, entities dealing in lottery tickets should ensure their tax classification and return-filing treatment align with the “Any Chapter” classification and the correct notified rate, so tax can be paid and returns filed without system errors or delay.

This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the rules for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax by furnishing either a bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, in response to inconsistent interpretations of Notification No. 16/2017–Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and earlier GST circulars. The key policy clarification is that the LUT facility is no longer limited to manufacturer exporters: **any registered person** may use LUT **if** they received foreign inward remittance in the preceding financial year equal to **at least 10% of export turnover, and in any case not less than Rs. 1 crore**; the circular states this effectively means the exporter must have received **whichever is higher: Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover** in the previous financial year. If that threshold is not met, the exporter must export under a **bond** rather than LUT.

The circular also clarifies the process for using and accepting the bond/LUT. The bond must be **executed on non-judicial stamp paper** for an amount determined as per the relevant bond format, and the exporter is required to furnish a **bank guarantee** along with the bond only to the extent required by the proper officer, not as a blanket requirement for all exporters. It further states that the LUT can be furnished on the exporter’s own letterhead in the prescribed format, and it must be accepted by the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner. The circular instructs tax officers not to insist on unnecessary guarantees or documentation beyond what the notification and circular require.

Another important compliance clarification is that the LUT/bond is a **pre-export** undertaking: it must be furnished **before exports are made** under the zero-rated/without payment route. The circular also explains that exports under bond/LUT are subject to the condition that the exporter will comply with the export provisions, including export of goods or services within the prescribed time limits and maintenance of proof of export. If the exporter fails to comply, the bond can be enforced for tax, interest, and any other applicable amount. The circular is intended to create uniformity across field formations, so compliance teams should ensure exporter eligibility is checked against the prior-year remittance threshold and that the correct instrument—LUT or bond—is used before undertaking exports without payment of integrated tax.

It is observed consign
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the bond/LUT procedure for **exports of goods or services without payment of integrated tax** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. It was issued by the **CBEC GST Policy Wing on 7 July 2017** under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017** to ensure uniform implementation after complaints from exporters and field offices about difficulties with the prescribed process. The core requirement is that any registered person making such zero-rated exports must furnish either a **bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11** before exporting without IGST payment.

The circular then distinguishes who may use an LUT and who must furnish a bond. It points to **Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 01-07-2017**, which specifies the class of exporters eligible to export under LUT, together with the applicable conditions and safeguards. **Exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond instead of an LUT.** The circular also reiterates that the **procedure for submission and acceptance of the bond was already laid down in Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST dated 4 July 2017**.

For the bond itself, the document requires that it be executed on **non-judicial stamp paper** of the **value applicable in the State where the bond is furnished**. A key clarification sought by the field was whether export bonds should be a **running bond with debit/credit facility** or a **separate one-time bond for each consignment/export**. The circular notes this issue and explains that the bond mechanism is intended to operate as a running bond, so exporters do not have to execute a fresh bond for every shipment.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that exporters making zero-rated supplies without IGST must first check whether they qualify for LUT under the 1 July 2017 notification; if not, they must arrange a bond in RFD-11 on the correct state stamp paper and follow the prescribed submission/acceptance process from the earlier circular. The circular is not imposing a new tax rate or deadline, but it does require adherence to the LUT/bond framework as a precondition to exporting without paying integrated tax.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 5 July 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs (GST Policy Wing), assigns “proper officer” status for specific GST functions under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (and related rules) to designated Central Tax officers, for matters other than registration and composition. It applies by virtue of section 2(91) of the CGST Act, read with section 20 of the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act, and it is intended to clarify which officer rank may legally exercise particular powers under the Act/rules.

For Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns the functions under section 67(7) and the proviso to section 78. For Additional or Joint Commissioners of Central Tax, it assigns powers under sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9); sections 71(1) and (2); the proviso to section 81; the proviso to section 129(6); and rule 139 sub-rules (1) to (4) and rule 140(2). For Deputy or Assistant Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns a broader set of functions, including sections 54(5), (6), (7), and (10); section 60(1), (2), and (3); sections 63, 64(1), and 65(6); and multiple powers under section 74, including sub-sections (1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), and (10), with the listing continuing on the next page. 

From a compliance standpoint, the practical impact is that taxpayers and company compliance teams must ensure that notices, orders, demands, recovery actions, inspections, access requests, search/seizure-related actions, refund-related actions, and other proceedings under the cited provisions are handled by the correct officer rank, because authority is being formally allocated to those officers. The circular does not set new monetary thresholds, tax rates, or filing deadlines; instead, it is an internal administrative authorization that determines which GST officer is empowered to act under the listed sections and rules, effective from the date of the circular itself, 5 July 2017.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (
rows.summary:
This circular addresses practical problems exporters were facing after GST implementation when supplying goods or services for export **without payment of integrated tax** and then trying to file **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST common portal. The government notes that these difficulties were causing export shipments to be held up, so it clarifies the procedure for furnishing the required **bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** under **rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**.

The core requirement is unchanged: any **registered person** choosing to export **without paying integrated tax** must furnish, **before export**, a **bond or LUT** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. The circular also confirms that, for **export of goods**, the rule 96A procedure applies **from 1 July 2017**, consistent with **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017**.

The new operational relaxation is that the bond/LUT does **not** need to be physically filed before the **jurisdictional Commissioner**, which had created hardship because many exporters are located far from that office. Instead, the circular allows this filing to be handled through the **proper officer** / jurisdictional tax administration mechanism in a way that avoids travel and administrative delay, so exporters can complete the requirement more easily and prevent export disruption.

For compliance purposes, the document is important because it confirms that exporters using the **zero-rated export without IGST payment route** must still ensure a valid **bond or LUT is in place before export**, but the process is being administratively simplified to reduce delays. The effective date tied to the export procedure is **1 July 2017**, and the requirement remains to use **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST portal.

Based on the title alone, the document is likely intended to identify which tax authority/officer is authorized to handle actions such as registration-related decisions, composition levy applications, compliance, and any related enforcement or procedural matters under the CGST framework.

rows.summary:
This circular amends Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018 on the question of who is the “proper officer” for adjudicating show cause notices issued under sections 73 and 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the IGST Act, 2017. It responds to two prior central tax notifications: Notification No. 02/2022-Central Tax dated 11 March 2022, which had already given certain Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners in specified Central Tax Commissionerates all-India jurisdiction to adjudicate DGGI-issued show cause notices, and Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax dated 25 November 2024, which expanded that arrangement to more such officers by substituting Table V in Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax. The 27/2024 notification took effect on 1 December 2024, and this circular is issued on 4 December 2024 to align the CBIC circular with that expanded adjudication framework.

The operative change is that paragraph 7.1 of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST (as previously amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST dated 12 March 2022) is substituted. The new text begins by stating that, for show cause notices issued by officers of the Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (DGGI), there may be cases where a single notice is issued to multiple noticees. In such cases, adjudication is to be handled in line with the all-India jurisdiction empowered officers specified under the amended notification framework, rather than being confined by the normal territorial jurisdiction approach.

For compliance purposes, the practical impact is on the adjudication of DGGI-issued show cause notices under sections 73 and 74: companies or other noticees facing such notices may have their matters adjudicated by the centrally empowered Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax designated under Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax as amended, including the broader set added by Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax. The document does not create a new tax rate, penalty, filing deadline, or monetary threshold; its significance is procedural and jurisdictional, clarifying which officers are authorized to adjudicate DGGI notices, including where one notice covers multiple noticees. The compliance team should therefore ensure that any DGGI show cause notices received on or after the effective change are tracked with attention to the designated adjudicating authority, and that internal responses, representation strategy, and escalation paths reflect this all-India jurisdiction framework.

The Tribunal set aside the order of the Adjudicating Authority and confirmed the provisional attachment of the shares and other assets. It also granted liberty to the Department to refer the matter to SEBI for investigation into the possible aspect of insider trading. During the survey, the books of account and other important documents belonging to M/s DCS Infotech Pvt. Ltd. were found at the business premises of the Deepak Group. The investigation revealed that DCS Infotech had purchased 46,48,720 shares of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. between FY 2004-05 and FY 2009-10 at a cost of approximately ₹5.47 crore. The market value of thos
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that an interest-free loan is **not automatically** a benami transaction, but it **will be treated as benami** where the funding structure shows that money was routed through a controlled company as a mere conduit to acquire shares for the benefit of the real controllers. In this case, the Tribunal found that funds were layered through group concerns and that the borrowing company’s directors/shareholders were only name-lenders, while the persons actually controlling the funds were the beneficial owners of the transaction; on that basis, the arrangement fell within **Sections 2(9)(A) and 2(9)(C) of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988**.

The underlying facts were that the Income-tax Investigation Wing surveyed Deepak Nitrite Ltd. and associated concerns, and during the survey it found books and other documents of **M/s DCS Infotech Pvt. Ltd.** at the Deepak Group’s premises. The investigation showed that DCS Infotech had acquired **46,48,720 shares** of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. during **FY 2004-05 to FY 2009-10** for about **₹5.47 crore**, while the market value of those shares at the relevant point was far higher (the document indicates a significant disparity). The Tribunal treated this as evidence that the share acquisition was not a straightforward independent investment by DCS Infotech, but part of a structured layering arrangement benefiting the controlling persons behind the funds.

As a result, the Tribunal **set aside the Adjudicating Authority’s order** and **confirmed the provisional attachment** of the shares and other assets. It also granted the Department liberty to **refer the matter to SEBI** for examination of a possible **insider trading** issue. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that corporate groups should not assume that interest-free or inter-company funding is safe merely because it is documented as a loan: if the lender, borrower, directors, shareholders, and source of funds indicate that the transaction is being used to mask beneficial ownership or to acquire assets for the real controller, it may be challenged as benami and exposed to attachment and related regulatory scrutiny.

The principal contention was that Mr. Udai Raj Cho
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court quashed the reassessment order passed under section 148A(3) and the consequential notice under section 148 in a case involving Khivraj Motors, a registered partnership firm, for AY 2023-24. The Income-tax Department had proposed to reopen the firm’s assessment on the allegation that ₹1,36,18,476 had escaped assessment, based on a show-cause notice dated 25 March 2026 issued under section 148A(1). However, the same amount had also been the subject of proceedings against one of the firm’s partners, Mr. Udai Raj Cho…, and those partner proceedings had already been restored for reconsideration.

The Court held that, because the same income amount was simultaneously under consideration in proceedings involving both the firm and the partner, the Assessing Officer should not proceed separately in a way that could lead to inconsistent findings or double taxation of the same income. Instead, the Court directed the same jurisdictional Assessing Officer to reconsider the firm’s case together with the partner’s case in a comprehensive manner. This means the Department must coordinate the two proceedings and examine the taxability of the ₹1.36 crore amount consistently before taking any final reassessment position.

Importantly for compliance purposes, the Court did not decide whether the ₹1,36,18,476 was ultimately taxable in the hands of the firm or in the hands of the partner. The order only restores the matter to the pre-reassessment stage, so the reassessment action based on the 29 June 2026 order under section 148A(3) and the follow-on notice under section 148 cannot stand as issued. For firms and partners facing parallel income-tax proceedings over the same amount, the case underscores the need for the Department to avoid fragmented proceedings that may result in duplicate assessments.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In re Airbus Defence and Space SA (GST AAR Gujrat) Summary: The Gujarat Authority for Advance Ruling considered whether Airbus Defence and Space S.A., Spain, through its Project Office in India, was liable to pay GST on the supply of forty C-295 aircraft to the Ministry of Defence and whether it was required to obtain GST registration in Gujarat. Under the Aircraft Contract dated 24.09.2021, Airbus was to supply fifty-six C-295MW aircraft, of which sixteen were to be delivered ex-works from Spain and forty were to be manufactured in India by Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL), the appointed Indian Aircraft Contractor, at its facility in Vadodara, Gujarat. Airbus entered into an IAC Contract dated 29.10.2021 with TASL for manufacture and supply of the forty aircraft. The Authority examined the transaction under [Section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017](https://taxguru.in/goods-and-service-tax/section-7-scope-supply-cgst-act-2017.html), including Schedule II, and noted that the aircraft constituted “goods” and that the transaction involved consideration in the course or furtherance of business. The applicant was to procure the aircraft from TASL at Vadodara and subsequently supply them ex-works to the Ministry of Defence at the same location. Title and ownership were to transfer to the applicant at the IAC facility upon execution of the Acceptance Certificate, following which the aircraft were to be accepted by the Ministry of Defence. The Authority therefore concluded that the transaction constituted a supply of goods under Section 7 read with Entry 1(a) of Schedule II and was liable to GST.
rows.summary:
The Gujarat Authority for Advance Ruling held that Airbus Defence and Space S.A. (Spain), acting through its Project Office in India, is making a taxable supply of goods when it procures and supplies the forty C-295MW aircraft manufactured in India by Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL) for the Ministry of Defence, and that this transaction is subject to GST under section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Entry 1(a) of Schedule II. The ruling arose from the aircraft contract dated 24.09.2021, under which Airbus was to supply 56 C-295MW aircraft in total: 16 ex-works from Spain and 40 to be manufactured in India at TASL’s facility in Vadodara, Gujarat under a separate IAC contract dated 29.10.2021. The Authority focused on the fact that the aircraft are “goods,” the transaction is undertaken in the course or furtherance of business for consideration, and Airbus is contractually positioned as the entity procuring the aircraft from TASL and then supplying them ex-works to the Ministry of Defence at the same Vadodara location.

A key compliance point in the ruling is the transfer of title and ownership: these were to pass to Airbus at the IAC facility upon execution of the Acceptance Certificate, after which the Ministry of Defence would accept the aircraft. Because the supply is structured as an actual transfer of goods for consideration rather than a mere facilitation or service arrangement, the Authority treated it as a taxable goods supply, not outside GST. The decision therefore confirms GST exposure for Airbus’s India-linked supply chain for the 40 aircraft and indicates that the Indian project office/arrangement must account for GST on this supply.

The ruling also addresses registration implications by recognizing the Vadodara, Gujarat location as the place tied to the supply and transfer mechanics, which is relevant for determining whether GST registration is required in Gujarat for the activities connected with this transaction. No explicit rate or monetary threshold is stated in the document, and no exemption is granted; instead, the substantive compliance conclusion is that the transaction falls within the GST net and must be treated accordingly.

rows.summary:
This Karnataka High Court decision in **Apoorva Harish Ruparel v. Assessment Unit** concerned **AY 2016-17** and arose after the Department issued a **section 148A(b) notice on 25 February 2023**, followed by a **section 148A(d) order and section 148 notice on 15 March 2023**. Because the assessee did not respond, the Department passed an **ex parte reassessment order on 25 January 2024** under **sections 147, 144, and 144B**, then went on to issue **three penalty orders**: one under **section 271(1)(b)** for non-compliance, one under **section 271F** for failure to file the return, and one under **section 271(1)(c)** for concealment or furnishing inaccurate particulars. The Department later issued a **section 226(3) notice on 14 November 2025** and attached the assessee’s **ICICI bank account**.

The Court quashed the entire chain of proceedings — including the **148A(d) order, 148 notice, reassessment order, penalty orders, consequential tax demands, and bank attachment** — because the statutory notices and communications had been sent to the assessee’s **secondary e-mail address** and an **old residential address**, even though he was **residing abroad** and no longer occupied the physical address used by the tax department. The key compliance point from the ruling is that reassessment and penalty proceedings can be invalidated where the Department relies on outdated or incorrect contact details rather than effectively serving notices on the assessee.

At the same time, the Court did **not** extinguish the reassessment permanently. It **restored the matter to the section 148A(b) stage** and allowed the assessee to file a response **by 5 October 2026**. For compliance teams, the practical lesson is that tax authorities must ensure notices are served at the current and properly usable contact details, especially where the taxpayer is non-resident or has changed address, because defective service can unwind the entire reassessment and enforcement process.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | UPI MDR and GST: Treatment of Tax on MDR and Input Tax Credit
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the GST and input tax credit implications of the proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on specified UPI transactions from 15th October 2026. Using a consultancy transaction of Rs. 10,000 plus 18% GST, it explains that where the customer pays Rs. 11,800 through UPI and MDR of 0.4% is applied, the MDR would be Rs. 47.20 and GST at 18% on the MDR would be Rs. 8.50, resulting in an additional MDR-related amount of Rs. 55.70. The article discusses the distinction between GST forming part of the underlying supply and GST charged on the separate payment-processing service represented by MDR, and considers whether the latter should be described as “GST on GST”. It outlines the stated UPI framework for specified Person to Merchant transactions exceeding Rs. 2,000, including the 0.4% standard MDR, the Rs. 300 cap for transactions of Rs. 75,000 and above, concessional treatment for certain sectors and capital-market transactions, and the absence of MDR for P2P transactions and specified small P2PM merchants. It further considers the availability of ITC on GST paid on MDR under the normal GST conditions, including the relevance of Section 16 and the restrictions under Section 17(5) of the CGST Act. For a GST-registered merchant making taxable supplies, the article states that the Rs. 8.50 GST on MDR would be available as ITC subject to eligibility and utilisation, making the MDR itself the economic cost. It also discusses cases involving exempt supplies, composition taxpayers and unregistered merchants, the effect of the Rs. 300 cap, accounting and reconciliation requirements, and concludes that the GST on MDR is GST on a separate payment-processing service rather than GST being charged again on the GST included in the customer’s invoice. Authors note: A GST registered client came to me asking, “Aman, my most of the business payments are received through UPI”, will I get ITC? What will be the treatment? So being a logical consulting engagement, I r
rows.summary:
The article explains the GST treatment of a proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) regime for specified UPI merchant transactions beginning **15 October 2026**. It uses an example where a consultancy raises a bill of **Rs. 10,000 plus 18% GST** (total **Rs. 11,800**) and the customer pays by UPI; if MDR of **0.4%** applies, the MDR would be **Rs. 47.20**, and GST at **18%** on that MDR would be **Rs. 8.50**, making the total MDR-related cost **Rs. 55.70**. The document emphasizes that this GST is not “GST on GST” on the original invoice amount; instead, it is GST on a **separate payment-processing service** represented by the MDR.

The stated UPI framework applies to **Person-to-Merchant (P2M)** transactions above **Rs. 2,000**. Under the discussed proposal, the standard MDR is **0.4%**, but there is a **cap of Rs. 300** for transactions of **Rs. 75,000 and above**. It also notes concessional treatment for certain sectors and capital-market transactions, while **P2P transactions** and specified **small P2M merchants** do **not** attract MDR.

On input tax credit, the article says a **GST-registered merchant making taxable supplies** can generally claim ITC on the **Rs. 8.50 GST** charged on MDR, provided the normal GST conditions are met, especially the eligibility requirements under **Section 16** and the restrictions under **Section 17(5) of the CGST Act**. In that case, the merchant’s economic cost is the MDR itself, because the GST paid on MDR is expected to be creditable and usable against output tax, subject to ordinary ITC rules and sufficient tax liability. For merchants making **exempt supplies**, **composition taxpayers**, and **unregistered merchants**, the article indicates that ITC would not be available in the same way, so the GST on MDR becomes a real cost rather than a creditable tax.

The article also flags practical compliance implications: merchants should track UPI receipts, reconcile MDR charges and GST charged on those charges, and account for the MDR and related GST separately from the underlying sale. Its conclusion is that the tax on MDR is properly viewed as GST on a distinct payment service, not as an additional tax layered on the customer’s invoice GST.

Anita Packaging, represented by proprietor Mr. Divij Agarwal, to pursue the statutory GST appellate remedy after it claimed that its former tax consultant failed to inform it of the adverse order. The challenge related to a Section 73 GST proceeding for the 2017–18 tax period, including a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 14.06.2022 and an Order-in-Original together with FORM GST DRC-07 bearing Reference No. ZD361223033724M dated 18.12.2023. Petitioner’s Submissions The petitioner submitted that there were no outstanding GST dues payable by him. rows.summary:
The Telangana High Court held that a GST registrant whose registration was cancelled for non-filing of returns may still be allowed to seek revocation of the cancellation even after the normal statutory time limit for appeal has expired. In this case, the petitioner, Ramesh, held GST registration No. 36DHMPR433SA1ZF, and his registration was cancelled by Form GST REG-19 dated 25.01.2024 on the ground of non-filing of returns for the relevant prescribed periods. The Court noted that by the time he approached it, the appeal period had already lapsed, but it nevertheless permitted him to move the competent GST authority for revocation of the cancellation.

The Court also recognized a practical fallback procedure if the GST portal does not accept the revocation application because of technical or time-bar issues: the taxpayer may submit the application manually/physically before the jurisdictional authority. The factual basis for relief included the petitioner’s assertion that no GST dues were outstanding and that the failure to file returns resulted from the accountant’s default rather than any intentional non-compliance. rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Bhandari Scrap & Safecon: 2 GST Judgments by SC & Genuine Buyer’s Dilemma
rows.desc: Summary: Two Supreme Court orders from July 2026 address different aspects of Input Tax Credit (ITC) exposure for genuine GST buyers where supplier-side defaults arise. In Bhandari Scrap Traders v. Union of India, the issue was the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act and whether the statutory condition requiring the tax charged on a supply to have actually been paid to the Government could be diluted for a bona fide purchaser; the condition was upheld, with ITC denied where the tax never reached the exchequer. In Additional Commissioner v. Safecon Lifesciences, the issue was narrower and concerned Section 74 of the UPGST Act and the use of the extended-period fraud machinery against a buyer without proof of fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression by that buyer; the Revenue’s SLP was dismissed and the High Court’s reasoning remained undisturbed. The supplied comparison therefore treats the decisions as addressing different legal questions, provisions and factual settings rather than as contradictory rulings. Bhandari Scrap concerned a situation where the supplier never deposited the tax, whereas Safecon concerned a transaction where the immediate supplier had filed GSTR-1/3B and paid tax at the time of the transaction, with the later irregularity relating to the supplier’s own upstream purchases. The practical position identified is that Section 16(2)(c) creates a hard-edged statutory condition, while invocation of the harsher Section 74 route still requires the statutory fraud-related threshold. The unresolved position concerning Sahil Enterprises, supplier due diligence, transaction-level documentation and the distinction between Sections 73 and 74 remain important for genuine businesses. This document summarizes two Supreme Court orders from July 2026 that deal with GST input tax credit (ITC) risk when a supplier defaults, but it emphasizes that the cases address different statutory issues and different fact patterns. In **Bhandari Scrap Traders v. Union of India**, the Court considered the constitutional validity of **Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act**, which requires that the tax charged on a supply must actually have been **paid to the Government** before the buyer can claim ITC; the Court upheld that condition and held that ITC can be denied even to a bona fide purchaser if the supplier never remits the tax to the exchequer. The practical effect is that this is treated as a strict, hard-edged statutory condition for ITC eligibility, so buyer-side good faith alone does not override the statutory requirement of actual tax payment by the supplier.

In **Additional Commissioner v. Safecon Lifesciences**, the issue was different: the Court dealt with **Section 74 of the UPGST Act** and whether the Revenue could invoke the extended-period fraud machinery against a buyer without proof of **fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression** by that buyer. The Revenue’s SLP was dismissed, leaving the High Court’s reasoning in place; the document presents this as confirming that the harsher Section 74 route cannot be used unless the statutory fraud threshold is met. The facts also differed materially from Bhandari Scrap: in Safecon, the immediate supplier had filed **GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B** and paid tax at the time of the transaction, and the later irregularity related to the supplier’s own upstream purchases rather than a direct non-payment at the buyer’s invoice level.

For compliance purposes, the document’s key message is that genuine buyers still need transaction-level diligence and documentation because ITC exposure may arise both from **supplier non-payment** under Section 16(2)(c) and from allegations of **fraud-based extended limitation** under Section 74, but the legal tests are not the same. It also flags that issues such as the treatment of **Sahil Enterprises**, the scope of supplier due diligence, the importance of invoice-by-invoice records, and the distinction between **Sections 73 and 74** remain important unresolved compliance considerations for businesses.

rows.summary:
The CGST Anti-Evasion Branch of Delhi South Commissionerate has arrested the proprietor of an iron-and-steel trading firm in connection with a large fake Input Tax Credit (ITC) fraud. According to the release, the alleged inadmissible ITC exceeds **Rs. 25.22 crore**, and it was claimed through bogus invoices with a stated value of about **Rs. 140.14 crore**. The investigation found that the firm took credit on invoices issued by multiple entities, several of which were allegedly **non-existent, non-functional, suspended, or cancelled**, and field verification suggested some suppliers were not carrying on genuine business at their declared places of business.

The case also alleges that the firm **claimed ITC without actually receiving goods** and then **passed on ITC to other recipients by issuing invoices without corresponding supply of goods**. The department relied on evidence gathered during investigation and statements recorded under **Section 70 of the CGST Act, 2017** before making the arrest. The proprietor was arrested on **17 September 2026** under **Section 69 of the CGST Act**, produced before the **Patiala House Court**, and remanded to **judicial custody for 14 days**.

For compliance purposes, this is a clear enforcement signal that businesses must ensure ITC is backed by **genuine underlying supply**, valid and active counterparties, and actual receipt of goods before availing credit. The release indicates that the department is actively pursuing fraudulent ITC chains involving bogus invoicing and paper entities, and the investigation is stated to be **ongoing**, so further action may follow.

The accident occurred at Thatimaakulapalli Cross Road in District Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh. The claimant received treatment at a hospital in Tirupati, and the FIR was registered at Yerravaripalem Police Station, District Tirupati. His address in the claim petition was shown as being in Chittoor District, Andhra Pradesh. However, the claimant filed the compensation claim under section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal at Chennai. National Insurance Company Ltd., whi
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a motor accident compensation claim under Section 166(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 cannot be filed in a tribunal location merely because the insurer has a branch office or does business there. For territorial jurisdiction, Section 166(2) is to be applied only by reference to the place where the accident occurred, the claimant’s residence or place of business, or the residence of the defendant; the Court clarified that the term “defendant” for this purpose does **not** include the insurance company. As a result, the presence of an insurer’s branch office or head office in a city does **not** by itself give the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal in that city jurisdiction over the claim.

On the facts, the accident occurred on 25 October 2022 at Thatimaakulapalli Cross Road in Tirupati District, Andhra Pradesh, when a mini truck struck the claimant’s two-wheeler. The claimant received treatment in Tirupati, the FIR was lodged at Yerravaripalem Police Station in Tirupati District, and the claim petition listed his address in Chittoor District, Andhra Pradesh. Despite these Andhra Pradesh connections, the claimant filed the claim before the MACT in Chennai, apparently relying on the insurer’s presence there; the Supreme Court’s ruling makes clear that this jurisdictional basis is invalid.

For compliance teams handling motor accident claims, the practical effect is that venue selection must be tested against Section 166(2) strictly and not on the basis of insurer convenience or office location. Any objection to territorial jurisdiction should be raised with reference to the statutory grounds: accident location, claimant residence/business, or defendant residence, and insurers should not be treated as qualifying “defendants” for this purpose. The ruling is especially important for litigation intake and early case assessment, because filing in a tribunal where only the insurer has an office is not a legally sufficient basis to maintain the claim there.

rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court upheld a GST search conducted on 25 July 2025 at the premises of Bass Legal LLP, including the cabin used by Advocate Puneet Batra, and refused to quash the seizure of his CPU, documents, and other materials. The petitioner argued that the search was unauthorized and violated advocate-client privilege because the seized electronic records were likely to contain confidential information relating to several clients, including Matkarma Technology Pvt. Ltd. (MTPL); the Court rejected the challenge and held that a search at a lawyer’s premises is not invalid merely because the location is occupied by an advocate, so long as the statutory authorization exists. The Court accepted the respondents’ position that the search was authorized under Section 67(2) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and noted that the investigation materials prima facie suggested the petitioner was not acting only as MTPL’s legal counsel but may have been involved in MTPL’s affairs and operations, which justified the search.  

The Court also addressed procedural issues raised in the writ petition, including the production of records in sealed cover, the fact that no show-cause notice had yet been issued to MTPL, alleged inconsistency in the department’s stance, and the relevance of departmental instructions and the Master Circular on SCN, Adjudication and Recovery dated 10 March 2017. It concluded that these points did not undermine the validity of the search authorization so long as the officers had the requisite “reasons to believe” under Section 67(2). However, the Court expressly recognized that advocate-client privilege and unrelated confidential client information must still be protected, indicating that any privileged or irrelevant material seized from the advocate’s premises cannot be treated as freely usable without safeguards. In short, for compliance purposes, the ruling confirms that GST officers may lawfully search an advocate’s office/cabin under Section 67(2) where there is sufficient investigative basis, but they must still handle privileged or unrelated client material with caution and privilege safeguards.

(Supreme Court of India) Unsuccessful Candidates Cannot Reopen A 15-Year-Old Selection By Raising New Grounds—Supreme Court Refuses CBI Probe Summary: The Supreme Court has dismissed a writ petition challenging the selection of Technician Grade-2 employees in the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited. The Court held that the petitioners could not enlarge the scope of proceedings by raising fresh allegations after having earlier confined their case to the contention that candidates lower in merit had been selected. The Court also declined to unsettle appointments made more than a decade ago, particularly when the selected candidates were not parties to the proceedings. The request for a CBI investigation was rejected because no specific pleadings or supporting material establishing manipulation or wrongdoing had been placed on record. Facts of the case On 4 March 2011, UPPCL issued an advertisement for filling 2,974 posts of Technician Grade-2 (Trainee) Electrical. The eligibility conditions included a two-year trade certificate in the electrician trade, the prescribed school qualification and a Course on Computer Concepts certificate issued by DOEACC. A written examination was conducted on 7 August 2011, in which 13,576 candidates participated. Of these, 6,288 candidates qualified for interviews conducted between November and December 2011. The results were declared on 21 May 2012. Several candidates were unable to produce their DOEACC certificates at the interview stage. UPPCL extended the time
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court dismissed a challenge to the selection process for **Technician Grade-2 (Trainee) Electrical** posts in **Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL)**, holding that unsuccessful candidates could not reopen a selection process conducted years earlier by introducing new allegations beyond the original case they had made. The recruitment was based on an advertisement dated **4 March 2011** for **2,974 vacancies**, with eligibility requiring a **two-year electrician trade certificate**, the prescribed educational qualification, and a **Course on Computer Concepts (CCC) certificate issued by DOEACC**. A written exam was held on **7 August 2011**, **13,576 candidates** appeared, **6,288** were shortlisted for interviews held in **November–December 2011**, and results were declared on **21 May 2012**.

The petitioners initially challenged the selection on the ground that candidates lower in merit had been selected, but later attempted to expand the dispute with fresh allegations. The Court rejected that approach, emphasizing that the scope of proceedings could not be enlarged after the fact, especially where the selection had already resulted in appointments made **more than a decade earlier**. The Court also noted that the selected candidates had **not been made parties** to the proceedings, making it inappropriate to disturb their appointments.

A request for a **CBI investigation** was also rejected. The Court found that the petitioners had not placed **specific pleadings or supporting material** on record showing manipulation, fraud, or any other actionable wrongdoing in the recruitment process. From a compliance perspective, the ruling reinforces that courts are reluctant to overturn long-settled hiring decisions absent concrete evidence, and that allegations introduced late without documentary support are unlikely to justify reopening appointments or triggering a criminal probe.

The finality of the settlement is not confined merely to the additional income offered by the assessee. Once the settlement application is admitted, the Commission considers the entire case for the relevant assessment year—including the returned income, additional income and deductions claimed while computing taxable income. The Court consequently upheld the Delhi High Court’s order quashing the reassessment notice and reassessment order disallowing Omaxe Limited’s deduction under Section 80-IB(10). Settlement application covering AY 2006-07 Omaxe Limited, a real-estate company, filed its return for AY 2006-07 declaring taxable income of approximately ₹89.21 crore after claiming a deduction of about ₹79 crore under Section 80-IB(10) in respect of its housing projects. During the pendency of the regular assessment, the company approached the Settlement Commission under Section 245C for AYs 2000-01 to 2006-07. For AY 2006-07, it offered additional income of ₹18 lakh. The Settlement Commission passed its final order under Section 245D(4) on March 17, 2008. While determin
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that once an assessment year is taken up by the Income Tax Settlement Commission and a final order is passed under Section 245D(4), the Assessing Officer cannot later reopen that same year under Sections 147 and 148 on a matter that was covered by the settlement proceedings. The ruling makes clear that the settlement’s finality is not limited to the extra income specifically offered in the application; it extends to the entire computation for that assessment year, including the returned income and the deductions claimed in arriving at taxable income.

This arose in the case of Omaxe Limited, a real-estate company, for AY 2006-07. Omaxe had filed a return declaring taxable income of about ₹89.21 crore and claimed a deduction of about ₹79 crore under Section 80-IB(10) for its housing projects. It then approached the Settlement Commission under Section 245C for AYs 2000-01 to 2006-07 and, for AY 2006-07, offered additional income of ₹18 lakh. The Settlement Commission passed its final order under Section 245D(4) on 17 March 2008.

After that settlement order, the Assessing Officer sought to reopen AY 2006-07 and disallow Omaxe’s Section 80-IB(10) deduction. The Supreme Court upheld the Delhi High Court’s decision quashing both the reassessment notice and the reassessment order, confirming that the reopening was impermissible because the issue had already been subsumed within the Settlement Commission’s final settlement. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that once a year is conclusively settled by the Commission, tax authorities cannot re-litigate deductions or other elements of that year’s income computation through reassessment proceedings on the same settled matter.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Supreme Court Holds Officiating Employees Have No Vested Right Under Old Promotion Rules
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13337 Case Name Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited And Another Vs G.N. Mani Ravinder And Others Etc. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited And Another Vs G.N. Mani Ravinder And Others Etc. (Supreme Court of India) Mere officiation on a higher post creates no vested right to promotion under old Rules; applicable Rules are those in force on date of consideration: Supreme Court The Supreme Court has held that employees merely officiating on a higher post do not acquire a vested right to regular promotion under the recruitment rules or administrative instructions that existed when the vacancies arose. The right of an eligible employee is only to be considered for promotion under the Rules in force on the date of such consideration. There is no universal principle that vacancies must necessarily be filled according to the Rules prevailing on the date on which they arose. The Court consequently set aside the High Court’s directions requiring BSNL to consider the employees for promotion as Rajbhasha Adhikari without insisting upon the written test prescribed under the 2005 Recruitment Rules. Administrative instructions providing automatic promotion The Department of Telecommunications created a separate official-language wing for promoting the use of Hindi. Posts of Hindi Translator Grade I, II and III were created, with the post of Hindi Officer constituting the next promotional level. An administrative order dated April 28, 1994 provided that Hindi Translators in Grades I, II and III would become eligible for promotion to the post of Hindi Officer after completing three, five and eight years of service, respectively. The private respondents were appoint
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that employees who are merely officiating in a higher post do **not** acquire any vested right to be regularized or promoted under the recruitment rules or administrative instructions that were in force when the vacancies first arose. Instead, the controlling rule is the one **in force on the date the promotion is actually considered**, and there is no general legal requirement that a vacancy must be filled under the rules that existed when it was created.  

This case arose from BSNL’s Rajbhasha/Hindi language cadre. The Department of Telecommunications had created Hindi Translator Grades I, II, and III, with **Hindi Officer** as the next promotional post. An administrative order dated **28 April 1994** stated that Hindi Translators in Grades I, II, and III would become eligible for promotion to Hindi Officer after **3, 5, and 8 years of service**, respectively. The private respondents had been appointed as officiating Rajbhasha Adhikari/Hindi Officer-like incumbents and argued they should be considered for promotion under the older regime without being subjected to the later written-test requirement.  

The Supreme Court rejected that position and held that the employees could not demand promotion under the old instructions merely because they had been officiating on the higher post. It specifically upheld the applicability of the **2005 Recruitment Rules**, including the **written test requirement**, and set aside the High Court’s direction that BSNL promote the employees as Rajbhasha Adhikari without insisting on that test.  

For compliance purposes, the decision means BSNL and similarly situated public employers may apply the promotion rules and selection procedures **current on the date of consideration**, even where employees have been performing higher duties for some time. Officiating service alone does not freeze the promotional framework or entitle an employee to be assessed under superseded rules.

Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar Vs Commissioner of Customs (Appeals) (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Foreign Assets Generated Before Section 37A but Continued to Be Held Abroad Thereafter Can Trigger Seizure of Equivalent Indian Assets: SAFEMA Tribunal Summary: The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has held that Section 37A of FEMA can be invoked where foreign assets or foreign exchange allegedly acquired before the provision came into force continued to be held abroad after its introduction on 09.09.2015. The Tribunal rejected the contention that such action amounted to retrospective application of Section 37A. It upheld the seizure of shares worth approximately ₹1.52 crore held by the estate in 33 Indian companies, as value-equivalent assets against suspected foreign exchange of approximately USD 690.65 million—₹5,718.59 crore—held outside India. Background of the case The Enforcement Directorate initiated an investigation against late Shri Anil Salgaocar based on information emerging from the Panama and Pandora Papers. The investigation revealed that five companies had been incorporated in the British Virgin Islands: Ling Tao Trading Ltd.; Sino Ling Tao Resources Ltd.; GBA Minmetals Trading Ltd.; Cheermark Global Ltd.; and Joyking Global Ltd. According to the Directorate, these companies procured iron ore from Salgaocar Group concerns in India and resold it in the Chinese market. During 2004-2012, approximately 22.75 million tonnes of iron ore were allegedly traded, generating turnover of about USD 1.794 billion and net trading profits of a
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA held that **Section 37A of FEMA can be applied to foreign assets or foreign exchange that were allegedly acquired before Section 37A existed, so long as those assets were still being held abroad after the provision came into force on 09.09.2015**. In other words, the Tribunal rejected the argument that seizure action under Section 37A is impermissibly retrospective merely because the original acquisition predates the provision; the relevant conduct is the **continued foreign holding after 09.09.2015**.  

On the facts, the Enforcement Directorate acted on information from the **Panama Papers and Pandora Papers** and investigated late **Shri Anil Salgaocar**. The probe found that five BVI companies—**Ling Tao Trading Ltd., Sino Ling Tao Resources Ltd., GBA Minmetals Trading Ltd., Cheermark Global Ltd., and Joyking Global Ltd.**—had allegedly bought iron ore from Salgaocar Group entities in India and resold it in China. During **2004–2012**, approximately **22.75 million tonnes** of iron ore were allegedly traded, with reported turnover of about **USD 1.794 billion** and net trading profits of about **USD 690.65 million** (around **₹5,718.59 crore**), which the authorities treated as suspected foreign exchange held outside India.  

As a result, the Tribunal upheld seizure of **shares valued at approximately ₹1.52 crore** held by the estate in **33 Indian companies** as **equivalent-value assets** against the suspected foreign exchange abroad. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that **holding foreign assets outside India after 09.09.2015 can expose a person or estate to equivalent-asset seizure in India under FEMA Section 37A**, even where the foreign asset was allegedly created before that date. The decision underscores the need to assess not only the timing of acquisition but also whether any suspected foreign exchange or offshore assets remained outside India after Section 37A became effective.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13329 Case Name Surendra Agrawal Vs Initiating Officer (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts SAFEMA Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Surendra Agrawal Vs Initiating Officer (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Flat Purchased in Relative’s Name but Loan Repaid and Property Used by Another Constitutes Benami Property: SAFEMA Tribunal Summary: The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has held that a flat registered in the name of a person having no financial capacity to purchase it was a benami property where the purchase negotiations, cash payments, housing-loan repayments and beneficial use of the property were attributable to his brother-in-law. The Tribunal rejected the explanation that the payments represented financial assistance extended in good faith during a financial crisis. It upheld the attachment after finding that the alleged owner was unaware of basic details of the flat, the loan was substantially repaid by the alleged beneficial owner and the property was utilised as collateral for the beneficial owner’s company. Facts of the case A residential flat in Blue Berry Apartment, DB City, Gwalior, measuring approximately 1,262 sq. ft., was registered in the name of Shri Surendra Agrawal. During an Income-tax search, the authorities found the property’s registration documents, chain documents, purchase agreement and receipts at premises connected with Shri Sandeep Mangal, the brother-in-law of the registered owner. The investigation revealed that the flat had initially been booked in the name of Sonu Mangal, alias Sandeep Mangal, who had negotiated its purchase. A cash-payment receipt of ₹6,79,320 was also issued in his name. The final agreement and sale deed were, however, executed in the name of
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that a residential flat registered in the name of Shri Surendra Agrawal was benami property and upheld its attachment because the evidence showed that his brother-in-law, Shri Sandeep Mangal (also referred to as Sonu Mangal), was the real purchaser and beneficial owner. The flat was in Blue Berry Apartment, DB City, Gwalior, measuring about 1,262 sq. ft.; the record showed that the property had originally been negotiated and booked by Sandeep Mangal, and a cash-payment receipt for ₹6,79,320 was issued in his name. Although the final agreement and sale deed were executed in Surendra Agrawal’s name, the Tribunal found that he had no demonstrated financial capacity to buy the flat, was unaware of basic particulars about it, and could not credibly explain the source of funds.

The Tribunal gave significant weight to the fact that housing-loan payments were largely made by the brother-in-law and that the property was also used as collateral for the beneficial owner’s company, which was inconsistent with Surendra Agrawal being the true owner. It rejected the explanation that the payments were merely financial help extended during a temporary crisis, treating that claim as unsupported by the surrounding records and conduct. In practical compliance terms, the decision reinforces that title in a relative’s name will not protect a transaction from benami scrutiny if the registered owner lacks financial capacity and the purchase, funding, repayment, and use of the asset all point to another person as the real owner.

For businesses and individuals handling property purchases, this ruling underscores the need for documentary consistency across who negotiated the deal, who paid the consideration, who services any loan, and who actually enjoys or controls the asset. Where those facts do not align with the registered titleholder, authorities may treat the arrangement as benami and maintain attachment, especially if the nominal owner cannot explain the transaction details or prove independent funding.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | PMLA Attachment Can Cover Property Held by Non-Accused Persons: SAFEMA
