Therefore, property held in the name of the wife or other family member of an accused can be attached even when such person is not named in the FIR or ECIR, provided the property represents proceeds of crime. The Tribunal accordingly upheld the attachment of properties valued at approximately ₹10.12 crore standing in the names of deceased accused Vikas Dubey, his wife, son and others. Facts of the case Two FIRs were registered following the incident in which a police team proceeding to arrest Vikas Dubey was attacked, resulting in the death of eight police personnel. During the subsequent investigation, it was alleged that Vikas Dubey was involved in several offences, including organised crime, corruption, embezzlement of funds meant for the Public Distribution System, forcible takeover of businesses and land-grabbing activities. The Enforcement Directorate registered an ECIR based on the scheduled offences and commenced an independent investigation under the PMLA. It provisionally attached properties valued at ₹10,12,27,216, treating them as having been acquired out of the proceeds of crime. The properties were held in the names of Vikas Dubey, his wife Mrs. Richa Du
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), attachment is aimed at the **proceeds of crime**, not only at property standing in the name of a person formally accused in the scheduled offence, so assets can be attached even if the holder’s name does not appear in the FIR or ECIR. In this case, the Enforcement Directorate registered an ECIR after two FIRs arising from the attack on a police team sent to arrest Vikas Dubey, in which eight police personnel were killed; the investigation alleged that Dubey was involved in organised crime, corruption, embezzlement of Public Distribution System funds, forcible takeover of businesses, and land-grabbing. Acting under PMLA, the ED provisionally attached properties worth **₹10,12,27,216** (about **₹10.12 crore**) that were standing in the names of **Vikas Dubey, his wife Richa Dubey, his son, and others**, on the theory that the assets were acquired from proceeds of crime.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **third-party ownership does not protect property from PMLA attachment** if the authorities can trace the asset to criminal proceeds. The Tribunal specifically upheld attachment of property held by family members and other non-accused persons where the asset appears linked to the scheduled offence, meaning corporate and individual holders should not assume that being outside the FIR/ECIR shields assets from enforcement action. The decision reinforces the need for enhanced source-of-funds diligence, beneficial ownership checks, and documentary support for acquisition of high-value assets, especially where there may be proximity to persons under criminal investigation or where funds could be alleged to derive from illegal activity.

rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that a bank cannot prevent confiscation of property found to be benami merely because it had taken a mortgage over the property before the benami-attachment order was passed. The case involved Flat No. B-304 in Blue Berry Apartment, DB City, Gwalior, which was registered in the name of Surendra Kumar Agrawal, but evidence from an income-tax search showed that the property had originally been booked and negotiated by Sandeep Mangal alias Sonu Mangal. The Tribunal relied on the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988, under which benami property is subject to attachment and eventual confiscation; it treated the attachment as an action against the property itself, not as an ordinary debt-recovery proceeding that could be displaced by a secured creditor’s priority claim under SARFAESI.

On the facts, the authorities found that Surendra Agrawal’s claimed income of only ₹5,000 to ₹7,000 per month from working in a shop was inconsistent with acquiring the flat. Although a housing loan of ₹22 lakh had been obtained from Canara Bank in Surendra Agrawal’s name, the investigation showed that loan repayments were substantially made from the bank account of Sandeep Mangal’s proprietary concern. The document states that out of total credits of ₹25.61 lakh into the housing-loan account, approximately ₹1.41 lakh was from Surendra Agrawal’s own account, while the rest was sourced from the concern linked to Sandeep Mangal, supporting the conclusion that the apparent owner was only a name-lender.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a mortgage or prior security interest does not “cleanse” a benami asset or create a defense against confiscation proceedings under the Benami law. Banks and other lenders should not assume that SARFAESI enforcement or mortgage priority will override a benami attachment/confiscation process if the property is later found to be benami. The case underscores the need for enhanced KYC, source-of-funds verification, borrower-beneficial-owner checks, and scrutiny of repayment flows where a property is financed in one person’s name but funded or serviced by another person or related concern.

The Tribunal rejected the appellant’s contention that the relied-upon documents were not furnished to him while he was in judicial custody. The offences alleged included cheating, forgery and criminal conspiracy under Sections 420, 467, 468 and 120-B of the IPC, apart from offences under the Uttar Pradesh Public Examination Act, 1998. The Special Task Force conducted an investigation and filed a charge sheet against 18 persons, including the appellant, Shri Rajeev Nayan Mishra. According to the prosecution, a group of persons connected with the logistics company responsible for transporting the question papers obtained access to the sealed boxes stored in a warehouse in Ahmedabad. The boxes were allegedly opened, the question papers photographed using mobil
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA upheld the provisional attachment of property linked to the alleged Uttar Pradesh Police Constable Recruitment Examination paper leak, rejecting the appellant’s claim that the “relied-upon documents” (RUDs) were not supplied to him while he was in judicial custody. The Tribunal held that because the appellant had signed an acknowledgment showing receipt of the envelope containing the RUDs, he could not later deny delivery nearly two months afterward, especially since he had made no contemporaneous complaint against the police officer who allegedly served the documents. In practical compliance terms, the decision reinforces that a signed acknowledgment of service/delivery is strong evidence against later non-service objections, and custodial recipients should document any alleged non-receipt immediately if they intend to challenge service.

The underlying enforcement action arose from an FIR dated 06.03.2024 relating to leakage of the question papers for the Uttar Pradesh Police Constable Recruitment Examination scheduled for February 2024. The alleged offences included cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 120-B of the IPC, along with offences under the Uttar Pradesh Public Examination Act, 1998. The Special Task Force investigated and filed a charge sheet against 18 persons, including the appellant, Shri Rajeev Nayan Mishra.

According to the prosecution narrative summarized in the document, persons connected with the logistics company responsible for transporting the question papers allegedly obtained access to sealed boxes stored in a warehouse in Ahmedabad, opened them, and photographed the question papers using a mobile phone. The Tribunal’s decision means the attachment connected with these allegations remains in force at this stage, and the appellant’s procedural challenge based on alleged non-supply of documents failed. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that in PMLA/SAFEMA proceedings, receipt acknowledgments and the absence of timely protest can defeat later service-based objections, so organizations or individuals served in custody should preserve records and raise immediate written objections if documents are not actually received.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Huge Receipts Without Gold Sales Justify Jewellery Seizure Under PMLA: SAFEMA
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13322 Case Name Vignesh Jewellery Vs Deputy Director (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts SAFEMA Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vignesh Jewellery Vs Deputy Director (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Huge Receipts from Accused Jeweller Without Corresponding Gold Sales Justify Retention of Seized Jewellery Under PMLA: SAFEMA Tribunal Summary: The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has upheld the retention of gold jewellery and bullion seized from two jewellery concerns which had received substantial amounts from an accused jeweller without establishing corresponding genuine sales. Background of the case An FIR was registered against M/s Pranav Jewellers, its founder, his wife and the branch manager on allegations that investors were induced to invest in various schemes on false promises of high returns. It was alleged that the funds collected from investors were diverted through bogus purchases and that corresponding bogus closing stock was created in the books. The offences alleged included Sections 406, 420 and 120-B of the IPC and Section 5 of the Tamil Nadu Protection of Interests of Depositors Act. Based on the scheduled offences, the Enforcement Directorate registered an ECIR and conducted searches at several premises connected with M/s Pranav Jewellers. Appellant Property seized Vignesh Jewellery Gold ornaments weighing 3,717 grams Ruby’s Jewellery Gold jewellery and bullion weighing approximately 5,885.140 grams, including 330 grams of bullion The Enforcement Directorate filed applications under Section 17(4) of the PMLA seeking retention of the seized property. The Adjudicating Authority allowed the applications. Both jewellers challenged the retention order before the Tribunal. Not named
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s retention of gold jewellery and bullion seized from two jewellery businesses, finding that the seizures were justified under the PMLA because the concerns had received large sums from an accused jeweller but could not show corresponding genuine gold sales. The underlying investigation began with an FIR against M/s Pranav Jewellers, its founder, his wife, and a branch manager for allegedly inducing investors to place money in schemes promising high returns, then diverting those funds through bogus purchases and reflecting bogus closing stock in the books; the alleged predicate offences included IPC Sections 406, 420, and 120-B, plus Section 5 of the Tamil Nadu Protection of Interests of Depositors Act. Based on those scheduled offences, the Enforcement Directorate registered an ECIR, carried out searches, and seized property from connected premises.

The seized property at issue was substantial: Vignesh Jewellery’s gold ornaments weighing 3,717 grams, and Ruby’s Jewellery’s gold jewellery and bullion weighing approximately 5,885.140 grams, including 330 grams of bullion. The ED then sought retention of the seized assets by filing applications under Section 17(4) of the PMLA, and the Adjudicating Authority approved those applications. On appeal, both jewellers challenged the retention order, but the Tribunal agreed with the ED’s position that the unexplained receipt of huge amounts from the accused jeweller, without proof of corresponding bona fide sales, supported continuing retention of the seized jewellery and bullion as proceeds connected to the alleged laundering scheme. For compliance purposes, the decision underscores that where a business receives large payments from an entity under PMLA scrutiny and cannot substantiate legitimate underlying transactions with proper records, invoices, stock movement, and sale corroboration, the authorities may treat the assets received or held in connection with those payments as retainable under PMLA procedures.

Vs Deputy Director (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) ₹784-Crore Compensation for Illegal Mining Does Not Wipe Out “Proceeds of Crime”; PMLA Attachment of ₹622-Crore FDs Upheld: SAFEMA Tribunal The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has upheld the attachment of fixed deposits and bank deposits valued at approximately ₹622.62 crore, holding that payment of compensation pursuant to the Supreme Court’s directions for illegal mining does not amount to compounding of the offence of money laundering or extinguish the alleged proceeds of crime. The Tribunal further held that quashing of criminal proceedings against certain individual partners did not terminate the PMLA proceedings against the partnership firm when the Orissa High Court had expressly permitted such proceedings to continue against the firm. Background M/s Serajuddin & Co., a partnership firm engaged in mining iron ore and manganese ore in Odisha, was accused of undertaking production exceeding the limits approved under its mining plan and environmental clearance. Following searches conducted on July 9, 2015, the Enforcement Directorate issued directions to various banks to freeze the firm’s current accounts and fixed deposits. The amounts lying in these accounts were stated to have originated from the sale of iron ore and manganese ore. The ED estimated the alleged proceeds of crime at ₹785.67 crore. Bank deposits and fixed deposits worth approximately ₹497.68 crore as of July 2015, together with accumulated interest, were valued at ₹622.62 crore when the provisional attachment order was passed on
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s provisional attachment of fixed deposits and bank deposits worth about ₹622.62 crore belonging to M/s Serajuddin & Co., a partnership firm engaged in iron ore and manganese ore mining in Odisha. The Tribunal held that the fact that the firm later paid ₹784 crore as compensation pursuant to Supreme Court directions for illegal mining did **not** amount to compounding the offence of money laundering, did **not** erase the alleged “proceeds of crime,” and therefore did **not** invalidate the PMLA attachment. The ED had estimated the proceeds of crime at ₹785.67 crore, and the attached deposits—originally about ₹497.68 crore as of July 2015, plus accumulated interest—were valued at ₹622.62 crore when the provisional attachment was issued.

The underlying allegations were that the firm exceeded the production limits approved in its mining plan and environmental clearance, generating funds from the sale of ore that were then treated as tainted. After searches on July 9, 2015, the ED instructed banks to freeze the firm’s current accounts and fixed deposits. The Tribunal’s ruling makes clear that compensation paid for illegal mining under the Supreme Court’s directions does not automatically wash out the money-laundering taint or restore attached assets, so entities involved in mining should not assume that paying environmental or mining compensation will resolve PMLA exposure.

The Tribunal also rejected the argument that quashing of criminal proceedings against certain individual partners ended the PMLA case. It held that the PMLA proceedings could continue against the partnership firm because the Orissa High Court had expressly allowed proceedings to proceed against the firm. For compliance purposes, the decision underscores that corporate or partnership assets can remain exposed even where individual accused persons secure relief in related criminal proceedings, and that parallel regulatory/money-laundering enforcement can survive separate compensation or settlement-related payments.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Company Liquidation Does Not End Director’s Liability for Unrealised Export Proceeds: SAFEMA
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13298 Case Name Arun Sogani Vs Joint Director (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts SAFEMA Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Arun Sogani Vs Joint Director (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi) Liquidation of Company Does Not Wipe Out Director’s Liability for Non-Realisation of Export Proceeds—₹3 Crore FERA Penalty Reduced to ₹30 Lakh Summary: The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has upheld the liability of a director for failure to realise export proceeds under the erstwhile Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973. It held that the subsequent liquidation of the company and transfer of its records to the Official Liquidator would not absolve a director who was in charge of the company when the exports were made and the period for realisation expired. However, considering the age of the proceedings, liquidation of the company and other surrounding circumstances, the Tribunal reduced the penalty imposed on the director from ₹3 crore to ₹30 lakh—the amount already deposited by him. Facts of the case The Reserve Bank of India informed the Enforcement Directorate that M/s Unicorp Industries Ltd. had been caution-listed for failure to realise substantial export proceeds relating to the period 1990 to 1998. Information received from various banks showed unrealised export proceeds of approximately ₹26.36 crore and USD 9,80,000. The company and its directors had allegedly failed to realise and repatriate these amounts within the prescribed period and had not obtained the RBI’s permission for such non-realisation or delay. Directives under Section 33(2) of FERA were issued to the company, its directors and concerned banks. The appellant, Shri Arun Sogani, sought 20 days’ time to furnish a reply but did not subsequ
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that a director’s liability for non-realisation of export proceeds under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA) does **not** disappear simply because the company was later liquidated and its records were handed over to the Official Liquidator. The Tribunal found that if the director was in charge of the company at the time the exports were made and when the realisation period expired, he can still be proceeded against for the earlier export-proceeds default, even after winding up. In this case, RBI had informed the Enforcement Directorate that M/s Unicorp Industries Ltd. had been caution-listed for failure to realise substantial export proceeds from the period **1990 to 1998**; bank information showed unrealised amounts of about **₹26.36 crore and USD 9,80,000**, and the company and its directors had allegedly neither realised/repatriated the money within the prescribed time nor obtained RBI permission for delay or non-realisation.

The enforcement action included directives issued under **Section 33(2) of FERA** to the company, its directors, and the relevant banks. The appellant, Shri Arun Sogani, had sought **20 days’ time** to file a reply but did not subsequently provide an effective response, and the Tribunal treated the failure to realise export proceeds as established enough to uphold liability. On penalty, however, the Tribunal took a lenient view because the proceedings were very old, the company had been liquidated, and there were other surrounding circumstances. As a result, the original penalty of **₹3 crore** was **reduced to ₹30 lakh**, which was the amount the director had already deposited.

For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that export realisation obligations and associated director exposure can survive corporate liquidation when the default occurred during the director’s tenure and before the prescribed realisation period expired. It also underscores the importance of timely export proceeds repatriation, obtaining RBI permission where realisation is delayed or not possible, and maintaining records and a credible reply to regulatory notices; failure to do so can lead to significant personal penalties even years later.

Investors were allegedly induced to invest ₹62,100 per bike on the assurance of monthly rent, EMI payments and bonuses. Following the registration of approximately 25 FIRs, the Enforcement Directorate recorded an ECIR and provisionally attached several properties as proceeds of crime or properties of equivalent value. One of the attached assets was a 6 MW biomass power plant, together with approximately seven acres of land, buildings and machinery situated at Nashik, Maharashtra. The property belonged to M/s Envirotech Pvt. Ltd., also referred to as M/s Mars. Subsequent Purchase of Attached Property The appellant, M/s Amanecer Green Pvt. Ltd., entered into an agreement dated December 17, 2020, to purchase the power plant for ₹10.17 crore. The agreement stipulated that, in case of default by the seller, the purchase price would stand reduced to ₹9 crore. Before executin
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal has held that a bona fide purchaser who acquired an attached asset through court-supervised sale proceedings is entitled to release of the property, even though the underlying criminal/financial investigation remains pending. In this case, Amanecer Green Pvt. Ltd. agreed on 17 December 2020 to buy a 6 MW biomass power plant in Nashik, Maharashtra, along with about seven acres of land, buildings, and machinery, for ₹10.17 crore; the agreement provided that if the seller defaulted, the purchase price would be reduced to ₹9 crore. The asset was already under provisional attachment by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in connection with the “BIKEBOT” investment fraud case involving M/s Garvit Innovative Promoters Ltd. and related persons, where around 25 FIRs had been registered and investors were allegedly induced to invest ₹62,100 per bike on promises of monthly rent, EMI payments, and bonuses.

The Tribunal noted that the purchase was undertaken after court-supervised procedures and treated Amanecer Green as a bona fide buyer, meaning the property itself should not remain blocked against the purchaser merely because it had previously been attached in the money-laundering proceedings. At the same time, the Tribunal protected the ED’s interests by allowing it to proceed against the sale proceeds held by the Court Receiver: the ₹6.95 crore sale consideration lying with the Court was permitted to be attached as a substitute for the property. For compliance purposes, the key point is that where an attached asset is sold through court-sanctioned process to an innocent purchaser, the attachment may shift from the physical asset to the realized sale proceeds, and agencies may pursue those proceeds rather than the property itself.

The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has directed the Enforcement Directorate to release a seized hard disk and mobile phone within 30 days after the ED admitted that the devices were not relied upon in the prosecution complaint and that their owner had not been arrayed as an accused. The Enforcement Directorate had seized a hard disk, mobile phone and locker belonging to Dr. Pradeep Makkar during proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The locker was subsequently released. However, the ED continued to retain the hard disk and mobile phone, prompting the appellant to approach the Tribunal against their continued seizure. During the hearing, counsel for the ED stated on instructions that the seized hard disk and mobile phone had not been relied upon in the prosecution complaint and that the appellant had not been named as an accused in the prosecution complaint. Thus, the ED did not demonstrate any continuing evidentiary or prosecutorial requirement for retaining the devices. In view of the ED’s statement, the Tribunal interfered with the impugned order to the extent it concerned the appellant and directed that the seized hard disk and mobile phone be released within 30
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal (in a PMLA matter) held that digital devices cannot be retained indefinitely once the Enforcement Directorate confirms they are not relied upon in the prosecution complaint and the person from whom they were seized is not named as an accused. In this case, the ED had seized a hard disk, a mobile phone, and a locker belonging to Dr. Pradeep Makkar during proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002; the locker was later released, but the ED continued to hold the hard disk and phone. During the hearing, the ED’s counsel stated that the hard disk and mobile phone were not used or relied upon in the prosecution complaint, and that Dr. Makkar had not been arrayed as an accused, meaning the ED could not show any continuing evidentiary or prosecutorial basis for keeping the devices.

Based on that admission, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order only to the extent it affected the appellant and directed the ED to release the hard disk and mobile phone within 30 days. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that under PMLA seizure/retention practice, continued custody of seized electronic devices needs a live justification tied to the complaint or proceedings; if the items are not relied upon and the owner is not an accused, indefinite retention is vulnerable to challenge and release may be required. The document does not announce any new statutory amendment or general rule change, but it is a clear tribunal direction limiting retention of seized devices in these facts and underscores the need to track whether seized items are actually cited in the complaint and whether the owner has been formally implicated.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | SAFEMA Tribunal Condones Delay in Review of Orders Based on Recalled Ganpati Dealcom Judgment
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal condones delay in review applications after Supreme Court recalled Ganpati Dealcom, restoring connected appeals for fresh consideration.The post SAFEMA Tribunal Condones Delay in Revie
rows.summary:
The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal has condoned delays in filing review applications because the Supreme Court has recalled its earlier judgment in **Ganpati Dealcom**, which had formed the basis for the challenged orders. As a result, the Tribunal has allowed the review process to proceed despite the late filing, restoring the connected appeals for **fresh consideration on the merits**.  

From a compliance perspective, the material point is that any orders or legal positions that were previously sustained by reliance on the now-recalled **Ganpati Dealcom** ruling may no longer be final, and affected parties should expect renewed judicial scrutiny. The document does **not** state any new monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, reporting requirements, or operational obligations beyond the Tribunal’s procedural decision to accept the delayed review applications.  

Entities potentially affected would be those with pending or concluded proceedings before the SAFEMA Tribunal that depended on the recalled Supreme Court ruling, especially where appeals or review rights may now be revived. The immediate compliance implication is to reassess any enforcement, litigation, or order-status assumptions that rested on Ganpati Dealcom and to monitor the restored appeals for outcomes that could alter prior positions.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Mere NDPS Accusation Cannot Justify Freezing Explained Assets: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal allowed release of an ancestral house and Tata Nexon after LIC, agricultural, business income and vehicle finance explained their sources.The post Mere NDPS Accusation Cannot Justify F
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi held that the freezing of Sonu’s ancestral residential house and Tata Nexon car could not be sustained merely because NDPS allegations had been made against him and others. The case arose from an alleged recovery of 157 grams of chitta/heroin on 02.04.2025 from Pradeep Kumar, Mohit, and Sonu, leading to FIR No. 0076/2025 under Sections 21 and 29 of the NDPS Act; the Freezing Authority issued an order under Section 68F(1), and the Competent Authority later confirmed it. Before the Tribunal, the appellants challenged only the house and the car, not the entire freezing action, and the Tribunal focused on whether those assets were “illegally acquired” within the meaning of the SAFEMA/NDPS framework.

On the house, the Tribunal accepted that it was ancestral property and noted the valuer’s view that the existing construction was about 10 to 12 years old. The only recent spending identified was renovation of ₹2.68 lakh, which the appellants explained through LIC-related receipts of ₹3 lakh and ₹1,03,800 received by Pushpa, followed by a cash withdrawal of ₹4 lakh; the Tribunal treated this explanation as sufficient to show legitimate funding rather than illicit acquisition. On the car, the Tribunal compared the actual vehicle cost of ₹8,73,032 including insurance with a higher valuation adopted by the SHO and found the lawful purchase explanation acceptable. As a result, the Tribunal allowed the appeal in substance for those assets and ordered release of the ancestral house and the Tata Nexon car.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that a bare NDPS accusation does not automatically justify continued freezing or forfeiture of property under Section 68F(1); the authority must still be able to connect the asset to illegitimate acquisition. If an owner can document legitimate sources for acquisition or renovation funds—such as inheritance/ancestral origin, insurance or other receipts, and bank withdrawals that reconcile to the expenditure—the Tribunal may lift the freeze even where serious drug-related allegations exist.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Penny-Stock LTCG Cannot Disguise Bribe Money; PMLA Attachment Upheld: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds PMLA attachment of assets linked to alleged bribe proceeds routed through inflated share transactions.The post Penny-Stock LTCG Cannot Disguise Bribe Money; PMLA Attachment Uph
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s provisional attachment of assets in a case alleging that cash bribes taken from medical students and their parents were laundered by converting them into apparently tax-exempt long-term capital gains through penny-stock/share transactions. The Tribunal accepted the ED’s case that funds were collected in cash for admissions and exam-related benefits, moved through cheque discounters, middlemen, and multiple bank accounts, and then channelled to so-called dummy purchasers who were funded by third parties to buy shares of non-functional companies at artificially inflated prices from the appellant and his family members. On that record, the Tribunal found the sharp share-price appreciation, lack of genuine underlying business activity, and evidence of third-party funding to be sufficient material to justify continuing the attachment pending completion of both the scheduled-offence case and the money-laundering proceedings.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that the decision reinforces the ED/tribunal approach that purported “LTCG” treatment will not protect proceeds if the underlying stock transactions are alleged to be sham or value-manipulated, especially where the share issuer has no real operations and the buyers appear to be name-lenders or funded conduits. The attachment was not lifted because the tribunal viewed the assets as potentially representing proceeds of crime until the merits are tested in the criminal trials. The document does not state any new statutory amendment, rate, threshold, or filing deadline; it is a case-law holding confirming that assets can remain attached under PMLA/SAFEMA where the evidentiary record suggests layering of illegal cash through share transactions.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Federalism: Constitutional Framework, Legislative Powers and GST Council
rows.desc: Examines Articles 246A, 269A and 279A, GST Council recommendations, cooperative federalism and Supreme Court rulings on GST powers.The post GST Federalism: Constitutional Framework, Legislative Powers
rows.summary:
This document is an analytical overview of India’s GST constitutional and legal framework, focused on how taxing power is allocated between the Union and the States after GST. It explains that Article 246A creates a special concurrent power for Parliament and State legislatures to make GST laws, while reserving exclusive Union control over inter-State GST through Article 269A, including the levy and collection of tax on inter-State supplies and the assignment of the resulting tax between the Centre and the States. It also examines Article 279A, which establishes the GST Council as the coordinating body for GST policy, and discusses how the Council’s recommendations function within a model of cooperative federalism rather than as ordinary executive directions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is not a new tax rate or filing deadline, but the legal effect of GST Council recommendations and how they interact with legislative power. The document reviews Supreme Court rulings on GST powers to clarify that while the Council is intended to guide harmonized GST policy, legislative competence remains grounded in the Constitution, and disputes may arise over whether recommendations are binding or persuasive in particular contexts. It is relevant to any entity subject to GST because it explains the constitutional basis for central and state GST legislation, inter-State supply taxation, and the institutional process by which GST rules are developed and coordinated.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTR-9 & GSTR-9C: Legal Framework, Threshold, Checklist & GST Reconciliation
rows.desc: GSTR-9 & GSTR-9C: A Complete Legal and Compliance Perspective on Annual GST Reconciliation Summary: Annual GST compliance is presented as more than a routine filing exercise, with GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C treated as year-end reconciliation documents carrying significant legal and compliance implications under the CGST Act, 2017. GSTR-9 is described as the annual consolidated return under Section 44 of the CGST Act, containing details of outward and inward supplies, ITC availed and reversed, tax paid, amendments, credit and debit notes, refunds, demands and HSN-wise information for the financial year. Applicability is linked to aggregate turnover on a PAN basis, with the supplied material referring to exemptions for taxpayers up to the prescribed threshold for relevant financial years. GSTR-9C is described as a self-certified reconciliation statement applicable where aggregate turnover exceeds Rs. 5 Crore, reconciling turnover, taxable turnover, tax liability, tax paid and ITC with books of accounts and financial statements. The article emphasises preparation of trial balances, financial statements, sales and purchase registers, GSTR-1/IFF, GSTR-3B, GSTR-2B, ITC workings, RCM details, credit/debit notes, refund and demand information and HSN-wise data. It recommends reconciliation between books and GST returns, checking RCM, Rule 42/43 reversals, HSN summaries and previous-year adjustments. Common errors identified include copying GSTR-3B figures into GSTR-9, ITC mismatches, missed reversals, incorrect RCM treatment, missing credit/debit notes and incorrect HSN reporting. The article concludes that GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C should be approached as a self-audit and reconciliation opportunity rather than merely as compliance forms. Table of Contents▸ 1. Understanding the Statutory Framework: GSTR-9 1. Threshold and Applicability a) For GSTR-9: b) For GSTR-9C – Reconciliation Statement: 2. GSTR-9C – The Reconciliation Statement 3. Basic Data Required – The Foundation of a Litigation
rows.summary:
The document explains that GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C are not just annual filing formats but legally important year-end GST reconciliation documents under the CGST Act, 2017. GSTR-9 is the annual consolidated return required under Section 44 of the CGST Act and must capture the financial year’s outward and inward supplies, input tax credit availed and reversed, tax paid, amendments, credit and debit notes, refunds, demands, and HSN-wise information. Its applicability is tied to aggregate turnover on a PAN basis, with the material noting exemptions for taxpayers up to the prescribed turnover threshold for the relevant financial years, so compliance teams should confirm whether the entity falls within an exempt or required category for the specific year being reported.

GSTR-9C is described as a self-certified reconciliation statement and becomes applicable when aggregate turnover exceeds Rs. 5 crore. It requires reconciliation of turnover, taxable turnover, tax liability, tax paid, and input tax credit as reported in GST returns against the books of account and financial statements. This means affected entities must be able to explain differences between their statutory books and GST reporting rather than merely replicate return figures.

The document highlights the underlying records a compliance team should gather and tie out before filing: trial balance, financial statements, sales and purchase registers, GSTR-1/IFF, GSTR-3B, GSTR-2B, ITC working papers, reverse charge mechanism (RCM) details, credit and debit notes, refund and demand records, and HSN-wise data. It specifically recommends reconciling books to GST returns, verifying RCM treatment, checking Rule 42/43 ITC reversals, validating HSN summaries, and reviewing prior-year adjustments. The process is presented as a self-audit exercise, so the filing should be supported by documented reconciliation logic and not prepared mechanically from GSTR-3B values.

The document also identifies common compliance errors that can create exposure: copying GSTR-3B figures directly into GSTR-9 without proper annual adjustments, ITC mismatches, missed reversals, incorrect RCM treatment, omission of credit/debit notes, and incorrect HSN reporting. For a corporate compliance team, the practical requirement is to ensure a complete annual reconciliation before filing, because the forms are intended to surface discrepancies and tax positions that may need correction, explanation, or disclosure.

However, where the alleged borrowing company is controlled by the persons providing the funds, its directors and shareholders are merely name-lenders, and the funds are layered through group concerns to acquire shares for the benefit of those controlling persons, the arrangement would fall within the definition of a benami transaction under Sections 2(9)(A) and 2(9)(C) of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988. The Tribunal set aside the order of the Adjudicating Authority and confirmed the provisional attachment of the shares and other assets. Facts of the case The Income-tax Investigation Wing conducted a survey in the case of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. and its associated concerns. During the survey, the books of account and other important documents belonging to M/s DCS Infotech Pvt. Ltd. were found at the business premises of the Deepak Group. The investigation revealed that DCS Infotech had purchased 46,48,720 shares of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. between FY 2004-05 and FY 2009-10 at a cost of approximately ₹5.47 crore. The market value of thos
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA held that **interest-free loans are not automatically or by themselves a benami transaction**, but the arrangement can still be treated as benami where the funds are **layered through a controlled company** and used to acquire shares for the real benefit of the persons who actually control the funding. In this case, the Tribunal found that the borrowing company was effectively controlled by the fund providers, its directors and shareholders were only **name-lenders**, and the money was routed through group entities to buy shares of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. for the benefit of the controlling persons; on that basis, the Tribunal concluded the arrangement fell within **Sections 2(9)(A) and 2(9)(C) of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988**.

The facts involved a survey by the Income-tax Investigation Wing in the Deepak Nitrite group, during which books and other documents of **M/s DCS Infotech Pvt. Ltd.** were found at the group’s premises. The investigation showed that DCS Infotech purchased **46,48,720 shares** of Deepak Nitrite Ltd. over **FY 2004-05 to FY 2009-10**, for about **₹5.47 crore**. The shares’ market value was stated to be much higher than the purchase cost, and the Tribunal treated the layering of funds and control structure as evidence that the acquisition was not a genuine independent investment by DCS Infotech but a benami holding for the real beneficial owners.

As a result, the Tribunal **set aside the Adjudicating Authority’s order** and **confirmed the provisional attachment of the shares and other assets** involved. It also granted the Department **liberty to refer the matter to SEBI** for examination of any possible **insider trading** issues. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that **internal or group-funded share acquisitions routed through an intermediary company can trigger benami exposure even if the loans are interest-free**, especially where the intermediary lacks real independence and appears to be acting only as a vehicle for the true controllers of the funds.

This note explains that once the company lists, it and all directors, key managerial personnel, employees, and connected persons come under the direct discipline of SEBI’s listed-entity framework, especially the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 as amended. Listing also means the company must simultaneously comply with multiple regimes, including the SEBI LODR Regulations, PIT Regulations, SAST Regulations, ICDR Regulations, and the Companies Act, 2013, rather than treating listing as a one-time event. The PIT framework specifically requires controls over insiders and connected persons, identification and handling of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI), designation of certain persons as “Designated Persons,” use of trading plans, trading-window closures, pre-clearance of trades, contra-trade restrictions, disclosures, Codes of Conduct and Fair Disclosure, appointment and functioning of the Compliance Officer, and maintenance of a Structured Digital Database.

The document highlights two recent regulatory changes that matter operationally. First, the 2025 amendment broadened the illustrative UPSI framework and added specific treatment for UPSI that originates outside the listed entity, so the company must be prepared to capture and control sensitive information even when it does not originate internally. Second, the earlier 2024 trading-plan amendment shortened the cooling-off period to 120 calendar days and removed the prior minimum plan-coverage requirement, which changes how trading plans may be used and scheduled by insiders. The note is intended to support immediate implementation from the listing date itself, so internal policies, controls, and training should be aligned at or before listing rather than after the fact.

From a compliance perspective, the note is not a standalone rulebook but a generic template for newly listed companies, with bracketed fields to be completed and company-specific thresholds and timelines to be finalized with the Compliance Officer before circulation. It expressly says it does not replace the company’s Board-approved Codes or legal advice on specific transactions, so a compliance team should treat it as a framework for tailoring internal procedures, not as the final authority. The practical implication is that the company must ensure its pre-clearance, disclosure, window-closure, insider-handling, and database procedures are ready on day one of listing, and that any company-specific thresholds or timing requirements are settled with the Compliance Officer before the document is used internally.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Repatriating UAE Business Profits to India: Tax and FEMA Rules
rows.desc: Summary: Repatriating money connected with a UAE business to India requires the payment to be identified by its legal character rather than simply described as business profit. The article explains that dividend, salary, directors’ fees, management or consultancy fees, interest, loan repayment, reimbursement, royalty, sale proceeds, liquidation distributions and branch profits can have different tax, accounting and FEMA consequences. Indian tax treatment depends substantially on the recipient’s residential status, the source and character of the payment, the point of accrual or receipt, applicable treaty provisions, the original investment route, transfer-pricing considerations and supporting records. A bank transfer to India is not necessarily a separate taxable event from the income-generating event. The article distinguishes company-level UAE Corporate Tax from Indian tax imposed on the shareholder and explains why UAE company tax is not automatically the shareholder’s foreign tax credit. It also addresses dividend declarations, salary for work performed in India, directors’ fees, services performed from India, shareholder loans, reimbursements, intellectual-property payments, sale of UAE company shares, deferred consideration, liquidation proceeds and branch profit remittances. For resident investors with ODI, the article highlights repatriation obligations, the designated authorised dealer bank, the 90-day period for specified dues and disinvestment or liquidation proceeds, purpose codes, banking documentation and the distinction between tax residence and FEMA residence. It further discusses NRE, NRO and resident accounts and emphasises that inward remittance is not governed by the LRS outward-remittance ceiling. The overall approach is to connect the UAE company’s accounts and corporate resolutions with tax records, ODI filings, banking evidence and the Indian income-tax return. Table of Contents▸ Introduction What Does Repatriation Mean? A Bank Transfer and a
rows.summary:
The document explains that money coming from a UAE business into India cannot be treated generically as “business profit”; the payment must be classified by its legal character, because dividend, salary, directors’ fees, management/consultancy fees, interest, loan repayment, reimbursements, royalty, sale proceeds, liquidation distributions, and branch profits can each trigger different tax, accounting, and FEMA consequences. For Indian tax purposes, the key issues are the recipient’s residential status, the source and character of the payment, when the income accrues or is received, any applicable treaty relief, the original investment structure, transfer-pricing exposure, and the supporting documents that substantiate the transaction; the article stresses that a bank transfer into India is not necessarily a separate taxable event from the underlying income event.

It also draws an important distinction between UAE Corporate Tax paid by the company and Indian tax obligations of the shareholder or recipient: UAE company tax is not automatically treated as a foreign tax credit for the individual shareholder. The document notes that specific payment types must be analyzed on their own facts—for example, dividend declarations, salary for work performed in India, directors’ fees, services performed from India, shareholder loans, reimbursement flows, intellectual-property/royalty payments, sale of UAE company shares, deferred consideration, liquidation proceeds, and branch profit remittances—because each may be taxed differently and may require different accounting treatment and documentary support.

On the FEMA side, the article is especially relevant for Indian residents who hold UAE interests through Overseas Direct Investment (ODI). It says repatriation must be routed through the designated authorised dealer bank and supported with proper banking documentation, purpose codes, and records that connect the UAE company’s accounts and corporate resolutions to ODI filings and the Indian income-tax return. For specified dues and for disinvestment or liquidation proceeds, the repatriation should be completed within 90 days. The piece also distinguishes FEMA residence from tax residence, and it states that inward remittance from the UAE is not subject to the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) outward-remittance ceiling.

Finally, the document addresses account-type mechanics for Indian recipients, including NRE, NRO, and resident accounts, and emphasizes that compliance teams should ensure the remittance trail, corporate documentation, tax reporting, and FEMA filings are all consistent with the true nature of the payment rather than the label used in the bank transfer. In practical terms, the compliance obligation is to verify characterization, taxability, treaty position, transfer-pricing and source records, banking purpose codes, ODI-related requirements, and the timing of repatriation where applicable.

rows.title: SEBI | Trust-to-LLP Conversion: Why AIF Investor Consent Should Be Value-Based
rows.desc: Summary: The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 proposes a framework for specified trusts regulated by SEBI and IFSCA to convert into limited liability partnerships, including a proposed Section 57A and Fifth Schedule to the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. The proposed Fifth Schedule, however, requires the consent of three-fourths of the investors without specifying whether the threshold is to be calculated by investor number or investment value. The article argues that this omission creates uncertainty because SEBI’s AIF framework has increasingly used value-based investor consent, including proposals concerning a 75 percent threshold by value. A headcount-based approach could produce materially different outcomes from a value-based approach where a small number of investors hold most of the fund’s capital. The article contrasts this issue with the dual-threshold mechanism under Section 230(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, which combines majority in number with three-fourths in value for schemes of arrangement. It argues that AIFs ordinarily comprise investors participating in a common investment structure and that conversion affects investors according to their economic exposure, making value-based voting more closely aligned with the proposed governance framework. The article therefore suggests that paragraph 4(a)(iv) should expressly require consent from investors holding at least three-fourths of the value of their investment. It also proposes that the value of each investor’s holding should be determined using the most recent SEBI-filed valuation and that non-responses should be addressed consistently with SEBI’s approach to AIF voting. The article concludes that these drafting clarifications could reduce uncertainty while retaining the broader objective of facilitating trust-to-LLP conversions. Keywords – Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), Trust-to-LLP Conversion, Investor Consent, SEBI, Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 Table of Contents▸ Int
rows.summary:
The document discusses a proposed legislative framework in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 that would allow specified trusts regulated by SEBI and IFSCA to convert into limited liability partnerships through a new Section 57A and a Fifth Schedule to the LLP Act, 2008. The key compliance issue identified is that the draft Fifth Schedule requires consent of “three-fourths of the investors” but does not specify whether that threshold is measured by investor headcount or by investment value, creating ambiguity for conversion approvals.

The article’s central point is that, for AIF-type structures, the consent threshold should be expressly value-based rather than based on the number of investors. It notes that SEBI’s AIF framework has increasingly moved toward value-based investor consent, including proposals around a 75% threshold by value, and argues that a headcount approach could distort outcomes where a few investors hold most of the capital. It contrasts this with Section 230(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, which uses a dual threshold for schemes of arrangement—majority in number plus three-fourths in value—and says that trust-to-LLP conversions should align with the economic reality of investor exposure.

For compliance purposes, the article recommends that paragraph 4(a)(iv) of the proposed schedule be clarified to require approval from investors holding at least three-fourths of the value of their investment, not merely three-fourths of the number of investors. It further suggests that each investor’s holding should be valued using the most recent SEBI-filed valuation and that any treatment of non-responses should follow SEBI’s existing approach to AIF voting. The overall implication is that funds and trust structures likely to be covered by the proposed conversion regime should prepare for a value-weighted consent process if the drafting is amended as suggested, and compliance teams should watch for final text because the current draft leaves the voting mechanics unsettled.

(Karnataka High Court) Capital Withdrawal Before Conversion Does Not Violate Section 47(xiii)—Karnataka High Court Upholds Tax-Neutral Succession of Firm By Company Summary: The Karnataka High Court has held that capital withdrawals by partners and changes in their profit-sharing or capital-sharing ratio before the conversion of a partnership firm into a company do not, by themselves, violate the conditions prescribed under section 47(xiii). For determining compliance, the relevant comparison is between the assets and liabilities of the firm immediately before succession and those taken over by the successor company. Where all such assets and liabilities were transferred to the company and the partners received no consideration or benefit at the time of conversion other than shares in the company, the exemption under section 47(xiii) could not be denied. The Court also held that board resolutions, legal opinions, valuation reports and documents relating to the conversion, generated in the ordinary course of business, do not become “incriminating material” merely because they were found during a search. Facts of the case Atria Wind (Kadambur) Pvt. Ltd. was formed by succession of the partnership firm, M/s Perpetual Investments. The business consisted of operating a 50-MW wind-power project in Tamil Nadu. The assessee filed its return for AY 2018-19 on 23 October 2018. The return was processed under section 143(1) on 17 May 2019. A search under section 132 was conducted at the assessee’s premises on 17 December 2020. Pursuant to
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court in **PCIT v. Atria Wind (Kadambur) Pvt. Ltd.** held that **capital withdrawals by partners, and changes in profit-sharing or capital-sharing ratios before a partnership firm is converted into a company, do not by themselves disqualify the conversion from tax neutrality under section 47(xiii)**. For purposes of section 47(xiii), the key compliance test is whether **all assets and liabilities of the firm immediately before succession are transferred to the company** and whether the partners receive **no consideration or benefit at the time of conversion other than shares in the successor company**. If those core conditions are met, the exemption cannot be denied merely because partner capital accounts were adjusted or money was withdrawn before conversion.

The case involved **Atria Wind (Kadambur) Pvt. Ltd.**, which succeeded the partnership firm **M/s Perpetual Investments**, a business operating a **50-MW wind power project in Tamil Nadu**. The assessee filed its return for **AY 2018-19 on 23 October 2018**, and the return was processed under **section 143(1) on 17 May 2019**. A **search under section 132** was conducted at the assessee’s premises on **17 December 2020**. In that context, the Court also ruled that **board resolutions, legal opinions, valuation reports, and other conversion-related documents created in the ordinary course of business do not become “incriminating material” merely because they were found during a search**.

From a compliance standpoint, the decision supports tax-neutral firm-to-company conversions where the firm’s assets and liabilities are fully taken over and the partners’ only consideration is shareholding in the new company. The ruling is significant for transactions involving **pre-conversion capital account movements**, because it clarifies that such movements alone are not fatal under section 47(xiii) unless they affect the substantive transfer conditions or confer prohibited consideration. There is **no new deadline or filing procedure** announced in the decision, but entities planning a conversion should ensure their documentation clearly shows the transfer of the entire business, the absence of impermissible consideration, and the ordinary-course nature of transaction records, so those records are defensible if later reviewed in a search or tax proceeding.

The principal contention was that Mr. Udai Raj Cho
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court quashed the reassessment order passed under section 148A(3) and the consequential notice under section 148 issued to Khivraj Motors, a registered partnership firm, for AY 2023-24, where the department alleged escapement of income of ₹1,36,18,476. The key compliance point is that the same ₹1.36 crore amount was also already the subject of reassessment proceedings against one of the firm’s partners, Mr. Udai Raj Choudhary, and the Court held that the tax authorities should not proceed in a way that could result in inconsistent findings or double taxation of the same income.  

The Court did not decide whether the amount is ultimately taxable in the hands of the firm or the partner; it only restored the matter to the pre-reassessment stage. It directed the same jurisdictional Assessing Officer to reconsider the proceedings for both the firm and the partner together, so the tax authority can make a coordinated determination on the correct taxable entity before moving forward.  

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that where the same item of income is being examined in parallel against a partnership firm and its partner(s), the department may be required to coordinate those proceedings and avoid duplicative reassessment actions. rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST applies on C-295 Aircraft Supply to MoD: Gujarat AAR
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13353 Case Name In re Airbus Defence and Space SA (GST AAR Gujrat) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts AAR/AAAR Gujarat, Advance Rulings Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In re Airbus Defence and Space SA (GST AAR Gujrat) Summary: The Gujarat Authority for Advance Ruling considered whether Airbus Defence and Space S.A., Spain, through its Project Office in India, was liable to pay GST on the supply of forty C-295 aircraft to the Ministry of Defence and whether it was required to obtain GST registration in Gujarat. Under the Aircraft Contract dated 24.09.2021, Airbus was to supply fifty-six C-295MW aircraft, of which sixteen were to be delivered ex-works from Spain and forty were to be manufactured in India by Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL), the appointed Indian Aircraft Contractor, at its facility in Vadodara, Gujarat. Airbus entered into an IAC Contract dated 29.10.2021 with TASL for manufacture and supply of the forty aircraft. The Authority examined the transaction under [Section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017](https://taxguru.in/goods-and-service-tax/section-7-scope-supply-cgst-act-2017.html), including Schedule II, and noted that the aircraft constituted “goods” and that the transaction involved consideration in the course or furtherance of business. The applicant was to procure the aircraft from TASL at Vadodara and subsequently supply them ex-works to the Ministry of Defence at the same location. Title and ownership were to transfer to the applicant at the IAC facility upon execution of the Acceptance Certificate, following which the aircraft were to be accepted by the Ministry of Defence. The Authority therefore concluded that the transaction constituted a supply of goods under Section 7 read with Entry 1(a) of Schedule II and was liable to GST.
rows.summary:
The Gujarat Authority for Advance Ruling held that Airbus Defence and Space S.A., Spain, acting through its Project Office in India, is making a taxable supply of goods when it procures forty C-295 aircraft from Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL) in Vadodara, Gujarat and then supplies those aircraft to the Ministry of Defence on an ex-works basis. The ruling arose under an Aircraft Contract dated 24.09.2021 for fifty-six C-295MW aircraft in total: sixteen were to be delivered ex-works from Spain, while forty were to be manufactured in India by TASL under a separate IAC Contract dated 29.10.2021.

For GST purposes, the Authority found that the aircraft are “goods” and that the arrangement is a supply made for consideration in the course or furtherance of business, bringing it within Section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017. It specifically relied on Section 7 read with Entry 1(a) of Schedule II to conclude that the transaction is a supply of goods. The ownership/title was to pass to Airbus at the TASL facility in Vadodara upon execution of the Acceptance Certificate, after which the aircraft would be accepted by the Ministry of Defence; that transfer of title at the Indian facility was central to the GST characterization.

The practical compliance consequence is that the forty aircraft supplied through the Indian manufacturing arrangement are subject to GST, rather than being treated as outside the scope of supply. The ruling also indicates that Airbus’s Project Office in India may need GST registration in Gujarat in connection with this transaction, because the supply is being made from/through the Vadodara location where title transfers and where the aircraft are procured from TASL. No specific rate, exemption, or filing deadline is stated in the document, but the ruling confirms taxability and the need to evaluate registration and related GST compliance for the Indian-side supply chain.

The relief was granted because the statutory communications were sent to the assessee’s secondary e-mail address and an old residential address, though the assessee was residing abroad and was no longer staying at the physical address used by the Department. This was followed by an order under section 148A(d) and notice under section 148, both dated 15 March 2023. As the assessee did not respond, an ex parte assessment order was passed on 25 January 2024 under sections 147, 144 and 144B. The Department thereafter passed three different penalty orders: under section 271(1)(b) for non-compliance, section 271F for failure to file the return and section 271(1)(c) for alleged concealment or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. The Department ultimately issued a notice under section 226(3) on 14 November 2025 and attached the assessee’s ICICI
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court quashed the reassessment proceedings for AY 2016-17 after finding that the Income Tax Department had served the key statutory notices at the assessee’s secondary email address and an old residential address, even though the assessee was residing abroad and no longer lived at that physical address. Because the notices under section 148A(b) dated 25 February 2023, the section 148A(d) order and section 148 notice dated 15 March 2023, and the later assessment and penalty communications were not properly brought to the assessee’s attention, the Court set aside the entire chain of action: the section 148A(d) order, section 148 notice, ex parte reassessment order dated 25 January 2024, all three penalty orders, the consequential demand notices, and the attachment of the assessee’s bank account under section 226(3) dated 14 November 2025. The penalty orders specifically covered section 271(1)(b) for non-compliance, section 271F for failure to file the return, and section 271(1)(c) for alleged concealment or furnishing inaccurate particulars.

At the same time, the Court did not permanently close the reassessment matter. It restored the case to the section 148A(b) stage, meaning the Department must restart the pre-reassessment process from that notice stage and give the assessee a proper opportunity to respond. The assessee has been permitted to submit a response by 5 October 2026. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that where the Department relies on email and address-based service for reassessment or penalty proceedings, it must ensure service reaches the correct, current contact details of the taxpayer; service to a secondary email and outdated residence was not enough to sustain the proceedings here.

The electronic filing process involves preparation of data, schema-based validations, utility validations, digital signatures, uploading and subsequent approval by the assessee. The Income Tax Department’s utility records themselves reflect subsequent releases and updates du
rows.summary:
This document is not a rule or notification changing the law; it is a formal representation dated 17 September 2026 from the Tax Bar Association, Jhalawar, Rajasthan to the Chairperson of the CBDT requesting that the due date for furnishing tax audit reports and related audit forms for AY 2026-27 be extended from 30 September 2026 to 31 October 2026. The request specifically covers tax audit reports in Forms 3CA/3CB read with Form 3CD, as well as audit reports in Forms 10B and 10BB. The stated compliance issue is that tax audit completion is interlinked with filing of the audited taxpayer’s return, especially ITR-3, ITR-5, and ITR-6, and the necessary filing utilities were released only progressively and later updated, making timely completion difficult.

The representation cites the utility-release timeline as a key operational constraint: ITR-3 was initially available on 18 June 2026 and updated on 1 September 2026, ITR-5 was initially available on 7 July 2026 and updated on 1 September 2026, and ITR-6 was initially available on 4 August 2026 and also shown as updated on 4 August 2026. It states that although the tax audit utility itself was available relatively early, the “complete ecosystem” needed to finalize audit cases became available only in stages, because electronic filing requires data preparation, schema validation, utility validation, digital signature, uploading, and assessee approval. The authors argue that these late and staggered utility releases reduced the effective working time available to taxpayers and professionals for audit completion.

The document also highlights broader practical difficulties said to be faced by taxpayers and tax professionals across the country, including the dependency between audit work and return-filing work and the need to reconcile audit reports with the corresponding ITR utilities before final submission. No penalty relief, statutory change, or mandatory compliance instruction is created by this letter itself; the only action sought is CBDT’s extension of the filing deadline to 31 October 2026 for the cited audit reports for AY 2026-27.

Since the underlying agricultural land had been compulsorily acquired and the compensation was exempt under section 10(37), the interest forming part of such compensation was also held to be exempt. However, the decision requires considerable caution because the assessee was assessed at Sonipat and the Tribunal did not consider the directly contrary jurisdictional decision of the Punjab & Haryana High Court in Mahender Pal Narang v. CBDT, wherein such interest was held taxable after the amendments made with effect from AY 2010-11. Facts of the case The assessee had not originally filed his return of income. Based on information appearing in the AIMS module, the assessment was reopened on the ground that the assessee had received interest from the Land Acquisition Officer on which tax had been deducted under section 194A. In response to the notice under section 148, the assessee filed his return on 30 October 2021 declaring income of ₹1,03,687. The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee had received ₹36,33,013 as interest on enhanced compensation. The assessee claimed that the amount represented interest awarded under section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act in connection with the compuls
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT in **Sandeep v. ITO** held that **interest awarded under section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on enhanced compensation is not to be taxed separately as “income from other sources” under section 56(2)(viii)**, because it is treated as **part of the compensation itself**. On that basis, where the underlying land is **compulsorily acquired agricultural land** and the compensation is otherwise exempt, the Tribunal held the **section 28 interest also qualifies for exemption under section 10(37)**. The assessee in this case had **not originally filed a return**; the assessment was **reopened on the basis of AIMS information** showing land-acquisition interest with TDS under **section 194A**. In response to the **section 148 notice**, the assessee filed a return on **30 October 2021** declaring income of **₹1,03,687**, while the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had received **₹36,33,013** as interest on enhanced compensation.

The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that the amount arose from **compulsory acquisition of agricultural land** and that the interest under section 28 was part of the exempt compensation package, so it could not be separately assessed as taxable interest income. However, this ruling should be applied cautiously for compliance purposes because the document expressly notes a **contrary Punjab & Haryana High Court decision in Mahender Pal Narang v. CBDT**, where such interest was held **taxable after amendments effective from AY 2010-11**. The case therefore highlights a potential jurisdictional conflict: although the Delhi ITAT allowed exemption on these facts, entities dealing with land-acquisition compensation must check the controlling jurisdiction and whether the payment is truly **section 28 interest on enhanced compensation** rather than other forms of interest.

Based on information received through the INSIGHT portal from CRIU/VRU, the Assessing Officer alleged that the assessee had obtained accommodation entries in the guise of purchases from M/s Gauri Shankar Trading Co. The purchases recorded in the profit and loss account from the said concern amounted to ₹50,96,555. The Assessing Officer, however, considered an amount of ₹60,13,941, apparently after including GST of ₹9,17,386, and treated the whole amount as unexplained expenditure under section 69C. The Department relied heavily upon the statement of the alleged proprietor of the supplier concern. The person concerned reportedly denied having carried on the business and claimed that his identity documents had been misused. The Assessing Officer also noticed that the supplier had substantial transactions in its GST records, whereas no corresponding turnover was reflected in its income-tax return. The assessee furnished purchase invoices, GST returns and stock records and submitted that the purchases were duly recorded in the regular books of account. It was further contended that the corresponding sales had been accepted and that it was commercially impossible to make the sales without making the underlying purchases. Nevertheless, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee had failed to establish the actual delivery of goods through transportation documents, e-way bills, d
rows.summary:
This Delhi ITAT ruling in **Anuj Sharma vs ITO** concerns an assessment year **2020-21** and addresses how far the tax department can go in treating alleged bogus purchases as unexplained expenditure under **section 69C**. The Assessing Officer relied on **INSIGHT/CRIU-VRU information** and a statement from the purported proprietor of **M/s Gauri Shankar Trading Co.** to allege that the supplier was only an accommodation-entry provider and that the assessee had taken bogus purchases. On that basis, the AO disallowed the entire purchase value of **₹60,13,941** (apparently **₹50,96,555** plus **₹9,17,386 GST**) as unexplained expenditure, even though the assessee had produced purchase invoices, GST returns, and stock records and argued that its sales had been accepted and could not have happened without underlying purchases.

The ITAT’s key compliance-relevant conclusion is that **the full purchase amount could not be treated as bogus merely because the supplier’s credibility was doubtful, especially where corresponding sales were accepted**. Instead of sustaining the entire **₹60.14 lakh** addition, the Tribunal **restricted the addition to ₹6 lakh**, effectively applying a much narrower estimate of possible inflation/benefit rather than disallowing the entire purchase cost. For corporate compliance teams, the case reinforces that tax authorities may still scrutinize purchases supported by suspicious third-party data, but if invoices, GST filings, stock records, and sales linkage exist, the risk is more likely to be confined to a limited addition rather than total disallowance. The practical compliance takeaway is to maintain robust documentation showing the movement of goods, purchase-to-sale linkage, and consistency across books, GST returns, and inventory records, because the absence of transport evidence such as e-way bills or delivery proofs was one of the factors the AO used to challenge the transactions.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | UPI MDR and GST: Treatment of Tax on MDR and Input Tax Credit
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the GST and input tax credit implications of the proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on specified UPI transactions from 15th October 2026. Using a consultancy transaction of Rs. 10,000 plus 18% GST, it explains that where the customer pays Rs. 11,800 through UPI and MDR of 0.4% is applied, the MDR would be Rs. 47.20 and GST at 18% on the MDR would be Rs. 8.50, resulting in an additional MDR-related amount of Rs. 55.70. The article discusses the distinction between GST forming part of the underlying supply and GST charged on the separate payment-processing service represented by MDR, and considers whether the latter should be described as “GST on GST”. It outlines the stated UPI framework for specified Person to Merchant transactions exceeding Rs. 2,000, including the 0.4% standard MDR, the Rs. 300 cap for transactions of Rs. 75,000 and above, concessional treatment for certain sectors and capital-market transactions, and the absence of MDR for P2P transactions and specified small P2PM merchants. It further considers the availability of ITC on GST paid on MDR under the normal GST conditions, including the relevance of Section 16 and the restrictions under Section 17(5) of the CGST Act. For a GST-registered merchant making taxable supplies, the article states that the Rs. 8.50 GST on MDR would be available as ITC subject to eligibility and utilisation, making the MDR itself the economic cost. It also discusses cases involving exempt supplies, composition taxpayers and unregistered merchants, the effect of the Rs. 300 cap, accounting and reconciliation requirements, and concludes that the GST on MDR is GST on a separate payment-processing service rather than GST being charged again on the GST included in the customer’s invoice. Authors note: A GST registered client came to me asking, “Aman, my most of the business payments are received through UPI”, will I get ITC? What will be the treatment? So being a logical consulting engagement, I r
rows.summary:
The document explains the expected GST treatment of the proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on certain UPI payments, stated to take effect from **15 October 2026**. It says that for **specified Person-to-Merchant UPI transactions above Rs. 2,000**, MDR is proposed at **0.4%**, with a **maximum cap of Rs. 300 for transactions of Rs. 75,000 and above**. It also notes that some sectors and capital-market transactions would receive **concessional treatment**, while **P2P transactions** and **specified small P2PM merchants** would not attract MDR.

Using an example of a **Rs. 10,000 consultancy supply plus 18% GST**, the customer pays **Rs. 11,800** via UPI; if MDR applies at **0.4%**, the MDR is **Rs. 47.20**, and **18% GST on that MDR is Rs. 8.50**, creating a total MDR-related cost of **Rs. 55.70**. The article emphasizes that this is **not GST being charged on the GST in the merchant’s invoice**; instead, the GST is charged on the **separate payment-processing service** represented by MDR. It explicitly addresses the common “GST on GST” concern and concludes that the GST on MDR is properly treated as tax on a separate service, not as a second layer of tax on the original supply.

For a **GST-registered merchant making taxable supplies**, the article says the **Rs. 8.50 GST on MDR should generally be available as input tax credit (ITC)**, assuming the merchant satisfies the normal ITC conditions under **Section 16 of the CGST Act** and is not blocked by the restrictions in **Section 17(5)**. In that case, the **economic cost** to the merchant is effectively the **MDR itself**, because the GST on MDR can be recovered through ITC. The document also flags that the analysis changes for **exempt supplies, composition taxpayers, and unregistered merchants**, for whom ITC may be unavailable or restricted, meaning the GST on MDR would then become a real cost.

The article also notes practical compliance implications, including the need for **accounting and reconciliation** of UPI receipts, MDR charges, and the GST charged on those charges. It makes clear that businesses should identify whether their UPI receipts fall within the proposed MDR framework, whether any **sectoral or transaction-specific cap** applies, and whether they are eligible to claim ITC on the GST charged by the payment-processing service provider. Overall, the key compliance message is that UPI-linked MDR is treated as a **separate taxable service**, and eligible registered businesses should be able to claim ITC on the GST charged on that MDR, subject to the CGST Act’s general conditions and restrictions.
