Vs Assessment Unit (ITAT Delhi) Excel-Sheet Entry Is Not “Money” Found With Assessee—Delhi ITAT Deletes Addition Under Section 69A Summary: The Delhi Bench of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal has held that an addition under section 69A cannot be made merely on the basis of entries appearing in an Excel sheet recovered during a search conducted on a third party. Section 69A applies where the assessee is found to be the owner of money, bullion, jewellery or another valuable article which is not recorded in the books. Where no cash, bullion, jewellery or valuable article was found in the possession of the assessee, an Excel-sheet entry by itself could not justify an addition under that section. Facts of the case The assessee filed its original return for AY 2018-19 on 14 September 2018, declaring nil income after reporting a loss of ₹16,20,383. The Department received information through the Insight Portal suggesting that the assessee had earned income from trading in equities and derivatives which had allegedly not been disclosed. The information originated from a search conducted on Shri Sushil Goel and other group entities on 31 January 2020. The Investigation Wing alleged that the searched group was involved in the purchase and sale of foreign currency and domestic and international hawala operations. Digital data was retrieved from devices belonging to Paras Goel. Based upon an Excel sheet forming part of that data, the Department alleged that the assessee had made an initial investment of ₹1 crore and earned profits from equity an
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT held that the Assessing Officer could not make an addition under section 69A merely because an Excel-sheet entry, recovered during a search on a third party, showed an alleged transaction or investment figure; section 69A requires the assessee to be found in possession of unexplained money, bullion, jewellery, or another valuable article, and an electronic entry by itself is not proof of such ownership. The assessee in this case had filed its original return for AY 2018-19 on 14 September 2018 declaring nil income and a loss of ₹16,20,383, but the Department later acted on information from the Insight Portal suggesting undisclosed equity and derivative income. That information traced back to a search on Shri Sushil Goel and related group entities on 31 January 2020, where the Investigation Wing alleged involvement in foreign currency dealings and domestic/international hawala operations, and digital data was taken from devices belonging to Paras Goel.  

Based on an Excel sheet in that digital material, the Department alleged that the assessee had made an initial investment of ₹1 crore and had earned profits from equity and derivatives trading, but the Tribunal found that no cash, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable article was actually found with the assessee, and the spreadsheet entry alone did not establish unexplained money in the assessee’s hands. The practical compliance point is that search material from third parties—especially loose digital records, spreadsheets, or inferred transaction ledgers—cannot automatically sustain a section 69A addition unless the Department can link actual unexplained assets or money to the assessee with proper evidence. For corporate taxpayers, this means alleged investments or profits reflected only in third-party electronic data should be challenged where there is no corresponding physical recovery, bank trail, or other direct evidence showing possession of unexplained assets by the assessee.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Allahabad HC Favours Mandatory Video Recording of BNSS Section 180 Statements
rows.desc: Allahabad HC Directs UP DGP To Consider Mandatory Audio-Video Recording Of Witness Statements Under Section 180 Of BNSS Summary: The Allahabad High Court, in Smt Chandrakanta vs State of U.P., Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 30325 of 2026, Neutral Citation No. 2026:AHC:192776, directed the Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh to consider making audio-video recording of statements recorded under Section 180 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 mandatory. The direction arose during consideration of a bail application concerning allegations of dowry death and related offences. The Investigating Officer admitted that the statement of the first informant under Section 180 BNSS had not been audio-video recorded, despite DGP circulars permitting such recording. The Court observed that the optional nature of audio-video recording had been used by several Investigating Officers and directed that statements should preferably be recorded through the E-Sakshya App and be made available to the concerned court on demand. The Court also issued several investigation-related directions concerning recording statements of independent witnesses, handling cases involving rape and sexual assault, medical examination, identification parades, collection of mobile-phone and call-detail records, and forensic examination of electronic evidence. The Court directed the DGP, U.P. to consider making audio-video recording of Section 180 BNSS statements mandatory and to apprise all Investigating Officers of the guidelines. On the bail application, the Court considered the applicant’s status as the mother-in-law of the deceased, the nature of the allegations, evidence, complicity, overcrowded jails and pendency of criminal cases, and granted bail subject to conditions. The Registrar (Compliance) was directed to send a copy of the order to the Director General of Police, U.P. for compliance with paragraph 20. Table of Contents▸ Allahabad High Court Considers Audio-Video Recording
rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court, in **Smt Chandrakanta v. State of U.P.** (Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 30325 of 2026; Neutral Citation No. 2026:AHC:192776), directed the **Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh** to **consider making audio-video recording of witness statements under Section 180 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 mandatory**. The issue arose in a bail matter involving allegations of **dowry death and related offences**, where the Investigating Officer admitted that the **first informant’s statement under Section 180 BNSS had not been audio-video recorded**, even though existing DGP circulars allowed such recording.

The Court noted that the **optional** nature of audio-video recording had led Investigating Officers to avoid using it, and therefore directed that Section 180 statements should **preferably be recorded through the E-Sakshya App** and **made available to the concerned court on demand**. The Court further asked the DGP, U.P. to **apprise all Investigating Officers of the guidelines** and to consider making the recording requirement mandatory, indicating a move toward a stronger evidentiary-preservation protocol in police investigations.

Beyond the recording issue, the Court also issued **investigation-related directions** affecting how police should handle certain evidence-gathering steps, including the recording of **independent witness statements**, procedures in **rape and sexual assault cases**, **medical examination**, **identification parades**, collection of **mobile-phone data and call-detail records**, and **forensic examination of electronic evidence**. These directions are not framed as a generalized policy note; they are court-ordered guidance intended to shape investigation practice, especially in serious criminal cases where evidentiary integrity is critical.

On the specific bail application, the Court considered the applicant’s position as the **mother-in-law of the deceased**, the nature of the allegations, the evidence and her alleged complicity, as well as broader custody concerns such as **overcrowded jails** and **pendency of criminal cases**, and ultimately **granted bail subject to conditions**. The **Registrar (Compliance)** was directed to send a copy of the order to the **Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh** so that the directions in **paragraph 20** could be complied with.

The Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer failed to account for the profit or loss embedded in the sales figure. It also deleted a disallowance under section 14A because the assessee had not earned any exempt income during the year. Facts of the case The assessee was engaged in trading in shares and securities. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer examined the purchase and sales ledgers and noticed the following figures: Opening stock of shares: ₹92,23,701; Purchases during the year: ₹12,91,194; Sales during the year: ₹53,12,935; and Closing stock declared by the assessee: ₹36,02,141. The Assessing Officer added the opening stock and purchases, arriving at total available s
rows.summary:
This ITAT Delhi decision for AY 2018-19 concerns a share-trading company, Blackrock Securities Private Limited, and clarifies how closing stock of shares should be computed for tax purposes. The assessee filed its return on 7 October 2018 declaring nil income and a current-year loss of ₹20,66,694, and the case was selected for compulsory scrutiny. During assessment, the Assessing Officer noted opening stock of ₹92,23,701, purchases of ₹12,91,194, sales of ₹53,12,935, and closing stock declared at ₹36,02,141, but then made an “suppressed closing stock” addition after effectively subtracting the sales value from the cost-based stock figures, which led to an inflated discrepancy of ₹16,22,549.  

The Tribunal held that this approach was fundamentally wrong because the sales figure represented sale proceeds, not the cost of the shares sold, and the profit/loss component embedded in the sales had not been properly recognized. In other words, the Assessing Officer could not deduct the gross sales value from opening stock and purchases recorded at cost and then treat the difference as understated closing stock; once the correct accounting treatment was applied, the addition could not stand. On that basis, the Tribunal deleted the addition relating to alleged suppression of closing stock.  

The Tribunal also deleted the disallowance made under section 14A, because the assessee had not earned any exempt income during the year. The practical compliance takeaway is that for share traders and similar businesses, stock valuations and sales must be matched on a proper accounting basis, and tax adjustments cannot be made by comparing cost figures with gross sales proceeds as if they were equivalent. It also reinforces that section 14A disallowance should not be sustained in a year where no exempt income has actually been received.

rows.title: Income Tax | Income from House Property under Income-tax Act, 2025: Sections 20 to 24
rows.desc: Summary: The Income-tax Act, 2025 consolidates the provisions relating to taxation of income from house property under Chapter IV. Sections 20 to 24 deal with chargeability, determination of annual value, deductions, taxation of arrears and unrealised rent, and treatment of co-owned properties. Section 20 provides that the annual value of a building or land appurtenant thereto owned by the assessee is chargeable under the head “Income from House Property”, subject to the specified conditions relating to the nature of property, ownership and use for business or profession. Section 21 provides the mechanism for determining annual value, including reasonable expected rent, actual rent, vacancy, municipal taxes, unrealised rent and self-occupied properties. Section 22 prescribes deductions including 30% of annual value and eligible interest on borrowed capital, with specified limits for self-occupied property. Section 23 provides for taxation of arrears of rent and unrealised rent subsequently recovered, with a 30% deduction. Section 24 deals with property owned by co-owners where their shares are definite and ascertainable, providing for separate computation in proportion to their respective shares and individual relief for self-occupied property. The article also sets out a broad computation of income under the head “Income from House Property”, beginning with Gross Annual Value, reducing municipal taxes to arrive at Net Annual Value, and thereafter providing for applicable deductions and eligible amounts in determining taxable income from house property. Table of Contents▸ Section 20: Income from House Property Section 21: Determination of annual value Section 22: Deductions from income from house property. Section 23: Arrears of rent and unrealised rent received subsequently Section 24: Property owned by co-owners. rows.summary:
The Income-tax Act, 2025 consolidates the rules for taxing income from house property in Chapter IV, and Sections 20 to 24 together govern when property income is taxable, how annual value is computed, what deductions are allowed, and how special cases such as arrears, unrealised rent, and co-owned property are treated. Section 20 makes the annual value of a building or land appurtenant to it chargeable under the head “Income from House Property” when the property is owned by the assessee, but only subject to the stated conditions relating to the nature of the property, ownership, and whether it is used for business or profession. For compliance purposes, this means entities or individuals holding property must first determine whether the property falls within this head and whether any business-use exception applies before treating rental or deemed rental income as taxable under these rules.

Section 21 sets out the mechanism for determining annual value, including use of reasonable expected rent, actual rent received, the effect of vacancy, municipal taxes, unrealised rent, and self-occupied property treatment. In practice, this requires taxpayers to compute gross annual value, then reduce municipal taxes to arrive at net annual value, and then apply the relevant adjustments under the section to determine the amount chargeable. Section 22 allows a standard deduction of 30% of the annual value and also permits deduction of eligible interest on borrowed capital, with specific limits applying where the property is self-occupied. Compliance teams should therefore verify that interest claims are within the applicable cap for self-occupied properties and that the 30% deduction is applied only after the annual value is correctly determined.

Section 23 covers arrears of rent and unrealised rent that are later recovered, making them taxable when subsequently received and allowing a 30% deduction from such amounts. This creates an ongoing reporting obligation to track recovered rent separately from current-period rent so it is included in the correct year and with the correct deduction. Section 24 addresses property owned by co-owners where their shares are definite and ascertainable: income must be computed separately in proportion to each co-owner’s share, and each co-owner is entitled to individual relief for self-occupied property where applicable. The document does not specify new filing dates or deadlines, but it does establish these substantive computation rules and requires accurate ownership records, rent tracking, municipal tax accounting, and interest documentation to support compliant reporting under the head “Income from House Property.”

rows.title: SEBI | Open Offer under SEBI SAST Regulations: Triggers, Pricing & Process
rows.desc: Summary: An open offer is a public offer made by an acquirer to purchase shares from existing public shareholders of a listed company when the acquirer acquires a substantial stake in, or control over, the company. The legal framework is contained in the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, commonly known as the Takeover Code, which replaced the 1997 Regulations and increased the initial mandatory open offer threshold from 15% to 25% of voting rights. The framework distinguishes ordinary market purchases from acquisitions crossing prescribed thresholds or resulting in acquisition of control. Key triggers include crossing 25% or more of voting rights, creeping acquisition beyond 5% in a financial year by existing holders of 25% or more, acquisition of control, indirect acquisition and voluntary offers. Mandatory offers generally cover at least 26% of the total voting share capital, while voluntary offers have a different minimum offer size. Regulation 8 prescribes pricing mechanisms, including the highest-price approach for frequently traded shares and valuation-based methodology for infrequently traded shares. The Takeover Code also provides a structured process covering appointment of the merchant banker, public announcement, escrow arrangements, detailed public statement, draft letter of offer, SEBI review, independent directors’ recommendations, tendering and payment settlement. Regulations 10 and 11 provide exemptions, while Regulations 19, 20 and 23 address conditional offers, competing offers and withdrawal. The framework also imposes responsibilities on the target company’s board and provides regulatory consequences for non-compliance, including penalties under Section 15H of the SEBI Act, 1992. Table of Contents▸ Understanding the concept of an Open Offer The Rationale behind the mandatory Open Offer Requirement Key Triggers for an Open Offer Size of a Mandatory Open Offer Pricing Methodology Pricing of Frequently Traded
rows.summary:
Under the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (“Takeover Code”), an open offer is the mandatory public offer an acquirer must make to existing public shareholders of a listed target company when the acquisition reaches prescribed shareholding thresholds or results in acquisition of control. The document explains that this 2011 framework replaced the earlier 1997 regulations and raised the initial mandatory open-offer trigger from 15% to 25% of voting rights, so any acquisition that crosses the new threshold must be assessed for open-offer obligations. It also makes clear that the code distinguishes ordinary market purchases from acquisitions that trigger regulatory duties because of size, control, or structure.

The key trigger points described are: acquisition of 25% or more of voting rights; creeping acquisition by an existing holder of 25% or more where additional purchases exceed 5% in a financial year; acquisition of “control” even if the shareholding threshold is not crossed; indirect acquisitions; and voluntary offers. Where a mandatory open offer is triggered, the offer generally must cover at least 26% of the total voting share capital, while voluntary offers are subject to a different minimum offer size. Compliance teams should treat both direct and indirect acquisition structures as potentially triggering the code, and not rely only on the nominal shareholding percentage.

Pricing is governed by Regulation 8 and depends on whether the target’s shares are frequently traded or infrequently traded. For frequently traded shares, the offer price follows the highest-price methodology; for infrequently traded shares, it is determined using a valuation-based methodology. This means pricing must be tested against the regulatory formula applicable to the trading status of the target’s shares, rather than set commercially at the acquirer’s discretion.

The document also outlines the procedural sequence required once an offer obligation arises: appointment of a merchant banker, public announcement, creation of escrow arrangements, issuance of a detailed public statement, filing of a draft letter of offer, SEBI review, recommendations from the target company’s independent directors, tendering by shareholders, and final payment settlement. In addition, Regulations 10 and 11 provide exemptions from open-offer requirements, while Regulations 19, 20, and 23 deal with conditional offers, competing offers, and withdrawal, respectively, so these provisions must be checked before finalizing a transaction. The target board has express responsibilities under the code, and non-compliance can lead to regulatory consequences, including penalties under Section 15H of the SEBI Act, 1992.

rows.title: Income Tax | UAE Corporate Tax for Indian Entrepreneurs: Key Tax & Compliance Issues
rows.desc: Summary: Indian entrepreneurs operating businesses in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and other UAE jurisdictions must analyse UAE Corporate Tax together with Indian tax, FEMA and cross-border compliance rather than treating the UAE company and its Indian owner as unrelated tax matters. The article explains the UAE Corporate Tax framework, including the standard 0% rate on taxable income up to AED 375,000 and 9% above that threshold, the distinction between taxable income and turnover, and the application of Corporate Tax to mainland, free-zone and other taxable persons. It sets out the conditional 0% regime for Qualifying Free Zone Persons, including requirements concerning adequate substance, qualifying income, excluded activities, the de minimis test, audited financial statements and transfer pricing. It also addresses Small Business Relief, natural persons, partnerships, deductible and non-deductible expenditure, related and connected persons, participation exemption, foreign Permanent Establishments and Corporate Tax compliance. For Indian entrepreneurs, the analysis extends to Place of Effective Management, Indian Permanent Establishment exposure, the India-UAE treaty, foreign tax credit, the distinction between company-level Corporate Tax and shareholder-level taxation, FEMA and Overseas Direct Investment, foreign-asset reporting, VAT, e-commerce, third-country trading, intellectual property, exit and liquidation. The article concludes with record-retention requirements, common mistakes and an annual cross-border tax checklist, emphasising that ownership, management, operations, revenue, related-party compensation, taxable profit and double-tax relief must be considered together. UAE Corporate Tax for Indian Entrepreneurs: Essential Considerations Indian entrepreneurs have established thousands of businesses in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and other UAE jurisdictions. These businesses range from consulting and technology companies to trading, logistics, manufacturing, real estate, e-co
rows.summary:
The document explains that Indian entrepreneurs with businesses in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and other UAE jurisdictions cannot treat the UAE company and the Indian owner as separate tax issues; instead, they must assess UAE Corporate Tax together with Indian tax law, FEMA, and cross-border reporting obligations. It states that the UAE Corporate Tax regime generally applies at **0% on taxable income up to AED 375,000** and **9% on taxable income above AED 375,000**, and it emphasizes that this tax is based on **taxable income, not turnover**. The article says the regime covers **mainland companies, free-zone entities, and other taxable persons**, so the compliance analysis must begin with whether the business is in scope under UAE rules.

For **Qualifying Free Zone Persons**, the document says the **0% corporate tax treatment is conditional**, not automatic, and depends on meeting substance and compliance requirements. Those requirements include maintaining **adequate substance**, earning **qualifying income**, avoiding or staying within limits for **excluded activities**, satisfying the **de minimis test**, preparing **audited financial statements**, and complying with **transfer pricing** rules. It also notes that businesses must determine whether income is qualifying or non-qualifying, because that affects whether the free-zone 0% treatment is preserved.

The document also highlights other UAE Corporate Tax reliefs and rules that may apply depending on the taxpayer’s status and activities. It mentions **Small Business Relief**, rules for **natural persons** and **partnerships**, and the treatment of **deductible versus non-deductible expenditures**, **related and connected persons**, **participation exemption**, and **foreign Permanent Establishments**. These provisions matter because they affect how taxable profit is computed and whether certain income or expenses are excluded from tax calculations.

For Indian entrepreneurs specifically, the document warns that the UAE structure can still create tax exposure in India through **Place of Effective Management**, **Indian Permanent Establishment** risk, and the interaction with the **India-UAE tax treaty** and **foreign tax credit** rules. It stresses the difference between **company-level UAE Corporate Tax** and **shareholder-level taxation**, meaning tax paid by the UAE company does not automatically resolve the owner’s individual tax position in India. The article also says entrepreneurs must consider **FEMA** and **Overseas Direct Investment** compliance, **foreign-asset reporting**, **VAT**, **e-commerce**, **third-country trading**, **intellectual property**, and **exit/liquidation** consequences.

Finally, the document says businesses must maintain adequate **record-retention** and follow an **annual cross-border tax checklist**, because common errors arise from failing to analyze **ownership, management, operations, revenue, related-party compensation, taxable profit, and double-tax relief together**. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that UAE entity classification, free-zone eligibility, transfer pricing, treaty relief, Indian reporting, and ongoing documentation all need to be reviewed on a recurring basis rather than only at incorporation or year-end.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Section 17(5) Blocked Credit: Safari Retreats, Telecom Towers & GST Remedies
rows.desc: Blocked Credit Under Section 17(5) of the CGST Act, 2017: Consequences and the Emerging Judicial Landscape Summary: The input tax credit mechanism is the structural spine of the Goods and Services Tax regime, while Section 17(5) of the CGST Act, 2017 operates as a principal statutory qualification by blocking credit for specified inward supplies despite the general entitlement under Section 16. An incorrect blocked-credit claim can require reversal of credit, payment of interest and potentially penalty, with proceedings arising under Sections 73 or 74 and, in appropriate circumstances, administrative blocking of the electronic credit ledger under Rule 86A. Two significant lines of litigation illustrate the evolving treatment of Section 17(5). In Safari Retreats, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Sections 17(5)(c), 17(5)(d) and 16(4), while holding that whether a building qualifies as “plant” under clause (d) could depend on a functionality test. Following dismissal of the review petition, the Finance Act, 2025 retrospectively amended Section 17(5)(d) from 1 July 2017 by replacing “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery”, thereby materially altering the practical position for construction-related claims. In contrast, litigation concerning telecom towers and passive infrastructure followed a taxpayer-favourable trajectory, with judicial authority treating dismantlable and relocatable towers and shelters as movable rather than immovable property. The Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue’s special leave petitions and subsequently dismissed review petitions in August 2026. The article examines these developments, the consequences of incorrect claims, available procedural and constitutional remedies, and the practical importance of distinguishing construction-related disputes from disputes involving relocatable telecom infrastructure. Table of Contents▸ Introduction The Structure of Section 17(5) Consequences of an Incorrect Claim The Construct
rows.summary: The document explains that input tax credit under GST is generally available under Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017, but Section 17(5) blocks credit for specified inward supplies, so a wrong claim can trigger reversal of credit, interest, and possibly penalty, with recovery proceedings under Sections 73 or 74 and, in appropriate cases, temporary blocking of the electronic credit ledger under Rule 86A. It highlights two major lines of litigation affecting compliance analysis: in **Safari Retreats**, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Sections **17(5)(c), 17(5)(d), and 16(4)**, but indicated that whether a building can qualify as **“plant”** under clause (d) may turn on a **functionality test**; after the review petition was dismissed, the **Finance Act, 2025** made a **retrospective amendment effective from 1 July 2017**, replacing the phrase **“plant or machinery”** with **“plant and machinery”** in Section 17(5)(d), which materially changes the position for construction-related input tax credit claims. In the **telecom towers and passive infrastructure** line of cases, courts treated **dismantlable and relocatable towers and shelters** as **movable property rather than immovable property**, which is significant because movable infrastructure is more likely to support input tax credit eligibility; the Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue’s special leave petitions and later dismissed review petitions in **August 2026**. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that blocked-credit determinations now require careful fact-specific review of the asset’s nature and use, especially for construction and real-estate projects versus telecom infrastructure deployments, because an incorrect characterization can create immediate tax, interest, and penalty exposure. The document also notes that the evolving judicial landscape makes it important to preserve documentation supporting the functionality, movability, and intended use of the asset, and to assess whether any claim falls within the now-retrospectively amended scope of Section 17(5)(d) from **1 July 2017 onward**.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Deepak Sahu Vs DCIT (ITAT Delhi) Section 153C Cannot Be Invoked For The Entire Block Through A Mechanical Satisfaction Note—Delhi ITAT Quashes Assessment Summary: The Delhi Bench of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal has quashed an assessment under section 153C after finding that the Assessing Officer of the non-searched person failed to record the mandatory satisfaction that the seized material had a bearing on the determination of the assessee’s total income for the relevant assessment year. The Tribunal held that the mere receipt of seized documents or digital data from the Assessing Officer of the searched person does not automatically justify proceedings under section 153C for every year falling within the block period. The Assessing Officer must independently examine the material, identify the relevant assessment year and record its potential impact on the assessee’s total income. Background of the search A search under section 132 was conducted on the Sushen Mohan Group on 2 January 2020. During the search, documents, books, mobile phones and other digital material were seized, and statements of various persons were recorded. The assessee, Deepak Sahu, was stated to be working as Manager-Finance and described as a key employee of the searched group. The Assessing Officer of the searched person recorded a satisfaction note on 30 September 2021. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction over the assessee recorded another satisfaction note on 9 April 2022 and issued notice under section 153C on the same day. The assessment was eventually completed under section 153C
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT quashed a section 153C assessment against Deepak Sahu for assessment year 2020-21 because the Assessing Officer of the non-searched person did not properly record the mandatory satisfaction that the seized material had a bearing on the determination of the assessee’s total income. The Tribunal held that section 153C cannot be triggered mechanically merely because documents, books, phones, or other digital material are handed over from the searched person’s Assessing Officer; the officer must independently examine the seized material, identify the relevant assessment year, and explain how the material could affect the assessee’s total income for that year.

The facts were that a search under section 132 was carried out on the Sushen Mohan Group on 2 January 2020, during which documents, books, mobile phones, and other digital data were seized and statements were recorded. Deepak Sahu was described as a Manager-Finance and key employee of the searched group. The searched person’s Assessing Officer recorded a satisfaction note on 30 September 2021, after which the jurisdictional Assessing Officer for Deepak Sahu recorded a second satisfaction note on 9 April 2022 and issued a notice under section 153C on the same day.

The ITAT found the second satisfaction note deficient because it did not demonstrate that the seized material had a bearing on the assessee’s total income, and therefore the jurisdictional precondition for section 153C was not satisfied. As a result, the notice and assessment made under section 153C were quashed. For compliance purposes, this ruling reinforces that in search-related third-party proceedings, the tax authority must show a specific and reasoned nexus between the seized material and the proposed addition for the relevant year; broad, routine, or block-period-based invocation of section 153C is vulnerable to challenge where that recorded satisfaction is absent or perfunctory.

rows.title: Finance | Cash Profit – The Driving Force for Business Resilience
rows.desc: Summary: In today’s dynamic world, Profit after tax is generally the first number in annual reports captured by the general public and is widely treated as an indicator of how a company has performed. Lenders, analysts and investors compare profit with corresponding periods and use it to assess growth, while management highlights it in presentations to shareholders. However, a healthy net profit does not necessarily guarantee a strong financial position because a business may report substantial profits while facing cash shortages affecting suppliers, debt servicing and payroll obligations. Conversely, a company with moderate or reasonable profit may have a strong cash position reflecting financial strength. The difference principally arises because net profit is determined on an accrual basis and includes non-cash items such as depreciation, provisions, impairment losses, fair value adjustments, expected credit loss adjustments and other accounting estimates, whereas cash profit focuses on actual cash generation by eliminating the effect of major non-cash expenses. Cash profit is therefore discussed in the context of business survival or going concern, creditworthiness, sustainable earnings, liquidity management, cash conversion cycle, management decisions, accounting estimates, investor outlook, dividend payout, capital allocation, financial reporting and early identification of financial stress. Strong earnings remain important, but their credibility is linked with cash generation ability. A disciplined cash conversion cycle, adequate liquidity and efficient capital allocation can support business resilience and financial stability, while excessive dependence on borrowings, long receivable periods, excessive inventory and interest burden can signal financial stress. The article accordingly emphasises that net profit and cash profit perform different roles and should not be interpreted in isolation. Net profit may indicate accounting performance, whereas cash profi
rows.summary:
This document is an explanatory finance article, not a rulemaking or formal regulatory filing, and it does not impose any new legal deadlines, thresholds, filings, or numeric compliance requirements. Its main point is that **profit after tax/net profit and cash profit are different measures and must not be read in isolation**: net profit is prepared on an accrual basis and can be inflated or reduced by non-cash items such as depreciation, provisions, impairment losses, fair value adjustments, expected credit loss adjustments, and other accounting estimates, while cash profit reflects actual cash generated by stripping out major non-cash expenses. For a compliance or finance team, the practical takeaway is that a company can show strong reported profit yet still face liquidity strain that affects **supplier payments, debt servicing, and payroll**, so cash-generation analysis is essential when assessing solvency, going concern risk, creditworthiness, and sustainable earnings.

The article stresses that cash profit is especially important for evaluating **business survival, liquidity management, the cash conversion cycle, management decision-making, investor expectations, dividend capacity, capital allocation, financial reporting, and early identification of financial stress**. It notes that strong earnings only matter if they are supported by real cash generation, and that a disciplined cash conversion cycle, adequate liquidity, and efficient capital allocation support resilience and stability. rows.title: Income Tax | Settlement Commission Order Bars AO Reopening Concluded Deduction Claim: Supreme Court

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that once the Settlement Commission has passed a final order under Section 245D(4) of the Income-tax Act, the Assessing Officer cannot reopen or reassess the same matter, including a deduction claim already concluded in that settlement. In this case, the deduction issue had been covered by the Settlement Commission’s final order, and the Court ruled that the tax authority was barred from starting a fresh assessment on that settled issue.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that a final settlement under Section 245D(4) has binding effect on the tax administration for the matters actually decided there, so the department cannot use reopening powers to revisit those concluded claims later. This protects finalized settlement outcomes from re-litigation by the Assessing Officer and means taxpayers should treat issues resolved by such an order as conclusively settled, at least as to the specific matters covered by the order.

No new filing deadline, rate, threshold, or procedural timeline is stated in the document. The practical compliance takeaway is to preserve the Settlement Commission order and ensure that any future tax notices or reassessment attempts are checked against the exact issues disposed of in that final settlement order.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Supreme Court Holds Officiating Employees Have No Vested Right Under Old Promotion Rules

rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court ruling involving BSNL employees who had been working in an officiating capacity on higher posts. The Court held that these employees do **not** acquire a vested or automatic right to promotion merely because they were temporarily placed in higher positions, and therefore they cannot insist on being promoted under the earlier promotion regime.

The practical effect is that BSNL may require such employees to be considered under the **2005 test-based promotion rules** rather than the prior rules they may have expected to apply. In other words, time spent officiating in a higher post does not lock in promotion eligibility or entitle the employee to promotion as of right under the old framework.

For compliance and HR administration, this means promotion decisions for affected BSNL personnel should follow the **current applicable rules**, including any test or assessment introduced in 2005, rather than treating prior officiating service as creating grandfathered promotion rights. The ruling reinforces that temporary or officiating assignment does not itself create a legally enforceable entitlement to elevation, so promotion processes should be documented as rule-based and not assumption-based.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Kolkata Deletes Section 271DA Penalty for Unproved Cash Receipt

rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Kolkata decision holding that a penalty under Section 271DA of the Income-tax Act cannot be sustained where the tax authorities fail to prove that actual cash was received. In the case described, the department relied on an unsigned, unexecuted sale agreement, but the Tribunal found that this document did not establish that any cash transaction had in fact occurred, so the penalty was deleted.

For compliance purposes, the key point is evidentiary: a proposed or draft sale agreement, by itself, is not enough to support a cash-receipt penalty unless the department can demonstrate actual receipt of cash in violation of the applicable cash-restriction provisions. The ruling reinforces that Section 271DA penalties require proof of the underlying cash transaction, not merely the existence of an unfinalized or unexecuted document suggesting one.

The document does not state any new statutory amendment, effective date, deadline, or numerical threshold; it is a case-specific judicial ruling. Its practical implication is that taxpayers facing Section 271DA exposure should review whether the revenue can substantiate actual receipt of cash, while compliance teams should continue to ensure that high-value transactions are documented through properly executed agreements and banking channels to avoid penalty risk.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Kolkata Deletes TDS and TCS Penalties on Bona Fide Belief Under Section 273B

rows.summary:

For compliance teams, the key point is not that TDS/TCS requirements are relaxed, but that penalty relief may be available if the taxpayer can substantiate a credible, bona fide basis for its position and demonstrate reasonable cause under Section 273B. The decision is relevant to entities responsible for withholding or collecting tax at source and reinforces the need to document tax positions, internal legal/tax advice, and the factual basis for any interpretation that differs from the Revenue’s view. No specific effective date, monetary threshold, or revised filing procedure is stated in the document; the takeaway is the tribunal’s penalty relief principle for Sections 271C and 271CA in cases of genuine good-faith error.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 68 Addition Deleted as Investigation Wing Failed to Prove Receipt: ITAT Kolkata

This ITAT Kolkata ruling holds that a Section 68 addition of ₹14.01 lakh could not be sustained where the Revenue’s case relied on an alleged accommodation entry but the Investigation Wing failed to prove that the assessee actually received the amount in question. The key compliance takeaway is that, for an unexplained cash credit addition under Section 68, the tax authority must establish a real receipt/credit in the assessee’s books and cannot rely only on suspicion, third-party allegations, or an unsubstantiated investigation report.

The decision effectively deletes the entire ₹14.01 lakh addition because the department could not demonstrate the receipt of the alleged entry. For companies and finance teams, this underscores the importance of maintaining clear books, supporting documentation, and evidence of actual transaction flow when dealing with any third-party credits, share capital, loans, or other inward receipts that could be scrutinized as accommodation entries. There is no new filing deadline, rate change, or prospective compliance rule in this document; it is a judicial finding on the evidentiary burden the Revenue must meet before Section 68 additions can stand.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kolkata ITAT Deletes Additions on Unrecorded Coal Purchases and Under-Invoiced Sales

The tribunal deleted the additions made by the tax authorities after finding that the evidence relied on was not strong enough to support the tax adjustment: specifically, third-party material and statements used against the taxpayer were deemed insufficient, and the statements had been retracted. In practical compliance terms, this is a taxpayer-favorable ruling that limits the ability of the tax department to sustain additions based only on third-party documents or withdrawn statements without stronger corroboration.

For a corporate compliance team, the key takeaway is evidentiary rather than procedural: if the company is ever challenged on alleged off-book purchases or suppressed sales, the tax authority must be able to substantiate the allegation with reliable, corroborated evidence, not merely third-party records or untested/retracted statements. The document does not announce any new statutory rule, filing requirement, rate, threshold, or deadline, and it does not describe a broader regulatory change; it is a case outcome showing how the ITAT evaluated the sufficiency of evidence in this fact pattern.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | FEMA Section 37A Applies to Continued Foreign Asset Holding: SAFEMA Tribunal
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds Section 37A seizure of Indian assets for suspected foreign exchange held abroad, rejecting retrospective application objection.The post FEMA Section 37A Applies to Continued Fo
rows.summary:
The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal upheld action under Section 37A of FEMA authorizing seizure of Indian assets where there is a suspicion that foreign exchange or foreign assets are being held abroad in violation of exchange-control rules. The key holding is that the tribunal rejected the argument that Section 37A was being applied retrospectively; instead, it treated the provision as applying to a continuing state of unlawful foreign asset holding, meaning that if the prohibited foreign assets continue to be held after the provision comes into force, enforcement action can proceed based on that ongoing condition.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that continued overseas holding of undisclosed or prohibited foreign exchange assets can expose an Indian person or entity’s domestic assets to attachment/seizure under Section 37A, even if the original acquisition occurred earlier, so long as the noncompliant holding persists. The document does not provide a separate effective date, monetary threshold, or deadline; rather, the trigger is the ongoing nature of the foreign asset holding and the enforcement authority’s suspicion of a FEMA violation. Compliance programs should therefore focus on identifying and remediating any continuing foreign asset positions that may be outside FEMA permissions, because the ruling indicates that the passage of time alone will not necessarily defeat enforcement if the breach is continuing.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Certified KYC Copy Facility Extended to FPIs: RBI Amendment Directions 2026

rows.title: Income Tax | Kolkata ITAT Deletes ₹18.83 Crore Section 69A Addition on Recorded Bank Credits

The document reports an income-tax appellate ruling by the Kolkata ITAT that deleted an addition of ₹18.83 crore made under Section 69A. The Tribunal held that bank credits that were already recorded in the books, or transactions that were otherwise explained, could not be treated as “unexplained money” merely because the tax authority believed the explanation was inadequate. In practical terms, this means the tax department’s Section 69A adjustment was rejected because the underlying banking entries and transaction trail were treated as sufficiently documented and not subject to unexplained-income characterization.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that properly recorded bank transactions should be supported by clear books, source documentation, and an explanation that links deposits/credits to identifiable transactions. The ruling reinforces that unexplained-money treatment is not appropriate where the receipt is already reflected in accounting records and the taxpayer can substantiate the nature of the funds. No new deadline, filing requirement, or procedural change is described in the text; this is a judicial outcome rather than a rule amendment, but it underscores the importance of maintaining contemporaneous records for all significant bank credits to defend against Section 69A exposure.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | SAFEMA Tribunal Upholds Benami Attachment Where Registered Owner Lacked Financial Capacity
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds benami attachment where brother-in-law funded, controlled and benefited from flat registered in another person's nameThe post SAFEMA Tribunal Upholds Benami Attachment Where Re
rows.summary: The document reports a SAFEMA Tribunal decision upholding a benami attachment over a flat that had been registered in one person’s name, where the evidence showed that the brother-in-law had actually funded the purchase, exercised control over the property, and received the benefit of ownership. For compliance purposes, the key point is that mere registration of title in a different person’s name did not protect the asset from benami proceedings when the named owner lacked the financial capacity to acquire the property and the real source of funds/control could be traced to another individual. The decision reinforces that authorities may look beyond formal ownership documents to the underlying funding, possession, control, and beneficial enjoyment of an asset when assessing benami risk. It is especially relevant for real estate and asset-holding arrangements where property is acquired in the name of relatives or other nominees without corresponding economic substance or documented consideration from the registered owner. No specific effective date, filing deadline, rate, threshold, or new procedural requirement is stated in the excerpt provided, but the practical compliance implication is that ownership structures should be supported by clear evidence of source of funds, genuine consideration, and beneficial ownership alignment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Legitimate Deductions Cannot Be Denied Merely for Non-Filing Revised Return: Madras HC

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court has held that legitimate income-tax deductions cannot be denied solely because the taxpayer did not file a revised return, and it remanded the trust’s assessment for fresh consideration on that basis. The ruling is relevant to charitable/trust taxpayers and assessing officers where a deduction or exemption is otherwise substantively allowable but was not properly claimed in the original return or was not supported by a revised return. The court’s key compliance point is that the tax authority should not mechanically reject a valid claim just for procedural non-filing of a revised return; instead, the claim must be examined on its merits.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that return-filing errors or omissions should still be corrected and documented promptly, but a missed revised return filing does not automatically eliminate an otherwise legitimate deduction. Entities should maintain adequate supporting records for the claim and be prepared to substantiate eligibility during assessment or appeal. The document does not provide a new statutory deadline, rate, threshold, or rule change; it reflects a judicial interpretation limiting the basis on which deductions may be denied in assessment proceedings.

rows.title: Income Tax | 29-Day Form 10B Delay Cannot Deny Section 11 Exemption: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai allows Section 11 exemption despite 29-day Form 10B delay as audit report was available with CPC before intimation.The post 29-Day Form 10B Delay Cannot Deny Section 11 Exemption: ITAT Ch
rows.summary:
The ITAT Chennai held that a charitable or religious trust’s exemption under Section 11 cannot be denied solely because Form 10B (the audit report) was filed with a 29-day delay, where the audit report had in fact already been available with the CPC before the intimation was issued. In other words, a minor procedural delay in filing the audit report did not defeat the substantive exemption claim when the underlying audit information was already on record and available to the tax authorities.

For compliance teams of trusts and institutions claiming Section 11 relief, the practical takeaway is that timely filing of Form 10B remains important, but this ruling indicates that a short delay may not automatically invalidate the exemption if the report was otherwise completed and available before the assessment intimation. The decision appears to protect exemption claims from being denied on a purely technical basis where there is no prejudice to the department and the audit report exists in the system before the decision is made.

The document does not announce a new statutory deadline or change the filing requirement itself; rather, it clarifies how the law is to be applied in a situation involving a 29-day delay. Compliance teams should still treat Form 10B as a mandatory filing for Section 11 eligibility, maintain evidence of the audit report’s preparation and submission date, and be prepared to demonstrate that any late filing was only procedural and that the report was available to the CPC before the intimation order.

rows.title: Income Tax | Belated Form 10B Before CPC Processing Sufficient for Section 11 Exemption: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai allows Section 11 exemption despite 33-day Form 10B delay as audit report was available before CPC processed return.The post Belated Form 10B Before CPC Processing Sufficient for Section

The key holding is that the late filing was still treated as sufficient because the audit report was available before the Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) actually processed the return, so the exemption could not be rejected solely on the basis of that delay. In practical compliance terms, this means that for Section 11 exemption claims, the timing of Form 10B submission relative to CPC processing mattered in this case, and a short filing delay did not automatically destroy eligibility where the report existed before assessment/processing occurred. The decision is relevant to entities claiming charitable or religious trust exemption under Section 11 and highlights that audit-report filing defects may be curable or non-fatal if the substantive reporting requirement is ultimately satisfied before processing.

rows.title: Income Tax | Agricultural Land’s Higher Stamp Value on NA Conversion Cannot Trigger Section 56(2)(x): ITAT Ahmedabad
rows.desc: Ahmedabad ITAT deleted Section 56(2)(x) addition where higher stamp value arose from land conversion funded by the purchaser.The post Agricultural Land’s Higher Stamp Value on NA Conversion Cannot Tri
rows.summary:
The document reports an Ahmedabad Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ruling that a higher stamp duty value arising from conversion of agricultural land for non-agricultural (“NA”) use does **not** by itself justify an addition under Section 56(2)(x) when the seller or purchaser has funded the conversion and the increase in value is attributable to that conversion rather than to an undervalued transfer price. In the case discussed, the ITAT deleted the Section 56(2)(x) addition, indicating that the tax authority cannot simply treat the post-conversion stamp valuation as the “value of property” for deemed income purposes if the higher value resulted from the NA conversion process.  

For compliance teams, the practical point is that property transactions involving agricultural land converted to NA use should be documented carefully, especially where the buyer bears the conversion cost or where the valuation jump arises only because of the conversion status change. Relevant records should show who paid for conversion, when the conversion occurred, and how the stamp value was determined, because those facts may be decisive in defending against a Section 56(2)(x) adjustment. The document does not announce any new statutory amendment, effective date, filing deadline, rate change, or procedural rule; it is a case-law clarification affecting how tax officers may apply existing Section 56(2)(x) anti-avoidance provisions in land transactions.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bank-Repaid Loan Cannot Be Deemed Accommodation Entry Solely on Third-Party Statement: ITAT Ahmedabad
rows.desc: ITAT Ahmedabad upheld Section 147 reopening but deleted additions for loans repaid through banking channels absent evidence of cash exchange.The post Bank-Repaid Loan Cannot Be Deemed Accommodation En
rows.summary:
The Ahmedabad ITAT held that the Assessing Officer could validly reopen Amigo Finstock Private Limited’s assessment under Section 147 for AY 2013-14, because the reopening was based on information and a statement recorded under Section 131, and the Revenue was not required to proceed under Section 153C merely because the information may have originated from a third-party search when no seized material from that search was actually relied upon. In practical terms, this means the reassessment jurisdiction was upheld, so the reopening itself was not quashed.

On the merits, however, the Tribunal deleted the addition made for alleged bogus/unsecured loan accommodation entries. The assessee had filed a return declaring total income of ₹42,52,820, and the disputed loans were held to be genuine because the assessee showed that the funds were received and repaid through banking channels within the same year; the Tribunal specifically noted there was no evidence of cash moving back to the lender or of any cash trail supporting the allegation of an accommodation entry. The decision emphasizes that a general third-party statement from an alleged entry operator, by itself, is not enough to disallow or treat a banking-channel loan transaction as bogus when the assessee’s own transaction trail is through bank transfers and no contrary direct evidence exists.

The order was issued in ITA Nos. 1540, 1541 and 1542/Ahd/2026 for AYs 2013-14 to 2015-16, dated 11 September 2026, but the summary provided is specifically focused on the AY 2013-14 findings. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that tax authorities may sustain reopening where they have information and recorded statements, but additions based only on generic entry-operator statements are vulnerable if the taxpayer can demonstrate the loan was actually received and repaid through formal banking channels without any cash component.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | PMLA Attachment Can Cover Property Held by Non-Accused Persons: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds PMLA attachment of family-held properties, holding that non-accused status does not prevent attachment of proceeds of crime.The post PMLA Attachment Can Cover Property Held by
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that attachment under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) is aimed at the **proceeds of crime**, not only at property standing in the name of a person formally accused in the FIR or ECIR. As a result, property may be attached even if it is held by a non-accused person such as a spouse, child, or other family member, so long as the authorities establish that the property represents proceeds of crime. In this case, the Tribunal upheld the provisional attachment of properties valued at **₹10,12,27,216 (about ₹10.12 crore)** that stood in the names of **Vikas Dubey, his wife, his son, and others**.

The facts involved **two FIRs** arising from the attack on a police team that had gone to arrest Vikas Dubey, in which **eight police personnel were killed**. The investigation alleged that Dubey was involved in multiple serious offences, including **organised crime, corruption, embezzlement of Public Distribution System funds, forcible takeover of businesses, and land-grabbing**. Based on the scheduled offences, the Enforcement Directorate registered an **ECIR** and conducted an independent PMLA investigation, leading to the attachment action.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that **title in the name of a non-accused does not by itself protect the asset from PMLA attachment**. The authorities can proceed against property if they believe it was acquired from illicit funds, even where the named holder was not included in the FIR/ECIR. In practical terms, entities dealing with asset tracing, freeze/attachment responses, KYC, beneficial ownership review, or transaction monitoring should assume that **family-held or nominee-held property may still be vulnerable to attachment** if linked to suspected criminal proceeds, and should be prepared to assess the source of funds and ownership trail accordingly.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kolkata ITAT Deletes ₹3 Lakh Additions Over Explained Cash and Credits

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that contemporaneous documentation and a clear audit trail for cash movements and account credits are critical to defending tax positions during scrutiny or appeal. The decision does not announce a new tax rate, deadline, or filing obligation; rather, it reflects an evidentiary standard in assessment proceedings and reinforces the need for robust recordkeeping and source verification for cash and credit transactions.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Surat Restricts Unaccounted Purchase Addition to Profit Under Section 44AD

For compliance purposes, the key implication is that where a taxpayer is assessed under presumptive taxation and an alleged unaccounted purchase is found, the tax exposure may be confined to the estimated profit embedded in that transaction rather than the gross amount, depending on the facts and the manner in which the income is characterized. The summary provided does not mention any new statutory amendment, filing deadline, rate change, or procedural deadline; it is a case-specific judicial interpretation affecting taxpayers and advisers handling additions for alleged unexplained purchases under Section 44AD and the possible application of Section 115BBE.
