rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal dismisses SBI’s appeal against benami attachment, holding mortgage priority cannot defeat confiscation; liberty granted under Section 27(2).The post SBI Mortgage Over Benami Property C
rows.summary:
The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal dismissed State Bank of India’s appeal involving a property attached as benami property, and held that SBI’s mortgage or secured-interest claim could not override the government’s confiscation/attachment action under the benami law framework. In practical terms, the tribunal found that even though SBI had a mortgage over the property, that interest did not defeat the confiscation process once the property was determined to be benami and subject to statutory action. The ruling therefore reinforces that lenders cannot assume their security interest will take priority over benami confiscation proceedings where the property falls within the scope of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) regime.

The summary also notes that the tribunal granted “liberty” under Section 27(2), indicating SBI may still have a procedural or remedial avenue under that provision, but not in a way that saves the mortgage from the confiscation outcome in this appeal. No tax rate, monetary threshold, filing deadline, or operational compliance timetable is stated in the provided text. For compliance teams at banks, NBFCs, or other secured creditors, the key takeaway is that lien/mortgage diligence must be more robust where title risk, benami risk, or ownership-concealment indicators exist, because a security interest may not protect the lender if the asset is later attached or confiscated as benami property.

rows.title: Income Tax | Rajasthan HC Quashes Section 148 Notice as Time-Barred and Issued by JAO
rows.desc: Rajasthan HC quashes AY 2017-18 reassessment notice as barred by limitation and invalid for being issued by JAO instead of FAO.The post Rajasthan HC Quashes Section 148 Notice as Time-Barred and Issue
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that the reassessment notice issued under Section 148 for Assessment Year 2017-18 was invalid on two independent grounds: it was issued after the applicable limitation period had expired, and it was issued by a jurisdictional assessing officer (JAO) rather than the faceless assessing officer (FAO) required under the post-Faceless Assessment regime. In practical terms, the court quashed the notice because the Revenue could not reopen the assessment once the statutory time limit had run, and because the notice was not issued by the proper designated authority under the applicable reassessment procedure.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that reassessment notices must be checked both for timeliness and for procedural authority. Where a notice under Section 148 is received for an older assessment year, the recipient should verify whether it has been issued within the legally permitted limitation period and whether it has been issued through the correct reassessment channel and officer as mandated by the faceless reassessment framework. If either requirement is not met, the notice is vulnerable to challenge as void or unenforceable.

rows.title: Income Tax | PMLA Attachment Upheld as SAFEMA Tribunal Rejects RUD Non-Supply Plea
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal dismisses Rajeev Nayan Mishra’s appeal, holding that RUDs were served in custody and the natural justice plea was unsupported.The post PMLA Attachment Upheld as SAFEMA Tribunal Rejects
rows.summary: The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal dismissed an appeal by Rajeev Nayan Mishra and upheld a PMLA attachment, finding that the challenge based on non-supply of relied-upon documents (RUDs) was not supported. The tribunal accepted the enforcement authorities’ position that the RUDs had already been served while the appellant was in custody, so the natural justice objection failed. In practical compliance terms, the ruling reinforces that a procedural defense alleging non-disclosure of documents will not succeed where the record shows the documents were in fact provided, even if the recipient was detained at the time. The decision therefore confirms the continuing validity of the attachment and underscores the importance, in PMLA matters, of maintaining clear evidence of service of investigative material and other relied-upon records.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Quashes Assessment for Invalid Section 148 Notice Issued by Non-Jurisdictional ITO
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashes reassessment after finding that the ITO lacked pecuniary jurisdiction to issue the section 148 notice.The post ITAT Delhi Quashes Assessment for Invalid Section 148 Notice Issued by
rows.summary:
The document reports a Delhi ITAT ruling that invalidated a reassessment because the notice under section 148 of the Income-tax Act was issued by an Income Tax Officer (ITO) who did not have pecuniary jurisdiction over the assessee. In other words, the tribunal held that the reassessment proceedings were legally defective from the start because the officer who initiated them was not the proper jurisdictional authority. As a result, the reassessment assessment was quashed in full.

For a compliance team, the key point is procedural: reassessment notices must be issued by the officer having valid territorial/pecuniary jurisdiction, and failure to do so can render the entire proceeding unenforceable. The document does not state any new tax rate, threshold, deadline, or substantive change to tax liability; it is a litigation outcome emphasizing that companies should verify the issuing authority’s jurisdiction when receiving a section 148 notice, because an invalidly issued notice may be challengeable and may invalidate the reassessment.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Surat Quashes Section 153C Assessments Over Delayed Satisfaction Note
rows.desc: ITAT Surat quashes four Section 153C assessments after finding the satisfaction note was recorded about 17 months after the searched person's assessment.The post ITAT Surat Quashes Section 153C Assess
rows.summary: The document reports that the ITAT Surat has quashed four income-tax assessments made under Section 153C because the mandatory “satisfaction note” was recorded too late—approximately 17 months after the assessment of the person searched had already been completed. For compliance purposes, the key point is that Section 153C proceedings depend on a timely recorded satisfaction that documents the Assessing Officer’s basis for proceeding against a third party in relation to seized material; if that satisfaction is not recorded within the legally relevant timeline, the assessment can be invalidated. The ruling affects cases where tax authorities seek to assess a person other than the one searched, especially where seized documents or assets are alleged to belong to or pertain to that other person. It underscores that timing and documentation are not procedural formalities but jurisdictional requirements: a delayed satisfaction note can defeat the entire Section 153C assessment. No new tax rate, threshold, or monetary limit is introduced here; the practical compliance takeaway is that taxpayers facing third-party search assessments should verify whether the satisfaction note was properly recorded and whether the Department met the required sequence and timing before issuing Section 153C notices or completing assessments.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Confirms Deletion of ₹2.99 Crore Addition Adopted From Section 143(1) Intimation
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai held that the Section 143(1) adjustment merged with the Section 143(3) assessment and upheld deletion of ₹2.99 crore addition.The post ITAT Mumbai Confirms Deletion of ₹2.99 Crore Addition
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Mumbai ruling involving an income-tax adjustment of ₹2.99 crore that had been added based on a Section 143(1) intimation. The Tribunal held that once a regular assessment is completed under Section 143(3), the earlier Section 143(1) adjustment effectively merges into that assessment, so the addition could not be independently sustained on the basis of the intimation alone. As a result, the ITAT upheld deletion of the ₹2.99 crore addition.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a preliminary processing adjustment under Section 143(1) does not necessarily remain separately enforceable if the return is later taken up for scrutiny and assessed under Section 143(3). The ruling matters for taxpayers facing add-backs or demand notices arising from automatic processing differences, because the final scrutiny assessment can supersede the earlier intimation-based adjustment. No new filing deadline, procedural change, rate, or threshold is stated in the document; the key point is the legal treatment of the ₹2.99 crore adjustment and the confirmation that it was deleted in this case.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Deletes TDS Demand Treating Outright Trademark Purchase as Royalty
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai deleted the TDS demand after holding the trademark assignment payment was not royalty and the assessee was not liable to deduct tax.The post ITAT Mumbai Deletes TDS Demand Treating Outrigh
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Mumbai ruling that deleted a TDS demand arising from an assessee’s payment for an outright purchase/assignment of a trademark. The tribunal held that the payment was **not “royalty”** for income-tax purposes, and therefore the buyer/assessee was **not required to deduct tax at source** on that consideration. In practical compliance terms, this means that where a transaction is structured as an actual transfer of ownership in a trademark rather than a license or right-to-use arrangement, the payment may fall outside the royalty TDS withholding regime.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the tax treatment depends on the **legal substance of the intellectual property transaction**: a full assignment of the trademark was treated differently from a royalty-bearing use arrangement. The ruling removes the specific TDS exposure in this case, but it does not create a blanket exemption for all trademark-related payments; each contract should be reviewed to determine whether it is a true purchase/assignment versus a license, and whether withholding obligations may still arise under the facts and applicable law.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Quashes Section 263 Revision Over Invalid Section 151 Sanction
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai held reassessment void for sanction under section 151(ii) by the wrong authority and quashed the section 263 revision order.The post ITAT Mumbai Quashes Section 263 Revision Over Invalid S
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Mumbai ruling with important procedural consequences for income-tax reassessment and subsequent revision proceedings. The tribunal held that the reassessment was invalid because the required sanction under section 151 was obtained from the wrong authority under section 151(ii), meaning the reopening itself was procedurally defective and could not stand. As a result, the ITAT quashed the section 263 revision order that had been passed in relation to that reassessment, because a revision order cannot be sustained where the underlying reassessment is void for lack of valid statutory approval.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that reassessment actions must strictly follow the sanction hierarchy prescribed in section 151, and obtaining approval from an incorrect authority can render the entire reassessment vulnerable to challenge. The ruling reinforces that taxpayers and tax teams should verify not only whether a reopening notice or reassessment has been issued, but also whether the officer who granted sanction had the proper statutory jurisdiction for the relevant case category. No numeric tax rate, filing deadline, or monetary threshold is discussed in the excerpt; the material issue is the legality of the approval process and the resulting invalidity of both the reassessment and the connected section 263 revision.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Huge Receipts Without Gold Sales Justify Jewellery Seizure Under PMLA: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds retention of gold jewellery linked prima facie to unexplained high-value transactions under PMLA.The post Huge Receipts Without Gold Sales Justify Jewellery Seizure Under PMLA:
rows.summary:
The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal upheld the retention/seizure of gold jewellery under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) where the items were linked prima facie to unexplained, high-value financial receipts. The key compliance takeaway is that authorities considered the absence of corresponding gold sales or other satisfactory source documentation for the large receipts as sufficient to justify continued retention of the jewellery as suspected proceeds of crime or property connected to money laundering.  

For a corporate compliance team, this underscores that unexplained high-value inflows can trigger asset seizure/retention exposure even where the underlying asset is jewellery rather than cash, and that a credible paper trail tying receipts to legitimate business activity or lawful asset disposal is critical. The decision appears to reinforce the enforcement approach that documentary mismatch—large receipts without supporting evidence of gold sales or other lawful consideration—can create a prima facie PMLA risk sufficient for interim action by authorities.  

No specific monetary threshold, effective date, or procedural deadline is provided in the text excerpt, and the note appears to be a case-based legal development rather than a new rule or regulation.

rows.title: Income Tax | Cash Balance Increase Alone Cannot Justify Income Addition: ITAT Indore
rows.desc: ITAT Indore deletes Rs.37.02 lakh addition based merely on difference between opening and closing cash balances in audited books.The post Cash Balance Increase Alone Cannot Justify Income Addition: IT
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Indore ruling that **a mere increase in cash balance, by itself, cannot be used to make an income addition**. In the case discussed, the tax authorities had made an **addition of Rs. 37.02 lakh** solely because the **closing cash balance in the audited books was higher than the opening cash balance**, but the tribunal deleted that addition.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **booked cash movement alone is not enough to establish unaccounted income** unless the tax authority can point to a proper basis for treating the increase as taxable receipts or unexplained money. The ruling indicates that **audited financial records should not be disallowed or income added merely because the cash balance has risen across the year**, without evidence of suppression of income, bogus entries, or some other specific tax discrepancy.

This affects taxpayers and finance teams where **cash balances change during the year in audited accounts**: if questioned by tax authorities, the position supported by this decision is that the increase must be evaluated in context rather than assumed to be income. There are **no new filing deadlines, rate changes, or procedural deadlines** in the text provided; it is a **case-law clarification** on the evidentiary standard required before an income addition can be sustained.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Nagpur Quashes Section 271(1)(c) Penalty for Limitation Delay
rows.desc: ITAT Nagpur quashed ₹4.62 lakh penalty under Section 271(1)(c) as barred by Section 275(1)(c) limitation.The post ITAT Nagpur Quashes Section 271(1)(c) Penalty for Limitation Delay appeared first on T
rows.summary:
The document concerns a penalty dispute under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act for Ganpati Industrial Spares Pvt. Ltd. for AY 2013-14, where the Assessing Officer alleged concealment of income of ₹14 lakh and imposed a penalty of ₹4,62,000. The assessment was completed under Section 143(3) read with Section 263 on 19 September 2024, and the assessment order specifically initiated penalty proceedings in that order; a later communication letter dated 1 October 2024 was not treated as the relevant date for limitation purposes. The key compliance/legal holding is that, under Section 275(1)(c), the limitation period for passing the penalty order runs from the date penalty is initiated in the assessment order, not from the date the order is communicated to the assessee.

Applying that rule, the Tribunal held that the penalty order had to be passed on or before 31 March 2025, but it was actually passed on 17 April 2025, i.e. 17 days late. Because the order was beyond the statutory time limit, the ITAT Nagpur quashed the penalty as barred by limitation, without needing to decide the merits of the concealment allegation in detail. The CIT(A)/NFAC had earlier confirmed the penalty, but the Tribunal overturned that outcome. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that in penalty matters under Section 271(1)(c), the date of initiation recorded in the assessment order is decisive for limitation tracking, and any penalty order issued after the Section 275 deadline is vulnerable to being annulled.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | SAFEMA Tribunal Upholds ₹622.62 Crore PMLA Attachment Despite Mining Compensation
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upheld attachment of ₹622.62 crore, holding mining compensation did not extinguish PMLA proceeds-of-crime proceedings.The post SAFEMA Tribunal Upholds ₹622.62 Crore PMLA Attachment Des
rows.summary:
The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal has upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s attachment of ₹622.62 crore under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), even though the underlying matter involved payment of mining compensation. The key compliance takeaway is that the Tribunal found that payment of compensation in the mining context does not, by itself, eliminate or “wipe out” the basis for treating funds as proceeds of crime for PMLA purposes, so attachment and related money-laundering proceedings can continue despite such compensation having been made.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical implication is that companies cannot assume that settling a mining-related liability, paying compensation, or otherwise regularizing a regulatory breach will automatically resolve exposure to PMLA attachment or money-laundering scrutiny. The order reinforces that authorities may still pursue attachment of property/value linked to alleged criminal proceeds, and that the existence of compensation payments does not necessarily defeat the legal characterization of tainted funds. The document does not provide any new compliance deadline, reporting date, or procedural filing requirement, but it does signal continued enforcement risk in mining and other regulated sectors where alleged illegal gains may be traced and attached under PMLA.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Company Liquidation Does Not End Director’s Liability for Unrealised Export Proceeds: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds director’s FERA liability for unrealised export proceeds but reduces ₹3 crore penalty to ₹30 lakh.The post Company Liquidation Does Not End Director’s Liability for Unrealised
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA held that a director’s liability for non-realisation of export proceeds under the former Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA) survives even if the company is later liquidated and its records are handed over to the Official Liquidator. In this matter, RBI had informed the Enforcement Directorate that M/s Unicorp Industries Ltd. was caution-listed for failing to realise substantial export proceeds from the 1990–1998 period; bank information indicated unrealised export proceeds of about ₹26.36 crore and USD 9,80,000. The company and its directors were alleged to have failed to realise and repatriate the export proceeds within the prescribed period and to have failed to obtain RBI permission for the delay/non-realisation, leading to directives being issued under Section 33(2) of FERA to the company, its directors, and the concerned banks.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that a person who was a director and in charge of the company when the exports were made and when the export-realisation period expired cannot escape liability merely because the company was later wound up. The Tribunal accepted that liquidation does not erase responsibility for past FERA contraventions tied to the period when the obligation arose. At the same time, it took into account the age of the proceedings, the liquidation status, and other surrounding facts to substantially reduce the penalty: the original penalty of ₹3 crore was reduced to ₹30 lakh, which had already been deposited by the appellant, Shri Arun Sogani. This means the monetary exposure can be moderated on appeal, but the underlying contravention finding and personal liability of the responsible director remained upheld.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Delhi HC Initiates Contempt Against Tihar Superintendent for Frustrating Parole Order
rows.desc: Delhi HC initiates contempt proceedings against Tihar Jail Superintendent for frustrating an order directing release of undertrial Anwar Hussain on parole.The post Delhi HC Initiates Contempt Against
rows.summary:
The document reports a Delhi High Court contempt action against the Superintendent of Tihar Jail for allegedly frustrating a court order that directed the release of undertrial prisoner Anwar Hussain on parole. The key compliance point is that the court had already issued a release direction, and the jail administration’s conduct is described as obstructing or failing to implement that judicial order. No detailed procedural deadlines, parole conditions, monetary penalties, or broader regulatory changes are provided in the text.  

For a compliance team, the substantive takeaway is limited but important: prison or custodial authorities must timely and faithfully execute court-ordered releases, including parole orders for undertrials, and failure to do so can expose officials and the institution to contempt proceedings. The document does not specify the underlying offense, the length or terms of parole, or any broader change in law or policy beyond this enforcement action.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | SAFEMA Tribunal Releases Power Plant for Bona Fide Buyer, Secures ₹6.95 Crore Sale Proceeds
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal releases a PMLA-attached power plant bought through court-supervised proceedings and permits ED to secure ₹6.95 crore sale proceeds.The post SAFEMA Tribunal Releases Power Plant for Bo
rows.summary: The document reports that the SAFEMA Tribunal has released a power plant that had previously been attached under the PMLA, on the basis that it was acquired by a bona fide buyer through court-supervised proceedings rather than through any tainted transaction. The key compliance point is that the Enforcement Directorate (ED) is allowed to retain and secure the ₹6.95 crore sale proceeds from that transaction, even though the underlying asset itself is released. In practical terms, the tribunal’s action distinguishes between the legitimacy of the buyer’s acquisition of the power plant and the government’s continuing interest in preserving the sale proceeds linked to the attached property. No new filing deadline, reporting cycle, rate, threshold beyond the ₹6.95 crore amount, or broader rule change is stated in the document; the notice is a case-specific enforcement outcome affecting the parties to this transaction and illustrating how attached assets and sale proceeds may be treated differently under PMLA/SAFEMA proceedings.

rows.title: Income Tax | Digital Devices Not Relied Upon in PMLA Complaint Cannot Be Retained Indefinitely: SAFEMA
rows.desc: PMLA Tribunal directs ED to release seized hard disk and mobile phone within 30 days after ED admits devices were not relied upon.The post Digital Devices Not Relied Upon in PMLA Complaint Cannot Be R
rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal held that digital devices seized in a PMLA investigation cannot be kept indefinitely when the Enforcement Directorate has not relied on them in the prosecution complaint and the owner has not been named as an accused. In this case, the ED had seized a hard disk, a mobile phone, and a locker belonging to Dr. Pradeep Makkar; the locker was later released, but the hard disk and phone remained in ED custody. At the hearing, the ED’s counsel stated that the hard disk and mobile phone were **not relied upon** in the prosecution complaint and that Dr. Makkar was **not arrayed as an accused**, which meant the ED could not show any continuing evidentiary or prosecutorial basis to retain the items.

On that basis, the Tribunal interfered with the impugned order only to the extent it affected the appellant and directed the ED to **release the seized hard disk and mobile phone within 30 days**. The practical compliance takeaway is that, in PMLA matters, retention of seized digital media must be justified by an actual ongoing investigative or evidentiary need; if the device is not relied upon in the complaint and the owner is not an accused, continued seizure may be challengeable and release may be ordered. No monetary threshold, filing deadline, or reporting requirement is discussed in the document beyond the 30-day release direction.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | SAFEMA Tribunal Condones Delay in Review of Orders Based on Recalled Ganpati Dealcom Judgment
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal condones delay in review applications after Supreme Court recalled Ganpati Dealcom, restoring connected appeals for fresh consideration.The post SAFEMA Tribunal Condones Delay in Revie
rows.summary: The document reports a procedural development before the SAFEMA Tribunal rather than a new substantive compliance rule: after the Supreme Court recalled its earlier judgment in the Ganpati Dealcom matter, the Tribunal accepted review applications filed out of time and condoned the delay, thereby allowing the related orders and appeals to be reconsidered afresh. In practical terms, this means that matters previously influenced by the now-recalled Ganpati Dealcom decision are not necessarily final and may be reopened or reexamined in the pending review/appeal process. No new filing deadline, monetary threshold, penalty rate, or compliance timeline is stated in the document itself. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is to identify any pending or concluded SAFEMA/FEMA matters that relied on the recalled Ganpati Dealcom ruling, because those cases may now face renewed judicial scrutiny and should be monitored for further orders.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Mere NDPS Accusation Cannot Justify Freezing Explained Assets: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal allowed release of an ancestral house and Tata Nexon after LIC, agricultural, business income and vehicle finance explained their sources.The post Mere NDPS Accusation Cannot Justify F
rows.summary:
The document summarizes a SAFEMA Tribunal decision in **Sonu & Another vs. Competent Authority (Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA, New Delhi)** concerning freezing action taken over property linked to an NDPS case. Police in Himachal Pradesh allegedly recovered **157 grams of Chitta/Heroin** from **Pradeep Kumar, Mohit, and Sonu on 02.04.2025**, leading to **FIR No. 0076/2025** under **Sections 21 and 29 of the NDPS Act**. Following that, the **Freezing Authority issued an order under Section 68F(1)** and the **Competent Authority confirmed it**, but the appellants challenged only two assets: an **ancestral residential house** and a **Tata Nexon car**.

For the **house**, the Tribunal accepted the claim that it was **ancestral** and noted the valuer’s finding that the construction was roughly **10–12 years old**. It found that the only recent spending shown was a **renovation expense of ₹2.68 lakh**, which the appellants explained through **LIC receipts of ₹3 lakh and ₹1,03,800 received by Pushpa**, followed by a **withdrawal of ₹4 lakh**. Because that explanation was supported by documents, the Tribunal treated the house as having a legitimate source and did not sustain freezing on that asset.

For the **Tata Nexon**, the Tribunal looked at the **actual vehicle cost of ₹8,73,032, including insurance**, and contrasted that with the higher value used by the SHO. The tribunal noted that the financing and ownership documents explained the purchase, so the car was also treated as legitimately acquired. The key compliance takeaway is that the Tribunal did **not** uphold freezing merely because the individuals were accused in an NDPS case; it required a demonstrated link between the asset and illegally acquired wealth, and where the owners could document **lawful inheritance/family ownership, renovation funding, and loan/other legitimate purchase sources**, the assets were released.

rows.title: Income Tax | Mere Work from Home in Meghalaya Does Not Exempt Salary: ITAT Guwahati
rows.desc: ITAT Guwahati denies Section 10(26) exemption as residence and work-from-home in Shillong did not prove salary arose from a specified-area source.The post Mere Work from Home in Meghalaya Does Not Exe
rows.summary:
The document reports a Guwahati ITAT ruling in **Aphidalin Syiemlieh v. ITO, Ward-1, Shillong (ITA No. 359/GTY/2026, AY 2024-25, order dated 11 September 2026)** holding that **working from home in Meghalaya, by itself, does not make salary income exempt under Section 10(26)**. The assessee, an employee of **Dell Technologies**, had filed a return showing only **₹11,450** of “Income from Other Sources” after claiming her salary as exempt under Section 10(26); the case was selected for scrutiny because of a **“large exemption claimed from Schedule Salary in the new tax regime.”**  

The Assessing Officer examined whether the statutory conditions for Section 10(26) were met and **disallowed the exemption**, making an **addition of ₹15,41,264** for salary income that had been claimed exempt; the **NFAC** later **confirmed** that assessment. The ITAT agreed with the lower authorities’ approach that the exemption cannot be claimed merely because the employee is physically working from a notified tribal area or from home there. Instead, the assessee must produce **cogent evidence** showing that the salary income **actually accrued or arose from a source situated within the specified area**, which is the key compliance requirement emphasized by the ruling.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that employees’ remote work location alone is not enough to support a Section 10(26) exemption claim. Employers and payroll/tax functions should ensure that any such exemption is supported by documentation proving the income source and statutory nexus to the notified area, because unsupported claims may be disallowed on scrutiny and lead to tax additions like the one sustained here.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Bangalore Deletes Section 68 Addition for Duplicate ITR Disclosure
rows.desc: ITAT Bangalore deletes Section 68 addition where partnership profit was mistakenly reported twice in Schedule EI without any double credit in the books.The post ITAT Bangalore Deletes Section 68 Addit
rows.summary:
This appeal concerns a section 68 addition made in the scrutiny assessment of a partnership firm, M/s Glass Tech India, for assessment year 2014-15. The firm had shown capital introduced by its two partners of Rs. 2 crore each, and the Assessing Officer treated the aggregate Rs. 4 crore as unexplained because the assessee’s explanation was that the amounts were only routed through cheques temporarily, never really intended as permanent capital, and were returned within two days to improve the firm’s bank ratio for credit facilities. The AO rejected that explanation, stating there is no recognized concept of “temporary” capital introduction of this kind, and made an addition under section 68.  

On appeal, the CIT(A) deleted the addition, and the Revenue challenged that deletion before the ITAT Delhi. The Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s relief and dismissed the Revenue’s appeal, effectively holding that the section 68 addition could not survive on these facts. The material compliance point from this order is that where capital receipts are reflected in the books and the surrounding evidence shows the funds were routed back quickly and were part of a disclosed banking arrangement rather than an undisclosed income inflow, the Tribunal did not sustain the unexplained cash credit addition against the partnership firm.  

There are no forward-looking regulatory deadlines or filing changes in the text, but the order is important for tax-compliance review because it addresses documentation and substantiation of partner capital movements during scrutiny. Entities with partner contributions or similar capital introductions should be prepared to explain the source and actual movement of funds, especially if amounts are reversed shortly after deposit and are used for bank-limit or ratio purposes.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 54EC ₹50 Lakh Limit Applied Per Financial Year: ITAT Bangalore
rows.desc: ITAT Bangalore holds pre-AY 2015-16 Section 54EC limit applied per financial year and allows ₹71 lakh invested within six months.The post Section 54EC ₹50 Lakh Limit Applied Per Financial Year: ITAT B
rows.summary:
This ITAT Bangalore ruling concerns the scope of the Section 54EC capital gains exemption limit before the law was tightened by later amendment. For Assessment Year 2013-14, the assessee sold a residential property and reported long-term capital gains of ₹70,90,317, then invested the gains in NHAI bonds in two separate tranches: ₹50 lakh in March 2013 and ₹21 lakh in July 2013, with allotment letters dated 31 March 2013 and 31 July 2013 and the bonds later credited to demat. Because the two investments fell in different financial years—FY 2012-13 and FY 2013-14—but both were made within the six-month statutory window, the Tribunal held that, for periods before insertion of the second proviso to Section 54EC(1) (effective from AY 2015-16), the ₹50 lakh cap applied separately to each financial year rather than as an overall cap for the six-month investment window.

As a result, the Tribunal allowed exemption for the full ₹71 lakh invested, even though that amount exceeded ₹50 lakh in aggregate. The compliance takeaway is that this decision is relevant only for pre-AY 2015-16 fact patterns involving Section 54EC investments straddling two financial years within six months of transfer; for those cases, the exemption claim could lawfully exceed ₹50 lakh if the investments were split across two different financial years. For later periods, the ruling is limited by the statutory amendment introducing the second proviso to Section 54EC(1), so the post-amendment position must be tested against the updated cap rules rather than this older interpretation.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Penny-Stock LTCG Cannot Disguise Bribe Money; PMLA Attachment Upheld: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds PMLA attachment of assets linked to alleged bribe proceeds routed through inflated share transactions.The post Penny-Stock LTCG Cannot Disguise Bribe Money; PMLA Attachment Uph
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s attachment of assets in a case alleging that cash bribes taken from medical students and their parents were laundered by converting them into purportedly tax-exempt long-term capital gains through stock transactions. The Tribunal accepted the ED’s theory that funds collected in cash were moved through cheque discounters, intermediaries, and multiple bank accounts, then routed to “dummy” purchasers who used those funds to buy shares of non-functional or inactive companies from the appellant and his family at artificially inflated prices; the later sale proceeds were then presented as legitimate LTCG. In substance, the ruling confirms that where share prices rise extraordinarily without any underlying business activity, and where the supposed buyers appear to be funded by third parties rather than acting independently, the authorities may treat the transaction chain as a facade for laundering illicit cash.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal found sufficient prima facie material to keep the attachment in place pending completion of both the scheduled-offence trial and the money-laundering proceedings, rather than accepting the gains as bona fide investment returns. The decision is relevant to institutions and individuals involved in admissions, educational trusts, share transfers, stock-based capital gains claims, or transactions showing unusual price appreciation in thinly traded or inactive companies, especially where funds originate from layered third-party transfers or “accommodation” arrangements. The document does not specify the exact appeal number or judgment date, but it indicates that the attachment under PMLA/SAFEMA remained valid because the alleged laundering structure was supported by the surrounding evidence and had not yet been disproved in the pending trials.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Telangana HC Permits GST Appeal Against Section 74 Common Adjudication Order
rows.desc: Telangana High Court grants two weeks to file appeal against Section 74 GST order with statutory pre-deposit and delay condonation application.The post Telangana HC Permits GST Appeal Against Section

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has directed the removal of Maharashtra Cooperation Minister Babasaheb Patil and seven other directors from the Latur District Central Cooperative Bank because they had exceeded the statutory maximum tenure of 10 years. The action was issued by RBI Assistant General Manager Kapil Goswami on Friday and was triggered after the Aurangabad bench of the Bombay High Court acted on a petition filed by bank member Satish Sheshrao Jadhav. The compliance issue is that directors of District Central Cooperative Banks and Central Cooperative Banks are subject to a hard 10-year tenure cap under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, as amended by the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025.

For compliance purposes, the affected entity is the Latur DCC Bank, and the affected individuals are the eight directors named in the RBI order, including Patil, who is identified as belonging to the Nationalist Congress Party led by Deputy Chief Minister Sunetra Pawar. The document does not describe any new reporting form, filing deadline, or remediation process beyond the immediate removal order, but it makes clear that any DCCB/central cooperative bank director exceeding 10 years of tenure is non-compliant and must be removed in line with RBI directions and the statutory amendment.

rows.summary:
The document says that a new merchant discount rate (MDR) on certain UPI payments could create a limited opening for India’s digital rupee (e-rupee), but it does not by itself make CBDC payments cheaper than UPI. Starting **October 15, 2026**, a **0.4% MDR** will apply only to **specified person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000**, with the charge **capped at Rs 300** for payments of **Rs 75,000 and above**. The article states that **about 96% of P2M transactions will remain unaffected**, and **consumers will not pay the MDR**; instead, the fee will be **shared among payment ecosystem participants**, not collected by the government.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that this pricing change may prompt merchants and payment providers to reassess alternative digital payment rails, including CBDC, but the document stresses that **digital rupee payments routed through interoperable UPI QR codes still incur existing NPCI switching fees**. In other words, e-rupee transactions using UPI infrastructure are **not automatically cheaper** than regular UPI transactions simply because MDR has been introduced on some UPI payments.

The article also says the e-rupee’s stronger commercial opportunity lies less in general retail payments and more in **programmable government payments**, especially **digital rupee-based food subsidy direct benefit transfers (DBT)** that are already being deployed in **select regions**. It notes that **more than 95% of person-to-merchant UPI transactions are below Rs 2,000**, which limits how much the MDR change alone can shift payment behavior toward CBDC. The overall compliance takeaway is that the MDR change affects only a narrow subset of UPI merchant payments, while CBDC adoption will depend more on the rollout of **programmable subsidy and other targeted use cases** than on any broad cost advantage over UPI.

rows.summary:
This document is an SBI Research article discussing the financial impact of mobilising foreign currency non-resident bank deposits (FCNR(B)) and is not a new legal rule, but it contains quantitative assumptions and estimates that banks and treasury/compliance teams may use in planning. It says that **$127 billion** raised through the FCNR(B) scheme could support about **Rs 25 lakh crore** of additional bank credit, assuming a **2.5 credit multiplier** and an **effective lending yield of 7.5%**. On that basis, banks would generate about **Rs 1.8 lakh crore** in annual notional yield from the extra lending, while paying roughly **Rs 75,000 crore per year** in interest on the FCNR(B) deposits, producing an estimated **net annual benefit of around Rs 1 lakh crore** and approximately **Rs 5 lakh crore over five years**.

It estimates **around $15 billion** of cumulative hedging costs using a **3% annual hedging cost** across the **one-year, three-year, and five-year maturity buckets**. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that the article frames FCNR(B)-driven funding as a potentially large balance-sheet and profitability support tool, but the headline profit figure depends heavily on assumptions about deposit mobilization, credit expansion, lending yield, interest expense, and hedging-cost treatment rather than on any mandated operational change.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India absorbed **Rs 2,22,629 crore** of liquidity in a **three-day variable rate reverse repo (VRRR)** auction, against a **notified amount of Rs 2.25 lakh crore**, at a **weighted average rate of 5.24%**. This was done against a banking system that still had an estimated **liquidity surplus of Rs 6.94 lakh crore as of September 17**, so the operation is part of a broader effort to drain excess cash from the system rather than an emergency liquidity measure. For compliance and treasury teams, the document’s main point is that this kind of continued liquidity withdrawal may gradually increase competition for deposits and wholesale funding, which could raise banks’ marginal funding costs over time and put pressure on net interest margins if the surplus liquidity continues to be taken out of the system.

The article says the immediate impact on margins is expected to be limited because **FCNR(B) inflows** have recently reduced banks’ dependence on wholesale funding, and **August certificate of deposit (CD) issuance fell to Rs 68,130 crore**. It also notes that **private banks’ fresh lending spreads widened by 22 basis points to 3.13% in July**, reflecting improved funding conditions, but warns that this improvement could reverse if liquidity withdrawal persists. The operational question for banks is how quickly they can deploy excess liquidity into lending and whether credit growth can absorb any increase in marginal funding costs.

A further liquidity-draining step is already scheduled: the RBI plans **Rs 50,000 crore of open market operation (OMO) sales** through **two auctions on September 21 and September 28**. For institutions affected by RBI liquidity operations, the practical compliance implication is to monitor short-term funding strategy, deposit pricing, wholesale borrowing plans, and margin sensitivity closely, because the direction of RBI operations suggests a sustained move toward tighter system liquidity.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has **not yet finalized** its proposed restrictions on revolving credit for NBFCs and is still reviewing the issue after receiving extensive stakeholder feedback. Deputy Governor S. C. Murmu said the RBI is assessing the risks of allowing revolving credit **both at the level of individual NBFCs and at the systemic level** before deciding whether the restriction will stand and, if so, in what final form it will be implemented. He indicated that the RBI may also hold further discussions with market participants to better understand the feedback, so firms should treat this as an **open regulatory question rather than a concluded rulemaking**.

The underlying proposal came from the RBI’s **August 6 draft amendments** to its NBFC credit facility directions, which would **restrict NBFCs to term loans** and **bar them from offering revolving credit products**. The document explains that a **term loan** is a fixed principal amount with a predetermined repayment schedule, while a **revolving facility** is a credit line that can be repeatedly drawn and repaid, renewing availability as balances are repaid. No final implementation date is stated in the article because the RBI has **not yet taken a final decision**.

For compliance teams at NBFCs and other affected lenders, the practical takeaway is that the proposed rule could materially change permitted product structures if adopted, especially for products currently offered on a revolving basis. Firms should monitor the RBI’s final decision closely, review any existing or planned revolving-credit offerings for potential exposure, and be prepared for the possibility that these products may need to be modified or discontinued depending on the final direction issued.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has expanded an existing KYC documentation option that was previously available to NRIs and PIOs so that it now also applies to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs). Under this revised facility, banks may accept an **original certified copy** of a customer’s KYC document instead of following only the usual process of comparing a copy against the original and recording the comparison on the copy.

For FPIs, the certified copy may now be authenticated by specific overseas authorities, including **authorized officials of overseas branches of Scheduled Commercial Banks registered in India**, **branches of overseas banks that have relationships with Indian banks**, **notaries public abroad**, **court magistrates**, **judges**, or an **Indian Embassy or Consulate General** in the country where the non-resident customer resides. RBI states that the existing KYC instructions were reviewed and the facility was extended to FPIs as part of that review.

The amendment applies across RBI’s KYC directions for **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, rural co-operative banks, and urban co-operative banks**. No separate effective date or deadline is stated in the text, but the change is presented as an immediate amendment to the applicable KYC framework. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to update onboarding and KYC verification procedures so that FPIs can use this overseas certification route, and to ensure staff understand which certifying authorities are acceptable under the revised RBI directions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) ordered the removal of Maharashtra Cooperation Minister Babasaheb Patil and seven other directors from the Latur District Central Cooperative Bank because they had served beyond the permitted 10-year tenure limit for directors of District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs/Central Cooperative Banks). The action was taken after a direction from the Aurangabad bench of the Bombay High Court, which acted on a petition filed by bank member Satish Sheshrao Jadhav. RBI Assistant General Manager Kapil Goswami issued the order on Friday.

For compliance purposes, the key rule is that directors of DCCBs/Central Cooperative Banks are subject to a maximum tenure of 10 years under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, as amended by the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025. The document does not provide a different numerical threshold or phase-in period beyond the 10-year cap, but the affected directors appear to have exceeded that limit, which triggered their removal.

The article says seven directors resigned after the RBI sought their responses to the complaint, indicating that the central bank had already initiated a response process before issuing the removal order. Patil said he would not challenge the RBI’s order, but he questioned whether the 10-year rule—he said came into force in 2021—could be applied retrospectively to appointments made before that year. That issue is material for governance reviews because it raises potential questions about how the tenure cap is being applied to pre-2021 appointments.

The affected entity is Latur District Central Cooperative Bank in Maharashtra, and the compliance lesson is that cooperative bank boards must monitor director tenure closely against the statutory cap and be prepared for regulatory action, including forced removal, if directors continue beyond the permitted period. The sequence in the document also shows that complaints may be escalated through a member petition, court direction, and RBI enforcement, so banks should ensure board composition records and tenure calculations are accurate and defensible.

"The next strike will be on 28, 29 and 30 September, three continuous days," AIBEA said. Advt "If it is still not solved, then from October 26 it will be a continuous indefinite strike."Also Read: FCNR(B) scheme could yield Rs 5.5 trillion notional profit for banks, RBI: SBI ResearchThe Centre has set up a crisis management group to deal with the proposed nationwide strikes by staff of public sector banks. rows.summary:
The document reports that Financial Services Secretary Sanjay Lohia has convened a meeting on Monday with the heads of public sector banks, regional rural banks (RRBs), and NABARD to make sure banking operations and essential customer services continue without interruption during a proposed employee-union strike. The immediate labor action is a three-day strike scheduled for September 28, 29, and 30, 2026, and the All India Bank Employees’ Association (AIBEA) has warned that if its demand for a five-day banking week is not resolved, it will begin an indefinite strike from October 26, 2026.

From a compliance/operations perspective, the government has already formed a crisis management group to handle strikes lasting three days or more, and that group is working with banks to strengthen standard operating procedures (SOPs) for business continuity. The affected institutions are public sector banks, RRBs, and NABARD, with the focus on maintaining uninterrupted banking services and essential customer-facing functions during the strike period. No rule change has yet been announced in the article, but the practical requirement is that these institutions should be prepared to activate and test continuity arrangements, staffing contingencies, and service-maintenance protocols ahead of the September 28 strike and the possible October 26 escalation.

rows.summary:
This article is not a new law or regulator-issued rule; it describes an operational shift in India’s gig economy where platforms are helping workers file income-tax returns so they can claim TDS refunds. The key development is that gig platforms, including Zomato and Swiggy, are integrating tax-filing assistance directly into their apps for delivery partners and other gig workers whose earnings have already been subject to tax deducted at source, and many of those workers are reportedly receiving refunds after filing.

From a compliance perspective, the practical obligation is not a new statutory requirement stated in the article, but an increasing expectation that gig workers who have had TDS withheld will file returns to reconcile withholding and recover excess tax. The article emphasizes that these filings are being facilitated at scale by the platforms, suggesting the platforms are acting as intermediaries in helping workers complete their tax compliance and refund claims.

A second material point is the financial-recordkeeping benefit: the tax filings create formal income documentation that workers can use for credit applications and other financial services. In other words, the compliance activity has a broader underwriting/financial-inclusion effect because it turns otherwise informal earnings into documented income history.

No specific effective date, deadline, threshold, rate, or filing window is mentioned in the article, and there is no indication of a change in tax law or a prescribed compliance timeline. The main takeaway for a corporate compliance team is that gig-work platforms are building tax-compliance support into their worker experience, which may increase filing volumes, strengthen audit trails for worker income and withholding, and create expectations around accurate TDS reporting, refund assistance, and documentation support.

rows.summary:
This article is a market update, not a regulatory notice, and it does not impose any new legal, compliance, filing, reporting, or operational requirements on companies. It reports that Indian equity markets declined for a sixth straight week amid continued foreign institutional investor (FII) selling and investor concern about a prolonged high-interest-rate environment. The Nifty fell 0.22% over the week, although it rose 0.33% on the final trading day to close at 23,346; the Sensex ended the day down 19 points, or 0.03%, at 74,294 and was down 0.65% for the week.

The piece attributes the partial late-week recovery to a pullback in crude oil prices from recent highs, which eased inflation concerns and reduced some pressure on sovereign yields after US and Japanese policy decisions came in broadly as expected. Even so, the policy tone in major economies was still described as hawkish/tightening, suggesting rates may stay elevated for longer, which continued to weigh on equity valuations. Persistent FII outflows also put pressure on the rupee and limited market recovery.

From a corporate compliance perspective, the only practical takeaway is macroeconomic and treasury-related: the article signals continued market volatility, a tougher funding/yield environment, and ongoing FX pressure, but it does not create any specific compliance action, deadline, threshold, or reporting obligation. It also notes that mid- and small-cap stocks outperformed large caps, with investors favoring domestically oriented businesses with stronger earnings visibility, order books, and balance sheets, and that healthcare and FMCG saw buying interest on defensive earnings characteristics.

rows.summary:
This article is a report about the FCNR(B) dollar deposit scheme’s impact on banks and the RBI, not a new rule or filing requirement. According to SBI Research, the scheme mobilized about **$127 billion** in **less than three months**, and that inflow could translate into a **notional profit of around Rs 5 trillion (Rs 5 lakh crore) for banks over five years** and about **Rs 0.5 trillion (Rs 50,000 crore) for the RBI**. The report says the regulator had already made a **wise decision to curtail the scheme by preponing its closure**, but the eventual inflows were much larger than expected, which shifted debate toward the scheme’s cost structure.

For compliance purposes, the substantive point is that the article discusses the **FCNR(B) deposit scheme’s economics** and the two main cost components identified by SBI Research: **interest outgo over the contractual maturity period at the contracted rates** and **hedging costs**. It frames the scheme as having been attractive in a period of elevated global borrowing costs, and it suggests the scheme’s overall effect was beneficial to the banking system despite criticism about costs. There are **no new compliance obligations, reporting deadlines, or entity-specific instructions** announced in this article, but institutions involved with FCNR(B) deposits would note the reported scale of mobilization, the closure timing change, and the cost mechanics referenced in the analysis.

rows.summary:
This article is a commentary from SBI Research on the **FCNR(B) deposit scheme** and its financial impact on banks and the RBI; it is not announcing a new rule or regulatory change, but it does discuss the scheme’s economics in compliance-relevant terms. SBI Research says the scheme has mobilized about **USD 127 billion** and argues that, over **five years**, it could generate a **notional profit of around Rs 5 trillion for banks** and add about **Rs 50,000 crore** to the **Reserve Bank of India’s balance sheet**. The report explicitly disputes estimates that the scheme costs roughly **Rs 5 trillion**, saying that this figure is based on double-counting the same foreign-exchange exposure: it combines about **Rs 1.75 trillion** of additional interest cost with about **Rs 3.18 trillion** of foreign exchange depreciation cost, even though the currency risk on the deposits has already been hedged through a **special USD-INR swap facility**.

For credit and treasury planning, the report says the deposits, using a conservative and time-lagged **credit multiplier of about 2.5**, could support **approximately Rs 25 lakh crore** of additional bank credit. It further states that, at an **effective yield of around 7.5%**, the interest income generated from that incremental credit could more than offset the interest paid on the FCNR(B) deposits, producing the claimed notional gain for banks. From a compliance perspective, the key operational point in the article is that the foreign-exchange exposure associated with FCNR(B) deposits is described as already hedged via the RBI swap mechanism, so the report is arguing that institutions should not treat the entire gross exposure as an unhedged cost. No new filing deadline, reporting obligation, or regulatory action is announced in the text; the content is a financial assessment of the scheme’s balance-sheet and profitability effects for banks and the RBI.

The preliminary work began before Thursday’s dramatic developments, which saw Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, who opposes a listing, pitted against other Tata Sons board members, who were in favour of it. rows.summary:
The document reports that Tata Sons has begun internal preparations for a possible stock market listing after the Reserve Bank of India directed it to comply with the regulatory framework applicable to upper-layer NBFCs. The company has already started assembling the financial and regulatory documentation needed for the process, but it has **not yet appointed investment bankers or other external advisers**.  

A key point for compliance teams is that **February 2027 is being treated only as an internal working target**, not a formal IPO deadline or approved timetable. The article makes clear that Tata Sons still must complete multiple **corporate and regulatory steps** before it can launch a public issue, so the listing process is still at an early preparatory stage.  

The trigger for these steps was the RBI’s **September 11 directive**, which followed the regulator’s rejection of Tata Sons’ application to surrender its core investment company status and instead requires the company to move toward compliance with **upper-layer NBFC** obligations. The article also notes that the situation has created internal disagreement: Tata Trusts chairman **Noel Tata is described as opposing a listing**, while other Tata Sons board members support it.

rows.summary:
The document reports on a governance and regulatory dispute involving Tata Sons, Tata Trusts, and the Reserve Bank of India’s requirements for Core Investment Companies (CICs). Harish Salve, who is advising Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran, says Tata Sons’ legal position is “legally perfect” and that the RBI issue is straightforward: Tata Sons must comply with the rules applicable to CICs, and in Salve’s view the key compliance step is for Tata Sons to become a public company.

The article says Tata Sons had earlier argued that after repaying its loans in 2019 it no longer needed to remain registered as a CIC, but the RBI did not accept that position because Tata Sons still holds majority stakes in companies that continue to have loans. As described, the RBI’s regulatory expectation is therefore tied not only to Tata Sons’ own borrowing, but also to the structure and financing of the companies in which it has majority holdings. The practical compliance implication is that Tata Sons cannot treat its 2019 loan repayment as ending CIC obligations if the RBI continues to view the group structure as within CIC rules.

Salve also says governance disagreements among Tata Trust trustees are impeding the move to a public company structure. He states that some trustees oppose the transition, and refers to a recent board meeting where two trustees were present, one voting in favor and the other against the proposal. The article presents listing/convertibility to a public company as the mechanism that would bring “transparency and professional management” to the group, indicating that this structural change is being framed as both a governance reform and a regulatory-response measure.

For compliance purposes, the document does not give a new formal deadline or specific monetary threshold, but it does identify an active regulatory posture: Tata Sons is expected to align with CIC-related RBI rules and may need to complete a public-company conversion to satisfy those expectations. The article also makes clear that the issue is currently unresolved and subject to internal disagreement at the trustee level, which may delay or complicate implementation of any required structural or governance changes.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India is reconsidering its draft proposal to impose a blanket ban on revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders/NBFCs, after industry feedback suggested the measure would affect far more of the NBFC sector than the RBI initially expected. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu met with NBFC representatives and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the central bank has already received about 350 industry feedback submissions on the draft proposal.

The main compliance issue under discussion is whether the RBI will proceed with a full prohibition on revolving credit or instead move to a partial restriction. Industry participants say the RBI originally believed the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but the consultation response indicates that a much broader set of lenders could be caught by the rule. One specific carve-out drawing repeated attention is an exemption for supply chain financing, which the industry has urged the RBI to preserve.

No final contours have been issued yet, so there is no confirmed operative rule to implement at this stage. However, sources cited in the article suggest the final guidelines may be issued in roughly two months, which is the only timeline provided. For compliance teams at NBFCs and other non-bank lenders, the key takeaway is that revolving credit products remain under active regulatory review, and firms offering such facilities should be prepared for either a narrower restriction or a broader ban depending on the RBI’s final decision, with supply chain financing potentially treated differently.

rows.summary:
The article describes a workforce shift in Indian banking driven by AI, automation, and other technology tools, but it does not announce a law, rule change, or formal regulatory requirement. The core business implication is that banks may be able to expand branches and operations without adding staff at the same pace as before, particularly in routine operational roles, while simultaneously increasing hiring for technology, data, AI, cybersecurity, and customer-facing specialist roles. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that workforce planning, role design, and reskilling priorities are changing, and banks should expect pressure to document how they are managing redeployment and capability-building as routine work is automated.

The article cites Axis Bank as the clearest example: in FY26 it added about 400 branches while employee strength fell 3% year over year to 101,337 from 104,453, and its branch count rose to 6,275 from 5,879. That suggests growth is becoming less dependent on proportional headcount expansion. Across the 10 largest private banks, combined employee strength fell by 10,114 in FY26 after a decline of 9,637 in FY25, reversing the addition of 83,645 employees recorded in FY24. This pattern indicates a material slowdown in incremental hiring at the sector level, especially for roles that can be standardized or automated.

The article also highlights role rebalancing inside banks. HDFC Bank reportedly reduced non-supervisory staff while expanding management roles, and Kotak Mahindra Bank cut net headcount while increasing hiring in AI, data engineering, software, cloud, and DevOps. For compliance officers, this points to a need to monitor whether staffing changes create gaps in supervision, controls, or segregation of duties, even as banks pursue efficiency gains. It also underscores that reskilling is becoming increasingly important, because existing employees may need to transition from routine operational tasks into more specialized digital and analytical functions.

No effective date, filing deadline, or compliance obligation is stated in the article. The only date reference is that the piece was published on Sep. 15, 2026, and it is reporting observed FY25/FY26 hiring and headcount trends rather than imposing requirements.

rows.summary:
The document reports a new UPI merchant discount rate (MDR) framework that becomes effective on **October 15, 2026** and is expected to create an annual fee pool of roughly **Rs 16,000–20,000 crore**, although the final amount will depend on the volume of eligible transactions, exemptions, and the transaction mix. The MDR applies only to **eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000**, not to all UPI payments, and it is set at **0.4%** of the transaction value. The fee is also **capped at Rs 300 per transaction**, which limits the MDR on large-value payments.

The article says the fee will be split among the **issuing bank, acquiring bank, UPI app, and the app’s payment service provider (PSP) bank**, with banks collectively receiving the largest share. Specifically, the **issuing bank will receive 40% of the MDR** for every Rs 100 collected, while the remainder is distributed across the other participants in the UPI ecosystem. Because of this allocation, the article identifies **Yes Bank, Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, and IndusInd Bank** as likely beneficiaries, depending on each bank’s role as issuer, acquirer, or PSP bank and the volume of eligible transactions they handle.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that the MDR is not a blanket charge on UPI, but a targeted levy on qualifying merchant payments above the **Rs 2,000 threshold**, with **specified exemptions and concessional rates for certain categories**. Institutions involved in UPI issuing, acquiring, or PSP functions will need to ensure their settlement, billing, and revenue-share processes are aligned to the new October 15 framework and to the capped fee structure. The document also notes that the government has tried to allay concerns about any increase in cash usage following the levy, but it does not indicate any additional direct compliance steps beyond implementing the new MDR allocation and eligibility rules.

rows.summary:
Public sector banks have raised substantially more than their original targets through the RBI’s special FCNR(B) deposit window, reflecting strong inflows from overseas depositors. From a compliance and treasury perspective, the material point is that these are foreign currency non-resident deposit inflows raised under the RBI’s special FCNR(B) window, and the banks are using the funds mainly to refinance more expensive liabilities rather than to materially change growth strategy. Bank of Baroda plans to use most of the proceeds to replace high-cost bulk deposits and maturing bonds while maintaining a balanced approach to incremental lending. Bank of India described its funding cost as roughly 6.5% plus operating expenses, compared with existing debt/bulk deposits and bonds costing around 7.3%–7.4%, indicating the deposits are being used to lower funding costs.

No new regulatory ratio, filing deadline, or explicit procedural compliance requirement is stated in the article itself. The only forward-looking business implication noted is that Bank of India has kept its credit growth guidance unchanged at 15%–17% despite the added liquidity, suggesting the inflows are not expected to trigger a change in lending policy or an immediate compliance change.

The amended provision empowers the Central government to specify, through notification, the electronic payment modes or transactions on which banks and system providers cann
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance issued a gazette notification on **September 14, 2026** stating that **no bank or payment system provider may levy any direct or indirect charge** on certain specified electronic payments. The protected payment types are **Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions of up to Rs 2,000** and **payments made using RuPay-powered debit cards**. This means institutions involved in processing or facilitating these transactions cannot reintroduce fees, surcharges, or other charges that would be passed on to either the payer or the recipient.

The notification was issued under the **amended Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, which gives the Central Government authority to identify, by notification, which electronic payment modes or transactions must remain charge-free. The document does not set a new effective date separate from the notification date, so the compliance requirement is triggered by the **September 14, 2026** notification itself.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that the prohibition applies not only to obvious fees but also to charges imposed **“directly or indirectly,”** meaning banks and system providers must ensure that any pricing, settlement, routing, or merchant-facing arrangements do not effectively transfer a cost to the user of these covered payment modes. The article also notes this is part of the broader policy debate over the possible return of **merchant discount rate (MDR)** on UPI, but for now the government has expressly preserved the **zero-charge regime** for the specified transactions.

The shift reflects stronger growth in consumer finance, gold loans and other asset-backed retail products, while large-ticket industrial and infrastructure lending faced greater competition from banks, according to CareEdge Ratings. Advt Gold loans recorded the fastest growth among major NBFC lending segments, rising 68.5% year-on-year to Rs 3.5 lakh crore. Higher gold prices increased collateral values and supported demand for quick, low-documenta
rows.summary:
The article reports a **financial sector trend, not a new rule or regulatory filing requirement**: NBFCs (including housing finance companies) expanded their credit book **14.9% year-on-year to Rs 59.9 lakh crore as of July 31, 2026**, up from **10.6% growth a year earlier**, with the loan book increasing by about **Rs 7.8 lakh crore** over 12 months. The growth acceleration was mainly driven by **retail lending**, which rose **21.4% year-on-year to about Rs 26.1 lakh crore** and increased its share of the total NBFC book to **43.5% from 41.2%** a year earlier; **industry credit** grew much more slowly at **7.4% to Rs 22.1 lakh crore**. Within retail, **gold loans** were the fastest-growing segment, surging **68.5% year-on-year to Rs 3.5 lakh crore**, helped by higher gold prices increasing collateral values and supporting demand for quick, low-documentation borrowing.

The document also notes that **consumer durables financing** grew **51.5%**, while **vehicle credit** rose **15.1%** and **housing credit** increased **11.9%**. By contrast, **NBFC infrastructure credit** grew only **6.2%**, slower than **bank infrastructure credit growth of 10.2%**, indicating that larger-ticket industrial and infrastructure lending is facing stronger competition from banks. **Agriculture credit** rose **18%**, but it still represented only **1.3% of the NBFC loan book**, so it remains a relatively small exposure for the sector. The article further states that credit grew about **1% month-on-month in July**, showing continued but modest near-term momentum.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this piece does **not impose any new compliance obligation, deadline, threshold, reporting duty, or procedural change**; it is a market update describing where NBFC lending growth is concentrated and how the book is shifting toward retail and asset-backed products. The practical relevance is primarily **risk and portfolio-monitoring related**: institutions active in NBFC lending should note the sharp expansion in retail, gold-backed, and consumer finance exposures, alongside slower growth in infrastructure and industrial lending.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s Informal Guidance response addresses whether securities purchased under a Non-Discretionary Portfolio Management Service (ND-PMS) can be pledged by the client. Geojit Financial Services said that in its ND-PMS model, clients maintain designated bank and demat accounts with an approved custodian, trades are executed through empaneled brokers, and clients give a power of attorney to the portfolio manager only to carry out transactions they have expressly consented to; the securities remain in the client’s beneficial ownership and are held in the client’s name in the demat account. The specific practical question was whether a client may pledge those securities in the ND-PMS demat account, either directly or through an instruction routed via the portfolio manager to the custodian, where the borrowing arrangement would be solely between the client and the lender and the portfolio manager would not be a party to the borrowing.

It records the facts and then frames the query for guidance; the excerpt provided does not yet contain SEBI’s actual interpretive conclusion or any approval, prohibition, or conditions, only the request and the factual basis for the question. For compliance purposes, the key issue presented is whether a portfolio manager under an ND-PMS arrangement may facilitate or permit pledging of client-owned securities that sit in the client’s demat account, and whether such action can be done directly by the client or through the portfolio manager-custodian channel without making the portfolio manager a counterparty to the loan transaction.

rows.summary:
The document is an informal guidance letter issued by SEBI on April 20, 2026, in response to a request from First Water Capital Advisory LLP regarding the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026. The applicant’s core question was whether a sponsor seeking an asset management company (AMC) licence under Route 2 may satisfy the required initial net worth contribution of ₹150 crore by providing ₹50 crore as equity share capital and ₹100 crore as redeemable preference shares, where the preference shares would be redeemable only after the AMC has earned profits for five consecutive years.

The letter records the applicant’s understanding of Regulation 5(1)(e) of the MF Regulations, 2026: a Route 2 AMC must have a minimum net worth of ₹150 crore at the time of registration, and that amount must be contributed by the sponsor. It also notes the continuing capital maintenance requirement that the AMC must continuously maintain net worth of at least ₹100 crore invested in assets specified by SEBI, but that this ongoing threshold may reduce to ₹50 crore if the company earns profits for five consecutive years. The sponsor is described as being responsible for ensuring that the required net worth is maintained at all times.

Because the text provided stops at the first query and does not include SEBI’s answer, the document as supplied does not yet show whether SEBI accepted or rejected the proposed use of redeemable preference shares as part of the sponsor contribution. What is clear from the quoted provisions is the compliance issue under review: whether the sponsor’s initial ₹150 crore contribution must be in a form that fully counts as net worth for registration purposes, or whether a mix of equity and long-dated redeemable preference shares is acceptable under Regulation 5(1)(e). If you share the remainder of the letter, I can summarize SEBI’s actual interpretation and any binding compliance implications.

rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal guidance letter dated **July 9, 2025** in response to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding the **extension of tenure for close-ended Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)** under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**. The applicant, which is a SEBI-registered portfolio manager (**registration no. INP000006271**) and the investment manager for **Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust** (Category III AIF, **registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291**) and **Sundaram Category II AIF** (**registration no. IN/AIF2/17-18/0340**), asked whether, during the extended period of a close-ended AIF, the fund may only liquidate existing investments or whether it may also make new investments in portfolio companies.

SEBI’s comment cites **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations, which allows a close-ended AIF’s tenure to be **extended for up to two years** if approved by **two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment** in the AIF. SEBI’s guidance indicates that, during the extended tenure, the AIF is **not restricted only to liquidation** of its existing portfolio; rather, it is also **permitted to make investments in portfolio companies**. This means compliance teams should treat the extension period as a continued investment period, not a wind-down-only period, unless the fund’s own constitutive documents or other applicable rules impose stricter limits. The letter is issued as an **interpretive response under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003**, and addresses the specific operational question raised by the applicant for its close-ended AIFs.

The document says the **Reserve Bank of India announced PPS in September 2020** as an additional security layer for cheques **above Rs. 50,000**, and that banks indicated enforcement from **1 September 2021**. Investors are advised to take note of the PPS requirement, although the sentence is cut off in the provided content before the full instruction is shown. The document also makes broad claims about the platform being **“highly secure”** and using **multiple layers of protection and data encryption** for mutual fund transactions.
