rows.summary:
SEBI has issued a Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for all SEBI Regulated Entities (REs) under circular SEBI/HO/ITD-1/ITD_CSC_EXT/P/CIR/2024/113 dated August 20, 2024. The stated purpose of the framework is to strengthen RE cyber defenses against evolving threats, align SEBI requirements with industry standards, promote more efficient audit practices, and improve overall compliance. This document is not the framework itself, but a set of FAQs prepared after SEBI received queries and feedback from REs; it is intended to give practical guidance and clarification on how to apply the CSCRF and the related Framework for Adoption of Cloud Services by SEBI REs.

The FAQs are organized around the main compliance areas that REs need to operationalize: governance and CISO responsibilities, how REs are categorized by thresholds, asset inventory and classification of critical versus non-critical systems, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) and patch management, cyber audit timelines, the Cyber Capability Index (CCI), Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), outsourcing rules, cloud service providers and hosted services, COTS product testing, log management and data security, ISO 27001 certification, SOC and Market-SOC requirements, threat intelligence, DC-DR drills, response and recovery, and classification/handling of cybersecurity incidents. From a compliance perspective, this means affected entities need to review the CSCRF obligations across the full security lifecycle, including governance, technology controls, incident readiness, third-party and cloud risk, and assurance activities.

A key point for compliance teams is that these FAQs are expressly guidance only: SEBI states that the explanations and clarifications in the FAQ document should not be treated as an interpretation of the CSCRF itself or as a binding opinion or decision of SEBI. In other words, the binding obligations are in the underlying CSCRF circular and related framework, and the FAQs should be used to understand SEBI’s intent and implementation expectations, not as a substitute for the actual legal requirements. The document excerpt provided does not include any specific deadlines, numerical thresholds, or technical rates beyond the citation and issue date of the CSCRF circular, so compliance teams should cross-check the FAQs against the original circular and any annexures for precise applicability, implementation dates, and control requirements.

rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), and it indicates that SEBI is **not accepting several requests to relax the compliance framework**. On the proposal relating to **identification/validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs**, commenters asked that existing FPIs not be required to provide additional proof because it would increase burden and paperwork; SEBI **disagreed**, saying the verification requirements will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry has already implemented. In practical terms, FPIs seeking the relevant status will still need to demonstrate the required conditions—such as diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios—but SEBI’s stated approach is to use a familiar verification model rather than introduce an entirely new process.

On **re-KYC and fee/payment periodicity**, commenters wanted the current periodicity to remain unchanged and opposed additional re-KYC requirements, arguing that material changes such as UBO updates would be caught through ordinary monitoring and that longer fee blocks would reduce SEBI’s flexibility. SEBI **disagreed with removing the re-KYC requirement**, stating that **material change reporting obligations remain in force** and that the additional re-KYC requirement is being retained for FPIs, consistent with treatment of other investors. The document also clarifies that there is **no yearly fee requirement currently**; instead, the proposal is to **increase the fee block period from 3 years to 10 years**, and this 10-year block is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC cycle**, rather than changing the underlying ability of SEBI to adjust fees.

A third item begins addressing comments that **FPIs should not be allowed to facilitate single demat accounts**, but the text provided is truncated, so the specific final regulatory outcome for that point is not visible in the excerpt. Based on the visible portions, the compliance takeaway is that SEBI is **preserving core identity, ownership, and status-verification controls for FPIs**, while trying to implement them through standardized existing frameworks rather than eliminating the obligations.

rows.title: Settlement Application
rows.summary:
This document describes the online **SEBI Settlement Application** process and the required supporting filings for applicants seeking settlement under SEBI’s settlement framework. It states that once the **non-refundable settlement application fee** is paid online, the applicant must **physically submit the printed settlement application together with all required documents, including proof of payment, to the SEBI Settlement Division within 7 calendar days** from the date the payment is successfully made. It also directs applicants to **refer to SEBI Circular dated June 18, 2019** before filing.

The application form requires the applicant to choose the **type of application** from the available categories: **Summary Settlement (SS), Suo Motu (SM), Pre-SCN, Post-SCN, Post Appeal (SAT), Post SAT Order (SO), or Settlement with Confidentiality (SC)**. The form asks for the relevant proceeding identifiers depending on the case type, including **Show Cause Notice number/date, Summary Settlement Notice number/date, SAT appeal number, and Appeal number**. It also requires the applicant to provide the **matter to which the application relates**, and includes controls to **save or withdraw** the application details.

For each applicant, the form requires entry of **name, PAN number, applicant type, and proposed settlement amount**, along with documentary uploads. The settlement amount entered **cannot be less than ₹3 lakhs**, as expressly required under the Settlement Regulations. The applicant must upload **certified true copies of the ITRs for the last 3 financial years** in **PDF format only, up to 20 MB**, and a **certified true copy of the PAN card** in **PDF format only, up to 500 KB**. These requirements apply to the applicant whether the applicant is an **individual or a body corporate**.

The form also requires a detailed **correspondence address**, the applicant’s **GST number**, **state/territory selection**, **10-digit phone number**, and a **primary email address**, with the email noted as the address that will be used for all communications with the entity. Overall, the compliance obligation is not just to complete the online submission, but to ensure the offline physical filing is sent to SEBI within the 7-day window and that all required identification, tax, and payment documents are accurate, complete, and in the specified file formats and size limits.

rows.title: Settlement Calculator BETA
rows.summary:
The document is an introductory description of SEBI’s **Settlement Calculator (BETA)**, which is built to estimate an **indicative settlement amount** under the **SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018**, using the computation matrix in **Schedule II** and factors under **Regulation 10**. It is explicitly stated that the calculator is only a guide: the final settlement amount can be modified by the **Internal Committee**, **High Powered Advisory Committee**, and the **Panel of Whole Time Members**, and in some cases SEBI may also impose **non-monetary settlement terms** under **Regulation 9**.

For compliance purposes, the core monetary floor is that the **Indicative Amount (IA)** cannot be lower than **Rs. 3 lakh for a first-time applicant** or **Rs. 7 lakh for other applicants**. A “first time applicant” is defined as a person against whom **no order has been passed by the adjudicating officer or SEBI**, and who has **never obtained a settlement order from SEBI** as of the date of the current application. The document also says the **Settlement Amount (SA)** is comprised of the IA plus any applicable adjustments under Regulation 10.

The calculator requires use of a **proceeding conversion factor (PCF)** depending on the **stage at which the relevant proceeding is pending** when the settlement application is filed. It further provides that, where a business or activity is **corporatized, converted into an LLP or partnership, or merged/taken over by new management**, the historical record of the erstwhile entity is treated as the record of the new entity. This means compliance obligations and past conduct do not reset simply because the entity form or ownership changes. The excerpt cuts off after mentioning “considerations including insolvency, change of name…,” so those additional conditions are referenced but not fully visible in the provided text.

rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/262 DOR.AML.REC.223/14.01.005/2026-27 September 18, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank has issued Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (hereinafter referred to as the Directions) in compliance with the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005. The Directions in paragraph 4(1)(v) allow the banks to alternatively obtain the original certified copy which are certified by any one of the authorities / authorised officials mentioned therein in case of Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs), as defined in Foreign Exchange Management (Deposit) Regulations, 2016 {FEMA 5(R)}. The extant instructions have since been reviewed and it has been decided to extend the above facility in case of Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs). 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by sections 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the Banking Regulation Act (AACS), 1949, read with section 56 of the Act ibid., section 10(2) read with section 18 of Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 (Act 51 of 2007), section 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, Rule 9(14) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and all other enabling laws in this regard, the Reserve Bank being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. Short Title and Commencement (1) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026. (2) These Directions shall come into force with immediate effect. 4. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co- operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Di
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026** on **September 18, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. These amendments modify the existing **RBI Rural Co-operative Banks KYC Directions, 2025** issued on **November 28, 2025**, which were originally framed under the **PMLA, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**.

The substantive change is that the RBI has decided to **extend to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** a facility that already existed for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under paragraph **4(1)(v)** of the 2025 Directions. That earlier facility allowed banks to **alternatively obtain an original certified copy** of the relevant document, certified by one of the specified authorities or authorised officials, instead of requiring the usual original documentation. After this amendment, **rural co-operative banks** may use the same alternative certified-copy process for **FPIs as well**, so institutions onboarding or maintaining accounts for FPIs must accept this document option where the applicable certification requirements are met.

The amendment is issued by the RBI using powers under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Banking Regulation Act (AACS), 1949 read with section 56**, **section 10(2) read with section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, **section 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and **Rule 9(14) of the PML Rules, 2005**. In compliance terms, affected entities are **rural co-operative banks**, and the practical obligation is to update KYC onboarding and document-acceptance procedures immediately so that **FPI customers are treated like NRIs/PIOs for this specific certified-copy alternative** under the amended KYC framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026** on **September 18, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. The amendment updates the RBI’s earlier **Urban Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**) to expand an existing KYC-documentation flexibility that previously applied only to **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under **FEMA 5(R)**.

Substantively, the RBI has decided to **extend the same facility to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)**. That facility allows urban co-operative banks, in the circumstances covered by paragraph **4(1)(v)** of the 2025 Directions, to **accept an original certified copy** of the relevant document, provided it is **certified by any one of the authorities/authorised officials specified in that paragraph**—instead of requiring the original document itself. The document does not introduce any new monetary threshold, rate, or deadline; the key compliance change is the **expanded eligibility set** for this alternative document-verification route.

For compliance teams at **urban co-operative banks**, the practical requirement is to update KYC onboarding/refresh procedures so that **FPIs are treated the same as NRIs and PIOs** for this specific certification-based document acceptance process. Since the amendment is effective immediately, banks should ensure front-office, operations, and AML/KYC staff apply the revised rule without delay and that internal KYC checklists, customer acceptance standards, and staff guidance reflect the new FPI inclusion.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the existing **RBI (Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025** to expand an already permitted KYC documentation alternative. Under the 2025 Directions, paragraph **4(1)(v)** allowed banks, for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)**, to obtain an **original certified copy** certified by specified authorities/authorised officials instead of the usual document form; the 2026 amendment **extends that same facility to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** as well. This means regional rural banks may now use the same certified-copy route for FPI onboarding/KYC verification, subject to the same authority/official certification framework referenced in the underlying KYC Directions.

The amendment is issued in reliance on the RBI’s statutory powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including the AACS variant and section 56), the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, the **Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and **Rule 9(14) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, and is stated to be made in the public interest. It has **immediate effect** from the date of issuance, **September 18, 2026**. The document does not introduce any new numerical threshold, rate, or deadline beyond immediate commencement; the substantive compliance change is the broader acceptance of certified copies for **FPI** KYC purposes under the existing RRB KYC framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately on September 18, 2026**. These amendments modify the **Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025**, which were originally issued in compliance with the **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**. The RBI states that it reviewed the existing KYC facility allowing banks to obtain an **original certified copy** of documents—certified by one of the specified authorities/officials—for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under paragraph 4(1)(v) of the 2025 Directions, and has decided to **extend the same facility to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)**.

This means that where the 2025 Directions permit acceptance of an original certified copy in lieu of standard document submission, FPIs are now included in that scope, subject to the same certification requirements and the same categories of certifying authorities/authorized officials referenced in the underlying Directions. The amendment is issued under RBI’s powers under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Banking Regulation Act (AACS), 1949 read with section 56**, **section 10(2) read with section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, **section 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and **Rule 9(14) of the PMLA Maintenance of Records Rules, 2005**.

The document does not introduce a delayed implementation date, grace period, threshold amount, or new numerical limit; instead, the operative requirement is an **immediate expansion of an existing KYC documentation flexibility**. Compliance teams at local area banks should therefore update onboarding/KYC procedures and staff instructions so that **FPI customers are handled consistently with the NRI/PIO certification-based alternative documentation process** from the date of issuance, ensuring the bank continues to meet AML/KYC and record-maintenance obligations under the 2025 Directions as amended.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the earlier **2025 KYC Directions** for small finance banks. The substantive change is narrow but important: the existing KYC rule in **paragraph 5(1)(v)**, which already allowed banks to accept an **original certified copy** of identification/related documents for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** when certified by specified authorities or authorised officials under **FEMA 5(R)**, is now being **extended to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** as well.

No monetary thresholds, reporting deadlines, or phased implementation periods are introduced in this text. Compliance teams at **small finance banks** should therefore update KYC procedures and staff instructions immediately so that FPI onboarding/document verification follows the same certified-copy option already available for NRIs and PIOs under the underlying 2025 Directions.

The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the existing **Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** and take **immediate effect** from **September 18, 2026**. The change is narrow but important: the RBI has expanded the existing KYC facility that already allowed banks, for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under FEMA 5(R), to accept an **original certified copy** certified by specified authorities/officials instead of insisting on the usual form of document submission, and this same alternative documentation facility is now being extended to **Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** as well.

VI in the table at paragraph 6.1 shall be partially modified as below: “Advances extended in India against out of the fresh FCNR (B) / NRE deposits (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity), qualifying for exemption from Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements, as per the Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Second and Third Fourth Amendment Directions dated June 08, 2026 and June 19, 2026 August 25, 2026, as applicable to various banks. 2 | Page Note: The amount to be excluded from ANBC for computation of priority sector targets shall not exceed the fresh outstanding FCNR (B) / NRE deposits eligible for exemption from maintenance of CRR / SLR in terms of the above Amendment Directions.” 3. The above amendment sh
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Third Amendment Directions, 2026 revise the Priority Sector Lending Directions, 2025 by shortening the end date for a specific ANBC exclusion related to advances against fresh foreign currency and non-resident deposits. Under the earlier Second Amendment Directions issued on August 7, 2026, advances extended in India against fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a tenor of 3 to 5 years, and advances against NRE term deposits of at least 3 years, were excluded from Adjusted Net Bank Credit if the deposits were mobilized during the relevant windows ending September 30, 2026; this amendment changes that cutoff date from September 30, 2026 to August 31, 2026.

As amended, the exclusion applies only to advances against fresh FCNR(B) deposits mobilized between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026, and to advances against NRE term deposits mobilized between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026, including deposits renewed at maturity, subject to the same deposit tenor conditions stated in the prior directions. The amendment also updates the cross-reference in paragraph 6.1, item VI, to reflect the relevant Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio exemption directions, and clarifies that the amount excluded from ANBC for priority sector lending computation cannot exceed the amount of fresh outstanding FCNR(B)/NRE deposits that are actually eligible for CRR/SLR exemption under those directions.

For compliance teams, the operational impact is that banks must stop applying the ANBC exclusion for deposits mobilized after August 31, 2026, even if the original September 30, 2026 date had been used in prior guidance. The amendment is dated September 11, 2026, and it amends the Priority Sector Lending Directions, 2025 as updated on August 7, 2026.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio Second Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the existing **2025 directions** to reflect that a **Local Area Bank has been included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, which means it is now being treated under the framework applicable to **scheduled banks** for these reserve requirements. The amendment is issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and it takes effect **immediately** on **September 11, 2026**.

The substantive change is the insertion of a new **“B. Incremental CRR”** provision after paragraph 7 of the 2025 Directions. The new paragraph **7A** states that, under **Section 42(1A) of the RBI Act, 1934**, the RBI may require **scheduled banks** to maintain, in addition to the balances required under **Section 42(1)**, an **additional average daily balance** at a rate specified by the RBI in a notification published in the **Gazette of India** (the text provided cuts off after “Ga…,” but the requirement clearly contemplates a Gazette notification). In practical compliance terms, this means affected institutions must monitor RBI notifications for any incremental CRR requirement and be prepared to maintain the additional average daily balance if the RBI imposes it.

Because the amendment is tied to the inclusion of a Local Area Bank in the Second Schedule, the key compliance point is that the affected bank(s) now fall within the regime applicable to **scheduled banks**, and the RBI has expressly preserved its power to impose an **incremental CRR** obligation over and above the normal CRR balance. No specific percentage, threshold, or implementation schedule for the incremental CRR is set out in this amendment itself; the operative rate will be whatever the RBI later specifies by separate notification.

rows.summary:
This RBI circular is part of the Reserve Bank of India’s continuing cleanup of the FEMA regulatory framework and specifically announces the withdrawal of seven older A.P. (DIR Series) circulars because they have become inoperative due to later amendments, duplication, overlap, or supersession. The circular is dated September 08, 2026 and is addressed to all Authorised Persons; they are instructed to bring its contents to the attention of their relevant constituents.  

The withdrawn circulars are: (1) AP (DIR) Series Circular No. 17 dated 29.09.2015 on ECB policy for issuance of rupee-denominated bonds overseas; (2) Circular No. 25 dated 03.09.2014 on ECB in Indian Rupees; (3) Circular No. 85 dated 06.01.2014 on liberalisation of the definition of “Infrastructure Sector” under ECB policy; (4) Circular No. 81 dated 24.12.2013 on borrowing and lending in rupees, specifically investments by persons resident outside India in tax-free, secured, redeemable, non-convertible bonds; (5) Circular No. 119 dated 26.06.2013 on ECB policy relating to import of services, technical know-how, and license fees; (6) Circular No. 49 dated 07.11.2012 on the Money Transfer Service Scheme list of sub-agents; and (7) Circular No. 48 dated 06.11.2012 on ECB policy for ECB by the Small Industries Development Bank of India.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is not a new substantive permission or restriction, but the removal from operative status of these seven specific circulars, meaning firms should not rely on them as current standalone guidance and should instead verify the applicable requirements against the latest FEMA/ECB/MTS scheme directions. The circular states it is issued under Section 10(4) and Section 11(1) of FEMA, 1999, and that it does not override any permissions or approvals that may still be required under other laws.

rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/253 DOR.AML.REC.219/14.06.001/2026-27 September 07, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 2 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16446, dated September 04, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries below on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 A. Individuals QDi.431 Name: 1: SANAULLAH 2: GHAFARI 3: na 4: na Name (original script): ثناء ﷲ غفار
rows.summary:
This RBI communication requires regulated entities to continue implementing Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 in line with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (dated November 28, 2025, as amended on December 29, 2025), meaning banks and other covered financial institutions must ensure they do not maintain accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorism-related lists circulated under UAPA. The letter is addressed to commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions. It specifically updates the UN Security Council’s 1267/1989 ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list based on UNSC press release SC/16446 dated September 4, 2026, which amended two entries on the sanctions list; the measures attached to listed persons/entities are the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo under UN Security Council Resolution 2734 (2024).

The document does not create a new sanctions framework, but it does require compliance teams to treat the updated UNSC list as operative and to screen/compare customer and counterparty names against the amended entries. The first amended individual listed in the excerpt is QDi.431, named Sanaullah Ghafari (original script: ثناء ﷲ غفار), indicating that the entry has been revised as shown in the UNSC notice. Because the RBI cites the UAPA Section 51A obligation and the KYC Directions, regulated entities must ensure they have no accounts in the names of any individuals/entities appearing on the circulated lists and must act on the updated designation information immediately upon receipt of this communication. The practical compliance action is to refresh sanctions screening/watchlists against the revised UNSC list and investigate any potential matches involving the amended entries without delay.

The Reserve Bank of India has removed two reporting obligations for Authorised Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I) banks with immediate effect, as of **September 2, 2026**. Previously, under Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 92 dated **April 4, 2003**, AD banks had to (1) send the RBI Central Office an up-to-date list of all offices/branches maintaining **rupee accounts of non-resident banks** as of **December 31** each year, by **January 15** of the following year, and (2) report **temporary overdrawals** by overseas branches/correspondents that exceeded the permissible limit if those overdrawals were not adjusted within **five days**.  

The circular states that, following a review, both of those requirements are now **dispensed with immediately**, so affected banks no longer need to make those specific annual and exception reports to the RBI under those provisions. The change applies to **all Authorised Dealer Category-I banks** and relates specifically to their handling of **non-resident bank rupee accounts** and monitoring/reporting of **overdrawals by overseas branches/correspondents**. The RBI notes that the directions are issued under **sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and that they do not affect any permissions or approvals that may still be required under other applicable laws.

rows.title: Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half-Yearly Return
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/250 CO.FIDD.FSD.No.S544/05-10-001/2026-27 September 02, 2026 The Chief Executive Officer / Managing Director All Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) All Local Area Banks/ Urban Cooperative Banks/ Rural Cooperative Banks/ Non- Banking Financial Companies / AIFIs Madam / Dear Sir, Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half- Yearly Return The regulatory framework governing the relief measures to be extended by the Regulated Entities (REs) in areas affected by natural calamities has been revised vide the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets dated April 29, 2026 (list enclosed), which came into effect from July 1, 2026. 2. These directions require REs to submit data relating to relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis. Accordingly, in order to align the existing reporting mechanism with the revised regulatory framework, REs shall furnish the required information in the revised reporting format through the CIMS portal. 3. The return shall be submitted within 30 days from the end of each half-year, i.e., by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. 4. REs shall ensure that the information submitted through the CIMS portal is accurate, complete, and duly validated. Appropriate internal systems and processes may be 2 established to facilitate timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the required information. 5. Further, the existing monthly return which was applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities stands discontinued with effect from July 1, 2026. Yours sincerely, (R Giridharan) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has revised the reporting framework for relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities under the amended Resolution of Stressed Assets directions dated April 29, 2026, which became effective on July 1, 2026. Under the new requirement, regulated entities must now report data on such relief measures through the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) portal in a revised format on a half-yearly basis, rather than under the prior reporting approach.

The half-yearly return must be filed within 30 days after the end of each half-year: by October 30 for the period ending September 30, and by April 30 for the period ending March 31. This applies broadly to all regulated entities covered by the circular, specifically Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks, as well as Local Area Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, and All India Financial Institutions. Entities are required to ensure the submitted information is accurate, complete, and properly validated, and they should establish internal systems and processes to support timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the data.

The circular also states that the existing monthly return for relief measures in natural calamity-affected areas, which applied to Scheduled Commercial Banks including Small Finance Banks but excluding Regional Rural Banks, has been discontinued effective July 1, 2026. In practical terms, compliance teams should treat the half-yearly CIMS filing as the operative reporting obligation going forward and stop the prior monthly submission for the affected bank categories from that date.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio** directions were amended on **September 2, 2026** through the **Second Amendment Directions, 2026**, and these amendments take effect **immediately from the date of issue**. The stated purpose is to reflect the establishment of the **Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC)** as the country’s central digital payment fraud intelligence platform and to allow UCBs to become members of IDPIC.

The key substantive change is in the treatment of eligible equity investments. **Paragraph 101(5)** of the 2025 Directions is replaced so that UCBs may invest in **equity shares of the Umbrella Organization (UO) of the UCB sector and of IDPIC, specifically for acquiring membership**. In other words, IDPIC is now expressly added as a permitted investment target in the membership context.

A related change is made to **Paragraph 107(1)**, which is also substituted to expand the list of permitted equity-share investments. The revised text includes **equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), the UCB sector’s Umbrella Organization (UO), IDPIC, and CCBs/StCBs where necessary for acquiring membership**. For compliance purposes, the amendment means UCBs should now treat IDPIC-related membership equity as expressly authorized under the investment portfolio framework, alongside the previously recognized entities, and apply the amended provisions as of **September 2, 2026**.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026** amends the earlier **Directions dated November 28, 2025** (updated June 17, 2026) that had granted a **temporary relaxation** on deposit pricing for rural co-operative banks. The underlying relaxation, which began **June 17, 2026**, had allowed the **temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and had also **restricted interest rates on NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above, including renewals upon maturity**, originally running through **September 30, 2026**. This amendment shortens that end date by replacing **“September 30, 2026” with “August 31, 2026”** in the relevant provisions, so the temporary relaxation now applies only until **August 31, 2026**.

The amendment is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and states that it is made in the public interest. It is titled the **Second Amendment Directions, 2026** and **takes effect immediately** upon issuance dated **August 25, 2026**. Operationally, compliance teams at affected rural co-operative banks should ensure that deposit-rate practices for the specified FCNR(B) and NRE categories are aligned to the revised sunset date and that any systems, product documentation, customer communications, or rate-setting controls referencing the earlier **September 30, 2026** deadline are updated to **August 31, 2026**.

rows.summary:
This RBI amendment narrows the time window for a specific CRR/SLR exemption available to rural co-operative banks under the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025. The original exemption applied to fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a tenor of at least three years and no more than five years, and to fresh NRE term deposits of three years or more (including renewals on maturity), but only if mobilized within the stated date ranges; the amendment changes the end date for those exemptions from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**. As a result, the FCNR(B) exemption now covers deposits mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026**, and the NRE term deposit exemption now covers deposits mobilized **between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026**.  

The change is made through the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026**, issued under RBI’s powers, and it takes effect **immediately** on **August 25, 2026**. Compliance teams at affected rural co-operative banks should therefore stop applying the CRR/SLR exemption to qualifying fresh FCNR(B) and NRE term deposits mobilized after **August 31, 2026**, even though the underlying 2025 Directions previously allowed the exemption through September 30, 2026. No other substantive eligibility criteria are changed in this amendment; the only operative modification is the shortening of the exemption period.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** shorten the window for a specific liquidity-reserve exemption previously available under the **2025 CRR/SLR Directions**. The earlier exemption applied to **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years** and to **fresh NRE term deposits of tenor 3 years or more** (including deposits renewed at maturity), but only if mobilized during the prescribed period; this amendment changes the relevant end date from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.  

For **FCNR(B) deposits**, the exemption period is now limited to deposits mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026**; for **NRE term deposits**, the amendment similarly changes the qualifying mobilization window to **between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026**. The practical effect is that urban co-operative banks will no longer be able to claim the CRR and SLR exemption for qualifying deposits mobilized after **August 31, 2026**, even though the original directions had allowed qualifying deposits through **September 30, 2026**.  

The amendment is issued under RBI’s statutory powers, including **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934**, and **Sections 18 and 24 read with Section 56 (AACS) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It is formally titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** and **takes effect immediately** upon issuance on **August 25, 2026**.  

For compliance purposes, urban co-operative banks should immediately update deposit-liability eligibility checks, internal CRR/SLR treatment, and any customer or treasury guidance tied to the earlier September 30 deadline, because only deposits falling within the revised date ranges remain exempt.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026 update the existing Regional Rural Banks CRR/SLR framework by shortening the temporary exemption window for certain foreign currency-linked and non-resident deposit mobilizations. Under the underlying 2025 Directions, fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years, and fresh NRE term deposits of three years or more, were exempt from CRR and SLR maintenance if mobilized within specified periods; the amendment changes the end date for both exemptions from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.

Specifically, in paragraph 20(5), the eligible FCNR(B) deposits must now be mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026** instead of through September 30, 2026. In paragraph 20(6), the eligible fresh NRE term deposits of tenor **three years or more**—including deposits renewed on maturity—must likewise be mobilized **between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026** rather than through September 30, 2026. The amendment does not change the deposit tenor requirements or the nature of the CRR/SLR exemption; it only accelerates the cut-off date for qualifying deposits.

These directions are issued under RBI’s powers under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and pursuant to **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. They are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** and came into force **with immediate effect** on **August 25, 2026**. Compliance teams at regional rural banks should ensure that internal deposit mobilization, CRR/SLR computation, and any customer-facing product or renewal processes reflect the revised **August 31, 2026** deadline for claiming the exemption.
