It replaces and organizes requirements across multiple subject areas into one framework covering branch customer service, customer protection and guidance, financial inclusion and accessibility, payment/remittance services, deposit and liability accounts, and responsible lending conduct. The document’s structure indicates that compliance obligations are not limited to a single policy area; they extend across day-to-day branch operations, product governance, account handling, customer communication, complaints, claims/settlement processes, and lending practices.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the RBI is imposing a **comprehensive conduct standard** on RRBs rather than only prudential rules. The directions require banks to maintain an institutional framework for implementation and oversight, deliver defined service standards in branches, and provide customer guidance and protection measures. They also create obligations around inclusion and accessibility—meaning RRBs must ensure their products and services are usable by intended customer segments, including those requiring special accessibility support—and around payment and remittance services, which suggests operational requirements for transaction processing and customer-facing service delivery. Because the document also contains a chapter on “deposit accounts and other liabilities,” compliance will need to review account-opening, account-operation, nomination/survivorship handling, claim settlement, and related documentation, including the referenced annexed forms and procedures.

The directions also cover **responsible lending conduct**, which means lending policies, underwriting, disclosures, communications with borrowers, and servicing/collection practices must align with the RBI’s conduct expectations. The presence of an annex titled **“Rates at a Quick Glance”** indicates that certain charges, rates, or standard pricing references are likely prescribed or summarized in the instrument and should be checked for any numeric limits or standardized rates that apply to deposits, lending, or service charges. Similarly, the annexes on **comprehensive notice period**, **inventory forms**, and **settlement of claims** indicate that the bank must follow specified notice and documentation procedures, not just internal discretion, when handling customer communications, branch inventories, and claim processing.

The document is relevant to **all regional rural banks** and any internal units that manage branch operations, customer service, deposit operations, payments, lending, complaints, accessibility, or legal/regulatory compliance. Because the document is marked **“Updated as on July 1, 2026,”** the compliance team should treat that date as the operative consolidated version and verify whether any provisions became effective earlier or were amended through that update. A full implementation review should focus on mapping every chapter’s requirements to internal policies, SOPs, branch processes, product terms, customer communication templates, claims forms, and lending controls, with special attention to any specific deadlines, notice periods, service standards, thresholds, or rates contained in the chapters and annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025” (DOR/2025-26/266, DOR.AML.REC.No.185/14.01.004/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025 and updated as of December 29, 2025) consolidates and updates the KYC/AML obligations that apply to Regional Rural Banks (RRBs). It takes effect from the stated commencement date in the directions and is organized to govern governance, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, and customer due diligence, with separate requirements for individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial ownership identification. For a compliance team, the key point is that these directions are not merely policy guidance: they impose mandatory procedures for onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and periodic updating of customer information, with the bank’s board and senior management responsible for ensuring implementation through approved policies and internal controls.

At the governance level, the directions require the RRB’s board of directors to approve a formal KYC/AML policy framework and to ensure it is aligned with RBI requirements. The bank must maintain a customer acceptance policy that defines which customers can be onboarded, how exceptions are handled, and how enhanced scrutiny is applied where risk is higher. A risk-based approach is required throughout, meaning customers must be categorized by risk level and subjected to corresponding due diligence intensity, monitoring frequency, and periodic review; the document also expects the bank to use internal risk management systems and controls to detect suspicious or unusual activity.

The customer identification procedure and CDD chapter require the bank to establish the identity of every customer before opening an account or entering into a relationship, and to identify and verify the beneficial owner where the customer is a non-individual. The directions distinguish between individuals, sole proprietorship firms, and legal entities, requiring different evidence and verification methods appropriate to the customer type. The bank must collect prescribed KYC information, verify it through acceptable documents or electronic means permitted by RBI, and ensure that the relationship is not established if identity cannot be satisfactorily verified or if the customer is unwilling to provide the required information.

The document also requires ongoing due diligence after account opening, including monitoring transactions against the customer’s declared profile and expected activity, and updating KYC records periodically based on risk classification. Where higher risk is identified, the bank must apply enhanced due diligence rather than routine onboarding checks, and it must be prepared to refuse, freeze, or discontinue a relationship where compliance requirements are not met or where suspicious indicators arise. The updated directions also imply specific operational obligations around recordkeeping, employee training, internal accountability, and escalation/reporting of suspicious transactions in line with India’s AML framework, so compliance officers should ensure that branch processes, digital onboarding workflows, and periodic KYC refresh cycles are all mapped to the new RBI-issued directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as of April 1, 2026, governs how Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) must prepare and disclose their financial statements. It replaces or consolidates the RBI’s prescribed presentation/disclosure framework for RRBs by setting mandatory formats for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account, along with detailed notes, instructions for compilation, and guidance on specific accounting-standard issues. It applies to Regional Rural Banks covered by RBI supervision, so compliance teams at affected RRBs should treat this as the controlling statement-format and disclosure rulebook for financial reporting.

The document is organized into four chapters: preliminary provisions, the required balance sheet and P&L presentation, disclosure requirements in notes to accounts, and other operational instructions. Chapter II requires RRBs to use the RBI-prescribed formats for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account and follow the accompanying compilation instructions; it also provides guidance on how to apply certain Accounting Standards in the RRB context. Chapter III sets the mandatory notes-to-accounts presentation and disclosure framework, including general presentation rules and specific disclosures that must appear in the financial statements.

Chapter IV adds separate compliance instructions on several accounting and provisioning topics that affect year-end close and audit readiness. It specifically covers provisioning for net debit balances in inter-branch accounts, reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, and provisioning for fraud. For compliance purposes, these areas require banks to have reconciled balances, documented treatment of unreconciled items, and appropriate provisions/transfers recorded in accordance with RBI direction rather than leaving them as purely internal accounting judgments.

Because the title states “Updated as on April 1, 2026,” compliance teams should verify that the version in use reflects all updates effective through that date and that reporting templates, accounting policies, and disclosure checklists have been aligned to the revised RBI directions before financial statements are finalized. The document excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, percentages, or line-item disclosure text, so the key compliance takeaway is the mandatory adoption of RBI’s prescribed formats and disclosures for RRB statutory financial statements, together with the specified special treatments for inter-branch balances, Nostro reconciling items, reserve transfers, and fraud provisioning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. The stated purpose is to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, natural-justice-based process** for classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters and to ensure that information on such defaulters is shared so that **further institutional finance is not extended to them**. These Directions are specifically aimed at **regional rural banks (RRBs)** and replace the prior framework on the same subject.

For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that RRBs must follow a formal process before classifying any borrower as a **wilful defaulter**, with the process designed to ensure fairness, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The document also introduces obligations to identify and report **large defaulters** in a prescribed format, alongside separate reporting for wilful default cases, so compliance teams should expect new or updated internal controls around borrower classification, documentation, escalation, and credit-information reporting. The Directions place emphasis on **board-level responsibility**, meaning the bank’s board must oversee the framework and related policies rather than leaving classification decisions purely to business units.

The document further requires **preventive measures** and assigns a role to **auditors**, indicating that compliance is not limited to post-default classification but also includes controls intended to detect or prevent wilful default and ensure proper audit scrutiny of relevant cases. It contains separate chapters on the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, and **repeal and other provisions**, which means institutions must align existing policies and reporting templates to the new RBI-prescribed structure and transition away from any superseded directions. The annexures provide the required **submission formats** for the list of large defaulters and the data on wilful default cases, so operational teams will need to use those exact formats when reporting to the RBI or other relevant channels.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the opening of Chapter I, the specific commencement date, thresholds for “large defaulter,” procedural timelines, and detailed reporting deadlines are not visible in the text shown here. However, even from the introductory material, the compliance impact is clear: RRBs should treat this as a formal RBI directive requiring a documented internal process, board oversight, audit involvement, and structured reporting for borrower default classification and dissemination of defaulter information.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025, as updated through July 1, 2026, set out the framework Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) must follow for identifying, reporting, disclosing, and resolving stressed assets, including restructuring, compromise settlements, technical write-offs, and special treatment for accounts affected by natural calamities. The document applies to RRBs and establishes mandatory board-approved policies, so compliance teams should ensure the bank has an updated policy framework covering early stress recognition, resolution options, prudential treatment, and reporting/disclosure obligations. The directions are organized to require early identification and reporting of stress, formal disclosures, and prudential norms for restructuring, with separate rules for special cases such as compromise settlements and technical write-offs, plus a dedicated chapter for accounts impacted by natural calamities.

For restructuring, the directions prescribe general instructions that must be followed when an account is to be restructured, and these prudential requirements govern how such accounts are to be classified and treated for regulatory purposes. The document also creates a specific process for natural calamity-affected accounts, involving the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC), Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC), and District Consultative Committee (DCC), indicating that resolution in such cases is coordinated through those local banking committees rather than handled solely at the branch level. Because the table of contents shows a distinct chapter for compromise settlements and technical write-offs, compliance teams should expect mandatory internal procedures for approving such actions and for ensuring proper accounting and regulatory recognition.

The title page and update note indicate the directions were issued on November 28, 2025 and are consolidated as updated on July 1, 2026, so that date should be treated as the current operative version for compliance purposes unless superseded later. The document’s structure suggests that the key obligations are not limited to one-time remediation; they include ongoing governance, timely identification of stress, and periodic disclosures to the RBI and/or in financial statements as required by the relevant chapters. Since the content excerpt provided does not include the full operative text of each chapter, a compliance officer should review the full directions for the exact timelines, reporting formats, approval authorities, asset-classification consequences, and any quantitative thresholds or exceptions that may apply to specific restructuring or settlement actions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning framework for **regional rural banks (RRBs)**, and it is issued as **DOR/2025-26/262** under **DOR.STR.REC.181/21.04.048/2025-26** dated **November 28, 2025**, with the text updated as of **July 1, 2026**. For a compliance team, the key point is that this is a consolidated prudential framework governing when RRBs may recognize income, how they must classify exposures and NPAs, what disclosures they must make, how security must be valued, how upgrades from NPA status are handled, and how IRAC processes are to be automated. The document is organized into chapters on preliminary matters, general instructions and disclosure requirements, asset classification, and provisioning norms, indicating that it is meant to be the operative supervisory rulebook rather than guidance only.

The applicability is to **regional rural banks**, and the directions appear designed to replace or update prior IRAC-related instructions by imposing a uniform classification/provisioning regime. The asset-classification chapter specifically covers the core classification norms, special treatment for particular cases of classification, valuation of security, the categories of non-performing assets, and the conditions for upgrading loan accounts once they have been classified as NPAs. It also contains a dedicated section on **automation of income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning processes**, which signals that banks must have systems capable of applying the rules consistently and electronically rather than relying only on manual review.

The general-instructions and disclosure chapters mean RRBs are expected not only to apply the prudential rules internally but also to make the required external disclosures in their financial reporting. The provisioning chapter indicates that the directions prescribe mandatory provisioning requirements tied to asset classification outcomes, so compliance teams should expect the rules to affect balance-sheet provisioning, capital planning, and loan monitoring workflows. Because the table of contents lists separate treatment for **specific cases**, **NPAs**, and **upgradation**, the document likely contains detailed trigger-based requirements that must be applied loan-by-loan and not merely at portfolio level.

From a compliance perspective, the operational impact is that RRBs should ensure their loan systems can: identify when income recognition must stop, classify assets in line with RBI’s prescribed norms, value security according to the stated rules, determine NPA categories correctly, apply the upgrade criteria only when permitted, and generate the mandated disclosures. The effective framework date is the issuance date (**November 28, 2025**), while the version cited is the **updated text as of July 1, 2026**; any compliance review should therefore confirm whether the bank is working from the updated consolidated version rather than the original issuance alone. Since the provided excerpt contains only the heading structure and not the substantive clause text, the exact thresholds, day-count triggers, provisioning percentages, or special carve-outs are not visible here and would need the full body of the directions to summarize precisely.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/261**, **DOR.LRG.REC.No.180/13-10-008/2025-26**) set out the RBI’s framework for how **regional rural banks (RRBs)** must govern, measure, monitor, and control **asset-liability management (ALM)** and **liquidity risk**. The document is structured as binding directions covering: when it takes effect, which institutions it applies to, how boards must oversee ALM, how ALM systems and organization must be designed, and how liquidity risk must be tracked through maturity-ladder monitoring.

A compliance team should note that these directions are intended to impose a formal **board-level governance framework** over ALM, rather than leaving it as a purely treasury function. The board is expected to approve the bank’s ALM-related policies, set and review risk limits, and oversee periodic review of ALM positions and liquidity risk management practices. The directions also require a dedicated ALM information system and organizational structure, implying that RRBs must have reliable internal data, reporting lines, and processes for analyzing maturity mismatches and liquidity needs.

The document specifically addresses **liquidity risk management** and introduces **maturity ladder-based monitoring** as the core mechanism for tracking cash inflows and outflows across time buckets. That means RRBs must maintain a structured view of their funding profile and asset maturities, identify mismatches, and ensure management action is taken where short-term liabilities exceed available liquid resources or where future cash outflows could exceed inflows. The substance of the directions indicates that compliance is not limited to reporting; banks must establish operational processes, controls, and escalation mechanisms to actively manage liquidity stress.

From the content provided, the directions clearly cover: **Chapter I** (preliminary matters such as short title, commencement, applicability, and definitions), **Chapter II** (board responsibilities and approval/review obligations), **Chapter III** (ALM governance, including information systems, organization, and process), and **Chapter IV** (liquidity risk management and maturity-ladder monitoring). However, the excerpt does **not** include the detailed operative clauses, so the exact commencement date, any quantitative thresholds, time-bucket requirements, reporting frequencies, or specific limits are not visible in the provided text. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the available material is that **all RRBs subject to these directions must have a formal, board-approved ALM and liquidity risk framework in place and must use maturity-ladder monitoring to control funding mismatches under RBI supervision**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **“Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** apply to **all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and lay out a comprehensive framework for how RRBs must set policy, classify securities, value them, transfer them between buckets, and report/operate their investment books. The directions are effective from **November 28, 2025** (with the document shown as updated through **May 18, 2026**), and they replace/standardize the investment-portfolio treatment for RRBs under RBI supervision.

At the governance level, the **Board of the RRB** is made responsible for approving and overseeing an investment policy that covers the bank’s overall investment objectives, risk appetite, prudential limits, internal controls, valuation approach, and delegation of operational authority. The policy must be robust enough to govern the entire investment portfolio and is not just a back-office treasury document; the Board is expected to ensure proper oversight, including regular review of compliance, limits, and exceptions. The directions also require a clear operational role for the **Sponsor Bank**, which must provide support and guidance as prescribed by the RBI, particularly where the RRB lacks infrastructure or expertise.

For **classification**, the directions require RRBs to categorize investments into the standard RBI buckets: **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Held for Trading (HFT)**, and **Available for Sale (AFS)**. The rules specify when an instrument can be held in each category and restrict arbitrary switching, so the initial intent and ongoing management of each security matter for accounting and prudential treatment. RRBs must follow the RBI’s instructions on **shifting securities between HTM, HFT, and AFS**, including the conditions under which transfers are permitted and the documentation/approval expectations for such moves.

On **valuation**, the directions require investment securities to be marked and carried according to their category, with valuation norms aligned to the RBI framework for market-linked instruments. The document covers the treatment of **depreciation and appreciation**, the recognition of valuation changes, and the operational procedures for periodic revaluation. Compliance teams should note that the classification bucket chosen directly affects valuation and profit-and-loss recognition, so controls around booking, reclassification, and period-end marking are material compliance points.

The directions also include instructions on the **operation of the investment portfolio**, meaning RRBs must ensure investments are acquired, held, transferred, and reported through controlled processes with proper authority, documentation, and internal checks. Where the document specifies special treatment or exceptions—such as transfers into or out of HTM, or investment actions requiring Board approval—those rules are mandatory and should be reflected in treasury SOPs, internal accounting policies, and management reporting. Overall, the compliance burden is to ensure the RRB’s investment book is managed under an RBI-consistent framework with Board-approved policy, accurate classification, proper valuation, and tightly controlled transfers and operations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they set the governing framework for how RRBs may charge interest on advances.

The document defines **“microfinance loan”** by reference to the definition in the RBI’s **Regional Rural Banks – Credit Facilities – Directions, 2025**, and defines **“rests”** as the periodicity with which interest is charged to borrowers. Any other undefined terms take their meanings from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, or their ordinary commercial meaning. From the excerpt provided, the substantive operative content shown is the issuance of a general interest-rate framework chapter, but the detailed rate-setting rules are not included in the text supplied.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **RRBs must align their advance-interest policies and charging practices with these new RBI directions as of the effective date**, rather than waiting for any future implementation window. Because the directions are mandatory RBI directions, affected institutions should treat them as a binding regulatory requirement for all applicable lending/advance products, including any products that meet the definition of microfinance loan under the linked RBI credit-facilities directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, creating a **comprehensive, self-contained framework** for how **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** may transfer or distribute credit risk. The stated purpose is to govern credit-risk transfer and distribution mechanisms used for **liquidity management, rebalancing exposures, strategic sales, and related lending arrangements**, replacing or consolidating prior RBI guidance in this area. The document is issued under the RBI’s powers under **sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

For compliance purposes, the most important point is that these Directions set out separate rules for multiple transaction types: **transfer of loan exposures**, **transfer of stressed loans**, **inter-bank participations**, and **transfer of borrower accounts at the request/instance of the borrower**. The framework applies specifically to **RRBs** and addresses not just outright loan sales but also other credit-risk distribution structures, meaning an RRB must assess every such transaction against the applicable chapter rather than treating all transfers the same. The document is structured to impose **general conditions applicable to all loan transfers** and then additional, distinct requirements for **stressed loan transfers**, signaling that distressed assets will be subject to tighter or different compliance handling than standard exposures.

The introduction makes clear that RBI is formalizing and standardizing these practices because credit-risk transfer arrangements have become important tools for banks, but they must be regulated to ensure orderly exposure management and risk distribution. Although the excerpt provided does not include the operative clauses, a compliance team should expect the Directions to require RRBs to follow the specific procedural and substantive conditions in each chapter before entering into any transfer or participation arrangement, and to treat these Directions as the governing RBI framework for such activities from the date of issuance unless the text states otherwise elsewhere. If your institution is an RRB, or is involved in transfer/participation arrangements with an RRB, this document is directly relevant and should be mapped to existing loan-transfer, stressed-asset sale, interbank participation, borrower-requested account transfer, and policy approval processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** replace and modernize the prudential framework for managing concentration risk in **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. The document states that RRBs have long been subject to exposure limits for single borrowers and borrower groups, originally tied to capital funds and later revised to **owned funds**, and that RBI is now exercising its powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen risk controls for exposures to a **counterparty, a group of connected counterparties, or specific sectors**.  

For compliance purposes, the key change is that RRBs must operate under RBI’s new concentration-risk directions instead of relying only on the older exposure framework. The introduction explains that the purpose is to mitigate asset-side concentration risk through prudential limits, and it specifically notes the historical expectation that banks establish **their own sectoral exposure limits** in addition to borrower/group limits. The document is organized into chapters on **Exposure Norms** and **Repeal and other provisions**, which indicates that it sets binding norms and also addresses what prior instructions are superseded.  

The excerpt provided does **not yet include the detailed operative limits, thresholds, or effective date provisions**, so a compliance team should review the full Chapter II and any annexes to identify the exact percentage caps, calculation bases, reporting/approval requirements, exemptions, and transition arrangements. Based on the introduction alone, however, the document clearly applies to **RRBs’ credit and exposure management policies** and is intended to require formal internal limits and controls to prevent over-concentration in individual borrowers, connected groups, and sectors.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The document is the Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025**, updated as of **July 1, 2026**, and it sets out the RBI’s binding framework for how RRBs must manage credit risk, structure credit decision-making, and comply with lending, documentation, and monitoring requirements. It applies to **Regional Rural Banks** and replaces/organizes the applicable credit-risk rules across multiple topics, including board-approved credit risk policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory and regulatory lending restrictions, property valuation, CERSAI filing, cash credit/current account/overdraft discipline, and loan-system requirements for bank credit. The title and chapter structure indicate that the directions are a consolidated operational compliance manual rather than a narrow rule change, so an RRB’s board, credit function, operations, and compliance teams would all be affected.

The directions require each RRB to maintain **board-approved policies** for credit risk management, meaning credit risk cannot be handled purely at the operational level; it must be governed by formal policies approved by the board and aligned with the RBI framework. The document also includes a dedicated chapter on **Credit Risk Evaluation**, signaling that banks must apply defined credit appraisal and monitoring standards before sanction and during the life of the facility. In addition, the directions cover **statutory restrictions** and **regulatory restrictions**, which means RRBs must ensure their lending practices stay within both legal limits and RBI-prescribed limits; any products or exposures that fall within those chapters must be checked for compliance before sanctioning or renewing credit.

A separate chapter addresses **valuation of properties and empanelment of valuers**, which means immovable-property collateral must be valued under a controlled process using approved/empaneled valuers rather than ad hoc valuation practices. Another chapter requires **filing of security interests in CERSAI** for security interests relating to **immovable property other than equitable mortgage**, **movable assets**, and **intangible assets**; this creates an explicit compliance obligation to ensure such charges are filed in the central registry rather than merely documented internally. The document also includes a chapter on **Maintenance of Cash Credit Accounts, Current Accounts and Overdraft Accounts by Banks**, indicating prescribed account-operation rules for these facilities, and a chapter on the **Loan System for Delivery of Bank Credit**, which typically means RRBs must use RBI-mandated credit delivery structure and monitoring discipline for working capital and similar lending.

Finally, the directions have a **miscellaneous** chapter and a **repeal/transition** chapter, which indicates some prior provisions are superseded and that implementation should be checked against the updated July 1, 2026 version rather than older circulars. Because the document is an “updated as on” compilation, compliance teams should confirm they are using the latest incorporated requirements, especially for policies, collateral valuation, CERSAI filing workflows, and account-operation controls. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** for an RRB or map the likely controls by function (board, credit, operations, legal, and compliance).

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Regional Rural Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025”** set out the mandatory framework for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** that report borrower credit data to Credit Information Companies (CICs). The directions apply to RRBs and govern both their **membership/participation in CICs** and the **end-to-end reporting, correction, and use of credit information**. The document is organized into requirements covering data formats, reporting timelines, reporting rules, rectification of rejected data and review of the **Data Quality Index (DQI)**, correction of Credit Information Reports (CIRs), use of credit information in credit appraisal, display of information, and the continuing applicability of other RBI Department of Regulation instructions.

For compliance purposes, the core obligation is that RRBs must **report credit information in the prescribed formats and within the specified timelines**, keep the reported data updated, and follow RBI-prescribed guidelines for submission and dissemination to CICs. The directions also impose obligations to **rectify rejected data** and address data-quality issues reflected in the **DQI**, meaning banks must monitor and improve reporting quality rather than treat reporting as a one-time submission. Where a borrower disputes information, the framework requires a process for **correction of the Credit Information Report**, so institutions need documented procedures for handling inaccuracies, dispute resolution, and timely updates to CIC records.

The directions further require RRBs to **use credit information reports in credit appraisal**, which means credit bureau data is not optional background information but part of the lending decision process. They also address **display of information**, implying that certain credit-information-related disclosures must be made available in the manner required by RBI. In addition, the document states that **other instructions issued by the Department of Regulation continue to apply**, so compliance teams must read these directions alongside any existing RBI rules on credit information, outsourcing/technology controls, lending operations, grievance handling, and related reporting obligations.

The title notes that the directions are **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** but the document excerpt provided does not show the specific operative amendments or implementation dates for individual provisions. The underlying instrument is dated **November 28, 2025** and identified as **DOR/2025-26/255 DOR.FIN.REC.No.174/20.16.056/2025-26**. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as on April 01, 2026**. The document is a consolidated set of directions for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** governing credit-facility related compliance, with a particular focus on **board-approved lending policies, digital lending, and lending against gold and silver collateral**. From the table of contents, the directions establish baseline preliminary rules and definitions, then impose specific operational, customer-protection, technology, reporting, loss-sharing, and collateral-management requirements. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are not merely guidance notes; they are structured directions that require RRBs to align internal policies, lending processes, third-party arrangements, and collateral controls with RBI-prescribed standards.

A major portion of the document is devoted to **digital lending**. The directions require RRBs to have **board-approved policies** governing digital lending and their arrangements with **Lending Service Providers (LSPs)** and Digital Lending Apps (DLAs), and they set out general requirements for those bank-LSP arrangements as well as conduct and customer-protection obligations. The document also covers **technology and data requirements**, which indicates that RRBs must ensure compliant handling of customer data, system controls, and digital infrastructure when offering lending through app-based or outsourced channels. In addition, it includes rules on **reporting of credit information and DLAs**, meaning compliance teams must ensure that loans originated digitally are properly reported to credit bureaus/credit information systems and that app-based lending channels are tracked and governed. Another specified area is **loss sharing arrangements in case of default**, so RRBs using third parties in digital lending must have documented arrangements that address who bears losses and under what conditions, while still remaining accountable for regulatory compliance.

The directions also separately regulate **lending against gold and silver collateral**. This chapter contains **general provisions**, **restrictions and ceilings**, and **valuation and assaying requirements**, which means RRBs must follow RBI-prescribed controls on accepting precious-metal collateral, including how such collateral is assessed and valued before credit is sanctioned. Although the excerpt does not show the detailed numeric limits, the presence of a dedicated “Restrictions and Ceilings” section indicates that there are specific caps or constraints on the amount, type, or structure of loans secured by gold/silver, and compliance teams should treat those as mandatory underwriting limits rather than discretionary policy choices. The valuation/assaying section signals that banks must use controlled, documented processes for purity testing and valuation, with implications for documentation, custody, and auditability of pledged collateral.

Because the document is organized as binding directions with a defined applicability section, compliance officers should assume it applies to **RRBs and their credit-facility operations**, including any digital lending partnerships and any lending secured by gold or silver. The update date of **April 01, 2026** is important operationally: it indicates the version should be treated as the current consolidated text as of that date, and internal policies, product notes, vendor agreements, customer disclosures, and control testing should be checked against that cut-off. If your institution offers digital loans, uses fintech/LSP partners, or takes precious metals as security, this document likely requires immediate review of board policies, outsourcing contracts, customer protection procedures, data governance controls, and collateral valuation workflows to confirm they match the RBI’s prescribed standards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits” Directions, 2025** set the deposit-interest framework that **regional rural banks (RRBs)** must follow for domestic rupee deposit products, and the document is marked **updated as of August 25, 2026**. It is a binding supervisory instrument issued by the RBI (dated **November 28, 2025**) and is organized around general interest-rate rules plus detailed requirements for **current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, payment periodicity, and treatment of deceased-depositor accounts**. The rules apply specifically to RRBs and their domestic rupee deposit business; the document’s substance indicates that the bank must align all deposit-interest practices, product disclosures, and operational systems to the RBI-prescribed framework.

A key compliance point is that the directions govern **how interest may be set and paid**, rather than allowing RRBs to freely determine deposit rates without constraint. The document establishes a **general interest-rate framework** under Chapter II, followed by product-specific rules in Chapter III, which means compliance teams must verify that every domestic deposit product’s rate-setting, compounding, accrual, crediting, and settlement processes conform to the prescribed RBI approach. The chapter on **domestic current accounts** implies interest restrictions typical for demand deposits, while the chapters on **savings deposits** and **term deposits** govern the rates, calculation method, and payment timing for those products; the directions also expressly address **additional interest**, **overdue deposits**, and **floating-rate term deposits**, so any special rate enhancements or rollover/renewal arrangements must be handled in the manner the RBI permits.

The document also imposes operational requirements for **when and how interest is credited**. It specifically covers the **periodicity of interest payment on domestic savings deposits**, which means the bank must ensure savings interest is credited at the mandated intervals, not merely calculated correctly. It also includes a rule for the **deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which is important for estate/claims processing and requires the bank to follow RBI’s prescribed treatment when interest continues to accrue or is payable after death. The mention of the bank’s **discretion to pay interest on the minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer** indicates a limited, product-specific permission or optional treatment that RRBs may apply only within the RBI framework and only where the account structure qualifies.

From a compliance perspective, the main action item is to ensure the RRB’s treasury, branch operations, core banking system, product manuals, and customer disclosures are consistent with the RBI directions as amended through the **August 25, 2026 update**. Any internal policies on rate publication, interest calculation, compounding/credit cycles, special rates, overdue handling, and deceased-account settlement should be checked against the exact chapter-specific rules in the final text, because the document is a prescriptive operational direction rather than a high-level policy statement. In practical compliance terms, this is the core prudential capital standard for RRBs: firms covered by it must maintain capital in the forms and amounts recognized by RBI, apply the prescribed deductions before capital is counted toward regulatory ratios, and compute RWAs using the framework specified in the directions.

The directions also signal that they are a **replacement/updated consolidation** of the RBI’s capital adequacy rules for RRBs, with the document itself marked **“Updated as on June 16, 2026.”** That means compliance teams should treat the June 16, 2026 version as the operative text and verify their policies, regulatory capital computations, internal controls, and reporting templates against that updated version rather than relying on earlier circulars. The document includes a **Chapter V on repeal and savings**, indicating that prior provisions covered by these directions are repealed to the extent specified, while preserving any actions already taken or liabilities already accrued under the earlier framework.

Because the excerpt provided is only the table of contents and header, it does **not disclose the specific numerical capital ratios, risk weights, deduction thresholds, reporting forms, or deadlines** that may appear in the body of the directions. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the available text is that RRBs are subject to a formal RBI capital adequacy regime covering capital composition, deductions, RWA computation, and reporting, and the operative version is the one updated through **June 16, 2026**. Any RRB or group providing support, capital instruments, or data for prudential reporting should ensure its systems and disclosures are aligned to the final updated text of these directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set replaces and consolidates the framework for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) undertaking specified fee-based financial services**. It was issued on **November 28, 2025** and is titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025,”** with the version provided marked **updated as on April 27, 2026**. The document applies to **RRBs** and governs when they may engage in certain non-fund-based financial services, the governance approvals required, and the conditions under which they may partner with other regulated entities. It also contains a repeal-and-savings section, meaning prior inconsistent directions are superseded, subject to any saved actions already taken.

At a governance level, the document places responsibility on the **board of the RRB** to oversee and approve these activities, ensuring the bank has proper internal controls, policies, and compliance monitoring before entering into such businesses. It specifically addresses the bank’s ability to make **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, indicating that such investments are permitted only within the RBI’s stated framework and subject to the conditions in the directions. Compliance teams should treat this as a board-governed activity requiring documented approval, policy coverage, and risk controls rather than as a routine treasury investment.

The financial-services portion of the directions covers **marketing of mutual fund units**, **insurance business as a corporate agent without risk participation**, **insurance business on a referral basis without risk participation (including sharing of physical space)**, and **merchant acquiring business**. In practical terms, the RRB may distribute or facilitate these products/services only under the specific regulatory conditions set out in the respective chapters, and the bank cannot assume underwriting risk or otherwise stray beyond the permitted agency/referral role where risk participation is barred. For insurance referral arrangements, the document expressly contemplates **shared physical premises** as an allowed operating model, but only if the required no-risk structure and other regulatory safeguards are met.

For merchant acquiring, the directions authorize RRB participation in the **merchant acquiring business**, which would allow the bank to support merchant payment acceptance activities subject to RBI conditions and operational controls. Compliance teams should expect obligations around due diligence, outsourcing/partner oversight if third-party service providers are used, customer disclosures, complaint handling, and adherence to the RBI’s broader payment-system and conduct requirements. Because the table of contents identifies this as a separate chapter, it is a distinct permission set rather than a general incidental activity, so implementation should be based on a formal internal approval and compliance framework.

The document also states that **other laws remain applicable and are not barred**, so any RRB undertaking these services must still comply with all relevant banking, insurance, securities, payments, consumer protection, AML/KYC, and contract-law requirements in addition to these directions. No specific monetary thresholds, fee caps, or quantitative limits are visible in the excerpt provided, but the key compliance point is that these activities are only permitted within the RBI-prescribed structure and subject to board-level oversight and the detailed conditions in the operative chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Regional Rural Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025”** (issued as **DOR/2025-26/247, DOR.LIC.REC.No.166/22-00-001/2025-26 on November 28, 2025**) sets the framework under which **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** may open and operate branches and certain other customer-access points, and it also governs the use of **Business Facilitators (BFs) and Business Correspondents (BCs)**. The document appears to replace or consolidate prior branch-authorisation instructions for RRBs into a single directions-based regime, and it is structured around (i) applicability and definitions, (ii) board governance, (iii) branch/outlet authorisation, (iv) off-site ATMs and cash-handling machines, (v) BF/BC arrangements, and (vi) reporting obligations. For a compliance team, the key point is that the RBI is not merely describing an internal best-practice framework; it is imposing a formal authorisation and governance regime that RRBs must follow when expanding access points or outsourcing customer-facing banking functions.

A central requirement is that each RRB must have a **Board-approved policy** governing branch authorisation and related outlet expansion, and the **Board of Directors** is assigned explicit oversight responsibility. Compliance should assume that decisions to open new banking outlets, deploy off-site or mobile ATMs/CDMs/BNAMs, and appoint BFs or BCs must be made within the parameters of that approved policy, with the board retaining accountability for controls, rationale, and monitoring. The directions therefore create a governance obligation as well as an operational one: management cannot treat branch expansion or third-party customer service arrangements as purely administrative actions; they must be embedded in a documented board-sanctioned framework and backed by internal controls and review.

In the branch-authorisation portion, the document regulates the **opening of banking outlets** by RRBs, meaning compliance teams must ensure that any new branch or customer service point is opened only in the manner and to the extent permitted by the RBI’s directions. The inclusion of a separate chapter for **off-site / mobile ATMs, cash deposit machines (CDMs), and bunch note acceptor machines (BNAMs)** indicates that these are treated as distinct deployment categories with specific regulatory treatment, not merely as ordinary equipment purchases. Any rollout of such machines should therefore be checked against the RBI’s authorisation criteria, location/operational conditions, and any reporting or approval thresholds that the full text may specify, because the directions expressly fold these devices into the branch-authorisation regime rather than leaving them entirely to internal discretion.

The document also establishes a dedicated regime for the **Business Facilitator / Business Correspondent model**. It contains separate sections on **eligibility**, **guidelines for engaging Business Facilitators**, and **guidelines for engaging Business Correspondents (BCs)**, which means an RRB must confirm that any outsourced agent arrangement is within the permitted eligibility rules and operational guardrails. From a compliance perspective, this typically implies controls over appointment, due diligence, scope of permitted activities, customer disclosure, oversight, and ongoing monitoring of agent performance; at minimum, the directions make clear that BF/BC use is not informal outsourcing but a regulated customer-service channel that must comply with RBI-prescribed conditions. If the bank uses agents for account opening, cash transactions, customer enrolment, or other service delivery, those arrangements should be reviewed for alignment with the RBI’s prescribed eligibility and engagement conditions before implementation or renewal.

Finally, the document includes a chapter on **information reporting**, signaling that RRBs likely have ongoing obligations to report branch/outlet openings, machine deployments, and BF/BC-related arrangements to the RBI in the manner and frequency set out in the full directions. Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed deadlines or thresholds, the presence of this chapter is important for compliance because it means expansion activities are not only permissioned but also subject to formal post-action or periodic reporting. In practice, a compliance team should treat these directions as requiring a controlled workflow: board approval of policy, pre-deployment legal/regulatory review, implementation only within the authorisation framework, and timely reporting to the RBI for any new branch, ATM/CDM/BNAM installation, or BF/BC engagement.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)

The most compliance-sensitive area beyond deposits is **responsible lending conduct**, meaning UCBs must ensure lending practices align with fair, transparent, and prudent treatment of borrowers throughout origination, servicing, and recovery. Although the excerpt does not list the specific lending thresholds or product-level limits, the chapter title indicates that lending practices are now formally part of the responsible-conduct rules rather than a standalone credit-policy issue. Finally, the presence of a **repeal and other provisions** chapter means prior overlapping instructions are being superseded or harmonized, so compliance teams should assume they must review legacy circulars and procedures against this consolidated 2025 directions set to identify any conflicts, updates, or documentation that must be retired or revised.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they took effect **immediately upon issuance**. The directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)** and are issued under **section 35A read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling provisions. For compliance purposes, the key point is that RBI has formally set prudential requirements governing **whether and when a UCB may declare dividends**, rather than leaving dividend declarations solely to internal board discretion.

The document indicates a dedicated framework in **Chapter II for declaration of dividend by a UCB**, meaning UCBs must review dividend decisions against RBI-prescribed prudential conditions before any declaration. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or tests in Chapter II, the title and structure make clear that these Directions create binding regulatory constraints on dividend distribution by UCBs and are intended to ensure dividends are declared only in a manner consistent with prudential soundness and regulatory compliance.

The document also includes **Chapter III on repeal and other provisions**, signaling that any prior RBI instructions on this subject may be superseded to the extent stated in the full text, while preserving actions taken or rights accrued under the earlier regime where applicable. It further states that the directions are **not intended to bar the application of other laws**, so UCBs must continue to comply with any parallel legal, accounting, corporate, or cooperative-law requirements that also govern dividend declaration. Finally, the document reserves RBI’s **interpretative authority**, meaning the central bank’s interpretation will control any ambiguity in these directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** (updated as of **April 1, 2026**) set out the mandatory format, presentation rules, note disclosures, and other accounting instructions for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**. The directions were issued by RBI on **November 28, 2025** and apply to the preparation of UCB financial statements from the specified effective date in the updated text; compliance teams should treat the April 1, 2026 update date as the operative reference point for the consolidated directions as presented here.

At a high level, the document requires UCBs to prepare their **balance sheet and profit and loss account in the RBI-prescribed format**, follow RBI’s detailed **notes and compilation instructions**, and apply specific guidance where accounting standards create presentation or disclosure issues. It also adds a separate chapter of **mandatory notes-to-accounts disclosures**, meaning the financial statements are not compliant unless the required qualitative and quantitative information is included in the prescribed presentation. Compliance officers should note that these are not merely “best practice” disclosures: the directions appear to convert several items into explicit regulatory reporting obligations for UCBs.

The document also contains additional operational/accounting requirements beyond the basic statement format. These include rules for **inter-branch account provisioning where there is a net debit balance**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries**, and rules for **transfer to or appropriation from reserve funds**. It further addresses **provisioning for fraud**, indicating that banks must apply RBI-prescribed provisioning treatment when fraud events occur, rather than handling such exposures solely under internal accounting policy.

In practical compliance terms, the directions affect **all UCBs covered by RBI’s applicability clause**, and they require banks to align internal financial reporting, year-end close processes, note drafting, and reconciliation controls to RBI’s stated presentation/disclosure regime. Because the document is expressly focused on **financial statement presentation and disclosures**, compliance teams should review not only the chart of accounts and statement templates, but also procedures for gathering source data for disclosures, reconciling inter-branch and Nostro items, and ensuring reserve-fund and fraud-related accounting entries are posted and disclosed in the required manner.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. These Directions are intended to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, and natural-justice-based process** for classifying borrowers of urban co-operative banks (UCBs) as wilful defaulters, and to ensure that credit information about such defaulters is shared so that lenders are cautioned against extending further institutional finance.

For compliance purposes, the document establishes a formal framework for **how UCBs must identify, classify, report, and monitor wilful defaulters and large defaulters**. It requires UCBs to follow prescribed procedures before making a wilful-defaulter determination, rather than using ad hoc or opaque internal practices, and it also sets up reporting obligations so that information on such cases can be disseminated to relevant credit-information channels and supervisory authorities. The Directions specifically cover both **wilful defaulters** and **large defaulters**, indicating that banks must maintain systems to detect, track, and report both categories, and not just internally flag them.

The document also makes clear that the **Board of the UCB has a defined role** in this process, which means compliance cannot be treated as only a branch-level or credit-officer function; governance oversight is required. In addition, the Directions include a chapter on **preventive measures and the role of auditors**, signaling that UCBs must have controls in place to prevent wilful default situations and that auditors have a responsibility in reviewing or validating the bank’s handling of such cases. The annexes provide the **required reporting formats** for submitting the **list of large defaulters** and the **data on wilful default cases**, so affected banks must ensure their internal data capture and reporting systems can populate those formats accurately and on time.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the beginning of Chapter I, it does **not yet show the detailed thresholds, deadlines, procedural steps, or classification criteria** that may appear later in the Directions. However, from the introductory material alone, the compliance impact is clear: any **urban co-operative bank** covered by these Directions must align its borrower-classification, credit-information sharing, governance, and audit processes with this RBI framework, and it should be prepared to use the prescribed annexed formats for reporting once the operative provisions apply.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (as updated on **July 1, 2026**) sets out the RBI’s framework for how urban co-operative banks must identify, report, disclose, restructure, classify, provision for, and recognize income on stressed borrower accounts. It applies specifically to **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and is intended to replace or standardize the bank-level handling of stressed assets through **board-approved policies**, early warning processes, and prudential norms for restructuring. The directions were issued by RBI on **November 28, 2025**, and the updated text reflects the rules in force as of **July 1, 2026**.

A core requirement is that each UCB must maintain a **board-approved policy** for resolution of stressed assets, so compliance is not optional or ad hoc at branch level. The policy must cover how the bank identifies stress early, what triggers reporting/escalation, how restructuring proposals are evaluated, and how the bank ensures appropriate accounting and supervisory reporting. The directions also require **early identification and reporting of stress**, meaning banks are expected to monitor accounts proactively rather than wait until default or severe delinquency, and to ensure the stress is tracked and escalated internally in a timely manner. In addition, the document requires **disclosures** relating to stressed assets and restructuring, so compliance teams need to ensure the bank’s public/regulatory reporting reflects the prescribed information accurately and consistently.

The document then lays down detailed **prudential norms for restructuring of accounts**. It specifies general instructions for when and how accounts may be restructured, and it governs the **asset classification impact after restructuring**, so the classification treatment cannot be decided solely by the bank’s internal credit judgment. It also creates a **special regulatory treatment** regime for asset classification in specified cases, and addresses **additional finance** extended to a stressed borrower under a resolution plan, meaning any fresh lending provided as part of resolution has to be handled under the RBI’s stated prudential framework rather than as ordinary new credit.

The directions further prescribe when an account may receive an **asset classification upgrade after satisfactory performance**, which means a restructured account does not automatically return to a better category unless the borrower demonstrates performance meeting the RBI’s required standard over the relevant period. The document also sets out the **provisioning requirements after restructuring**, so banks must hold specific loss provisions against restructured/stressed exposures as required by the framework, and it includes rules for **income recognition** on such assets, meaning interest recognition cannot be assumed to follow standard accrual treatment if the account is stressed or under restructuring. For compliance purposes, the key operational implications are that UCBs must align credit, treasury/accounting, regulatory reporting, and board oversight processes to this RBI resolution framework, and they must apply the classification/provisioning/income rules exactly as prescribed for stressed accounts, including any additional finance and post-restructuring performance monitoring requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the income-recognition, asset-classification, and provisioning framework for urban co-operative banks (UCBs), with the document shown as **updated through July 1, 2026**. It applies to the regulated UCBs covered by the RBI’s prudential framework and replaces/updates the earlier rules on how loans and other credit exposures must be classified, when income may be recognized, and how much provision must be made. The key compliance point is that these are mandatory prudential requirements, so affected banks must align their board-approved policies, lending practices, system-based classification logic, disclosures, and provisioning calculations to the prescribed RBI standards.  

The directions require UCBs to follow RBI’s asset-classification norms in determining whether an exposure is standard, non-performing, or otherwise impaired, and to stop recognizing income on accounts once they become non-performing under the prescribed rules. The document includes detailed rules on general asset-classification principles, the conditions under which an account becomes an NPA, treatment of accounts regularized close to the balance-sheet date, special/edge-case classifications, NPA categories, valuation of security, and the conditions for upgrading loan accounts after they have been classified as NPAs. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to ensure that overdue tracking, days-past-due logic, interest accrual, and NPA tagging are implemented consistently and reviewed regularly, because these classifications directly drive provisioning and financial reporting.  

The directions also emphasize the role of the board and senior management in prudence in lending and consumer education, and they impose disclosure requirements that UCBs must satisfy in relation to their asset quality and prudential reporting. In practice, this means the board must oversee credit-risk policy, monitoring, and compliance with RBI prudential norms rather than leaving classification/provisioning decisions entirely to operations or finance teams. UCBs must also ensure that any required public or regulatory disclosures accurately reflect asset quality, classification status, and related prudential information.  

Because the title says the document is “updated as on July 1, 2026,” the effective operating rule is that the version in force includes amendments through that date, so compliance should use the updated consolidated text rather than the original 2025 issue alone. The excerpt provided does not show the detailed numeric provisioning percentages or all threshold definitions, so a compliance review should verify the exact day-count triggers, provisioning rates, and any transitional or implementation dates in the full text before finalizing policies or controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025” sets out a formal, board-led framework for liquidity risk and asset-liability management (ALM) for urban co-operative banks, with the stated framework applying to UCBs and expressly noting that the liquidity risk management provisions also apply to Level I UCBs. The document appears to be a comprehensive replacement/updated supervisory standard issued by RBI on November 28, 2025 (reference DOR/2025-26/285 and DOR.LRG.No.204/13-10-006/2025-26), and its effective/commencement details are expected to be specified in Chapter I, though those details are not included in the excerpt provided. At a high level, the direction requires banks to maintain a structured ALM governance system, including a robust ALM information system, a defined ALM organization, and a formal ALM process, all under board oversight.

For compliance purposes, the most material requirement is that the board is made explicitly responsible for approving the bank’s ALM and liquidity-risk policies, setting and reviewing limits, and ensuring periodic review of the framework rather than leaving these decisions solely to management. The document establishes that liquidity risk must be actively managed, not merely monitored, and that banks must prepare a Structural Liquidity Statement (SLS) as part of their liquidity management process. It also indicates that behavioral pattern analysis is required, meaning banks cannot rely only on contractual maturities and must incorporate customer behavior and product behavior into their liquidity assessment and planning.

Because the document is organized around governance and process rather than a single numeric capital-style ratio in the excerpt, the key compliance obligation is ongoing internal control and reporting discipline: UCBs must maintain a documented ALM framework, ensure board-approved policies and limits, and operate a systematic process for measuring and managing liquidity mismatches and behavioral assumptions. The specific thresholds, time buckets, reporting frequencies, and any filing deadlines or implementation timelines are not visible in the excerpt provided, so a compliance team would need the remaining chapters to identify any exact ratios, limit bands, statement formats, escalation triggers, or submission timelines. Based on the visible portion alone, however, the direction clearly imposes a formalized, governance-heavy ALM regime on UCBs and extends liquidity-risk expectations to Level I UCBs as well.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 2, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** set out the governing framework for how **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** must classify, value, move, and otherwise manage their investment portfolios. The document is **effective on issuance as of November 28, 2025**, and the copy provided is **updated through September 2, 2026**; compliance teams should therefore treat it as the operative version unless later amended. Although the excerpt provided shows only the table of contents, it is clear the directions cover the board’s oversight role, mandatory investment-policy requirements, general portfolio-management rules, and the detailed treatment of securities by category.

At a high level, the directions require UCBs to maintain a formal **investment policy** approved and monitored at board level, and to manage investments through prescribed categories, including **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Held for Trading (HFT)**, and **Available for Sale (AFS)**. The framework also addresses **shifting securities among categories**, including movement **to and from HTM** and **between AFS and HFT**, which means banks must have internal procedures and documentation controls for reclassification decisions, valuation impacts, and any related accounting treatment. Because the document specifically distinguishes between classification and valuation requirements, compliance teams should expect obligations tied not only to where instruments are booked, but also to how they are marked, monitored, and reported over time.

The title and structure indicate that the directions regulate the **operation of the investment portfolio**, so they likely apply to all UCB investment activity covered by the RBI’s UCB framework, with particular attention to securities holdings and trading/investment book management. The board’s responsibilities and the “General Guidelines” section suggest the RBI expects governance over investment limits, approval processes, risk controls, and ongoing monitoring, rather than leaving these decisions solely to management. Any institution classified as a UCB should therefore confirm that its policies, accounting systems, trade capture, valuation practices, and internal approvals are aligned to the RBI’s category-specific rules and any permitted exceptions or transfer conditions.

Because the excerpt does not include the substantive chapter text, specific thresholds, percentages, valuation rates, time limits, or numerical limits cannot be confirmed from the provided content alone. From a compliance standpoint, the key action item is to review the full directions for any mandatory approval steps, permissible frequency and conditions for reclassification, valuation methodology for AFS/HFT securities, and any restrictions or caps on the HTM bucket. If you want, I can also summarize the full operative provisions chapter by chapter if you provide the remainder of the document text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions are issued under RBI’s powers in **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act and take **effect immediately upon issuance**. The document defines “microfinance loan” by cross-reference to the **RBI (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025**, and defines “rests” as the **periodicity of charging interest to borrowers**; other undefined terms take their meanings from the Banking Regulation Act and related RBI framework.

For compliance purposes, the key operative change is that UCBs must follow RBI’s rules on how interest rates on advances are determined and applied, rather than relying on ad hoc pricing practices. The excerpt provided does not yet include the substantive rate-setting clauses, but it establishes that the directions are binding on all affected UCBs from the date of issue and that they are meant to govern the interest-rate framework for loans/advances, including the treatment of interest “rests.” The document also signals that these directions are part of a broader 2025 RBI overhaul for UCB credit regulation, so compliance teams should align this instrument with the linked **Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** when reviewing loan pricing, interest computation, and borrower disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued a new consolidated framework for urban co-operative banks on **transfer and distribution of credit risk**, titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**). The document is intended to replace and unify earlier RBI guidance covering **loan transfers, stressed-loan transfers, consortium lending, multiple banking arrangements, and other credit-risk transfer arrangements**, creating a self-contained regulatory regime for urban co-operative banks (UCBs). From a compliance perspective, the key change is not a single isolated rule but the creation of an overarching framework governing how UCBs may sell, transfer, participate in, or otherwise redistribute loan exposures and associated credit risk.
