Based on the introduction, the key compliance point is that RBI is not issuing an advisory but a **binding regulatory direction** that will govern both ordinary loan transfers and stressed-loan transfer arrangements, so affected banks should expect obligations around transaction structure, eligibility, and procedural compliance once the operative chapters are reviewed in full.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The Directions apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks** and are intended to strengthen prudential management of **concentration risk** arising from exposures to counterparties and sectors of the economy. RBI states that the framework is issued under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, including **Sections 21, 27, and 35A read with Section 56**.

Substantively, the document establishes a regulatory framework for how Rural Co-operative Banks must manage exposure concentration risk, replacing or supplementing earlier prudential norms issued through **Credit Monitoring Arrangements (CMA)** and other RBI instructions. It is not a generic policy statement: it is a binding direction requiring these banks to follow RBI-prescribed exposure norms and related controls for managing concentration in lending and other exposures. The introduction makes clear that the purpose is to reduce systemic and institution-specific risk from overexposure to particular borrowers/counterparties or sectors.

The table of contents shows the Directions are organized into **Chapter I – Preliminary**, **Chapter II – Exposure Norms**, and **Chapter III – Repeal and other provisions**, with **Annex I** and **Annex II** supporting the exposure framework. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed exposure thresholds, the structure indicates that the core compliance obligations are set out in Chapter II and likely include specific caps, measurement rules, and reporting/monitoring requirements that Rural Co-operative Banks must apply in practice.

For a compliance team, the key immediate takeaway from the excerpt is that this is a **new RBI binding direction with immediate effect** for the rural co-operative banking sector, focused on concentration risk governance and exposure management. Any compliance review should check the full Chapter II text and annexes for the exact exposure limits, methodology, exceptions, transitional treatment, and any repeal or grandfathering provisions contained in Chapter III.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction updates the credit-risk framework for Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) and consolidates both prudential expectations and hard limits on lending and account conduct. It applies to RCBs and is issued as the “Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025,” updated as of July 1, 2026; the text provided here is only the opening portion and states the regulatory purpose but does not yet contain the substantive chapter-by-chapter requirements.

From the introduction, RBI explains that RCBs face significant credit risk because their exposures span multiple sectors, borrower types, and products, and because interconnectedness can create broader systemic effects. The document signals that credit-risk control for RCBs will rely on a combination of board-approved policies, credit-risk evaluation requirements, statutory restrictions, regulatory restrictions, property valuation rules, CERSAI filing requirements for security interests, and rules for maintaining cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts. The table of contents shows the main compliance areas: Chapter II on board-approved policies; Chapter II-A on credit risk evaluation; Chapter III on statutory restrictions; Chapter IV on regulatory restrictions; Chapter V on valuation of properties and empanelment of valuers; Chapter VI on filing security interests in CERSAI for immovable, movable, and intangible assets; Chapter VIA on maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts by banks; and Chapter VII on repeal and other provisions.

Because the excerpt stops at the introduction, it does not yet provide the actual thresholds, prohibited activities, reporting deadlines, valuation rules, CERSAI filing timelines, or account-maintenance procedures that compliance teams would need for implementation. On the basis of the portion supplied, the key takeaway is that RBI is treating rural co-operative bank credit risk as a governance and operations issue requiring formal policies and multiple control mechanisms, and a full compliance review would need the remaining chapters to identify the exact obligations and effective dates attached to each rule.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** set out a mandatory framework for how **rural co-operative banks** must participate in and use India’s **Credit Information Companies (CICs)** system. The document applies to the covered rural co-operative banks and governs both their **membership obligations with CICs** and their ongoing responsibilities for **reporting, updating, correcting, and using credit information**. It is issued as RBI circular **DOR/2025-26/304, DOR.FIN.REC.No.223/20.06.056/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025**, and the text provided is the version **updated as on July 01, 2026**.

The directions require affected banks to provide credit information in the **prescribed RBI/CIC data formats** and to do so within specified **reporting timelines**, with continuing **updation obligations** for changes in borrower account status. The document also lays down **reporting guidelines** intended to ensure data accuracy and consistency, including procedures for handling **rejected data**, required remediation, and review of the institution’s **Data Quality Index (DQI)**. Where credit information reports contain errors, the directions require the bank to follow a defined process for **correction of the Credit Information Report**, rather than leaving inaccuracies unresolved.

A key compliance requirement is that rural co-operative banks must use credit information reports in their **credit appraisal process**, meaning loan decisions should incorporate bureau/CIC data rather than relying only on internal records. The directions also require **display/disclosure of information** in the manner specified by RBI, so compliance teams should expect obligations that affect what customer-facing or internal information must be shown or made available. In addition, the document states that other applicable instructions issued by the **Department of Regulation** continue to apply, so these directions are not a standalone regime but operate alongside other RBI requirements.

The structure of the document shows that it also covers **technical coordination** through a **Technical Working Group** and includes further custom provisions in later chapters. Because the content provided is only the table of contents and not the full operative text, no specific numeric thresholds, filing dates, or exact technical parameters can be extracted here beyond the document’s issue date and the July 1, 2026 update date. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that rural co-operative banks must ensure they are registered/operational with CICs, maintain accurate and timely borrower reporting, actively fix rejected or inaccurate data, and integrate credit bureau information into lending decisions and required disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2025** take **immediate effect** and apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, specifically **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **NABARD Act**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A and Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they replace prior RBI instructions on this subject once the repeal provisions operate.

For compliance purposes, the document is a comprehensive framework governing how RCBs may **issue, manage, and conduct debit card operations**. It requires each bank to have a **Board-approved policy and procedures** covering issuance, customer onboarding, risk controls, operational processes, and ongoing conduct around debit cards. The directions also regulate the **form factor** of debit cards, meaning the bank must ensure the card design and format comply with RBI requirements, and they set rules for any **co-branding arrangements**, so banks cannot freely partner or brand cards without meeting the specified regulatory conditions.

The directions additionally lay down **general operating guidelines** for debit cards, which means RCBs must follow RBI-mandated rules for issuance and use, and implement the relevant controls and customer-facing processes prescribed in the document. Compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory update to product governance, card operations, and vendor/co-brand oversight, with responsibility likely extending to policy revision, approval workflows, and monitoring to ensure all debit card activity is aligned with the new directions.

The document’s structure also indicates a **Chapter VII repeal and savings framework**, so compliance officers should verify which earlier RBI circulars or directions are superseded and whether any transitional obligations continue to apply. Since the text provided does not include the later chapter details, a full implementation review should confirm any specific operational thresholds, card issuance conditions, security requirements, customer disclosures, or exception handling provisions contained in the remaining chapters and annexed provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (updated **as on April 1, 2026**) set out the RBI’s binding framework for how rural co-operative banks may extend credit, with special emphasis on governance, digital lending, and lending against gold/silver collateral. The document is issued under RBI authority on **November 28, 2025** and applies to the covered rural co-operative banking entities identified in the directions; compliance teams should treat it as a consolidated operating rulebook rather than a narrow advisory circular.

A major portion of the directions governs **board-approved policies** and requires covered banks to have formal, approved internal frameworks for credit-related activities rather than ad hoc practices. The document then sets detailed requirements for **digital lending**, including rules for bank–LSP (lending service provider) arrangements, conduct and customer-protection controls, technology and data safeguards, credit-information reporting for digital lending applications (DLAs), and loss-sharing arrangements when borrowers default. Compliance teams should expect obligations around how digital products are designed and delivered, how customers are informed and treated, how data is handled, and how outsourcing/LSP relationships are monitored and documented.

The directions also contain a separate chapter on **lending against gold and silver collateral**, indicating that rural co-operative banks may do so only within RBI-prescribed controls. That chapter includes general provisions plus specific **restrictions and ceilings**, and it addresses **valuation and assaying** of gold and silver, meaning the bank must follow standardized procedures for testing, appraisal, and loan sizing against precious-metal collateral. For compliance purposes, this is important because it implies not just product authorization but also operational requirements around collateral acceptance, valuation integrity, and limits on exposure.

Because the text provided is only the table of contents and cover portion, the exact numerical ceilings, operational deadlines, and any specific thresholds are not visible here; however, the document clearly signals that those details are embedded in the substantive chapters and are binding on the affected banks. A compliance officer should therefore review the full directions for the precise approval, disclosure, reporting, and collateral-handling obligations that apply from the effective/updated date, and should verify whether current policy, customer documentation, digital-lending controls, and gold/silver loan processes already match RBI’s requirements or need to be revised.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the interest-rate framework for **rural co-operative banks’ deposit products** and applies to the **rural co-operative bank category** covered by the RBI’s regulatory framework (the document is titled “Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits”), with the updated version noted as **effective/updated through August 25, 2026** and originally issued on **November 28, 2025**. It governs how these banks may set and pay interest on **domestic rupee deposits**, and the table of contents shows it also extends to **rupee deposits of non-resident depositors** in a later chapter, so compliance teams should treat it as a comprehensive deposit-rate and deposit-interest compliance instrument rather than a narrow pricing note.

For **domestic current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits**, the direction prescribes the general framework banks must follow in setting interest rates, including how interest is to be applied to these products and how payment timing is handled. It also specifically addresses **additional interest on domestic deposits**, **interest on overdue domestic deposits**, **floating-rate domestic term deposits**, the **periodicity of interest payment on savings deposits**, and **interest payable to the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which means banks need procedures covering rate calculation, accrual, payment timing, and account handling in death-settlement situations. The document further includes rules on **penalties for premature withdrawal of domestic term deposits**, so product terms and system controls need to reflect whatever penalty structure the directions require.

The table of contents also shows a dedicated chapter on **rupee deposits of non-residents**, which indicates the directions are not limited to resident customers and likely impose separate conditions for those accounts as well. Because the excerpt provided is only the opening portion and does not include the operative provisions, the compliance-critical takeaway is that rural co-operative banks should review the full text for the exact rate-setting permissions, any prohibited practices, and any operational deadlines or recordkeeping requirements, then ensure all deposit-rate policies, customer disclosures, and core-banking system rules are aligned to the RBI’s 2025 directions as updated on **August 25, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy” Directions, 2025** set the capital adequacy framework for **rural co-operative banks** and replace the prior regime for these entities, with the text updated as of **May 15, 2026**. The document establishes the rules for what counts as **regulatory capital**, how banks must compute **risk-weighted assets (RWA)**, and the reporting and governance requirements tied to capital adequacy. It is organized to cover: applicability and definitions; capital requirements and the composition of **Tier 1** and **Tier 2** capital; RWA calculation; special instructions on refund of share capital, investor protection in regulatory capital instruments, and reporting; and repeal/saving provisions.  

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is that covered rural co-operative banks must maintain capital under RBI’s prescribed prudential norms rather than legacy capital treatment. The directions specify the regulatory treatment of capital instruments in detail: what can be recognized as Tier 1 capital, what may qualify as Tier 2 capital, and how those amounts feed into the overall capital adequacy calculation against RWAs. The document also lays out the methodology for determining RWAs, which is critical because it directly affects the capital ratio a bank must hold and therefore impacts balance-sheet composition, lending capacity, and supervisory compliance status.  

The directions further impose additional operational and investor-protection rules in connection with **regulatory capital instruments** and **share capital refunds**, indicating that banks cannot treat these instruments purely as ordinary equity/funding arrangements without observing RBI’s prescribed conditions. In practical terms, the compliance team should expect requirements around issuance, recognition, redemption/refund, and treatment of such capital instruments to be tightly controlled, with reporting to RBI required under the chapter on reporting. The repeal and saving provisions mean the new directions supersede earlier capital adequacy instructions for rural co-operative banks, while preserving any actions already taken or rights accrued under the old framework to the extent specified in the text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on **Rural Co-operative Banks’ Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** formally govern how **rural co-operative banks** must maintain mandatory reserves and report compliance, and they are issued under RBI’s powers under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the RBI Act, 1934. The document is a consolidated instrument, **updated as of August 25, 2026**, and its operative chapters cover CRR, SLR, the method for computing SLR, reporting, penalties, and repeal/transition provisions. It applies specifically to the class of institutions covered by the title—rural co-operative banks—rather than to commercial banks generally.

At a high level, the directions require affected banks to maintain prescribed minimum balances with the RBI and/or maintain approved liquid assets in the manner the RBI specifies, and to compute and report those requirements according to the procedures in the directions. The document indicates that the RBI may enforce compliance through the penalties framework in the Banking Regulation Act and its own directions, so failure to maintain the required CRR/SLR or to follow the reporting/computation rules can have regulatory consequences. Because the table of contents separately includes a chapter on the **procedure for computation of SLR**, the directions are not only substantive but also operational: banks must use the RBI-prescribed method for determining eligible assets, calculating the ratio, and evidencing compliance in periodic returns.

The document also appears to include detailed annexures and a dedicated reporting chapter, which means compliance officers should expect specific forms, statement formats, or operational definitions to control how holdings are classified and disclosed. The inclusion of a repeal/other provisions chapter suggests these directions may supersede prior RBI instructions on the same subject and contain transitional or saving clauses for existing arrangements. Since the excerpt provided does not show the actual numerical CRR/SLR percentages, reporting deadlines, or asset eligibility rules, a compliance team should treat this as the controlling framework and then review the body of the directions and annexures for the exact ratios, calculation base, maintenance periods, submission dates, and any exemptions or special treatment for particular categories of rural co-operative banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and updated through **May 25, 2026**) establish a consolidated governance framework for rural co-operative banks, covering board constitution, appointment and conduct of the CEO/MD, board meeting discipline, and board committees. The document applies to **rural co-operative banks** and sets out mandatory governance standards that replace earlier scattered provisions; the repeal/transition provisions are referenced in Chapter VI, so compliance teams should treat this as the operative governance rulebook unless a specific grandfathering or savings clause preserves an earlier requirement.

A major area of the directions is the **constitution of the board and appointment of the CEO/MD**. The RBI prescribes how the board is to be formed and governs the process for selecting and appointing the bank’s chief executive function, indicating that board composition and leadership appointments are not merely internal matters but subject to RBI governance standards. Compliance teams should expect these provisions to require documented appointment processes, fit-and-proper style vetting, and adherence to any RBI-prescribed eligibility or tenure rules in the full text.

The directions also impose formal duties on the **board as a collective** and on **individual directors**. Chapter III requires the board to carry out oversight and governance responsibilities directly, and it includes a **code of conduct** for directors, meaning directors must comply with explicit behavioral, independence, confidentiality, and conflict-management expectations rather than informal local practices. For compliance purposes, this typically requires maintaining director declarations, training, attendance/participation records, and processes to address conflicts, recusals, and breaches of conduct.

The document further standardizes **board meeting procedures**. It includes a **model agenda** for board meetings and a **calendar of reviews**, which means boards are expected to conduct recurring oversight of specified control, risk, finance, and compliance matters at defined intervals instead of ad hoc. Compliance officers should ensure the board calendar is aligned to the RBI’s required review cycle, that agenda items are actually placed before the board on schedule, and that minutes evidence review, challenge, and closure of action items.

Finally, the directions establish governance expectations for key **board committees**, specifically the **Audit Committee of the Board** and the **Risk Management Committee**. These committees are intended to formalize oversight of financial reporting, internal controls, audit findings, risk identification, measurement, monitoring, and mitigation, and they must function within the RBI’s governance framework rather than as purely advisory bodies. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to verify that committee charters, membership, meeting frequency, reporting lines, and issue-tracking processes satisfy the RBI’s directions and that committee decisions are documented and escalated appropriately.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025” (issued November 28, 2025 and updated through April 27, 2026) set out the RBI’s framework for what rural co-operative banks may do when offering selected financial services beyond core banking. The directions apply to rural co-operative banks and cover four main areas: governance and board oversight, investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), insurance distribution, merchant acquisition services, and issuance of prepaid payment instruments. The document is structured as operative directions, with Chapter I establishing short title/commencement, applicability, and definitions; Chapter II laying out general governance rules; Chapter III setting the service-specific permissions and restrictions; and Chapter IV addressing repeal, saving, and application of the new framework.

A key compliance point is that the board is expressly given a central supervisory role, meaning the bank must ensure board-level control and oversight over any permitted financial-services activity rather than treating these as informal add-ons. The AIF section indicates that rural co-operative banks are subject to RBI’s policy on investments in Alternative Investment Funds, which is typically an area requiring close monitoring because of concentration, exposure, and regulatory restriction risks. Compliance teams should assume any AIF-related investment or exposure must be checked against the specific RBI constraints in the operative text and be approved and tracked at board or equivalent governance level.

On insurance, the directions distinguish two different models. First, a rural co-operative bank may act as a corporate agent for insurance business, but only without taking on risk participation, meaning it can distribute insurance products but cannot underwrite or share insurance risk. Second, the bank may do insurance referral business on a referral basis without risk participation, including by sharing physical space; this means the bank can facilitate customer referrals to an insurer while staying out of insurance underwriting and risk-bearing functions. These permissions are limited and compliance-sensitive: the bank must keep the activity clearly segregated from core banking, ensure the arrangement remains referral/corporate-agency only, and avoid any structure that implies risk participation or unauthorized insurance intermediation.

The directions also allow merchant acquisition business, which means the bank may support merchant payment acceptance activities, and they specifically permit the issue of prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), subject to the RBI’s conditions in the operative provisions. Because PPIs and merchant-acquiring are payments activities with AML/KYC, customer onboarding, settlement, and operational-risk implications, the bank will need documented policies, approved processes, and controls to ensure it stays within the permitted scope. The final chapter repeals earlier provisions covered by the new directions while preserving actions already validly taken under the prior framework to the extent stated in the savings clause, and the document’s updated-as-of date indicates later amendments through April 27, 2026 should be read into the operative requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they take effect on **January 01, 2026**. The directions apply to **rural co-operative banks operating in India**, specifically **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981**. The document is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, so it is a binding RBI direction for the covered institutions.

Based on the material provided, the document is structured to set out the framework for **authorising digital banking channels** for these banks, beginning with preliminary scope and definitions and then moving into **prudential requirements, technological guidelines, general guidelines, and exemptions/repeal provisions**. From what is available, the key compliance point is the **effective-date deadline of January 1, 2026** and the fact that the directions are targeted at rural co-operative banks’ use of digital banking channels, meaning affected banks should treat this as a forthcoming RBI authorization framework and review the full text for any pre-launch or ongoing compliance conditions once available.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, under **Section 44A and Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, as amended by the **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020**, and read with **Section 56**. These Directions establish the RBI’s framework for the **voluntary amalgamation of rural co-operative banks**, replacing prior guidance for these transactions and setting out a formal process covering shareholder approval, RBI approval, implementation of the amalgamation scheme, and repeal/saving provisions. The document is aimed at the banks involved in a proposed voluntary merger and creates mandatory procedural requirements rather than merely advisory guidance.

For compliance purposes, the key change is that a rural co-operative bank seeking to merge voluntarily must follow the sequence and conditions laid down in these Directions: first obtain the required **shareholder approval**, then secure **RBI approval**, and only then implement the **scheme of amalgamation** in the manner specified. The Directions also indicate that they govern the full process from preliminary definitions and scope through to post-approval implementation, so institutions planning a merger must align internal approvals, member communications, statutory filings, and operational transition steps with this RBI-mandated workflow. The document’s structure makes clear that compliance is not limited to the execution of a merger agreement; the amalgamation must satisfy both the bank’s governance requirements and the RBI’s supervisory approval process.

The Directions apply specifically to **rural co-operative banks** involved in **voluntary amalgamation** transactions, meaning compliance teams at such institutions should treat any proposed merger as a regulated event requiring prior regulatory engagement and adherence to the prescribed scheme format and approval mechanics. Because the document includes a **repeal and saving** chapter, it appears intended to supersede earlier RBI instructions on the same subject while preserving any actions validly taken under those previous provisions, so teams should confirm whether any legacy merger steps or pending schemes are grandfathered or must be transitioned to the new regime. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, voting percentages, filing deadlines, or implementation timelines contained in the chapters, so a full compliance review would need those operative sections to identify exact approval levels, submission requirements, and timing obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“All India Financial Institutions – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** under RBI reference **RBI/DoR/2025-26/338** and **DoR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.257/13-04-001/2025-26**. The document is a consolidated set of operational and governance directions for **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, with its substantive requirements organized into chapters covering governance, audit oversight, market operations, regulatory compliance, human resources, and repeal/transitional provisions. The table of contents shows that the directions are not limited to one subject; they impose requirements on board functioning, audit committee responsibilities, reporting of market transactions, FATCA-related registration, staff certification, and staff rotation/audit.

From the chapter headings, the document requires AIFIs to ensure their **Board** and **Audit Committee of the Board** discharge specified oversight duties, and it introduces or reinforces compliance expectations around internal governance and control. It also addresses **services and market operations**, specifically including **deferment of option premium** and **reporting of corporate bond transactions**, indicating that institutions engaged in these activities must follow RBI-prescribed procedures and timelines for market reporting and any permitted premium deferment. The compliance chapter specifically covers the **Inter-Governmental Agreement (IGA) with the United States under FATCA**, with a dedicated **registration requirement**, so affected institutions must make sure their FATCA registration obligations are satisfied and maintained where applicable.

The directions further impose **human-resource and capacity-building** obligations, including a chapter on **certifications** and a specific provision on **staff rotation and audit**, which suggests compliance expectations for training/qualification records, role rotation controls, and related audit review. The document also includes a **repeal and other provisions** chapter, meaning some earlier RBI directions may be superseded or transitioned by this 2025 framework; compliance teams should therefore verify which prior instructions are repealed, amended, or carried forward. The excerpt provided does **not** include the operative text of the chapters, so specific numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, frequencies, or dates of phased implementation are not visible here; however, the effective date is tied to the **November 28, 2025** issuance unless the body of the directions states otherwise in the omitted sections.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025** establish a revised outsourcing risk-management framework for the entities covered by the directions, with the stated purpose of strengthening governance, accountability, and controls over outsourced activities, especially **outsourcing of information technology (IT) services**. The document is organized as a binding directions framework beginning with **Chapter I (Preliminary)**, which sets out the short title, commencement, applicability/scope, and definitions, followed by **Chapter II**, which assigns specific oversight responsibilities to the **Board**, and **Chapter III**, which addresses IT outsourcing in detail. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that outsourcing is not treated as a purely operational procurement matter; it is a regulated risk area requiring formal board-approved policy, senior management oversight, and defined internal control arrangements.

The document specifically requires each covered institution to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and for the Board to retain responsibility for governance over outsourced arrangements. The Board’s role includes approving the policy and ensuring that management puts in place effective controls, while senior management is responsible for implementation and monitoring. The directions also create a structured governance framework for **outsourcing of IT services**, requiring the institution to maintain accountability for outsourced functions rather than transferring responsibility to service providers. This means the institution must be able to demonstrate oversight over the outsourced provider, the associated risks, and the control environment.

Within the IT outsourcing chapter, the directions call for an explicit **outsourcing policy**, a defined role for **senior management**, and a defined role for the **IT function** in overseeing outsourced technology arrangements. The policy is intended to govern authorization, accountability, oversight, and risk management for outsourced IT services, and the framework indicates that institutions must maintain internal ownership of the risk even where the service is performed externally. The outline of the chapter also shows a dedicated **Risk Management Framework**, signaling that institutions will need formal processes to identify, assess, mitigate, and monitor outsourcing-related risks rather than relying on ad hoc vendor management.

From the material provided, the document’s operative scope is centered on **All India Financial Institutions**, and the compliance obligation is to align outsourcing practices with the RBI’s prescribed governance and risk-management expectations. The excerpt does not provide the detailed substantive clauses beyond the chapter headings and section titles, so no specific numerical thresholds, deadlines, or rates are visible in the supplied content. However, the structure makes clear that affected institutions should expect mandatory board-level policy approval, documented management responsibilities, and formal controls around outsourced IT services as core compliance requirements under the 2025 directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025” set a consolidated conduct framework for all AIFIs, replacing the prior pre-existing directions on Fair Practices Code, loan penalties, prepayment charges, and recovery-agent conduct once these 2025 Directions became operative. The document is addressed to all All India Financial Institutions and places direct responsibility on their boards to approve, oversee, and periodically review policies and internal controls that ensure fair, transparent, and responsible customer treatment across the lending lifecycle.

AIFI boards must institutionalize governance for responsible business conduct rather than treating it as a purely operational matter. The Directions require board-approved policies on fair practices and responsible lending, effective complaint-handling and monitoring mechanisms, and clear internal accountability for ensuring compliance by branches, employees, and outsourced agents; the board is expected to review the effectiveness of these arrangements and satisfy itself that the institution’s conduct is aligned with regulatory expectations. The institution must also maintain sufficient documentation and oversight to evidence compliance with the RBI’s conduct rules.

On lending conduct, the Directions require a Fair Practices Code that makes loan terms, fees, interest, and borrower obligations transparent and non-misleading from sanction through closure. The institution must communicate sanction decisions and loan conditions clearly, avoid unfair or coercive collection practices, and ensure that loan documents and disclosures are understandable and accessible to borrowers. The document also standardizes treatment of penal charges in loan accounts: any penal charge must be reasonable, transparent, and linked to borrower non-compliance rather than being used as an additional source of income through hidden or compound charges. The RBI specifically requires that penal charges be clearly disclosed in the loan agreement and communicated at the time of sanction, and that they not be applied in a manner that is punitive, arbitrary, or opaque.

The Directions also regulate pre-payment charges on loans, requiring AIFIs to apply the RBI’s restrictions on when such charges may or may not be levied. Where pre-payment charges are prohibited under the applicable RBI framework, they cannot be imposed directly or indirectly, and institutions must ensure that product design, documentation, and collection systems do not circumvent this restriction. AIFI recovery-agent arrangements are subject to explicit conduct obligations: the institution remains responsible for the behavior of agents, must put in place controls over engagement, training, monitoring, and borrower-contact rules, and must prevent harassment, intimidation, or misrepresentation in recovery activity.

A separate miscellaneous provision requires compliance with the Supreme Court’s order dated April 30, 2025 in the matters of Pragya Prasun and Ors. v. Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 289 of 2024) and Amar Jain v. Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 49 of 2025), meaning affected institutions must align their practices with that judicial direction in addition to RBI’s conduct rules. The Directions also include provisions for “declaration of calamity,” under which institutions must adopt measures consistent with RBI requirements when borrowers are affected by a notified calamity, typically involving relief-oriented treatment of loan obligations and operational flexibility.

The document is dated November 28, 2025 and is marked “Updated as on July 1, 2026,” so compliance teams should treat the July 1, 2026 version as the operative text reflected in the update. It also contains repeal and saving provisions, preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework to the extent specified, while making clear that other applicable laws are not displaced by these Directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer (KYC) Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/335; DOR.AML.REC.No.254/14.01.011/2025-26, issued **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through December 29, 2025**) set out the KYC/AML framework applicable to covered **All India Financial Institutions**. From the table of contents alone, the document is structured to require these institutions to maintain board-approved policies and controls, define customer acceptance standards, implement risk management, perform customer identification and customer due diligence, and continue due diligence over the life of the relationship. It also specifically addresses special CDD treatment for **individuals, sole proprietary firms, legal entities, and beneficial owners**, which signals that the directions are not generic—they are intended to govern onboarding, verification, and ongoing monitoring across multiple customer types.

For compliance teams, the document’s material significance is that it appears to codify a full lifecycle KYC regime: institutions must establish a **customer acceptance policy**, a **risk management framework**, and a **customer identification procedure (CIP)** before or at onboarding, then apply **customer due diligence (CDD)** measures tailored to the nature of the customer and the risk posed. The presence of separate sections for **legal entities** and **beneficial ownership** means the institutions must look through entity structures and identify the natural persons who ultimately control or own the customer, rather than relying only on incorporation documents. The “ongoing due diligence” section indicates that KYC is not a one-time onboarding exercise; firms must periodically refresh and monitor customer information and transaction behavior over time.

The excerpt provided does **not** include the operative text of the requirements, so specific thresholds, documentary standards, periodic review frequencies, monetary limits, or exact timelines for implementation cannot be confirmed from the excerpt itself. However, the title and structure clearly indicate a binding RBI direction applicable to the covered institutions, and the updated date of **December 29, 2025** suggests compliance teams should use the consolidated version rather than the original issuance alone. In practice, a compliance officer should treat this as a directive to confirm that internal KYC/AML policies, customer onboarding workflows, beneficial ownership checks, and ongoing monitoring procedures are aligned to the final RBI text in each of the listed chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025**, and this version is marked **“Updated as on April 1, 2026.”** It sets the mandatory financial-statement presentation, disclosure, accounting guidance, and consolidated prudential reporting framework for **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, so compliance teams at covered entities need to ensure their statutory financial reporting, notes to accounts, and group reporting are aligned to these directions rather than relying only on generic accounting standards.

The directions prescribe the **required balance sheet and profit and loss account format** and also govern the **preparation of consolidated financial statements**. They then provide **guidance on specific issues under certain accounting standards**, meaning AIFIs must apply RBI-prescribed interpretations or presentation rules where these directions speak to an accounting topic. The document also contains a detailed **“Notes to Accounts” disclosure regime**, organized into general presentation rules and mandatory disclosure requirements, which indicates that compliance is not limited to statement formats but extends to the content, structure, and completeness of footnote disclosures.

A separate chapter imposes **Consolidated Prudential Reporting (CPR)** requirements. For CPR, the directions specify the **scope of entities covered, the reporting frequency, the required format, and other consolidation instructions**, so relevant institutions must identify which consolidated group entities fall within RBI’s prudential consolidation perimeter and ensure the reports are prepared on the cadence and in the template mandated by RBI. Even from the table of contents alone, it is clear that this is a comprehensive reporting instruction set affecting both standalone and consolidated reporting processes, with a compliance obligation to monitor RBI-specified presentation, disclosure, and consolidation rules as of the updated effective reference date of **April 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** to create a standardized, transparent, and non-discriminatory process—consistent with natural justice—for classifying borrowers as **wilful defaulters** and for disseminating information about such defaulters so other lenders are warned and do not extend further institutional finance. The Directions are issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**, and they apply to **All India Financial Institutions** (the document’s regulated entities). The stated structure of the Directions shows they cover: the board’s role, treatment of wilful defaulters, reporting of wilful defaulters and **large defaulters**, preventive measures, auditor responsibilities, and repeal/transition provisions, with annexed reporting formats for large-defaulter lists and wilful-default data.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive change is that regulated institutions must follow the RBI’s prescribed procedure before branding a borrower a wilful defaulter, rather than using ad hoc internal classifications. The document specifically requires a **fair process** that includes principles of natural justice, and it establishes a formal mechanism to **collect and share credit information** on wilful defaulters so that lenders are cautioned against extending fresh finance. It also adds a separate reporting obligation for **large defaulters**, with a dedicated Annex I format for submitting the list of such defaulters, alongside Annex II for reporting wilful default cases.  

The Directions also assign governance responsibility to the institution’s **Board**, which must oversee the framework for identifying and handling wilful defaulters and ensure implementation of the preventive and reporting controls. In addition, the document contemplates a role for **auditors** in the preventive-control framework, indicating that compliance should not be treated only as a lending or recovery function but also as an internal-control and assurance issue. The presence of a distinct chapter on preventive measures indicates institutions are expected to maintain procedures that deter misuse of funds, detect default behavior early, and support accurate classification and reporting.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is identified as **DOR/2025-26/333** and **DOR.FIN.REC.No.252/20-16-003/2025-26**. The excerpt provided does not include the full operative commencement clause, so the exact effective date and any transition timelines cannot be confirmed from the supplied text; however, the Directions are clearly intended to take effect as the governing RBI framework for wilful-defaulter and large-defaulter treatment for all in-scope All India Financial Institutions. A compliance team should therefore review internal credit, recovery, reporting, board-governance, and audit procedures against the final text and the two annexed reporting templates to ensure the institution can identify, classify, notify, report, and share information on affected borrowers in the manner RBI prescribes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025”** (dated **November 28, 2025**, and **updated as on July 1, 2026**) sets out the RBI’s framework for how specified **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** must identify, report, and resolve borrower stress, and what additional provisioning applies if resolution is delayed or not implemented properly. In practice, the document requires covered institutions to maintain **board-approved policies** for handling stressed assets, establish processes for **early identification of stress**, make the required **disclosures**, and remain subject to **supervisory review** by RBI. The directions appear organized around a formal **review period**, an **Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA)** process where multiple lenders are involved, and a structured **resolution plan** requirement, indicating that the institution cannot simply delay action once stress is identified.

For compliance teams, the most important operational point is that the RBI is replacing ad hoc workout behavior with a prescribed, time-bound resolution framework: once an account shows signs of stress, the institution must escalate it through its internal governance process and, where applicable, coordinate with other lenders through an ICA and resolution plan. The document also introduces or reinforces **additional provisioning** consequences when there is **delayed implementation of a resolution plan**, meaning that failure to execute the required solution within the specified timeframe can create a direct capital/provisioning hit. Because the title and structure indicate applicability to **AIFIs**, compliance should assume this is relevant to RBI-regulated all-India development/financial institutions rather than ordinary commercial banks unless the institution is explicitly brought within scope elsewhere in the text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 01, 2026**) set the prudential rules that covered all-India financial institutions must follow for recognizing income, classifying assets, and making provisions. The directions apply to the institutions covered by the RBI’s definition in the document and replace/organize the framework under which they must identify non-performing assets, disclose asset quality, and maintain board-approved governance over lending and credit risk practices. The document is structured as binding directions effective from **November 28, 2025**, with later updates reflected through **July 01, 2026**.

At a compliance level, the directions require the **Board** to play a direct oversight role in prudential lending, asset classification, and provisioning policy, rather than leaving these as purely operational decisions. The institutions must also implement prudence in lending and consumer education measures and meet specified disclosure requirements, meaning compliance teams need to ensure credit policies, customer-facing communications, and reporting controls are aligned with the RBI framework. The directions are not merely accounting guidance: they govern how loans are treated when repayment weakness emerges, when income can no longer be recognized, and what provisioning must be charged against exposures that deteriorate.

The core substantive change area is **asset classification**, including the rules for when an account becomes a **non-performing asset (NPA)**, how such accounts are categorized, and how accounts can be upgraded after they are cured. The document includes detailed instructions on general asset classification, classification as NPA, accounts regularized near the balance sheet date, specific classification cases, NPA categories, and the conditions for upgradation of NPA loan accounts. Compliance officers should treat these sections as the operative rules for determining whether a credit exposure may continue to be treated as performing, what internal triggers must move it into NPA status, and how to document any subsequent regularization or upgrade.

Although the table of contents in the provided text does not show the numerical thresholds or provisioning percentages, the directions clearly contemplate a separate **Chapter IV – Provisioning Norms**, which indicates that the institutions must make provisions in accordance with RBI-prescribed standards once assets are classified as impaired or non-performing. In practice, this means compliance and finance teams need to ensure the institution’s systems, MIS, and accounting controls can automatically reflect the RBI’s recognition/classification/provisioning outcomes, including around balance-sheet date cutoffs and any special treatment for accounts that are regularized close to reporting dates.
