rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** are a consolidated set of binding rules for NBFC lending activities, with the version provided **updated as of July 15, 2026**. The document applies to **NBFCs** and, for the digital lending chapter, to NBFCs using **lending service provider (LSP)** arrangements and **digital lending applications (DLAs)**. It establishes board-level governance requirements, detailed conduct and customer-protection rules for digital lending, technology/data controls, reporting obligations, loss-sharing rules for defaulted loans, and specific restrictions and ceilings for lending against **gold and silver collateral**.

At a high level, the directions require the **board of an NBFC** to approve and oversee lending policies, including controls over outsourcing and digital lending arrangements, and to ensure the NBFC remains responsible for compliance even where third parties are involved. For **digital lending**, the NBFC must ensure that any LSP relationship is structured and monitored so that customer-facing practices, disclosures, consent, and grievance handling meet RBI requirements; the NBFC cannot shift regulatory responsibility to the platform or intermediary. The chapter also imposes **technology and data safeguards**, meaning data collected through digital lending must be limited, appropriately protected, and used only for permitted purposes, with controls over access, storage, sharing, and deletion as required by the directions.

The document further requires **credit information reporting** and oversight of any DLAs used in the lending process, so that loans originated or serviced digitally are properly reflected in credit bureau/reporting systems and the lender maintains traceability of the transaction chain. It also includes rules on **loss sharing in case of default**, which means NBFCs that enter arrangements with LSPs or similar service providers must allocate and document responsibility for default losses in a way that complies with RBI’s framework; this is intended to prevent hidden credit risk transfer and ensure the NBFC remains accountable for prudent underwriting and collection practices. In addition, the directions contain **general provisions** that govern implementation, compliance monitoring, and any residual obligations not covered by the chapter-specific rules.

For lending secured by **gold and silver collateral**, the directions establish dedicated rules that constrain how NBFCs can accept, value, and lend against precious-metal collateral. The document includes **restrictions and ceilings** for such lending, meaning compliance teams must check the specific collateral type, valuation practices, concentration limits, and any caps or prudential thresholds set by RBI before originating or renewing these loans. Because the excerpt does not include the detailed numerical ceilings, a compliance review would need to verify the full chapter text for exact loan-to-value limits, eligibility conditions, and any operational conditions attached to gold and silver-backed lending.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acceptance of Public Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the framework for when and how NBFCs may accept public deposits and how deposit-taking NBFCs must manage repayment, liquidity, disclosures, reporting, and compliance after the rules take effect. It is issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acceptance of Public Deposits) Directions, 2025**; the document shown is an **updated version as on April 15, 2026**. The introductory clause states that the Directions become effective **on the date they are placed on the official website** (the text provided cuts off after “official…”), so the operative start date is the publication/website-placement date rather than a fixed calendar date in the excerpt.

The core substance of the Directions is that they govern **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** that accept or propose to accept **public deposits** and impose the RBI’s framework on eligibility, restrictions, and ongoing conduct. The document is organized into chapters covering: preliminary definitions and application, **maintenance of liquid assets**, **restrictions on acceptance of public deposits by NBFCs**, **general provisions for repayment of public deposits**, **miscellaneous instructions**, **reporting requirements**, and **repeal/other provisions**, with two annexes. From the chapter headings alone, the compliance implication is that firms in scope will need to verify whether they are permitted to accept deposits at all, maintain the required liquid assets, follow prescribed repayment rules and timelines, and meet any recurring reporting obligations.

Because the excerpt provided ends in Chapter I before the substantive rules appear, the text available here does **not** include the specific numerical thresholds, deposit caps, liquidity percentages, maturity restrictions, reporting forms, or penalty/transition details that may be contained in later chapters and annexes. For compliance purposes, the key item visible in this excerpt is the **existence of a comprehensive RBI regime for NBFC public deposits** and the fact that it is a formal direction under statutory authority, meaning affected entities must treat it as binding once effective. If you share the remaining pages, I can produce a fuller operational summary with the exact limits, deadlines, filing requirements, and any amended or repealed provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the capital-adequacy framework for **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** and related entities covered by the applicability provisions. The document is organized around regulatory capital, risk-weighted assets, securitisation exposures, and leverage ratio, and it replaces/updates earlier prudential capital norms by prescribing how NBFCs must calculate eligible capital, deductions, and asset risk weights for regulatory reporting and compliance.

A core compliance obligation is that affected entities must determine **regulatory capital** by classifying capital into **CET1, Tier 1, and Tier 2**, and apply the RBI’s prescribed deductions and adjustments before using those amounts for capital-adequacy calculations. The directions also address the treatment of **owned funds**, **deferred tax assets (DTA)** and **deferred tax liabilities (DTL)**, and require specific regulatory adjustments to be made from capital rather than treating all balance-sheet items as freely available capital. The framework further introduces or maintains a **leverage ratio** requirement, meaning firms must monitor not only risk-weighted capital adequacy but also an exposure-based leverage measure.

The directions require NBFCs to compute **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** under RBI-prescribed rules, which then drive the minimum capital requirement. The document specifically includes a separate section on **securitisation exposures**, indicating that NBFCs holding or originating securitised exposures must apply special capital treatment rather than relying solely on general asset risk weights. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that securitisation positions, off-balance-sheet exposures, and any other assets subject to special treatment are mapped to the correct regulatory buckets and risk weights.

Because the document is titled as **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** firms should treat that date as the version control point for the current requirements and verify whether any changes through that update affect their capital computation methods, deductions, or exposure classifications. The document’s structure indicates that the applicable rules begin with **short title and commencement** and **applicability** provisions in Chapter I, so compliance officers should confirm whether the firm falls within the defined NBFC categories and whether any exceptions or special applicability rules apply before implementing the capital and RWA calculations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Governance) Directions, 2025** set out the governance framework for NBFCs and, in several places, impose stricter requirements on **NBFCs in the Middle Layer (NBFC-ML) and Upper Layer (NBFC-UL)**. The directions are issued by the RBI under its supervisory powers and are intended to standardize board composition, committee oversight, fit-and-proper expectations, and senior management controls across regulated NBFCs. Because this document is titled as **updated as on June 24, 2026**, compliance teams should treat the updated version as the operative text and verify internal policies against that current version.

At a high level, the directions require each NBFC to have a **board-approved governance policy** and to **periodically review** it, rather than relying on informal practices. The board is expected to oversee governance, risk, compliance, and management succession/change control, and the directions specifically call for procedures addressing **changes in directors and/or management**. For all NBFCs, the document also addresses **board experience requirements**, meaning the board must have the appropriate level of expertise and collective capability to govern the institution; this is not a purely ceremonial requirement and should be reflected in board nomination, fit-and-proper assessment, and succession planning processes.

A separate set of obligations applies to **NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL**, which face enhanced governance expectations. These include requirements on the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**, periodic **reviews** of governance arrangements, and mandatory **committees of the board** with specified oversight responsibilities. The document also introduces requirements around key control functions, including the appointment of a **Chief Risk Officer (CRO)** and a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)** for the relevant layers, signaling a formalized second-line control structure and clearer accountability for risk and compliance management. Compliance teams should ensure that the roles are not merely created on paper but are supported by documented reporting lines, authority, and independence consistent with the RBI’s governance expectations.

The directions are binding on the NBFCs within scope as defined in the document, and the practical compliance task is to map every applicable requirement to existing policies, board terms of reference, committee charters, and senior management appointments. Where the document specifies board reviews, appointment standards, or committee composition, those requirements should be checked against actual board minutes and governance documents, especially for NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL. In addition, any internal triggers for **director or management change approvals, notifications, and onboarding/offboarding controls** should be aligned to the RBI framework so that changes are handled through a documented governance process.

Because the provided excerpt is mainly the table of contents and title page, it does not show the detailed thresholds, exact committee composition rules, or any transitional deadlines in the visible text. However, from the portions shown, the compliance significance is clear: the RBI has issued a formal governance code for NBFCs, with heightened obligations for middle- and upper-layer entities, and firms in scope should confirm that their board structure, committees, senior appointments, and policy review cycles conform to the final updated directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025** (updated **July 1, 2026**) consolidates the RBI’s rules on when and how NBFCs may expand into other financial services, with the document specifically covering governance by the board, investments in AIFs, overseas investments, expansion through the automatic route, and entry into insurance business. It applies to NBFCs within the scope of the Directions, and the table of contents indicates separate treatment for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs**, **NBFC-CICs**, and **HFCs** where relevant, so compliance teams should first map their entity type to the correct subchapter before assessing permissibility. The document is not just informational; it sets out the regulatory framework and procedural requirements that govern whether an NBFC may undertake new financial activities directly, through subsidiaries, joint ventures, or overseas investment structures, and it places responsibility on the board to oversee these expansions.

A key subject of the Directions is **investment in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, which is addressed as a standalone compliance area in Chapter II. The inclusion of AIFs alongside board governance signals that NBFCs must review their investment practices against RBI’s specific constraints and any related approval/monitoring expectations before making such investments. The Directions also cover **overseas investment by NBFCs**—with separate provisions for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs** and for **NBFC-CICs**—indicating that foreign subsidiaries, JVs, or investment structures are regulated differently depending on the NBFC category. For compliance purposes, this means cross-border expansion is not presumed permissible and must be tested against the exact entity-specific conditions in the relevant section.

The document further addresses **expansion of activities through the automatic route**, meaning some service expansions may be allowed without case-by-case prior approval if the NBFC satisfies the prescribed conditions. It also includes a dedicated section on **entry into insurance business**, with separate rules for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs and HFCs**, implying that insurance forays are tightly controlled and depend on the institution’s regulated status. Because the table of contents shows multiple activity-specific chapters rather than a single omnibus permission, the compliance obligation is to verify the exact route, entity type, and activity before launching any new line of business, forming a subsidiary, entering a JV, or making an overseas investment.

The excerpt provided does not include the body text of the specific provisions, so no exact monetary thresholds, capital ratios, filing deadlines, or approval forms can be confirmed from the visible text alone. However, the document’s structure makes clear that it is intended to be the operative RBI framework for these expansion activities and that the relevant obligations are likely detailed in the later sections under each chapter. A compliance team should therefore treat this as the controlling document for business-expansion approvals and confirm the exact procedural requirements, restrictions, and any thresholds in the full text before proceeding with any AIF investment, overseas structure, or insurance-related activity.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025** (as updated through **April 15, 2026**) set the framework for when and how NBFCs may open, close, or operate branches and overseas representative offices. The document applies to **NBFCs** subject to RBI supervision under these Directions and replaces earlier branch-authorisation guidance, with a **repeal-and-saving** structure preserving actions already taken under prior rules where applicable. Although the excerpt provided is only the table of contents, the operative structure shows that the Directions specifically regulate **opening branches in India, opening branches abroad, closing branches, and opening representative offices abroad**, with some prior provisions marked **deleted**, indicating a consolidation and revision of the earlier regime.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that branch-related expansion or overseas presence by an NBFC is not treated as a purely internal business decision; it is governed by RBI authorization rules under these Directions. Any NBFC planning a new branch in India, a branch outside India, or a representative office abroad should assume a **pre-approval/authorisation-based process** rather than an automatic right to open such offices, and should confirm that the proposed activity falls within the specific permissions and procedural requirements in the relevant chapter. The document also contemplates **branch closures**, meaning compliance teams need controls not only for opening new locations but also for proper RBI-compliant winding down or closure of existing ones.

The title page indicates the Directions were issued on **November 28, 2025** and then **updated on April 15, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the April 15, 2026 version as the current authoritative text. Because the excerpt does not include the body text of the rules, no specific numerical thresholds, filing deadlines, or approval criteria are visible here; however, the table of contents confirms that the Directions are organized around procedural requirements for branch authorization and overseas presence, so the full text should be reviewed before any expansion, relocation, or closure decision is implemented. In short, the document is a dedicated RBI rulebook for **where NBFCs may establish physical offices or representative presence and how those actions must be handled under RBI oversight**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and apply to **all categories of NBFCs at all regulatory layers**, unless a specific provision says otherwise. The RBI issues these directions under its powers in **sections 45K, 45L, and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934**, and the purpose is to govern how voluntary amalgamations of NBFCs are to be handled under RBI oversight.

From the material provided, the document establishes the RBI’s framework for **granting a No Objection Certificate (NOC) and/or approval** for voluntary amalgamation transactions involving NBFCs. That means any NBFC seeking to merge voluntarily with another entity must follow the RBI’s prescribed process rather than proceeding purely as a corporate law matter; the RBI is asserting regulatory control over the transaction before it can be completed. Because the applicability is stated broadly, the compliance impact is not limited to a particular size or layer of NBFC unless later provisions carve out exceptions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that these Directions create a **mandatory RBI approval/NOC route** for voluntary amalgamations of NBFCs, and they are not future-dated—they are operative immediately upon issuance on **November 28, 2025**. The document excerpt does not yet include the detailed procedural steps, eligibility conditions, forms, timelines, or substantive approval criteria, but it clearly signals that NBFCs contemplating amalgamation must treat RBI consent as a required precondition and align internal transaction planning, board approvals, and regulatory filings accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under Sections **45JA, 45K, 45L, 45M, and 45MA** of the RBI Act, 1934. The document is a replacement/updated framework governing **acquisition of shareholding or control in NBFCs** and is structured around when RBI prior approval is required, what information must be filed, what public notice must be given before a change in control/management, and how investments from **FATF non-compliant jurisdictions** are treated. It applies specifically to **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** and transactions that result in an acquisition of shareholding or a change in control or management of an NBFC.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that **prior RBI approval is required before acquiring shareholding or control in an NBFC** where the transaction crosses the thresholds or otherwise falls within the scope set out in the Directions. The document also lays down a formal **application process for prior approval**, meaning the acquirer and the NBFC must prepare and submit the prescribed information to RBI before closing the transaction. In addition, where there is a proposed **change in control or management**, the Directions require a **prior public notice** to be issued, so the parties cannot treat the transaction as purely private; the notice obligation is intended to inform the market and stakeholders in advance of the change.

The Directions further impose restrictions or additional scrutiny for transactions involving **investment from jurisdictions identified by FATF as non-compliant**. That means any proposed acquisition funding or ownership chain involving such jurisdictions will trigger enhanced regulatory concern and may be disallowed or subjected to special conditions under RBI’s framework. The document also includes a **repeal and saving clause**, indicating that prior inconsistent directions are revoked while preserving actions already taken or rights/liabilities accrued under the earlier regime, and it clarifies that other applicable laws are **not barred** by these Directions.

Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not yet disclose the specific numerical ownership thresholds, exact filing forms, timelines, or the detailed content of the public notice**; those are likely contained in the body and annex. A compliance team should therefore treat this as confirmation that RBI has issued a formal new control-acquisition regime for NBFCs effective from the date of issuance, and should review the operative chapters immediately for any transaction involving acquisition of shares, voting rights, managerial control, or a change in ownership structure of an NBFC.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This document is the RBI’s consolidated 2025 framework for NBFC registration, exemptions, reporting, and scale-based regulation, issued under the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and it applies to every Non-Banking Financial Company unless a specific exemption or carve-out is stated. It is dated November 28, 2025 and is presented as “updated as on July 01, 2026,” so compliance teams should treat it as the operative version incorporating amendments up to that date. The RBI states that the directions are issued in the public interest to regulate the financial system and to prevent NBFC affairs from being conducted in a way detrimental to depositors, investors, or the NBFC itself.

The document’s core substantive change is the creation and operation of a scale-based regulatory framework for NBFCs, meaning compliance obligations are not uniform across all entities but depend on the size, type, and risk profile of the NBFC. The framework is organized into chapters covering preliminary provisions, scale-based regulation, registration requirements, exemptions from the RBI Act, reporting obligations, and repeal/other transitional provisions. For a compliance team, this means the first task is to determine the entity’s classification under the RBI’s framework, because that classification will drive registration status, prudential requirements, reporting frequency/content, and which provisions of the RBI Act continue to apply versus which are exempted.

The document expressly addresses registration requirements, so any entity carrying on NBFC activities must assess whether registration with the RBI is required and whether any statutory exemption applies. It also creates a separate chapter on exemptions from the provisions of the RBI Act, 1934, indicating that certain NBFCs, activities, or classes of entities may be relieved from some statutory requirements only to the extent specified in these directions. Compliance teams should therefore review not just whether the business is an NBFC, but also whether it falls within an exempt category and whether the exemption is conditional or limited.

The reporting chapter indicates that NBFCs have ongoing reporting obligations to the RBI, and these obligations are part of the directions themselves rather than a separate standalone circular. Because the document is a consolidated framework, the compliance posture should be assumed to include continuing RBI reporting and internal controls to support classification under the scale-based regime, registration/renewal monitoring, and any exemption reliance. The final chapter on repeal and other provisions indicates that prior directions are being superseded or read together with transition rules, so teams should verify whether legacy policies, filings, or compliance calendars need to be updated to align with the 2025 framework as updated through July 1, 2026.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Asset Reconstruction Companies – Know Your Customer” Directions, 2025 (DOR/2025-26/377, DOR.AML.REC.No.296/14.01.010/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025; updated as on December 29, 2025) establish the KYC/AML framework specifically for Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) to prevent their use for money laundering or terrorist financing and to preserve financial-system integrity. The document is structured into eleven chapters covering preliminary provisions, general requirements, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, customer due diligence, recordkeeping, FIU-India reporting, handling communications from international agencies, other instructions, and repeal/transition provisions, with two annexes. From the excerpt provided, the core regulatory change is that ARCs are now expressly subject to RBI’s consolidated KYC expectations under these Directions, rather than only general AML principles, and the directions are intended to govern how ARCs identify customers, maintain records, and report suspicious or prescribed information.  

For compliance teams, the key implication is that ARCs must implement a formal customer acceptance policy, risk-based controls, customer identification procedures, and customer due diligence procedures tailored to the ARC business model, and must maintain records and reporting processes aligned to those obligations. The directions also require ARCs to report to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND) where applicable and to comply with obligations arising from international agreements and communications from international agencies. Chapter XI indicates there are repeal and other transitional provisions, meaning prior related instructions are superseded or modified and firms must confirm which legacy directions cease to apply once the new framework is in force.  

The excerpt you provided does not include the operative chapters’ detailed thresholds, dates, or procedural steps, so I cannot reliably state specific deadlines, numeric thresholds, or category-by-category customer requirements from the text shown. However, a compliance officer should treat the November 28, 2025 issue date and the “updated as on December 29, 2025” status as signals that the final, consolidated directions may contain amendments or clarifications relative to the original issue, and should review the full chapters and annexes for exact onboarding, identification, record retention, reporting timing, and escalation requirements before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 12 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005** to create a formal system for **disseminating credit information on wilful defaulters** so lenders can be cautioned and **additional institutional finance is not extended** to such borrowers. The Directions are titled as above and **come into force immediately** on issuance. They apply to **all Asset Reconstruction Companies**; the document also states that the restrictions relating to **further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters** and the provisions on **large defaulters** apply to the relevant entities covered by the Directions, with detailed treatment to be administered through the reporting framework set out in the next chapter.

The substantive compliance focus of the document is the **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters** by ARCs, with the objective of feeding reliable credit information into the financial system. The Directions introduce reporting requirements backed by prescribed formats: **Annex I** sets the **format for submission of the list of large defaulters**, and **Annex II** sets the **format for submission of data on cases of wilful default**. For a compliance team, the key operational implication is that ARCs must maintain internal processes to identify relevant default cases, compile the required borrower/case information in the RBI-prescribed templates, and ensure that the information used for cautioning the market is reported in a consistent and timely manner.

The document is also structured to include a **repeal and savings framework** in Chapter III, meaning prior directions or instructions on the same subject are being replaced or superseded to the extent covered by this 2025 instrument. No monetary thresholds, rates, or numerical limits are visible in the excerpt provided, so a compliance officer should review the full text and annexures for any definitions of “wilful defaulter,” “large defaulter,” reporting cutoffs, submission timelines, or specific data fields that create additional operational obligations. Based on the text shown, the immediate compliance takeaway is that **ARCs must be prepared to implement RBI’s mandatory reporting and caution-listing framework for wilful and large defaulters without delay**, using the annexed reporting formats.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) and credit information reporting set out the reporting, membership, data-quality, customer-service, and governance obligations that apply to ARCs in their role as credit information providers. The directions are issued by RBI under the cited circular reference and, according to the title, are updated as of July 1, 2026; the document itself is framed as the operative compliance instrument for ARCs with respect to credit information reporting and dissemination to credit information companies (CICs). At a high level, the directions require ARCs to participate in the CIC ecosystem, submit and maintain accurate credit information in the prescribed formats, and comply with RBI’s reporting timelines, rectification processes, and customer redress requirements.

A major substantive requirement is membership of CICs: ARCs must be members of credit information companies and operate in the manner specified by RBI for furnishing and receiving credit information. The reporting chapter then governs how ARCs must transmit loan/account-level data, including use of RBI-prescribed data formats and adherence to reporting timelines and periodic updation requirements. The directions also require ARCs to follow reporting guidelines designed to ensure data consistency and completeness, and they specifically contemplate rejection of non-compliant data submissions, with a mandated rectification process for rejected data and review of the ARC’s Data Quality Index (DQI), which implies that persistent data-quality failures may be tracked and assessed by regulators.

The document also addresses correction of Credit Information Reports, meaning ARCs must participate in correcting inaccurate bureau records when discrepancies are identified. It further requires ARCs to use credit information reports in credit appraisal, so credit decisions and recoveries must be supported by CIC data rather than handled informally. There is also a display/disclosure obligation for information, which indicates that certain prescribed credit-information-related details must be made available in the manner required by the directions.

Finally, the directions establish a Technical Working Group and a customer service and grievance redressal framework, which means ARCs will need internal processes and designated accountability for technical implementation, complaint handling, and escalation. For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that these directions are not merely advisory: they create ongoing obligations to become and remain CIC members, report accurately and on time, correct rejected or inaccurate data, monitor data-quality metrics, and maintain a functioning grievance process tied to credit information reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on March 10, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) Directions, 2025** are a comprehensive regulatory framework for ARCs, issued under RBI authority on **November 28, 2025** and marked as **updated through March 10, 2026**. The document reorganizes and consolidates requirements across registration, governance, asset reconstruction and securitisation activities, prudential regulation, accounting/disclosure, and miscellaneous compliance obligations, so any entity operating as an ARC in India—or seeking to register as one—would need to treat this as its core rulebook. The title and structure indicate that the directions supersede prior fragmented instructions and create a single continuing framework for ARCs’ conduct, board oversight, reporting, and operational standards.

From a compliance perspective, the document specifically governs **the role of the board of directors, registration and related matters**, implying formal requirements around governance and eligibility before an entity can function as an ARC. It then sets out **guidelines on asset reconstruction and securitisation**, meaning the manner in which ARCs may acquire, manage, restructure, and resolve financial assets is subject to RBI-prescribed conditions rather than general commercial discretion. A separate chapter on **prudential regulations** indicates ongoing capital, exposure, asset-quality, provisioning, or similar risk-management requirements, while the **governance and conduct** chapter signals that ARCs must comply with conduct standards beyond pure prudential rules. The **accounting and disclosures** chapter means the directions also impose specific financial reporting and transparency obligations, and the **miscellaneous instructions** plus **repeal and other provisions** chapters indicate the document also addresses transition, applicability, and the treatment of prior directions.

For compliance teams, the most important operational takeaway is that these directions are meant to be **binding regulatory instructions for ARCs**, not merely guidance, and they likely require internal policies, board approvals, reporting controls, and monitoring procedures to be aligned with RBI expectations. The document reference to **Annexes I–VI** suggests that detailed formats, definitions, forms, or technical criteria are attached and must be consulted for exact implementation. Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not** show the substantive thresholds, ratios, deadlines, or detailed procedural steps; however, the title and chapter layout make clear that affected entities should review the full text carefully for registration conditions, ongoing prudential limits, disclosures, and any transition provisions that became effective with the 2025 directions and subsequent March 10, 2026 updates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Credit Information Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** establishes a formal outsourcing-risk framework specifically for **credit information companies (CICs)**, with the stated aim of ensuring that outsourcing arrangements do not weaken governance, data protection, security, confidentiality, accountability, or regulatory compliance. The directions are issued by the RBI under its supervisory authority and apply to outsourcing of relevant activities by CICs; they are organized around board oversight, senior management responsibility, IT outsourcing governance, and risk management controls. The document indicates a structured compliance regime beginning with a board-approved outsourcing policy and ongoing oversight responsibilities, rather than leaving outsourcing decisions to operational teams or vendors.

At the governance level, the **Board must approve the outsourcing policy** and remains ultimately responsible for outsourced activities even when functions are performed by external providers. The board is expected to set the risk appetite, review material outsourcing arrangements, and ensure that the CIC has adequate systems to identify, manage, and monitor outsourcing risk. Senior management is tasked with implementing the policy, maintaining effective controls, and ensuring that business, IT, legal, and risk functions coordinate on outsourcing decisions; the IT function has a defined role in assessing technical risk, security, resilience, and vendor performance where technology services are outsourced.

For **IT outsourcing**, the directions require CICs to adopt a governance framework that provides **authorization, accountability, and oversight** over outsourced technology services. The compliance focus is on ensuring that outsourced IT arrangements are properly approved, risk-assessed, documented, and monitored, with attention to service continuity, cybersecurity, data access controls, and the ability of the CIC to supervise and audit the provider. The document also indicates that the outsourcing policy and controls must be designed to prevent over-dependence on third parties and to preserve the CIC’s capacity to meet its regulatory and operational obligations.

The directions further require a **risk management framework** for outsourcing, meaning CICs must identify and assess risks before entering into arrangements and continue monitoring them throughout the relationship. Although the excerpt provided does not show the later chapter details, the structure indicates the document will include requirements on risk assessment, contractual safeguards, due diligence, monitoring, and escalation/termination controls. The effective date is tied to the issuance date shown on the document—**November 28, 2025**—and compliance teams should treat the directions as operative from that date unless a later commencement date is specified in the omitted sections.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Credit Information Companies Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the operating, governance, reporting, customer-service, and grievance-handling requirements for **credit information companies (CICs)** and the entities that participate in the credit-information ecosystem. The directions apply to CICs operating under RBI regulation and address their board oversight, statutory compliance, investment limitations, membership rules, data submission and dissemination processes, technical governance, and customer redress systems.

A key area is **governance and board responsibility**: the directions assign the board of a CIC explicit responsibility for ensuring compliance with the RBI framework and for overseeing the CIC’s policies, systems, and controls. They also restate the **statutory framework governing CICs** and the RBI’s authority over their functioning, meaning compliance teams must treat the directions as the operative regulatory baseline rather than just internal policy guidance.

The directions also cover **investment in CICs**, indicating that ownership and investment structures are regulated and that any shareholding or investment activity in a CIC must fit within the RBI’s prescribed framework. For compliance purposes, this means changes in control, investment arrangements, or ownership percentages need to be reviewed against the directions before implementation.

A substantial portion of the document governs **credit information reporting and dissemination**. It addresses **membership of CICs**, the obligations of **credit institutions (CIs)** when submitting data, and the CIC’s role in ensuring that information is collected, validated, maintained, and shared properly. The directions require CICs to have processes for receiving data from reporting institutions, handling errors and corrections, and disseminating credit information only in accordance with permitted purposes and access conditions. Compliance officers should note that this is not just a technical IT requirement: it imposes ongoing procedural obligations around data quality, timeliness, accuracy, and controlled access.

The document also establishes a **Technical Working Group (TWG)** and a **standing sub-group**, indicating an ongoing governance mechanism for technical standards, operational issues, and coordination within the credit-information framework. This signals that CICs may be expected to align systems and reporting practices with standards or decisions emerging from these bodies, so regulatory monitoring should include TWG-related developments.

Finally, the directions include a chapter on **customer service and grievance redressal**, which means CICs must maintain formal processes to handle consumer complaints, dispute resolution, and service-quality expectations. In practical terms, compliance teams should expect obligations around complaint tracking, turnaround times, escalation, and the correction of inaccurate credit information where required. Because the document is an updated 2026 version of the 2025 directions, compliance staff should use the updated text as the operative version and verify any implementation dates, thresholds, or procedural changes against the full chapters referenced in the table of contents before relying on prior versions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI circular titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026”** is a consolidated supervisory directions document for commercial banks, issued by the **Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office, Mumbai**, dated **July 31, 2026**. It brings together and standardizes compliance expectations across several operational areas, including **IT system access, monitoring end-use of funds, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), fair practices in charging interest, inoperative accounts/unclaimed deposits, nomination facility, and fraud prevention**. The document is aimed at **commercial banks** and is intended to function as a supervisory framework that banks must follow, with chapter-wise requirements applying depending on the relevant business activity or control area.

For **IT systems access**, the directions require banks to establish controlled and monitored access arrangements to their information technology systems, implying governance over who can access systems and how access is tracked and restricted. The **monitoring of end use of funds** chapter indicates that banks must have procedures to verify that funds are used for their intended purposes, which would typically require post-disbursement checks, documentation, and escalation where misuse or diversion is detected. These requirements are compliance-relevant for lending, treasury, operations, and internal control teams because they affect the bank’s ability to demonstrate oversight of customer and borrower funds.

The document also contains a dedicated **Prompt Corrective Action Framework** chapter, meaning banks must comply with RBI’s intervention framework when financial or supervisory indicators weaken. Although the excerpt does not show the exact thresholds, the existence of a formal PCA chapter means banks should expect **trigger-based regulatory restrictions, monitoring, and remediation obligations** once RBI-prescribed capital, asset quality, profitability, or leverage benchmarks are breached. Compliance teams should treat this as a requirement to maintain continuous monitoring, board-level escalation, and readiness to implement RBI-imposed business restrictions if PCA thresholds are crossed.

Under **Fair Practices Code – Charging of Interest**, banks are required to follow prescribed fair-lending and disclosure standards when levying interest, which would ordinarily include transparent communication of rates and adherence to internal policy and contractual terms. The **Inoperative Accounts / Unclaimed Deposits** chapter requires banks to manage dormant or unclaimed balances according to RBI-prescribed procedures, which generally involves identifying such accounts, undertaking customer contact efforts, and maintaining safe custody and reporting controls. The **Nomination Facility** chapter requires banks to provide and administer nomination options in line with regulatory requirements, so account opening and maintenance processes must ensure customers are informed of nomination rights and that nominations are correctly captured and updated.

The final portion shown covers **fraud prevention measures**, including frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **retail loan bulk proposal sanctions**, and **frauds involving fake title deeds of property**. This means banks must have stronger internal controls, segregation of duties, due diligence, and exception reporting around these specific fraud channels, with heightened scrutiny where staff collusion or document fraud is involved. Since the table of contents indicates more detailed subparts beyond the excerpt, compliance officers should assume the full directions contain operational obligations and reporting/escalation steps for fraud detection, sanction controls, and preventive monitoring, and should review the complete text for any explicit timelines, thresholds, or mandatory reporting formats not visible here.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns Directions, 2026** are issued by the **Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office** and are dated **July 31, 2026**. They apply to **commercial banks** and establish the governance, data, and filing framework for RBI supervisory returns. The directions are organized around board/senior management accountability, reporting infrastructure, and detailed return-filing requirements.

A key requirement is that the **board and senior management remain responsible for the completeness, accuracy, and timeliness of supervisory reporting**, and banks must maintain appropriate oversight and internal controls over the return-filing process. The directions also require banks to have adequate **data architecture and IT infrastructure** to support supervisory reporting, with systems capable of producing reliable regulatory data and ensuring integrity of reporting across source systems, reconciliations, and submission workflows. Banks are expected to implement processes that ensure **accuracy and integrity in reporting**, which implies validation, review, and governance over data used in supervisory returns.

The document then sets out the **filing of supervisory returns**, including **operational guidelines, a list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, and penalties**. Although the excerpt does not list the individual returns or exact due dates, the directions clearly indicate that commercial banks must comply with the RBI’s specified reporting calendar and any prescribed formats/instructions for each return. Banks should therefore identify all returns covered by the directions and align internal reporting ownership, data collection, and sign-off processes accordingly.

For compliance purposes, the most important operational takeaway from the document excerpt is that the RBI is formalizing a structured supervisory-return regime with explicit expectations around governance, system readiness, accuracy controls, and punctual submission. Because the document includes a dedicated **penalties** section, failures in filing, data quality, or adherence to timelines may attract regulatory consequences. A compliance team should review the full schedule of returns and deadlines in the complete text and ensure the bank’s control environment is set up to meet the RBI’s reporting requirements from the applicable commencement date of the directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** under the Department of Supervision, and these directions replace/update the RBI’s framework for the appointment, independence, tenure, and oversight of statutory auditors for commercial banks. The document applies to **commercial banks** and sets out mandatory requirements for the **board and senior management**, who must oversee the audit function and ensure compliance with the RBI’s appointment and governance standards. It also specifically governs the **number and coverage of Statutory Central Auditors and Statutory Auditors**, the **eligibility and independence criteria** for auditors, the **professional standards** they must follow, and the **rules on tenure and rotation**.

For banks, a major compliance obligation is that statutory audit appointments must be made only through the RBI-prescribed process, with the board and management responsible for ensuring that auditors meet the RBI’s **eligibility criteria** and do not compromise **independence**. The directions also address **audit fees and expenses**, meaning banks must structure compensation and reimbursements in line with the RBI framework rather than ad hoc arrangements. The document further indicates a formal **appointment procedure**, so banks will need to align internal governance, nomination/approval workflows, and documentation practices with the RBI requirements rather than relying solely on prior board-level practice.

Because the table of contents shows dedicated sections on governance, eligibility, independence, tenure, fees, and appointment procedure, compliance teams should expect these directions to impose both **substantive auditor-qualification requirements** and **process controls** around selection, rotation, and oversight. The key date visible in the document is the **issue date: 31 July 2026**; the excerpt provided does not include the detailed effective date or transition timetable, so those would need to be confirmed in the operative text before implementation planning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Internal Audit Function” Directions, 2026** are a new supervisory framework issued by the RBI’s Department of Supervision on **31 July 2026** (circular reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/413**, **DoS.CO.PPG.7/11.01.005/2026-27**). The document is directed at **commercial banks** and sets out mandatory requirements for how the internal audit function must be governed, structured, and operated. Its stated focus is to strengthen the **risk-based internal audit framework**, with explicit expectations for board oversight, senior management accountability, functional independence, audit planning, and communication/reporting processes.

From the table of contents, the Directions apply across several core compliance areas: **preliminary applicability and commencement**, **governance and oversight**, and **risk-based internal audit framework**. Under governance, the document assigns specific responsibilities to the **Board** and to **senior management**, indicating that internal audit can no longer be treated as a purely operational function; it must be actively overseen at the highest levels. The internal audit framework chapter shows that banks must have a formal **policy on internal audit**, ensure **functional independence** of the function, conduct structured **risk assessment**, define the **scope** of audits, establish **communication** channels for findings, and implement **performance evaluation** of the function itself.

The excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative text of each requirement, so the precise thresholds, deadlines, reporting formats, or transition periods are not visible here. However, the document clearly signals that compliance officers should expect a formal RBI-mandated internal audit regime for commercial banks that likely requires board-approved policy governance, documented risk-based audit planning, and demonstrable independence from the business and control functions being audited. The effective date is tied to the issuance date in the title block (**31 July 2026**), but because the substantive commencement clause is not visible in the excerpt, any implementation date or transitional grace period would need to be confirmed from the full text before finalizing compliance actions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** (issued **31 July 2026**) establish a consolidated fraud-risk governance and detection framework for **commercial banks** subject to RBI supervision. The document requires banks to put in place a formal **governance structure for fraud risk management**, including board and senior-management oversight, so that fraud prevention, detection, reporting, and remediation are handled through defined institutional responsibilities rather than ad hoc responses. It also introduces a structured **Early Warning Signal (EWS)** and **Red Flagging Account (RFA)** framework for identifying stress or suspicious activity in advance of a confirmed fraud.

The document is issued by RBI’s Department of Supervision and is intended to strengthen the security of payment channels such as internet/mobile banking and other digital payment applications operated by covered banks. It is a supervisory direction, so compliance is not optional: banks must align their internal governance, technology controls, and customer-facing processes with the requirements in the directions.

A key compliance obligation is that the bank’s Board must approve a policy framework for digital payment security and oversee implementation through governance arrangements that assign accountability for security risk management. The directions require banks to maintain structured security controls across the full application life cycle, including secure development, testing, change management, deployment, and ongoing vulnerability management. They also require stronger authentication controls for customer access and transaction approval, meaning banks must ensure authentication frameworks are risk-sensitive and resilient against unauthorized access, rather than relying only on weak or legacy login methods.

The document also places explicit obligations on fraud risk management and reconciliation. Banks must have systems to detect suspicious or fraudulent digital payment activity, respond to it promptly, and reconcile digital payment transactions with internal records and settlement outcomes to identify breaks or failures. In addition, banks must maintain customer protection measures, including customer awareness initiatives and a grievance-redressal mechanism so customers can report issues and receive timely resolution for failed, disputed, or unauthorized digital payment transactions.

The document’s title page shows it was issued on July 31, 2026, and the directions are identified as RBI/DoS/2026-27/411 and DoS.CO.CSITEG.5/31.01.015/2026-27. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** (issued **July 31, 2026**) set out the mandatory framework for appointing, rotating, supervising, compensating, and replacing statutory auditors of **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The directions apply to all SFBs and are intended to govern the statutory audit process under RBI supervision, with emphasis on board responsibility, auditor independence, and regular rotation of audit firms and partners.

For governance, the document requires the **Board and senior management** of each SFB to take active responsibility for the audit process rather than treating it as a routine administrative exercise. They must ensure proper appointment procedures, monitor auditor performance and independence, and maintain oversight over any issues that arise during the audit cycle. The directions also establish detailed rules for how many statutory central auditors/statutory auditors may be appointed and how branch coverage is to be allocated, meaning the scope of audit work must be structured in accordance with RBI-prescribed limits rather than left entirely to bank discretion.

The directions specify **eligibility criteria** for auditors, including requirements intended to ensure competence, independence, and professional standing, and they impose explicit restrictions to prevent conflicts of interest. Auditors must comply with professional standards, and the bank must verify that the chosen audit firms and partners are not disqualified under RBI rules or otherwise impaired in their independence. The document also addresses **tenure and rotation**, requiring periodic rotation of audit firms and, where applicable, audit partners, so the same auditor cannot continue indefinitely in a way that would compromise objectivity.

The directions further regulate **audit fees and expenses**, implying that compensation must be structured and approved in a manner consistent with RBI expectations and not in a way that could undermine auditor independence. They also provide a formal **appointment procedure**, meaning the bank must follow a prescribed process rather than making ad hoc appointments. Overall, the compliance impact is that SFBs must review their auditor appointment governance, independence screening, rotation tracking, and board oversight processes to ensure they align with the RBI’s 2026 statutory audit requirements from the date the directions take effect.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026

A key requirement is that the **board** must approve and oversee the internal audit policy and ensure the audit function has adequate authority, resources, independence, and access to records and personnel. **Senior management** must implement the framework, ensure timely remediation of audit observations, and support the internal audit team without interfering with its objectivity. The directions also require a formal **risk assessment process** to determine audit priorities and frequency, meaning audit coverage must be driven by the bank’s risk profile rather than a fixed or purely calendar-based plan.

The internal audit function must be **functionally independent**, properly documented, and structured to cover the bank’s material activities, processes, systems, and control environment. The directions set expectations for the **scope of audit**, including review of governance, operations, compliance, risk management, and internal controls, and require that audit findings be formally communicated and tracked through corrective action and closure. The framework also contemplates clear reporting lines, escalation of significant issues, and periodic reporting to the board or its audit committee so that unresolved weaknesses and high-risk issues receive prompt attention.

Where the document becomes operationally important for compliance teams is that it creates an enforceable requirement for each SFB to maintain a **policy on internal audit**, ensure **adequate staffing and competence**, and conduct audits using a documented, risk-based methodology. Compliance officers should expect to review whether the bank’s existing audit charter, reporting structure, issue-tracking process, and board oversight arrangements align with these directions once they take effect. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026

It applies to payments banks and is issued under RBI supervision effective from the date of the circular dated **July 31, 2026**; compliance teams should treat it as binding from that issuance date unless the text specifies a later operative date. The directions place responsibility on the **Board and senior management** to ensure that the statutory audit process is properly governed, including selection, independence safeguards, and ongoing oversight of the auditors’ work.

A major substantive requirement is the new or clarified framework for **appointment of statutory central auditors/statutory auditors**, including limits on how many auditors may be appointed, eligibility conditions, independence requirements, professional standards, tenure limits, and rotation rules. The document explicitly addresses the **number of auditors permitted**, which indicates RBI is controlling concentration and ensuring appropriate scale of coverage for payments banks. It also sets out detailed **eligibility criteria** for auditors, meaning the bank must verify that any proposed audit firm or individual meets RBI’s standards before appointment; the compliance burden is not just to appoint an auditor, but to document that the auditor satisfies the prescribed qualifications and independence tests. The directions further require the bank to follow RBI’s rules on **independence, professional conduct, and audit standards**, so audit committees should expect stricter conflict-checking, confirmations from audit firms, and documentation around any relationships that could impair objectivity.

The document also introduces a structured regime for **tenure and rotation**, meaning payments banks cannot retain the same statutory auditor indefinitely and must track service periods to ensure timely replacement when the maximum tenure is reached. Because the table of contents separately identifies **audit fees and expenses**, the directions also regulate how audit compensation and reimbursable costs are handled, which is material for budgeting and for avoiding arrangements that could appear to compromise auditor independence. In addition, the **appointment procedure** is expressly covered, so the bank must follow the RBI-prescribed process rather than using an ad hoc hiring approach; compliance teams should expect formal board/committee approvals, required declarations or certificates, and documented submissions/records for regulatory review.

The document further includes a separate chapter on the **Long Form Audit Report**, signaling that statutory auditors of payments banks must provide more than a routine financial-statement opinion and must report in a detailed format that likely covers internal controls, compliance observations, and other matters RBI expects to be surfaced to governance bodies. Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed operative clauses, the structure makes clear that payments banks will need procedures to manage auditor onboarding, independence attestations, rotation tracking, fee approvals, and the receipt and review of the Long Form Audit Report. Compliance officers should therefore assess whether current audit governance documents, board committee terms of reference, and appointment calendars align with these RBI directions and prepare for immediate implementation from the July 31, 2026 circular date.

A key substantive requirement is that payments banks must implement an operational process for early detection of frauds, rather than relying only on post-event investigation. The document’s Chapter III directs banks to create governance around early warning signals for banking transactions and to treat red flags as part of a controlled fraud-risk workflow, which implies defined monitoring rules, escalation triggers, and action steps when suspicious activity is identified. This is a compliance obligation affecting transaction monitoring, account surveillance, and internal reporting processes across the bank’s retail and operational channels.

The directions further require independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals, where relevant, before relying on their outputs or certifications. This means payments banks cannot simply accept third-party representations at face value in fraud-sensitive contexts; they need a verification step and supporting controls around outsourced or external dependencies. The document also includes staff accountability and penal measures, indicating that employees involved in fraud-risk management may face internal consequences where controls are not followed, and the bank must have a clear discipline or accountability framework tied to fraud-related lapses.

Although the excerpt provided ends before the full text of the later chapters, the document is organized to cover governance, early detection, and general instructions, which signals a comprehensive compliance regime rather than advisory guidance. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026** under RBI’s Department of Supervision (reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/450** and **DoS.CO.PPG.44/11.01.005/2026-27**). A key substantive requirement concerns **fair practices in charging interest**. Local area banks must ensure their interest-charging practices comply with RBI’s fair-practice expectations, meaning interest must be levied transparently and in a manner that is not arbitrary or misleading to customers. The direction is meant to govern how banks calculate, disclose, and apply interest so that borrowers and depositors are treated consistently and the bank’s internal systems align with RBI’s supervisory standards.

The directions also impose requirements for handling **inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits**. Local area banks must maintain processes for identifying accounts that have become inactive/inoperative and for dealing with balances that remain unclaimed, with the aim of protecting customer funds, preventing misuse, and ensuring proper recordkeeping and follow-up. Compliance officers should expect obligations around periodic review, customer outreach, and internal controls so that dormant balances are not neglected and can be properly reported or transferred in accordance with RBI’s rules.

A substantial portion of the document is devoted to **fraud prevention measures**. The RBI specifically addresses frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, and **frauds involving fake title deeds of property deposits**. It also requires safeguards for the **safe custody of critical documents** and sets expectations for **accounts opened by employees**, indicating that banks must have internal controls to detect conflicts of interest, unusual transactions, document tampering, and staff misuse of account-opening processes. The document further includes “other instructions,” indicating that fraud controls are not limited to the enumerated scenarios and that banks must maintain broader anti-fraud governance, escalation, and monitoring arrangements.

The final major area is a **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which establishes a channel for confidential reporting of wrongdoing. The table of contents shows that the scheme covers **scope and coverage**, indicating that the directions will specify who can make protected disclosures, what types of misconduct can be reported, and how such reports are to be handled. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that the bank must have procedures to receive, protect, investigate, and escalate whistleblower-style complaints without retaliation, while maintaining confidentiality and documentation.

Overall, the document is a supervisory instruction package for local area banks that tightens expectations on customer fairness, dormant-account management, anti-fraud controls, document security, employee-account controls, and protected reporting. Because the excerpt provided shows the structure but not the detailed chapter text, the compliance significance is that the bank should treat these chapter headings as mandatory control areas requiring operational procedures, monitoring, and staff accountability effective from the direction’s issuance date unless a chapter specifies a different implementation timeline in its detailed provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:

At a high level, the document requires local area banks to maintain a **concurrent audit system covering identified business areas, transactions, and control points on an ongoing basis**, rather than relying only on period-end or statutory review. The board and senior management are expected to oversee the audit framework, ensure the scope is commensurate with the bank’s size, risk profile, and operations, and make sure audit observations are tracked to closure. The Directions also require the bank to maintain a reporting system so that material irregularities, exceptions, and control failures identified through concurrent audit are escalated appropriately and promptly addressed.
