The Directions further provide that the appointment should be for a defined **tenure** and that **remuneration** must be structured and approved in a manner consistent with the bank’s governance framework, rather than being left to informal negotiation. The reporting system under the Directions is intended to ensure periodic communication of audit findings and follow-up on unresolved issues.

The contents also indicate that the Directions contain a **repeal and other provisions** chapter, which means earlier RBI instructions on the same subject are being superseded or consolidated by this 2026 framework. For compliance purposes, local area banks should treat this as the operative RBI direction governing concurrent audit from the stated effective date in the final text, and they should review existing audit charters, committee oversight processes, auditor engagement terms, and reporting templates to ensure alignment with the new requirements. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** or a **board memo format**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Local Area Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026” are a new supervisory framework for local area banks, issued by the Department of Supervision and dated July 31, 2026, under circular reference RBI/DoS/2026-27/444 and DoS.CO.PPG.38/11.01.005/2026-27. The directions set out mandatory requirements for how a local area bank must organize, govern, staff, and operate its compliance function, with the intent of making compliance a formal, board-supervised function rather than an ad hoc operational activity. The document’s effective date is not visible in the excerpt provided, so the compliance team should confirm the commencement date in the full text or associated notification.

From the portion shown, the directions specifically address chapter-level obligations on governance and oversight, the role of the board, the role of senior management, and the need for a formal compliance policy. They also cover the scope of the compliance function, including group-wide compliance, the internal structure of the function, and staffing expectations. Because the table of contents shows a dedicated staffing section, the directions likely require banks to assign sufficient resources and define reporting lines and responsibilities, rather than relying on a dispersed or informal control arrangement.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that local area banks will need to evidence a documented compliance framework, board involvement in oversight, senior-management accountability, and a defined internal compliance organization with adequate personnel. The excerpt does not include the detailed thresholds, timelines, or procedural steps within each chapter, so a full implementation assessment should review the complete directions for any specific approval requirements, reporting frequencies, independence standards, escalation obligations, or transition deadlines that may apply.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) - Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026”** on **31 July 2026** under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including **Section 35-A read with Section 51**). The document states that these directions are issued in the public interest and are intended to govern certain supervisory and compliance matters for **regional rural banks**. The excerpt provided shows that the directions are structured into four parts: preliminary provisions, fair practices rules for lenders on charging interest, fraud-related requirements for loans and advances, and repeal/savings and interpretation provisions.

From the table of contents and opening text, the directions apply specifically to **RRBs** and are framed as supervisory directions rather than a standalone policy note. The document explicitly includes a **Chapter on “Fair Practices Code for Lenders - Charging of Interest”**, which indicates that RRBs will have to follow RBI-prescribed fairness standards in how interest is levied on lending products. It also includes a **Chapter on “Frauds in Loans and Advances”**, signaling that RRBs must comply with RBI requirements concerning identification, reporting, and handling of frauds linked to lending activity. However, the excerpt does not yet show the detailed operational rules in those chapters, so the specific procedural steps, thresholds, reporting timelines, or exceptions are not visible in the provided text.

The preliminary chapter indicates the directions will contain provisions on **short title and commencement**, **applicability**, and **definitions**, which means the final document will specify when the directions take effect, which entities and activities are covered, and how key terms should be interpreted for compliance purposes. The closing chapter is also noted to contain **repeal and saving provisions**, an **application of other laws not barred** clause, and **interpretation** rules, which are typically used to clarify that prior inconsistent directions may be superseded while existing legal obligations under other laws remain unaffected unless expressly excluded. In practical terms, a compliance team at an RRB should treat this as a new RBI supervisory framework for interest-charging practices and loan/advance fraud controls, but the excerpt does not provide the operative deadlines, rates, reporting formats, or enforcement consequences beyond the issuance date and statutory basis.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on **31 July 2026** as **RBI/DoS/2026-27/454** and titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026,”** establishes a dedicated fraud-risk framework for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. It is intended to govern how RRBs prevent, detect, escalate, and report fraud-risk events, with an emphasis on formal governance, early-warning systems, and red-flagging of accounts.

The document requires RRBs to maintain a **board-approved governance structure for fraud risk management**, with clear oversight responsibility and internal accountability for identifying and managing fraud risk. It also introduces a structured **Early Warning Signal (EWS) and Red Flag Account (RFA)** framework for **credit facilities/loan accounts**, under which accounts showing suspicious indicators must be monitored, escalated, and, where warranted, marked as red-flagged rather than left to ad hoc branch-level judgment. The framework is not limited to lending: it also covers **other banking/non-credit related transactions**, meaning compliance teams must ensure fraud-monitoring controls extend beyond loan books to operational and transactional activity as well.

A material compliance obligation is the requirement that once a **credit facility/loan account is classified as a Red-Flagged Account**, the RRB must follow the specified reporting and fraud-classification process under Chapter IV, rather than delaying action until loss is fully crystallized. The directions also require **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where such external parties are involved in the transaction or account activity, which means banks cannot rely solely on internal records when validating potentially fraudulent activity. This creates a direct need for documented verification procedures, third-party corroboration, and escalation workflows that can stand up to supervisory review.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the full operational thresholds or every procedural step, the table of contents shows that the directions are comprehensive and organized into: **preliminary provisions, governance and oversight, early detection/EWS-RFA controls, and general instructions on red-flagging and fraud reporting**. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the RBI is moving RRBs toward a more formal, system-driven fraud-risk regime with mandatory governance oversight, account-level warning signals, broader transaction monitoring, and stronger evidentiary requirements before concluding or closing out suspected fraud matters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026”** (dated **July 31, 2026**, issued under **RBI/DoS/2026-27/443**, Ref. **DoS.CO.PPG.37/11.01.005/2026-27**) consolidate supervisory requirements for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** across several operational and compliance areas, including core banking, prompt corrective action, fair practices, nomination, and fraud prevention. The document is organized into chapters covering **preliminary provisions, core banking solution implementation, PCA, fair practices code on charging interest, nomination facility, and fraud prevention measures**, indicating that it is intended as a broad supervisory framework rather than a narrow rule change.

For compliance purposes, the most material operational requirement referenced in the table of contents is the mandate on **Core Banking Solution (CBS) implementation**, which signals that covered UCBs must meet RBI-prescribed CBS-related standards and timelines. The document also includes a dedicated **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework** chapter, meaning banks will be subject to RBI’s risk-based supervisory triggers and restrictions when financial/operational thresholds are breached; compliance teams should expect explicit monitoring obligations, escalation processes, and potential business constraints once PCA conditions are met. Because the actual chapter text is not fully included here, the summary cannot state the specific PCA ratios or cutoffs, but the direction clearly establishes that UCBs must maintain internal surveillance and reporting to detect breach conditions early.

The directions also address **Fair Practices Code requirements relating to charging of interest**, which indicates that UCBs must follow RBI rules on interest computation/disclosure and customer communication, and that any deviations or opaque interest practices may be a compliance issue. The **Nomination Facility** chapter indicates obligations for banks to provide and administer nomination for customer accounts/deposits in accordance with RBI procedures, including the operational processes needed to accept, record, and honor nominations. These are standard customer-facing compliance obligations, but the document’s inclusion as a separate chapter means RBI is treating them as enforceable supervisory requirements rather than optional best practices.

A substantial portion of the document is devoted to **Fraud Prevention Measures**, with subparts covering **coordination among agencies, legal and administrative measures, and precautions/safeguards**. The visible contents show detailed operational controls for safeguarding **cash and valuables, negotiable instruments, and books of account**, implying that UCBs must maintain internal controls, custody procedures, and escalation/reporting mechanisms to reduce theft, misappropriation, or fraud risk. Compliance officers should treat this as a requirement for both preventive controls and incident response: the bank is expected to coordinate internally and externally where fraud risk arises, maintain proper records, and implement physical and documentary safeguards over assets and records.

Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not** reveal the specific effective-date provisions, thresholds, numerical limits, or procedural deadlines that may appear in the chapter text. However, as a July 31, 2026 supervisory direction from RBI’s Department of Supervision, it is clearly intended to be binding on the UCBs within its scope, and compliance teams should review the full chapter text for any implementation dates, reporting timelines, or quantitative trigger points tied to CBS, PCA, interest charging, nomination processing, and fraud-control controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026** under its Department of Supervision, dated **July 31, 2026**. These directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)** and are intended to govern the **preparation, accuracy, governance, and timely filing of supervisory returns** with the RBI. The document makes clear that compliance is not just a filing exercise: the bank’s **board and senior management** are responsible for overseeing the return-reporting framework, maintaining adequate **data architecture and IT infrastructure**, and ensuring the **accuracy and integrity** of all reported information.

A key requirement is that UCBs must file the supervisory returns listed in the directions in the **prescribed manner and within the specified timelines**, with separate treatment for operational guidance, exceptions, and penalties. The document establishes a formal structure for returns submission, including a list of applicable returns and timing rules, which means banks need to map each return they are required to file to the exact RBI timetable rather than relying on ad hoc internal reporting practices. Where exceptions apply, they are addressed explicitly in the directions, indicating that deviations from the standard filing process are only permissible if covered by the RBI’s stated exception framework.

The directions also emphasize governance obligations around the reporting process: management must ensure the bank has systems that can generate reliable supervisory data and support consistent reporting. This implies a compliance expectation that the bank’s internal controls, data validation, and IT systems are capable of producing regulator-ready information without manual rework or reconciliation issues. The requirement for **accuracy and integrity in reporting** suggests that incomplete, incorrect, delayed, or poorly controlled submissions could trigger supervisory consequences.

The document further provides for **penalties** for non-compliance, although the excerpt does not show the penalty amounts or exact enforcement mechanics. From a compliance perspective, the important point is that this is a binding supervisory framework, effective from the date of issue unless the full text specifies otherwise in the commencement section. UCBs should therefore review the complete list of applicable returns, filing deadlines, and any exceptions immediately, then confirm that their governance, systems, and controls are aligned to the RBI’s 2026 reporting regime.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026”** on **31 July 2026** under **RBI/DoS/2026-27/441**. The document sets the statutory audit framework for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**, with the stated purpose of governing how statutory auditors are appointed, how many may be appointed, their eligibility, independence, professional standards, tenure/rotation, and audit fee arrangements. The excerpt provided shows the structure of the directions but does not include the detailed operative clauses beyond the table of contents, so a compliance team should expect the full text to impose mandatory audit-governance requirements on UCB boards and senior management.

From the contents shown, the directions expressly cover: **applicability and definitions**, **board and senior management oversight**, and **appointment rules for statutory auditors/statutory central auditors**, including the **number of auditors and branch coverage**, **eligibility criteria**, **independence requirements**, **professional standards**, **tenure and rotation**, **audit fees and expenses**, and the **appointment procedure**. Because the document is a statutory directions instrument from RBI’s Department of Supervision, it is not merely guidance; it is intended to establish binding compliance expectations for affected banks. The table of contents indicates that the appointment framework is likely to prescribe concrete limits or thresholds for how many auditors a UCB can engage and how audit coverage must be allocated across branches, as well as conditions auditors must satisfy before appointment.

The document also indicates that governance responsibility is placed not only on the auditors but on the **bank’s board and senior management**, implying internal oversight obligations around selecting, approving, and managing the audit process. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as a governance and control requirement affecting the annual statutory audit cycle, including documentation of auditor eligibility, independence checks, rotation/tenure monitoring, and proper approval procedures. No effective date beyond the issuance date is visible in the excerpt, and no numeric thresholds or fee caps are provided in the text supplied; those would need to be confirmed from the full directions before implementation planning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Internal Audit Function” Directions, 2026** (issued **31 July 2026**, circular reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/440** and **DoS.CO.PPG.34/11.01.005/2026-27**) set out mandatory governance and internal audit requirements for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**. The document establishes a **risk-based internal audit framework** and assigns clear accountability to the **board** and **senior management** for approving, overseeing, and ensuring the effectiveness of the internal audit function, rather than treating internal audit as a purely operational task. It also requires the bank to maintain a formal **internal audit policy**, define the **scope and objectives** of internal audit, and ensure the function has appropriate **authority, stature, and independence** so it can operate without undue influence from the business it audits.

The directions appear to require a structured **risk assessment process** to determine audit coverage and priorities, and the internal audit work must be converted into a formal **audit plan** based on the bank’s risk profile. Compliance officers should expect the directions to prescribe how internal audit should identify and prioritize higher-risk areas, and to require periodic review and updating of the audit plan as risks change. Because this is a Reserve Bank supervisory direction, the bank will need to document the methodology used for risk assessment, the rationale for audit selection, and the approval/monitoring trail at board or board-level committee level.

More broadly, the directions are aimed at ensuring UCBs have an internal audit function that is **independent, board-approved, risk-sensitive, and capable of supporting governance and regulatory compliance**. The document is organized into chapters on preliminary matters, governance and oversight, and the risk-based internal audit framework, indicating that obligations likely cover not only audit execution but also reporting lines, escalation, and management responses to findings. The document excerpt provided does not include the later chapters or any specific numerical thresholds, deadlines for phased implementation, or exemptions, so those details would need to be checked in the full text before determining whether any bank-specific transition period or size-based carve-out applies.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management” Directions, 2026** were issued on **July 31, 2026** and are directed at **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**. The document is a comprehensive fraud-risk governance framework, so the key compliance takeaway is that UCBs must maintain a formal, board-supervised fraud risk management structure, with clear accountability for detecting, escalating, investigating, and reporting fraud or suspected fraud across credit and non-credit banking activities. The directions appear to replace or update earlier RBI expectations by codifying a more structured regime around governance, early warning signals, third-party confirmations, and fraud incident handling.

A central requirement is the establishment of a **governance structure for fraud risk management**. UCBs must have a defined internal framework overseen at senior levels, with responsibility for fraud prevention and detection not left to ad hoc operational handling. The bank must ensure that fraud risks are monitored at the institutional level, with escalation channels and oversight mechanisms sufficient to identify suspicious activity early and prevent concealment or delay in reporting. Compliance teams should treat this as requiring board/management ownership, documented internal roles, and ongoing supervisory review of fraud-control effectiveness.

The directions also introduce a formal **Early Warning Signal (EWS) framework** for detecting fraud in **credit facilities/loan accounts** and in **other banking or non-credit transactions**. This means banks must implement systems and processes to identify indicators of suspicious behavior before a fraud fully crystallizes, rather than relying only on post-event detection. The document specifically distinguishes between loan-account risk indicators and other transaction types, so institutions need separate controls appropriate to credit exposures and to operational/payment/service activities. The compliance burden here is to ensure these warning signals are built into internal monitoring, reviewed consistently, and acted upon promptly through defined escalation and investigative procedures.

Another material requirement is the need for **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**. Where a bank relies on external entities or professionals in connection with transactions, underwriting, verification, valuation, audit, legal certification, or related services, it must not treat those representations as automatically reliable; instead, the framework requires independent confirmation in the circumstances contemplated by the directions. This is aimed at reducing fraud risk arising from forged, manipulated, or collusive third-party inputs. For compliance purposes, banks should review vendor, professional, and outsourced-service controls to ensure they can verify external confirmations and detect inconsistencies before relying on them.

The document’s structure also indicates **general instructions** for handling cases where credit facilities, loan accounts, or other banking transactions show indications of fraudulent activity. That implies banks must have a formal response process once red flags arise, including internal review, documentation, escalation, and compliance with any RBI reporting requirements. While the excerpt does not show the detailed reporting timelines or thresholds, the title and chapter headings make clear that the directions are intended to impose institution-wide obligations on UCBs to detect, investigate, and control fraud risk systematically. A compliance team should therefore map the full text into policies, controls, investigation protocols, and staff training, with particular attention to how early warning signals are generated, who reviews them, and how suspicious cases are escalated.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026” were issued on July 31, 2026, by the Department of Supervision and are directed at urban co-operative banks in relation to their digital payment systems and related security controls. The document is a supervisory directions framework that sets out mandatory governance, risk-management, authentication, fraud-management, reconciliation, and customer-protection requirements for banks offering digital payment services; from the table of contents, it is clear the directions are organized into binding chapters on preliminary matters, board responsibilities, general controls, and internet banking, indicating these are not merely advisory best practices but formal compliance obligations.

For compliance purposes, the most important takeaway from the available text is that the RBI is requiring boards of affected banks to approve formal policies covering digital payment security and to ensure governance over security risks, application security, authentication, fraud risk management, reconciliation, and customer grievance redressal. The directions explicitly apply to urban co-operative banks, so compliance teams should assume the obligations attach to any such bank operating digital payment channels, including internet banking and other digital payment activities referenced in the chapter structure. Because the excerpt provided ends at the table of contents and does not include the substantive clauses, the specific control thresholds, implementation timelines, technical requirements, and any exceptions are not visible here; however, the document’s structure shows that the RBI has established a comprehensive control framework that will likely require documented board-approved policies, ongoing monitoring, and formal customer-facing complaint and protection processes.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, issued on 1 April 2025 to all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs), is a consolidation of all housing finance instructions/guidelines issued up to 31 March 2025; it expressly states that it does **not introduce any new instructions or requirements**, but replaces and updates the prior master circular dated 2 April 2024 by incorporating all changes issued through 31 March 2025 (with the full list of updates referenced in Annex 3). For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs should treat this as the current consolidated reference for housing finance and verify their policies, lending practices, and disclosures against the updated circular rather than the earlier version.

The circular governs UCB housing finance activities broadly, including housing loans to eligible borrower categories, loan terms and conditions, financing limits, security, loan tenor, graduated instalments, aggregate housing finance exposure, additional/supplementary finance, lending to housing boards, advances to builders/contractors, priority sector treatment of housing loans, and precautions, with a separate section on the National Building Code. It also includes specific requirements on matters such as maximum loan amount and margin, interest-rate/reset/foreclosure and prepayment provisions for EMI-based housing loans, penal charges, and the Key Facts Statement (KFS) for loans and advances. Compliance teams should understand that these topics are the substantive operational framework for UCB housing finance and must be applied in accordance with the consolidated RBI instructions referenced in the circular and its annexures.

The document also highlights that housing finance to specified categories up to prescribed limits qualifies as priority sector lending, which is relevant for regulatory classification and reporting. However, the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, rates, margins, tenure limits, or category-specific eligibility rules themselves; those would be set out in the body of the circular and annexes, and should be checked in the full text before making lending or reporting decisions. Since the RBI specifically says the circular only consolidates existing instructions, the effective compliance obligation is to ensure the bank’s housing finance products and processes are aligned with the latest consolidated instructions as of 31 March 2025.

This April 1, 2025 RBI master circular for all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) is a consolidation of every instruction issued on income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, and related prudential matters through March 31, 2025. The RBI explicitly says it does **not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it replaces/updates the prior April 2, 2024 master circular only to reflect the full body of existing directions, including the items listed in Annex 9. Compliance teams should therefore treat this document as the current consolidated reference point for prudential norms on advances, rather than as a source of new policy changes.

The circular covers the full framework for identifying and treating non-performing assets (NPAs), including when an account becomes NPA, how to maintain records of recovery, how to apply borrower-wise rather than facility-wise treatment, and how to handle special cases such as agricultural advances affected by natural calamities, housing loans to staff, and credit facilities guaranteed by the Central or State Government. It also consolidates directions on project financing, restructuring of advances, treatment of other advances, recognition of income on investments classified as NPA, NPA reporting to the Reserve Bank, and consumer education requirements. In addition, it includes the broader asset classification framework, with definitions, classification rules, and guidance for advances covered by rehabilitation packages approved by term lending institutions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must continue applying the prudential norms and procedures already in force as of March 31, 2025, with no relaxation or new operational rule implied by this issuance. The circular serves as the authoritative compilation for internal policy, loan monitoring, NPA recognition, provisioning, and reporting controls, so banks should ensure their credit policies, classification engines, board-approved processes, and reporting templates are aligned to the consolidated instructions contained in the circular and its annexures.

The circular covers the full RBI framework for: issuing guarantees, including broad guidelines, permissible purposes, maturity, volume, secured versus unsecured guarantees, and deferred payment guarantees; guarantees relating to commodities under selective credit controls; safeguards for issuing guarantees; immediate settlement of claims under bank guarantees; handling delays in obtaining certified copies of judgments; and correspondence with government departments. From a compliance perspective, this means UCBs must review the annexed consolidated instructions and verify that all current business practices for guarantees, co-acceptances, and LCs comply with the RBI’s applicable limits, approval controls, documentary safeguards, and settlement expectations as in force through March 31, 2025. No new effective date, threshold, rate, or deadline is introduced in the circular text provided beyond the publication date and the cut-off date for consolidation, but the institution must treat the revised master circular as the current consolidated reference for these products.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/09 (DOR.CAP.REC.03/09.18.201/2025-26), applies to all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) and supersedes/consolidates the earlier master circular dated 1 April 2024. It states that it updates all instructions and guidelines on prudential norms for capital adequacy issued up to 31 March 2025, with the detailed rules collected in the annexures referenced in the circular.

Substantively, the circular reiterates that capital is a buffer against losses and a licensing/continuation requirement for a bank, and then restates the statutory minimum capital position for co-operative banks under the Banking Regulation Act (AACS): a bank may not commence or carry on banking business unless its aggregate paid-up capital and reserves are at least ₹1 lakh. It also indicates that the circular covers the computation of net worth, capital adequacy norms/CRAR, risk weights, market risk capital, share-linking to borrowings, refund of share capital, and investor-protection measures for regulatory capital instruments, with specific operational guidance contained in Annexes 1 through 5.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that UCBs must use this Master Circular as the current consolidated source for capital adequacy compliance as of 31 March 2025, and must follow the detailed requirements in the annexures on: how to compute net worth; the applicable risk weights for capital adequacy calculations; the rules for issuing preference shares and debt capital instruments; the format for returns; and any procedural safeguards for investors in such instruments. The document also includes a section on returns, implying ongoing reporting obligations under the prescribed pro forma.

No new numerical capital adequacy ratio, deadline, or rate is stated in the excerpt beyond the ₹1 lakh statutory minimum paid-up capital and reserves threshold; the circular’s primary compliance change is the consolidation and update of the earlier instructions into one current master circular effective from 1 April 2025.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular updates and consolidates all RBI instructions on the **Board of Directors of Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, superseding the prior circular dated **April 1, 2024**. It is addressed to the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all UCBs and reiterates that boards must consist of persons of **high integrity and knowledge**, with the bank required to maintain **at least two professional directors at all times**—meaning directors with suitable banking experience (at middle/senior management level) or relevant professional qualifications. The circular applies to the governance of UCBs under the RBI’s supervisory powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **RBI Act, 1934**.

The document covers the **constitution of the Board**, the **role and responsibilities of directors**, the **committees of the Board**, the **calendar of reviews and matters to be placed before the Board**, and controls relating to **donations to trusts/institutions where directors or their relatives have an interest or position**. It also includes rules on **payment of fees and allowances to directors**, and it consolidates earlier RBI circulars and the related guidance annexed in the master circular, including the **Madhava Das Committee recommendations** and the prescribed **reviews to be submitted to the Board**. For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that UCBs must ensure their governance structure, board composition, committee oversight, and periodic review mechanisms continue to satisfy RBI expectations as set out in the updated consolidated instructions.

The circular is effective from **April 1, 2025** and is intended to be read as the current master reference on board governance for UCBs. Compliance teams should treat the circular as the governing compilation of all existing instructions on this subject, and should verify that board composition, director suitability, board committee structure, agenda/calendar items, donation approvals, and director compensation arrangements are aligned with the consolidated RBI framework.

It is issued as a **statutory guideline under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The circular **revises and consolidates** the RBI’s earlier Master Circular on the same subject dated **April 24, 2024**, and the RBI states expressly that this version **contains no new instructions or guidelines**; it only compiles all instructions issued on the topic **up to March 31, 2025**.

For compliance purposes, the document confirms that banks must follow the RBI’s existing rules on lending to NBFCs across the full set of subject areas covered in the circular, including: finance to **NBFCs registered with RBI**, finance to **NBFCs not requiring registration**, **activities not eligible for bank credit**, finance to **factoring companies**, other prohibitions on bank finance, **bridge loans/interim finance**, **advances against collateral security of shares to NBFCs**, restrictions on **guarantees for placement of funds with NBFCs**, **prudential exposure ceilings** for banks’ aggregate exposure to NBFCs, restrictions on **bank investments in securities/instruments issued by NBFCs**, and the **risk weight** applicable to bank credit to NBFCs. The document’s operative effect is therefore to serve as the current consolidated reference for all existing RBI requirements governing bank funding and related exposures to NBFCs, rather than introducing a substantive policy change.

The key practical point is that compliance teams should treat this as the **current, consolidated master reference** for bank-to-NBFC finance as of **April 1, 2025**, and ensure internal credit policies, exposure monitoring, permissibility checks, and investment/guarantee controls are aligned to the annexed RBI instructions referenced in the circular. rows.summary:
This Master Circular, effective **April 1, 2025**, consolidates and updates RBI’s existing **Basel III capital adequacy / prudential capital guidelines** for **all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks**. It supersedes the prior consolidated Master Circular dated **April 1, 2024** and states that the earlier instructions have been **suitably updated/amended** to reflect all relevant circulars issued up to the date of this circular; the list of source circulars is in **Annex 26**. The RBI also expressly notes that **Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks are not covered by this circular** and should instead follow their own licensing and operating guidelines for capital adequacy.

From the content shown, the circular is a comprehensive restatement of the Basel III capital framework for covered banks, including the **minimum capital requirement (Pillar 1)**, the **scope of application**, **composition of regulatory capital**, **recognition of minority interest**, **regulatory deductions/adjustments**, and **transitional arrangements**. It then sets out the detailed **credit risk capital charge** framework, covering exposures to **domestic and foreign sovereigns and central banks, public sector entities, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, primary dealers, corporates and NBFCs, retail portfolios, residential mortgages, commercial real estate, NPAs, specified categories, other assets, and off-balance-sheet items**. The table of contents also shows specific treatment for items such as **counterparty credit risk on off-balance-sheet exposures**, indicating that the circular is not merely high-level policy but a detailed operational rulebook that affects how banks calculate risk weights and capital charges across major asset classes.

For compliance purposes, the key action is that affected banks must ensure their **capital adequacy calculations, exposure classifications, deductions, and transitional treatment** are aligned with the updated consolidated instructions as of **April 1, 2025**. Because the circular consolidates prior instructions rather than creating a single isolated rule change in the excerpt provided, a compliance team would need to check the annexed consolidated circular list and the body of the Master Circular for any **new or revised risk weights, deduction thresholds, reporting expectations, or capital composition requirements** applicable to their portfolios and regulatory filings.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated **June 16, 2025** and addressed to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, consolidates all Reserve Bank instructions issued up to that date on **credit facilities to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs)**. It does not introduce a single new standalone rule in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and consolidates the RBI’s existing requirements and expectations for banks to **step up advances to SC/ST borrowers**.

A key compliance point is the **planning and coordination framework** banks must use. The **District Level Consultative Committees (DLCCs)** under the Lead Bank Scheme remain the principal coordination mechanism between banks and development agencies, and the **district credit plans** prepared by Lead Banks must clearly show how credit is linked with **employment generation and development schemes**. Banks are also expected to maintain **closer liaison with District Industries Centres (DICs)** in the districts for promotion of **self-employment** opportunities. At the **block level**, planning must give **weightage to SC/ST communities**, meaning credit planning is not to be neutral in a purely population-agnostic way but should deliberately reflect SC/ST participation and needs.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure the bank’s **district credit planning, branch/block-level business planning, and developmental coordination processes** explicitly incorporate SC/ST lending objectives and can demonstrate that linkage in records and planning documents. Because the circular is a **master consolidation**, the operative compliance requirement is not just monitoring one policy note, but ensuring internal credit policy, rural and priority sector planning, and reporting systems align with the consolidated RBI instructions listed in the appendix. The document excerpt does not specify numerical lending targets, caps, dates for phased implementation, or special pricing terms; the material requirement shown is the **institutional obligation to plan, coordinate, and weight credit delivery in favor of SC/ST borrowers through formal district and block-level mechanisms**.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular consolidates RBI’s Lead Bank Scheme instructions issued up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to SLBC/UTLBC convenor banks and lead banks, superseding/compiling prior guidance rather than introducing a single isolated rule. For compliance teams, the key point is that the circular is a consolidated operational framework covering the governance structure for Lead Bank Scheme forums, credit-planning and monitoring responsibilities, data-flow requirements, and banking-penetration obligations, with the detailed operative instructions contained in the circular’s sections and the appendix of source instructions. It applies to institutions participating in the Lead Bank Scheme framework, especially lead banks, convenor banks, and the bodies they service at district, state, block, and local levels.

The document establishes the fora under the Lead Bank Scheme, including Block Level Bankers’ Committees, District Consultative Committees (DCCs), District Level Review Committees (DLRCs), and State Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs), and lays out requirements for their constitution, meeting conduct, agendas, annual meeting calendars, and related reporting/review processes. It specifically identifies the role of Lead District Managers (LDMs), requires quarterly public meetings and grievance-redressal mechanisms at the district level, and standardizes the SLBC website information/data architecture and liaison with state governments. It also calls for capacity-building, training, and sensitization programmes, indicating that compliance is not just documentary but includes active operational coordination and stakeholder engagement.

On implementation, the circular covers preparation of credit plans and Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs), monitoring performance against those plans, and a revised mechanism for data flow for Lead Bank Scheme forum meetings. That means banks and convenor institutions must ensure timely, accurate submission and consolidation of data used for LBS meetings and reviews, and must maintain planning and monitoring processes that can evidence progress against district/state credit objectives. The circular also includes rules on assignment of Lead Bank responsibility, which is relevant for any institution taking on or continuing that role.

A material compliance area is banking penetration and branch/service expansion. The circular continues the roadmap for providing banking services in unbanked villages and the roadmap for opening brick-and-mortar branches in villages with population above 5,000 where there is no branch of a scheduled commercial bank, while also aligning the roadmap for such unbanked villages with revised branch authorization guidelines. Even though the text provided here does not state the detailed thresholds or timelines beyond the “population more than 5,000” criterion, the compliance implication is that affected banks must track coverage gaps, service delivery obligations, and branch-opening priorities for eligible villages under the revised framework. The circular itself is dated April 1, 2025, and consolidates guidance effective through March 31, 2025.

rows.summary:
RBI has issued a new **Master Circular on Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** dated **April 1, 2025** under **RBI/2025-26/02 FIDD.GSSD.CO.BC.No.01/09.01.003/2025-26**. rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by the RBI on 1 April 2025 (RBI/2025-26/01, FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26), is addressed to the Chairman/Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all scheduled commercial banks and consolidates all RBI instructions on the Self Help Group (SHG)-Bank Linkage Programme up to 31 March 2025. It does not itself announce a new standalone policy change in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and compiles the existing regulatory framework governing SHG lending and related bank obligations.

The document explains the policy rationale for SHG-bank linkage: SHGs are intended to connect the formal banking system with the rural poor, with NABARD studies cited as showing higher SHG loan volumes, a shift from consumption/non-income-generating borrowing toward productive activities, near-100% recovery in some cases, lower transaction costs for banks and borrowers, and rising member incomes. It also notes that around 85% of bank-linked SHGs were formed exclusively by women, highlighting the program’s gender dimension. On this basis, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, following the Union Budget 2008-09 direction on “Total Financial Inclusion.”

The excerpted text says scheduled commercial banks should meet the full credit needs of SHG members for: income-generation activities, social needs, and other approved purposes referenced in the underlying Budget language. For a compliance team, the key point is that this Master Circular is the authoritative consolidation of RBI guidance on SHG-bank linkage as of 31 March 2025, so internal policies, credit processes, product structures, and monitoring arrangements for SHG lending should be checked against the consolidated RBI instructions contained in the full circular and its appendix.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026”** for public comment, following its existing **KYC Directions, 2025** provisions on **Operations of Bank Accounts and Money Mules** and in response to the **Hon’ble Supreme Court’s order dated August 4, 2026**. The Supreme Court directed RBI to adopt and circulate a **Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)** setting out what banks must do when placing **temporary debit holds** on amounts or accounts linked to **money-mule activity** and **cyber-enabled fraud**.  

The draft amendment is intended to update the current instructions on bank account operations and money-mule controls and to advise banks on the procedure for imposing these temporary debit holds in cases connected to money-mule activity and cyber-enabled financial fraud. RBI is issuing this as a **consolidated draft** for consultation, and it is stated to be applicable to **all Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Local Area Banks, as well as Urban Cooperative Banks**. RBI notes that, after reviewing feedback, it will issue **final directions separately for the relevant regulated entity types**.  

Comments and feedback from regulated entities, stakeholders, and members of the public must be submitted **on or before October 2, 2026**. Submissions can be made either through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Draft Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026”**.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued for public comment the draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”**, following the announcement in the RBI’s **Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 05, 2026**. The draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of interest-rate instructions with a **harmonized, principles-based framework for all regulated entities (REs)** covering both **fixed-rate and floating-rate loans and advances**, with the framework to be calibrated to the **nature, complexity, and scale** of each RE’s operations.

The RBI says the existing regime is uneven: for **Commercial Banks** (including **Small Finance Banks** and **Local Area Banks**), there are detailed rules already in place for **internal and external benchmark-based lending**, including the setting of **spreads over benchmarks**; by contrast, the rules for **NBFCs, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks** are mostly limited to conduct-related requirements. The RBI also notes that among commercial banks it has observed **divergent practices in determining the MCLR (internal benchmark) and its components**, and that current guidance on **fixed-rate loans** is very limited. The proposed directions are meant to address these gaps and align interest-rate setting practices more consistently across REs.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is still a **draft consultation document**, so the immediate obligation is to **review and submit comments/feedback** rather than to implement final rule changes yet. However, the substance of the proposal signals that, once finalized, it may impose a more uniform supervisory standard on all REs for how loan and advance interest rates are determined, including both benchmark-linked floating-rate structures and fixed-rate lending. The document excerpt provided does not yet give a final effective date, transition period, or operative thresholds/rates; those would need to be checked in the final directions once issued.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’
rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. The comments on the draft Directions are invited from Regulated Entities, market participants, and other interested parties till August 28, 2026. The comments / feedb
rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft revised Directions on the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework and invited public comments by August 28, 2026. The draft replaces the RBI’s existing CVA framework issued in 2011, which had been based on the 2010 Basel Committee standards, and is intended to align Indian rules with the Basel III revisions to CVA treatment.

Substantively, the RBI is proposing to allow Indian banks to use the Basel “basic approach” for CVA capital calculation (BA-CVA), with banks permitted to adopt either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. In addition, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may, consistent with BCBS guidance, calculate their CVA capital charge at 100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge instead of using the BA-CVA methodology. The draft also clarifies when CVA hedges are eligible for recognition, increases the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties based on sector and credit quality, and separates systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation to better reflect indirect CVA hedges.

The RBI states that these changes are meant to make the framework more risk-sensitive and more consistent with current international standards. The new draft Directions, titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**, apply to commercial banks in India that are subject to RBI regulation and to their CVA capital computation for derivative exposures. The consultation is open to regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties, who may submit comments up to the August 28, 2026 deadline.

rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft directions for public comment to update the concentration risk framework applicable to rural co-operative banks (RCBs). The package consists of two instruments: a new **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026**, which would replace the existing **2025** concentration risk directions, and a **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which would amend certain provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

The draft changes are intended to set out prudential exposure limits for **single and group counterparties**, raise **housing loan limits**, and specify prudential limits for **unsecured advances**. RBI also proposes to give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** more flexibility to determine the **tenor and moratorium** for housing loans, while for **other RCBs** it proposes to **increase the ceilings** for those housing-loan parameters. In addition, RBI proposes to **withdraw the general prudential sectoral exposure limits**, with the stated exception that the **real estate sector** exposure limit would remain in place.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that these are **draft directions** open for consultation, not yet final rules. RBI has set **August 28, 2026** as the deadline for comments/feedback from regulated entities and other stakeholders, which may be submitted either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the RBI website or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. Compliance teams at RCBs should review the draft closely for any changes to counterparty exposure, unsecured lending, and housing finance policies, especially where deposits exceed the **₹1,000 crore** threshold.

rows.title: Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments
rows.desc: July 21, 2026 Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments Foreign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules'). The Union Budget 2026- 27 announced a comprehensive review of the NDI Rules to create a more contemporary, user-friendly framework for foreign investments, consistent with India's evolving economic priorities. Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. The salient features of the proposed draft Rules, inter alia, are as under: a) Simplified and principle-based framework: Rationalization of provisions, harmonization of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity. b) Alignment with the FDI Policy: Clear demarcation of procedural FEMA provisions from policy and sector-specific requirements, improving regulatory coherence and facilitating timely policy changes. c) Enhanced ease of doing business: Streamlined procedures, reduced compliance burden and greater operational flexibility through a transparent and investor-friendly regulatory framework. d) Future-ready regulatory framework: Adoption of principle-based, investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions aligned with evolving business practices, while preserving necessary regulatory safeguards. � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 The Rules will be finalized after wider public consultations
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **draft rationalised Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (NDI Rules)** for public comments on **July 21, 2026**, following the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the foreign investment framework. The draft is intended to update and simplify the existing foreign investment rules in India by creating a more contemporary, user-friendly structure that better aligns with India’s current economic priorities and the evolving foreign investment environment.

For compliance teams, the key substantive change is that the RBI, based on a committee review and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, is proposing a **simplified, principle-based framework** with **harmonized definitions** and a more coherent regulatory architecture. The draft also aims to **separate FEMA procedural requirements from FDI policy and sector-specific requirements**, which should make it clearer which obligations arise under FEMA rules versus sectoral policy conditions and may allow policy changes to be implemented more efficiently. The document also emphasizes **reduced compliance burden, streamlined procedures, and greater operational flexibility**, with the stated goal of improving ease of doing business and making the regime more investor-friendly while retaining necessary safeguards.

No specific numeric thresholds, ownership caps, rates, deadlines, or sector-specific eligibility changes are stated in the press release itself. The only procedural deadline mentioned is that the draft will be **finalized after wider public consultations**, meaning the current publication is a consultation stage rather than an immediately effective rule change. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as a signal that the NDI Rules are likely to be materially reworked, but should wait for the final notified text to identify any actual legal obligations, transition requirements, or date-specific implementation steps.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as potentially applicable to their data governance frameworks and control environment.

The RBI’s stated objective is to respond to the increasing digitalisation of financial services and the growing dependence on technology-driven business models, where data has become a critical asset. The draft explains that as data volume, variety, and velocity increase, regulated entities need stronger governance so that data remains **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose** across business functions and systems. The RBI also highlights that weak data governance can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks**, indicating that the guidance is intended to support broader risk management and supervisory expectations, not just IT controls.

The RBI is seeking comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders **by August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted via the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”** No final compliance obligations are imposed yet in this press release, but the issuance of the draft signals that regulated entities should review their data governance practices and be prepared for future final guidance once the consultation closes.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), on June 10, 2026, issued a public consultation on draft Amendment Directions for the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR). The document explains that the current framework still requires banks to compute counterparty credit risk (CCR) exposure using the Current Exposure Method (CEM), even though RBI had already issued final SA-CCR-based guidelines in 2016 for “Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions” and “Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties,” originally intended to apply from April 1, 2018 but later deferred.

RBI says the earlier SA-CCR framework has now been comprehensively reviewed because of major legal and regulatory changes since 2016, including the enactment of the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020 and the implementation of the margining framework under the RBI’s “Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives” Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also issued multiple FAQs over time to clarify SA-CCR application, and the draft amendments are intended to align the directions with those developments.

The draft directions are described as making several substantive changes to the 2016 version currently reflected in the “Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025.” These include clarifying the scope of CCR across both banking book and trading book exposures; setting out how multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets should be treated in light of the new netting and margining framework; and giving specific treatment for transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments. The draft also adds guidance on deferment of option premium, how to compute the effective notional amount for options, and begins incorporating disclosure-related requirements, though the excerpt cuts off before the full disclosure provisions are listed.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that RBI is preparing to replace or materially update the deferred SA-CCR framework and is seeking comments before finalizing the rules. Banks and other affected institutions should review their derivative exposure measurement, netting set documentation, margining processes, clearing-member activity on SEBI-recognised exchanges, and option valuation/exposure calculations to assess whether systems and policies need to change once the amended directions are finalized and brought into force.

rows.title: Adherence to Compliance Requirements for Handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: Non-Confidential Circular Department: LISTING Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/19 Date: August 07, 2026 To, All Listed Entities Subject: Adherence to Compliance Requirements for Handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 Suggested Best Practices SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 “(PIT Regulations)”, as amended from time to time, and the relevant circulars issued by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges detail, inter-alia, the manner in which the listed companies are required to deal with Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI). The provisions of the PIT Regulations are further supplemented and clarified through the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) issued by SEBI. In light of the observations made in certain cases, it is considered imperative that listed companies diligently adhere to best practices to ensure full compliance with the PIT Regulations as amended from time to time including the following: 1. Listed companies shall maintain a structured digital database containing the nature of UPSI, the names and PANs (or any other identifier authorized by law) of persons who have shared the information, and the names and PANs of persons with whom such information has been shared. In case where UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediaries, or fiduciaries, the names and identifier of the individuals handling such information shall be recorded. 2. Listed companies shall diligently implement and periodically review internal policies designed to prevent the leakage of UPSI. Such measures must be in alignment with the statutory and regulatory provisions prescribed under the PIT Regulations. 3. To ensure a culture of compliance, companies shall conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries regarding the prescribed manner of handling UPSI. 4. Listed companies shall ensure compliance with the Code of Conduct formulated by the company wi
rows.summary:
This circular is addressed to **all listed entities** and is issued by the NSE Listing Department as **Circular Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/19 dated August 07, 2026**. It does not create a wholly new regulatory regime; rather, it reinforces and reiterates the obligation to strictly comply with the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT Regulations)**, as amended from time to time, together with SEBI and stock exchange circulars and the SEBI FAQs that supplement those regulations. The circular says recent observations in certain cases make it necessary for listed companies to follow stated best practices to ensure full compliance in how **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)** is handled.

The first key requirement is that listed companies must maintain a **structured digital database** of UPSI disclosures. That database must record the **nature of the UPSI**, the **names and PANs** (or any other legally authorized identifier) of the people who shared the information, and the **names and PANs** of the people with whom it was shared. Where UPSI is shared with a **listed company, intermediary, or fiduciary**, the company must also record the **names and identifiers of the individuals** who actually handled the information. This is a concrete recordkeeping obligation, not just a general control expectation.

The circular also requires listed companies to **diligently implement and periodically review internal policies** intended to prevent UPSI leakage, and those policies must be aligned with the PIT Regulations and related legal requirements. In addition, companies must run **periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries** on the proper handling of UPSI, reflecting an expectation of ongoing compliance education rather than one-time training. Further, listed entities must ensure compliance with their own **Code of Conduct** formulated under the PIT framework, meaning internal insider-trading policies and procedures must be actively followed and enforced.

No new monetary thresholds, reporting deadlines, or rate changes are introduced in this circular, but the compliance expectation is immediate in the sense that listed entities are expected to already be following these requirements under the PIT framework and to strengthen execution wherever gaps have been observed. For a compliance team, the practical implication is to verify that the structured digital database is complete and capture-ready, that internal UPSI controls are documented and periodically reviewed, that training is conducted on a recurring basis, and that the company’s Code of Conduct and related insider-trading procedures are actually being implemented in day-to-day operations.

rows.title: Update of single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges
rows.summary:
This circular updates NSE’s single filing system under the earlier circular dated September 30, 2024 and applies to **all listed entities** that make **Regulation 30 disclosures under the SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015**. Effective **June 20, 2026**, the single filing system is being **extended to XBRL filing** for the newly covered event(s), and the Exchange has also released additional XBRL utilities. For the initial phase, companies may continue to submit the **PDF filing first**, and NSE will treat that PDF submission as compliance under Regulation 30; however, the listed entity must then **submit the corresponding XBRL filing within 24 hours** of the PDF submission. The XBRL utility for the newly covered events will be available in the Exchange portal under **COMPLIANCE >> Common XBRL Upload >> Equity Announcement- XBRL**, and the same filing will also be made available in **iXBRL/readable format** on NSE’s website at the specified corporate filings/announcements XBRL page.

The circular also states that the **XBRL utility and separate filing process for the Para B event in Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR 2015**—specifically **“Awarding, bagging/receiving, amendment or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the normal course of business”**—will be **discontinued effective June 20, 2026** and **merged into the single utility for Para B events**. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that, from that date, these disclosures are routed through the updated single filing/API-based integration workflow and that the 24-hour XBRL follow-up requirement is met after any PDF submission.
