The document contains no implementation mechanics, deadlines, numerical thresholds beyond the “top 100” criterion, or procedural details for how AGMs must be held; those obligations are contained in the referenced SEBI circular, not in this NSE cover letter. The only explicit administrative instruction in this notice is to review the enclosed SEBI circular (also available on the NSE website) and act accordingly.

rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs -Amendments
rows.summary:
This NSE communication simply forwards SEBI’s July 22, 2021 notification, titled **“Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs - Amendments,”** to the Company Secretaries of **all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs)**. The letter itself does **not** spell out the amended disclosure requirements; it says the SEBI notification is enclosed and should be reviewed for “necessary action,” with the circular also available on the NSE website. For compliance purposes, the key point is that **SEBI has issued amendments affecting continuous disclosure/compliance obligations for InvITs**, and any InvIT should treat this as a regulatory update requiring review against its current disclosure processes and reporting calendar.

The notice is dated **23 July 2021** and references the underlying SEBI notification dated **22 July 2021**. No thresholds, rates, filing dates, or specific procedural changes are described in the body of this NSE letter, so the operative requirements are contained only in the attached SEBI circular/notification, which is not reproduced here. Therefore, from this document alone, a compliance team should note the **applicability to all InvITs**, the **effective regulatory update date of July 22, 2021**, and the need to obtain and implement the enclosed SEBI amendment text.

rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by REITs - Amendments
rows.summary:
This communication from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited dated 23 July 2021 is a forwarding notice to all Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) about SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/599 dated 22 July 2021, titled “Continuous disclosures in compliances by REITs - Amendments.” The NSE letter itself does not spell out the revised compliance requirements; it states that the SEBI notification/circular is enclosed and is to be reviewed and acted on by the recipients, and that the circular is also available on the NSE website for reference.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that SEBI has amended the continuous disclosure framework applicable to REITs, so REIT issuers and their compliance teams must review the underlying SEBI circular to identify what periodic or event-based disclosures have changed, what reporting formats or timelines now apply, and whether any additional filings, certifications, or internal controls are required. The notice is addressed to the Company Secretary of all REITs, indicating the change is relevant to all REIT entities subject to SEBI’s continuous disclosure regime. No specific effective date, deadline, thresholds, or quantitative requirements are provided in the NSE forwarding letter itself; those details are expected to be contained in the enclosed SEBI notification dated 22 July 2021.

rows.title: Guidance note for companies undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
rows.summary:
This NSE guidance note, issued on 9 July 2021 and addressed to all listed companies, does not create a new standalone rule; it points companies to a January 3, 2018 circular of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) and reminds them that companies undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) must continue to comply with listing regulations and all other applicable laws as amended from time to time. The note is explicitly described as guidance for assistance only, so the underlying obligations remain those in the applicable regulations and the IBBI circular.

The cited IBBI circular places responsibility on the Interim Resolution Professional, Resolution Professional, or Liquidator (as applicable) to exercise reasonable care and diligence and take all necessary steps to ensure that the corporate debtor complies with applicable laws during CIRP or liquidation. It also clarifies that if the company incurs any loss, including any penalty, because of non-compliance with applicable laws during the process, that loss is not to be treated as insolvency resolution process cost or liquidation process cost under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. However, if non-compliance occurs because of the insolvency professional’s conduct, the insolvency professional can be held responsible for that non-compliance.

For listed entities, the practical compliance message is that CIRP does not suspend legal and disclosure obligations under SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) and related regulations; the company and the appointed insolvency professional must still ensure timely compliance with all applicable filing, disclosure, and governance requirements throughout the process. No new thresholds, monetary limits, or specific deadlines are introduced in this note beyond the issuance date, but companies are instructed to review and comply with the current version of all applicable listing and regulatory requirements during CIRP.

rows.title: Standard Operating Procedure for listed subsidiary company desirous of getting delisted through a Scheme of Arrangement wherein the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary are in the same line of business
rows.summary: This NSE communication is a forwarding notice to all listed entities that have issued listed equity shares or listed convertible securities, pointing them to a SEBI notification dated 6 July 2021 on a new “Standard Operating Procedure” for delisting a listed subsidiary company through a Scheme of Arrangement when both the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary operate in the same line of business. The document itself does not set out the procedure in detail; instead, it announces that SEBI has issued the controlling circular and that the circular is attached and also available on the NSE website for reference and necessary action. The operative change for compliance teams is that any listed group structure contemplating this specific delisting route should review and follow the SEBI-issued SOP referenced by circular number SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL1/CIR/P/2021/0585, dated 6 July 2021. No separate deadline, threshold, rate, or filing date is stated in this NSE covering letter beyond the circular’s issue date, and the only affected parties identified here are listed entities with equity and convertibles, particularly listed parent-subsidiary groups in the same business line considering delisting of the subsidiary through a scheme of arrangement.

rows.title: Issue of No Objection Certificate for release of 1% of Issue amount
rows.summary:
This NSE communication is an informational forwarding letter dated 6 July 2021 to all companies whose securities are listed on SEBI-recognized stock exchanges. It transmits SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/OIAE/IGRD/CIR/P/2021/588 dated 5 July 2021, titled “Issue of No Objection Certificate for release of 1% of Issue amount,” and states that the SEBI circular is enclosed and also available on the NSE website. The letter itself does not set out the detailed rule changes or procedures; rather, it directs listed companies to review the SEBI notification and take necessary action as applicable.

From this letter alone, the only specific compliance implication is that the new SEBI instruction concerns the issuance of a No Objection Certificate that would permit release of 1% of the issue amount, suggesting a process connected to securities issuance and funds release. The communication does not specify the effective date of the underlying SEBI requirements beyond the SEBI notification date of 5 July 2021, nor does it state deadlines, thresholds beyond the 1% reference, or the exact entities/processes impacted. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a notice to retrieve and assess the underlying SEBI circular for operative obligations, implementation steps, and any filing/approval conditions that may apply to issuers or other market participants involved in public issues.

rows.title: Guidance Note on Analyst/Institutional Investors meet
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by NSE on June 29, 2021, explains the effect of SEBI’s May 5, 2021 amendments to the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, specifically the enhanced disclosure requirement under point 15 of para A of Part A of Schedule III. For listed companies, disclosure of **group meetings** with analysts/institutional investors is now **mandatory**, including both the **schedule** of such meetings and the **post-meeting disclosures**; however, disclosure of **one-on-one meetings** is **not mandatory** under this clarification. The note also requires that **all audio/video recordings and transcripts of post-earnings or quarterly investor calls**, whether held physically or digitally and whether organized by the listed entity or any other entity, must be **disclosed to the recognized stock exchange**.

In addition, the Exchange says it has been advised to issue further guidance under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 to strengthen disclosures where **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)** is shared during analyst/research/investor meetings. This second requirement is explicitly limited to situations where UPSI is in fact shared during the meet, and it applies even if the meeting was **not organized by the listed company**, because the possibility of sharing price-sensitive information in such meetings cannot be ruled out. The practical compliance implication is that listed entities must treat analyst/institutional investor interactions as potentially disclosure-relevant when UPSI may be discussed, and ensure the required disclosures and filings are made in line with these clarified expectations.

rows.title: FAQ’s - LODR amendments dated May 05, 2021
rows.summary:
SEBI’s May 5, 2021 amendments to the LODR Regulations, 2015, as explained in this NSE FAQ circular dated June 28, 2021, clarify how listed entities should determine applicability and the compliance timeline for certain risk-management-related changes. For Regulation 3(2), the market-capitalization cutoff date to determine whether a listed entity is subject to the relevant provisions is **March 31, 2021**. Listed companies are also reminded that they must comply with the amended LODR requirements and any other applicable regulations as updated from time to time; the FAQ is only interpretive assistance and does not replace the regulations.

The substantive amendment addressed in the FAQ is to **Regulation 21(2)**, which now requires the **Risk Management Committee (RMC)** to have **at least three members**, with a **majority from the board of directors**, including **at least one independent director**; and for entities with **outstanding SR equity shares**, **at least two-thirds of the RMC must be independent directors**. Regulation **21(3A)** changes the frequency requirement from **“once” to “twice”**, and Regulation **21(5)** changes the threshold from **500 to 1000** (as amended in the regulation text). The amendment to **Schedule III, Part D** requires formulation of a **detailed risk management policy**.

On timing, the FAQ says compliance periods are available for the amended provisions, but the visible text in the provided document cuts off before the full timing table is shown. It does clearly indicate that the time available differs by provision, and specifically references **Regulation 21(2), 21(5), and Schedule III, Part D** as items for which a compliance period is being provided. The circular is addressed to **all listed companies** and issued by the **National Stock Exchange of India Limited** as a response to common implementation questions about the SEBI amendment.

rows.title: Action(s) to be initiated against listed companies for non-payment of outstanding Annual Listing Fees (“ALF”)
rows.summary:
This circular informs all listed entities that have not paid their outstanding Annual Listing Fees (ALF) that the NSE will initiate enforcement action in line with SEBI’s SOP on non-payment of ALF. The process is staged: first, the Exchange will issue reminder letters during the six-month period after the ALF invoice is issued; second, once those six months expire, the Exchange will send a formal notice requiring payment within 15 days, and if the entity still does not pay within that 15-day period, the Exchange will withhold approval for any further listing of securities by that defaulting listed entity.

If the listed entity still fails to clear the ALF after that notice period, the Exchange will escalate the matter to the promoter(s) of the defaulting entity. A notice will be sent to the promoter(s) using the information available with the Exchange, requiring them to ensure compliance and arrange payment of the outstanding ALF within 30 days from the date of that promoter notice. The circular also states that the concerned promoter(s) may submit a representation to the Exchange by email at listingsop@nse.in (the text provided cuts off immediately after this, so any additional filing details or subsequent steps are not visible in the excerpt).

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is to ensure ALF is paid promptly after invoice issuance, because the enforcement timeline begins with the invoice date and quickly escalates from reminders to formal notice, then to restriction on further listing approvals, and finally to promoter-level action. The document applies specifically to listed entities with unpaid ALF and, at the final stage, to their promoter(s); no other fee amounts or numeric thresholds are specified beyond the six-month reminder window, the 15-day cure period, and the 30-day promoter payment period.

The practical compliance implication is that listed companies administering employee share plans under the **SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014** should review their plan rules and internal procedures so that vesting treatment on an employee’s death follows the SEBI circular rather than any default minimum vesting timeline. The circular is addressed to **all listed entities**, so any company with SEBI-governed share-based employee benefit schemes may be affected.

rows.title: Guidance note on communications by Listed Entities
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by NSE on 11 June 2021 under confidential reference NSE/CML/2021/18, applies to all listed companies and is aimed at how they communicate publicly through the Exchange website/platform and other disclosures. It reminds listed entities that they often publish performance updates, awards and recognition, leadership claims, and interview-based statements by key managerial personnel or other representatives about prospects or future plans, but that stakeholder protection remains paramount and such communications must not compromise market integrity.

The core requirement is that no price-sensitive information may be disclosed to the public unless it has first been disclosed to the stock exchanges. In addition, any public statement made by the listed entity must be truthful, fair, evidence-based, and not manipulative, deceptive, distorted, untrue, or misleading; the entity must not make unsubstantiated promises or forecasts. Communications must also be written in clear, concise, understandable, simple, and easy-to-understand language, avoiding excessive technical, legal, or otherwise complex wording.

If the company presents financial data, it must include corresponding data for the past three years, and that disclosure must cover sales, gross profit, net profit, share capital, reserves, earnings per share, dividends, debts, and book values. The note also says companies should provide a link to the company’s website where the underlying details are available and can be verified. Finally, the level of detail must be adequate and appropriate so that investors are not misled or distracted by incomplete or promotional presentation.

The amendment is issued under Sections 101A(2) and 101A(4) of the Insurance Act, 1938, after consultation with the Advisory Committee under Section 101B and with the prior approval of the Central Government.

Substantively, the required percentage cession of the sum insured on each general insurance policy to Indian reinsurer(s) is fixed at 4% for insurance attaching during the financial year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. This means insurers writing general insurance business must cede 4% of the sum insured on each applicable policy into the obligatory cession framework for that period.

There are explicit carve-outs: no obligatory cession is required for premium ceded to the Terrorism Pool, Nuclear Pool, or Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool, where the cession is stated to be “NIL.” In addition, the entire obligatory cession must be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re); no other reinsurer may receive this mandatory cession. The notice is effective as the amended regulatory requirement for the 2026–27 financial year and should be reflected in reinsurance placement, treaty/cession administration, and compliance reporting for policies attaching between 1 April 2026 and 31 March 2027.

The document does **not** specify a phased implementation, monetary threshold, or separate compliance deadline; its effect appears immediate from the date of notification/publication. Any entity underwriting or servicing tariff-based policies in the listed lines should ensure internal templates and customer-facing documents no longer rely on the de-notified arbitration provisions.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Other Forms of Capital) Regulations, 2022 were notified on 5 December 2022 and are intended to replace and standardize the framework under which insurers can raise capital through instruments other than ordinary share capital. The regulations apply to insurers regulated under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, and they sit within the broader IRDAI regulatory framework governing capital raising and solvency. They define key terms such as “equity share capital,” “other forms of capital,” “preferential issue,” “private placement,” “promoter,” “controlled,” and related expressions, so companies using or issuing non-equity capital must align their instrument structures and disclosures with these regulatory meanings.

A major substantive requirement is the creation of a regulatory framework for issuance, treatment, and monitoring of “other forms of capital,” including instruments that are not pure equity but are intended to count toward an insurer’s capital base subject to conditions. The regulations provide for classification and treatment of instruments based on their features, including terms around priority, redemption, maturity, and loss absorption, and they require insurers to ensure that these instruments are structured so they do not undermine policyholder protection or solvency. Where instruments are held by promoters or related parties, or are issued through private placement or preferential issue, the regulations impose additional scrutiny and compliance conditions. The document also sets out the regulatory expectations for disclosures, approval processes, and ongoing compliance in relation to these instruments.

The regulations appear to include an explicit quantitative treatment for a particular category of capital instruments, showing a phased recognition or crediting of capital value over time. The text references a table in which the recognized value declines in steps from 100% to 80%, 60%, 40%, 20%, and then 0% as maturity approaches, with the example indicating a value of 1.50 plus 20% = 1.80 at one stage, which suggests the instrument’s regulatory value is amortized or progressively reduced before maturity. Compliance teams should treat this as a key capital-adequacy feature: instruments may not retain full regulatory capital recognition throughout their life, and the insurer must monitor residual tenor and the corresponding amount eligible for capital credit.

The regulations also specify conditions around the number and type of investors and the mechanics of issuance. The text references a threshold of 50 and mentions private placement/procedural requirements, suggesting limits or gating conditions for certain offers or placements, and it also refers to a 15-day timeline in at least one procedural context. In addition, the instrument documentation must contain prescribed features and cannot conflict with the regulatory definition of capital; the regulations appear to require careful drafting of offering documents and issuer resolutions before issuance. Where instruments are to be issued or transferred, the insurer must ensure the transaction is approved and documented in the manner prescribed by IRDAI.

Finally, the regulations include amendments or references to prior IRDAI regulations dated 2022 and 2015, indicating that this notification integrates with or modifies existing capital and insurer governance rules rather than operating in isolation. The practical compliance impact is that insurers planning to raise capital through hybrid, subordinated, or otherwise non-equity instruments must review the new definitions, valuation/recognition rules, issuance procedures, and ongoing reporting requirements before launching any transaction. In short, the document does not merely permit alternative capital forms; it imposes a structured legal and prudential framework that controls what can be issued, how it is recognized in capital calculations, and what approvals/disclosures are required.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI notification fixes the **obligatory cession for financial year 2022–23** under **Section 101A of the Insurance Act, 1938**, and applies to **Indian reinsurers and other insurers that are required to comply under that section**. For policies attaching in the period **1 April 2022 through 31 March 2023**, insurers must cede **4% of the sum insured on each general insurance policy** to the Indian reinsurer; however, the cession is **NIL** for **terrorism premium** and for **premium ceded to the Nuclear Pool**. The notification also requires that the **entire obligatory cession be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**, so no portion of this mandated cession may be routed to any other reinsurer.

The document then sets out the operating conditions for the cession. It states that **there is no sum-insured limit** applicable for cessions made during the year, and it specifies different cession percentages for certain classes/segments of business and treaty structures, including figures of **5%**, **7.50%**, **10%**, **15%**, **50%**, **78%**, and **14%** as referenced in the notification’s schedule/terms. These percentages appear to govern how the obligatory cession is to be allocated across different categories of general insurance business and/or arrangements, so compliance teams should verify the applicable line of business and corresponding percentage before ceding premium or sum insured.

From a compliance perspective, the key action item is to ensure that all eligible general insurance policies attaching in FY 2022–23 are identified and that the prescribed **4% obligatory cession** is calculated and routed correctly to **GIC Re only**, with exclusions properly carved out for **terrorism** and **Nuclear Pool** premium. The notification is dated **10 January 2022** and published in the Gazette of India on **17 January 2022**; the operative period is tied to the **financial year beginning 1 April 2022 and ending 31 March 2023**.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued a notification on 5 August 2021 reconstituting the Insurance Advisory Committee, exercising its powers under Section 25(1) of the IRDA Act, 1999 and Regulation 3A of the Insurance Advisory Committee (Meetings) Regulations, 2000. The reconstituted committee takes effect from 10 August 2021, so any references to the committee’s composition or participation after that date should use the new membership list.

The notification replaces the committee membership with a specified set of industry and professional representatives, indicating the body is meant to reflect both life and general insurers as well as market institutions and professional associations. The listed members include the Chairperson of Life Insurance Corporation of India; the Chairman-cum-Managing Director of The Oriental Insurance Company Limited; the Chairman-cum-Managing Director of General Insurance Corporation of India; the Chief Executive Officer of Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance Company Limited; the Chief Executive Officer of ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Limited; and the Chairman-cum-Chief Executive Officer of Star Health & Allied Insurance Company Limited.

It also includes representatives from key industry and technical institutions: the Director of the National Insurance Academy; the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India; the Secretary General of the Insurance Institute of India; the President of the Insurance Brokers’ Association of India; and the President of the Indian Institute of Insurance Surveyors & Loss Assessors. The document continues with additional committee membership beyond the excerpt shown, including the Insurance Ombudsman, but the core compliance point is that the committee’s constitution has been formally reset and becomes operative on the stated effective date.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure internal governance materials, committee references, and any stakeholder engagement or regulatory communication involving the Insurance Advisory Committee are aligned to this 10 August 2021 reconstitution, rather than any prior composition. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or substantive operational rules are introduced in this notification beyond the change in committee membership and effective date.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021** on **7 July 2021**, and the amending text appears to take effect from the date of publication unless a specific provision in the underlying regulations says otherwise. The amendments revise several provisions of the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, and also make related changes to the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015** and the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**.  

A key change is the insertion of a new **regulation 31** in the 2015 Indian Insurance Companies Regulations, stating that an insurer must comply with **regulation 5** of the 2021 amendment framework, which appears to introduce updated requirements tied to the insurer’s structure and governance. The document also amends **regulation 5(2)(vi)** of the 2015 regulations to update the cross-reference language, replacing earlier references so that the provision now points to the relevant clause(s) under the amended framework; similarly, **regulation 7** is amended to change the wording around **promoter/promoter group ownership and control** and the related cross-references to the 2000 and 2015 rules.  

The amendment makes conforming edits to **regulations 16 and 17** of the 2015 regulations by replacing the prior cross-references with references to **regulation 5(2)** of the amended 2021 framework, indicating that compliance obligations under those provisions now track the updated ownership/control standard. It also deletes or updates references in **regulations 29, 30 and 31** to align them with the new 2021 rule set, and amends the textual reference in the older rules so that the compliance regime is read together with the **2015** and **2021** amendments.  

In the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015**, the amendment substitutes the cross-reference in **regulation 5(2)(vi)** and updates **regulation 7** and **regulation 13** to reflect the revised 2021 wording and the applicable ownership/control concepts. The same type of conforming changes are made in the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**, again updating **regulation 5(2)(vi)**, **regulation 7**, and **regulation 13** so that those provisions refer to the amended regime rather than the superseded language.  

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that insurers, and especially those affected by **foreign investment**, **Indian ownership and control**, and the linked **promoter/promoter group** provisions, must apply the updated cross-references and the new/modified compliance standard introduced by the 2021 amendment. The document does not set out a monetary threshold or percentage in the extracted text provided here, but it clearly requires regulated entities to realign their internal compliance, ownership-control assessments, and regulatory filings/interpretations to the amended regulatory structure immediately upon the amendment’s commencement.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) issued the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021** on **19 May 2021** (G.S.R. 337(E)), after publishing draft rules on **15 April 2021** and inviting public comments for **15 days** from publication. The amendments were made under **section 114(2)(aaa)** read with **section 2(7A)(b)** of the **Insurance Act, 1938**, and they amend the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015**.

The most significant substantive change is a revised definition of **“foreign investment”** in the 2015 rules. The amendment also revises related definitions and references in the rules (including terms used in rule 2 and rule 5, and an updated statutory citation in rule 8), so compliance teams should treat this as a definitional and cross-reference update rather than a stand-alone licensing regime. The document specifically changes rule 4 to state that **foreign investment up to 74%** of the paid-up equity share capital is permitted in an Indian insurance company, subject to the conditions in the rule and the broader insurance-law framework. In practical terms, the rule change reflects the increase in the foreign investment ceiling for Indian insurance companies from the earlier level to **74%**, and compliance teams should ensure ownership tracking, board/governance checks, and foreign investor reporting are aligned with that cap.

The amendment applies to **Indian insurance companies** and the foreign investment they receive, so any insurer with existing or proposed foreign shareholding must review whether its capital structure, approvals, and internal compliance procedures now fit within the revised **74%** limit and the conditions attached to rule 4. Because the document is an amendment notification rather than a full restatement of the rulebook, affected firms should read it together with the **2015 Foreign Investment Rules** and the **Insurance Act, 1938** to identify every updated definition and cross-reference that may affect filings, ownership monitoring, and regulatory correspondence. The notification does not set a separate operational deadline beyond its issuance date, but it became effective upon publication on **19 May 2021**.

The document is dated 28 August 2026 and is issued under IRDAI reference number IRDAI/REINS/CIR/MISC/114/08/2026. No separate monetary thresholds or penalty rates are stated in the visible text, but the operational requirement is clear: entities covered by the circular must shift their relevant reinsurance filings and approvals to BAP for the specified financial years and functions.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **27 August 2026** to **all insurers** permitting investment in **New Development Bank (NDB) “Maharajah INR Bonds” / onshore rupee bonds** as part of insurers’ **approved investments**. NDB has requested this permission to support issuance of bonds with a proposed total size of **INR 25,000 crore over a five-year period**, and the stated use of proceeds is for **general corporate purposes** and **financing/onward lending for sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

The circular clarifies that these NDB onshore rupee bonds are treated as **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**. IRDAI’s permission is not unconditional: insurers may invest only if the bonds are governed by **any applicable Government of India norms**, the **public issue is duly approved by SEBI**, and insurers comply with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when making the investment. The bonds must also satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, as amended from time to time; the circular further notes that where **SEBI exempts the rating requirement** because the bonds have been rated by an **international rating agency**, that SEBI position is relevant to the compliance assessment.

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that NDB onshore rupee bonds are now eligible for insurer investment, but only within the existing statutory and regulatory framework for approved investments. Insurers should verify, before investing, that each issuance has the necessary **SEBI approval**, that any **Government of India conditions** are satisfied, that the investment remains consistent with **Section 27E limits/requirements**, and that the issue meets the applicable **Schedule III approved-investment rating standards** or a valid SEBI exemption applies. The circular is a **permission to invest**, not a relaxation of existing insurer investment controls, and there is no separate date-specific operational deadline beyond the effective applicability of the circular from its issuance on **27 August 2026**.

The IRDAI has issued a circular dated 07-08-2026 requiring all life insurers, and all general and health insurers other than reinsurers, to begin monthly submission of specified financial information for the purpose of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s Index of Service Production (ISP). The reporting starts from **July 2026 onward** and requires insurers to provide, on a monthly basis, the relevant income and claims data used for ISP compilation.

For **general and health insurers (excluding reinsurers)**, the required monthly data are **Gross Direct Premium, Claims Paid (Direct), and Investment Income of Policyholders and Shareholders**. For **life insurers**, the required monthly data are **Gross Premium, Benefits Paid (Gross), and Investment Income for Policyholders and Shareholders**. The information must be submitted through the **National Informatics Centre (NIC) online data templates** created for this purpose; IRDAI says the **online link will be shared separately**, and the template formats are identified as **Annexure A for life insurers** and **Annexure B for general and health insurers**.

The filing deadline is strict: the NIC form must be submitted **on or before the 15th day of the month following the reporting month**. IRDAI also expressly instructs insurers to ensure the information is **complete and accurate at the time of submission**. The circular is issued under **Section 14(2)(h) of the IRDA Act, 1999** and is stated to be for the limited purpose of meeting ISP data needs only; it **does not change** the disclosure requirements or financial statement preparation requirements under the **Insurance Act, 1938** or the **IRDA framework**.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **31 July 2026** and addressed to **all CEOs/CMDs of all insurance companies, including life insurers and stand-alone health insurers**, responds to the **flood-related natural disaster in Assam** that began on **19 July 2026** and affected the districts of **Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat** (declared a natural disaster). IRDAI states that insurers must take **immediate steps** to reduce hardship to affected policyholders and accelerate **claim registration and settlement**.

The circular requires insurers to **mobilize all resources immediately**, including **surveyors and investigators**, and to appoint **senior Nodal Officers** to oversee claims in the affected areas. The appointment of the Nodal Officer must be **communicated immediately to the Chief Secretary**, and claims in each district may be handled by a designated **District Claims Service Head**. Insurers must also activate and publicize **24x7 customer support/helplines** to assist claimants, and they must run an **extensive awareness campaign** describing the measures being taken; the **contact details of the district heads** must be published on the insurer’s website and additionally publicized through **press and digital media**.

On claims handling, insurers are directed to use **special, empowered district desks** so claims can be processed quickly in the affected districts. The document’s focus is operational readiness and speed of service delivery rather than changing policy coverage terms: the compliance obligation is to ensure rapid claim intake, escalation, and settlement support for customers impacted by the Assam floods, with visible local points of contact and continuous assistance availability.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued a circular dated **23 July 2026** to **all insurers except reinsurers** requiring them to improve the timeliness and completeness of submissions made to the **Office of the Insurance Ombudsmen (IO)**. The regulator says that, based on a recent orientation programme for Insurance Ombudsmen, insurers have been causing **inordinate delays** by submitting **Self-Contained Notes (SCNs)**, supporting documents, and follow-up information **piecemeal** and **late**, which in turn delays resolution of policyholder/beneficiary complaints.

The circular emphasizes that SCNs and any further documents requested by the Ombudsman are essential for deciding complaints, and that insurers must provide the materials sought under **Rule 15(2) of the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017** promptly. This is tied to **Rule 17(4)**, which requires that a complaint be decided **within 90 days of receipt of all required information from the complainant**; delayed insurer responses undermine this statutory timeline. To improve disposal efficiency, IRDAI advises insurers to submit the required SCNs **duly supported by relevant documents**, rather than sending information in fragments after repeated follow-ups.

Although the excerpt cuts off before listing every procedural instruction, the document clearly establishes a compliance expectation that insurers must treat Ombudsman requests as time-sensitive and provide complete, organized, and prompt responses to avoid delaying complaint adjudication. The practical compliance impact is on all insurer complaint-handling and Ombudsman-response processes: insurers should ensure that SCNs and requested documents are compiled and submitted without unnecessary delay, and that subsequent information requests are tracked and answered comprehensively, since the regulator views delayed or partial submissions as a matter of concern.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 14 July 2026 and addressed to all insurers, issues additional clarifications on implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), building on Circular No. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/45/4/2026 dated 1 April 2026. The stated purpose is to ensure consistent implementation of the regulatory framework and it specifically clarifies three areas: the role of the Appointed Actuary, the requirement for independent validation, and the use of Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation.

On the Appointed Actuary’s role, the circular says that under Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, the Appointed Actuary must provide actuarial expertise and support for preparation of financial statements under applicable Ind AS, but this role is limited to actuarial inputs and valuation-related support; the Appointed Actuary is not the person responsible for actually drafting or signing the financial statements. The circular then clarifies that the insurer’s management remains responsible for the preparation and approval of Ind AS financial statements, while the Appointed Actuary contributes required actuarial inputs, assumptions, and valuations.

A major change concerns independent validation and timing. For the financial year 2026–27, and for every year thereafter, an independent validation of the insurer’s Ind AS financial statements is required before finalization. The circular specifies that this independent validation must be completed by 31 August 2026 for the 2026–27 financial year, and similar timelines will apply in subsequent years in line with the year-end reporting process. The validation is intended to cover the proper application of Ind AS, including actuarial assumptions, policy liability measurements, and consistency of disclosures, and it must be carried out by an independent professional or firm with the relevant expertise and no conflict of interest.

The circular also clarifies how Ind AS-compliant financial statements are to be used for consolidation. For any insurer that is part of a group, the Ind AS financial statements prepared by the insurer are to be used for group consolidation purposes, provided they are prepared in accordance with the applicable Ind AS and have undergone the required independent validation. The document implies that insurers must ensure their subsidiary/parent consolidation packs are based on validated Ind AS numbers rather than on separate local-compliance figures.

Finally, the circular indicates that insurers must align their internal processes, governance, and reporting timelines with these requirements immediately for the 2026–27 cycle. Compliance officers should ensure the Appointed Actuary’s responsibilities are properly documented and limited to actuarial support, that an independent validation mechanism is in place well before the 31 August 2026 deadline, and that finance, actuarial, and consolidation teams are coordinating so that the validated Ind AS financial statements can be used for reporting and consolidation without delay.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **8 July 2026** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, updates the **formats for publishing financial results under SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015** for listed insurance entities. It explains that SEBI’s master circular on financial-results publication already required listed insurers to use IRDAI-prescribed formats, but those formats now needed revision because of the **adoption of Ind AS by insurers**. As a result, the circular says the **unaudited/audited quarterly financial-results formats submitted to stock exchanges have been updated** for **all listed Life Insurers, General Insurers, Health Insurers, and Reinsurers**.

The updated requirements apply specifically to listed insurers/reinsurers **that are required to prepare financial statements under Ind AS**. For these entities, **quarterly financial results must be presented in the format set out in Annexure I**, and the **segment-wise Revenue, Results, and Capital Employed** must also be reported along with the quarterly results, in the format prescribed in **Annexure II**. The circular also refers to a further format in **Annexure III** and indicates another annexure tied to **SEBI LODR Regulation 47(1)(b)**, implying additional publication-format obligations where applicable to listed entities.

The circular also notes an important exception: insurers that have been granted **forbearance for Ind AS implementation for FY 2026–27** are treated differently, because the format changes are driven by Ind AS adoption and therefore apply to the entities that are actually operating under Ind AS. It further references earlier IRDAI directions/circulars from **25 January 2016** and **30 January 2017**, indicating that the current update is a replacement or revision of prior publishing formats rather than a wholly new reporting regime. For compliance purposes, listed insurers should ensure their stock-exchange financial-result disclosures are revised immediately to match the new annexed formats, including the quarterly statement and the required segment reporting, so that their disclosures remain aligned with IRDAI’s standards under the SEBI LODR framework.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the transitional arrangements governing **payment of annual fee and issuance of Certificate of Registration** for insurance intermediaries, and for surveyors/loss assessors where applicable. These arrangements had originally been issued by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026**, with applicability extended to surveyors and loss assessors by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/54/4/2026 dated 7 April 2026**. The earlier transitional framework was due to expire on **30 June 2026**, but IRDAI has now decided that it will continue **beyond 30 June 2026 until the date the relevant amended Regulations are notified**.

More specifically, the circular amends the timing in the earlier circulars so that the period referenced in **paragraph 4.3 of Circular 41/3/2026** is extended from **30 June 2026 to 31 August 2026, or to the date of notification of the relevant amended Regulations, whichever is earlier**. It also states that **paragraph 4.1 of Circular 54/4/2026** is to be read in line with this extension. The practical effect is that entities covered by those circulars should continue following the interim process for annual fee payment and certificate issuance until the new regulations are formally notified, rather than assuming the transitional mechanism ends on 30 June 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that firms in the affected categories must keep using the existing transitional arrangement and should monitor closely for the notification of the amended Regulations, because that notification will end the transitional regime even if it occurs before **31 August 2026**. No new fee rate or threshold is introduced in this circular; the only substantive change is the **extension of the interim compliance period and related operational process** pending the final regulatory amendments under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, as amended by the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025**.

This IRDAI circular, dated 25.05.2026 and issued under Ref. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/72/5/2026, amends the remuneration framework for Key Managerial Persons (KMPs) under the IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024. It specifically modifies Regulation 8.1(b) and 8.3, and also updates the related definitions/wording in Regulation 9.2, so insurers must review their KMP pay structures under the 2024 corporate governance regime rather than treating this as a standalone guidance note.

The core change is a new cap methodology for KMP remuneration for FY 2026–27, with a formula driven by the insurer’s size/financial metrics and thresholds. The document lays out a graded structure with three bands and corresponding maximum remuneration percentages: for one band the cap is linked to 90% of a benchmark amount, for another it references a 30/40/50 threshold structure tied to the “(G + …)” measure, and for another it uses 15, 30, and 60 as review/approval trigger points; in addition, the circular mentions a “10%” and “50%” limit in connection with certain components and an overall ceiling for specific KMP remuneration categories. It also explicitly distinguishes fixed and variable compensation and sets out how variable pay should be computed, including a formula based on a ratio of one amount to another, and it describes that certain remuneration components may be excluded or restricted depending on the applicable band and conditions.

For compliance purposes, insurers must examine remuneration proposals not only for whole-time KMPs but also for other managerial/technical roles covered by the revised wording, and they must apply the new calculation rules when determining whether pay is within the permitted ceiling. The circular indicates that some remuneration arrangements require prior approval/escalation when they cross specified thresholds, and it introduces a staged approach using annual compensation levels and band-based percentage caps rather than a flat, universal limit. It also appears to require that remuneration be split and evaluated by component, with special treatment for variable pay and other allowances, so boards and nomination/remuneration committees will need to document the basis for each KMP package under the new framework.

The practical compliance action is to reassess FY 2026–27 KMP compensation plans, map each KMP into the relevant category under the amended regulations, and ensure that any proposed fixed pay, variable pay, or other perks comply with the new formula and ceiling structure before approval or payment. Because the circular amends the underlying regulations themselves, insurers should update internal remuneration policies, committee approval templates, and governance papers to reflect the revised provisions, and they should be prepared to justify any compensation above the lower benchmark percentages only where the circular’s conditions and approval route are satisfied.

This circular from IRDAI clarifies how the post-amendment annual-fee and certificate-of-registration transition applies to **Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs)** under the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025**. It states that the circular applies to **all SLAs** and is issued in continuation of IRDAI’s earlier circular dated **16 March 2026** on transitional arrangements for annual fee payment and CoR issuance for intermediaries. The background noted is that the SBSR Act amended **Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938** so that intermediary registration continues in force subject to payment of the annual fee prescribed by regulation, unless suspended or cancelled by the Authority.

The key operational change is the treatment of the **annual fee for SLAs for the period 5 March 2026 to 30 September 2026**. The circular provides the applicable fee structure and the **18% GST** component: for the first fee slab, the base fee is **₹400**, GST is **₹72**, and the total payable is **₹472**; for the second fee slab, the base fee is **₹2,000**, GST is **₹360**, and the total payable is **₹2,360**. The document also indicates that the annual-fee mechanism must be read in light of the transitional framework, with SLAs continuing to be subject to registration and fee requirements during the transition rather than falling outside the regime.

The circular also clarifies timing around the transition. It states that **from 5 March 2026 to 5 March 2027**, the relevant arrangements continue, and it specifically notes the applicability of the clarified fee and registration treatment during that period. It further references that the earlier circular had already set transitional arrangements for intermediaries generally, and this document narrows that guidance to SLAs because of their distinct operational and fee structure. The practical compliance takeaway is that SLAs should ensure their annual fee payments are made in accordance with this updated structure and timeline so that their **registration remains in force** and their **Certificate of Registration** is properly issued/maintained under the revised framework.

The IRDAI has issued this circular on 1 April 2026 to all insurers, under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999, and Regulations 7 and 8 of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, to provide implementation clarifications on Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS). The circular follows amendments notified to the 2024 Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions Regulations, and the clarifications are intended to govern how insurers should apply the amended Ind AS framework from 1 April 2026 onward.

The document is structured around multiple specific issues, with the clarifications stated in the body and Annexure-II. It covers, among other things, the treatment of items in relation to the insurer’s balance sheet and financial reporting under Ind AS, including references to products, liabilities, and other insurer-specific accounting items. The circular also clarifies the handling of certain matters under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDAI regulatory framework, including the application of provisions linked to Sections 11, 13, 49, and 64 of the Insurance Act, 1938, as well as references to regulatory reporting/filing obligations and treatment of assets or investments under the revised regime.

A key operational deadline in the circular is 30 April 2026, which is mentioned as a required date for a specified submission/action under the clarifications. The circular also refers to the 2026–27 period in connection with implementation, indicating that insurers must align their accounting and related compliance processes for that financial year. The document points insurers to Annexure-I and Annexure-II for the detailed question-and-answer clarifications that drive the actual implementation requirements.

The circular makes clear that insurers should follow the clarified interpretations for their Ind AS implementation and related regulatory compliance, rather than relying on prior practice that may be inconsistent with the new amendments. It also references the need to comply with linked provisions of the Insurance Act, 1938, including Sections 11, 13, 49, and 64, implying that the accounting treatment cannot be viewed in isolation from statutory insurance reporting and investment requirements. If insurers need clarification, they are instructed to contact IRDAI at the email address provided: indas-team@irdai.gov.in.

IRDAI has issued a transitional circular for insurance intermediaries under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (“SBSR Act”), which became effective on 5 February 2026. Exercising powers under section 42D(4A), IRDAI is changing the mechanism for two compliance areas: the payment of annual fee and the issuance of the Certificate of Registration for insurance intermediaries.

The circular applies broadly to all registered insurance intermediary categories, specifically Insurance Brokers, Corporate Agents, Insurance Marketing Firms (IMFs), Web Aggregators, Common Service Centres (CSCs), Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors, Insurance Repositories, Third Party Administrators (TPAs), and any other entities registered as insurance intermediaries under the applicable regulations. It states that the SBSR Act has amended section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938, and the new transitional framework is meant to govern the move to the amended regime.

The key operative dates are 5 February 2026, when the SBSR Act came into force, and the transitional payment/registration window from 5 March 2026 to 30 June 2026. During this period, intermediaries are required to follow the transitional arrangements prescribed by IRDAI for annual fee payment and certificate issuance; the circular refers to specific forms/annexures and procedural provisions to be used in this period, indicating that existing or legacy procedures are not simply continuing unchanged.

For compliance teams, the practical point is that annual fee and registration certificate administration is no longer just a routine pre-existing renewal process; it is now governed by a statutory transition under the amended law, with a defined compliance window and IRDAI-specified procedures. Intermediaries in any of the listed categories should ensure their registration status, annual fee payments, and certificate issuance/renewal activities are aligned with the new transitional requirements applicable from 5 March 2026 through 30 June 2026.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a clarification circular on insurers’ investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), dated 12/02/2026, to supplement para 1.5 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17/05/2024. The circular confirms that the existing framework already permits insurer investment only in Fund of Funds (FoFs) that comply with section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938; insurers must have the FoF’s offer documents include a clause preventing that FoF from investing into AIFs that invest in overseas companies or funds; insurers must ensure AIFs do not invest in securities of companies incorporated outside India; and an insurer cannot invest in an AIF that has exposure to a FoF in which that insurer already has exposure.

The new circular is being issued because insurers sought clarification on how these rules apply where AIFs use “excuse rights” and how investee limits should be treated for direct and indirect exposure through FoFs. IRDAI states that compliance with the newly clarified conditions will satisfy sub-paras 4(b), 4(c), and 5 of para 1.5 of the Master Circular, and it introduces a specific exception-based framework for AIFs using excuse rights. Under the clarified approach, insurers may invest only in AIFs that do not, either directly or indirectly, breach the section 27E restriction on overseas exposure, and the insurer must ensure the relevant AIF/FoF structure is consistent with the clarified investment restrictions before committing funds.

The circular therefore broadens the permissible avenues for insurer investment in AIFs, but only within the clarified compliance guardrails. For compliance teams, the key action is to review AIF and FoF structures, fund offer documents, and any excuse-rights mechanics to confirm that the underlying investment chain does not create prohibited overseas exposure or impermissible cross-exposure through FoFs. The document does not state a separate implementation deadline beyond the circular date itself, so the clarifications should be treated as effective from issuance unless a later operative date is specified in the full text.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **6 January 2026** to **all insurers and insurance intermediaries** directing them to implement TRAI’s mandatory **1600-series** calling framework for consumer-facing communications. The circular responds to TRAI’s **16 December 2025 Direction**, issued under **section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997**, intended to curb **Unsolicited Commercial Communication (UCC)**, reduce impersonation-based fraud, and improve consumer trust.

The key compliance requirement is that **all service and transactional voice calls** to consumers must be moved to the **1600 series**, and this adoption must be **completed by 15 February 2026**. After that date, insurers and intermediaries **must not initiate service or transactional voice calls from any number other than one allocated under the 1600 series**, and this restriction applies **regardless of whether customer consent is explicit or implied**. In other words, consent does not create an exception for using non-1600 numbers for these call types.

The circular also warns that **any UCC complaint** against an entity that does not comply will be dealt with under the **regulatory provisions applicable to unregistered telemarketers under TRAI**, and this is **in addition to any further action** that the Authority (IRDAI) may deem appropriate. For compliance teams, this means firms should urgently confirm allocation of 1600-series numbers, complete technical and operational migration before the deadline, and ensure all outbound service/transactional calling workflows, vendor arrangements, and telephony systems are blocked from using non-1600 numbers after **15 February 2026**.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular permitting **insurers and reinsurers** to invest not only in bank AT1 and Tier 2 instruments, but also in the **same types of capital instruments issued by RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. Specifically, insurers may now invest in **AT1 bonds** and in **Debt Capital Instruments and Preference Share Capital Instruments (excluding Perpetual Cumulative Preference Shares)** that form **Tier 2 capital** of such AIFIs. The circular states that this expansion is intended to broaden insurers’ investment options and support portfolio diversification.

This permission is tied to the fact that **RBI enabled AIFIs to issue Additional Tier 1 Bonds and Tier 2 capital effective 1 April 2024** under its Basel III prudential framework. IRDAI’s instruction is not a new standalone investment regime; instead, insurers must apply the **existing IRDAI investment provisions already applicable to investments in banks**, specifically the rules in **paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024**. In other words, compliance teams should treat these AIFI instruments as fitting within the same framework used for bank AT1/Tier 2 investments, rather than creating a separate internal policy basis.

The circular also imposes an administrative/compliance requirement: insurers must use the **existing category codes specified for investments in PSU banks** when recording these investments. The document does not introduce a separate later implementation date beyond the circular date itself; it is dated **19 December 2025**, and the permission is presented as effective immediately from that issuance. For compliance purposes, the key action is to ensure that investment policy, limits, approvals, classification/reporting, and system coding are updated so that investments in these AIFI AT1 and Tier 2 instruments are processed consistently with the bank-investment framework and mapped using the existing PSU-bank category codes.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular dated **10 October 2025** announces a **full cessation of the earlier practice of allowing individual Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs) to add an additional line of business/department to their surveyor licence on the basis of the categorization letter issued in 2001–02**. It applies to **all licensed Surveyors and Loss Assessors**, and specifically addresses the category of individual SLAs who had been categorized into multiple lines of business before the **IRDA Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (Licensing, Professional Requirements and Code of Conduct) Regulations, 2000** took effect. The circular explains that, under the earlier system, an individual SLA was categorized in several lines of business/departments, and later was permitted to retain only **3 LOBs** from among those categorized on the licence.

The regulator had already relaxed this framework through **Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020**, which allowed an individual SLA to **add LOBs based on the 2001–02 categorization letter** if the person had the relevant educational qualification and had maintained **continuous renewal of the licence without break** up to the date of filing the modification application. That 2020 circular also removed the earlier **cap of 3 LOBs** on an individual surveyor licence. However, IRDAI states that it has now received multiple applications under this 2020 route from SLAs who are seeking to add new LOBs but have **not carried out the required survey work in the relevant line(s) of business in recent times / as required under the applicable norms**, indicating that the earlier concession was being used beyond its intended scope.

As a result, IRDAI is ending this practice: **the option to seek addition of LOB/department to an SLA licence solely on the basis of the old 2001–02 categorization letter is no longer available**. Compliance teams should treat this as a change affecting the **licensing and scope of work of individual surveyors/loss assessors**, particularly those who may have been relying on the 2020 circular to expand their licence coverage. Going forward, any SLA licence modification requests should be reviewed under the current regulatory framework rather than the old categorization-based relaxation, and firms should ensure that internal records, authorizations, and engagement assignments reflect that the prior facilitation for adding LOBs from the 2001–02 categorization has been discontinued.

IRDAI has issued Circular No. IRDAI/RBC/CIR/MISC/94/8/2025 dated 14 August 2025 on **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** under the Risk Based Capital (RBC) framework for the Indian insurance industry. The circular explains that RBC implementation is a key IRDAI initiative to align Indian insurance regulation with global best practices, and that QIS 2 follows the first quantitative impact study (QIS 1) conducted in 2023. Based on the results of QIS 1 and feedback from insurers, IRDAI is requiring a second impact study to refine the framework further.

The requirement applies to **all Life Insurers, General Insurers, Standalone Health Insurers, Reinsurers, Branches of Foreign Reinsurers, and Lloyd’s India**. Insurers must complete QIS 2 **using the Technical Guidance document** and must base the exercise on the **data used for actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025**. IRDAI says the technical guidance, the data submission template, the requirements for the associated template used to submit results, the submission mode, and the supplementary information will be communicated separately to insurers.

The circular states that **QIS 2 is a pivotal step toward the RBC framework**, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal regulatory exercise rather than a voluntary consultation. The only deadline explicitly visible in the text provided is the use of the **31 March 2025 valuation data**; the circular also references that the separate technical guidance and submission instructions will follow, so insurers should monitor for those documents and prepare to meet any resulting submission requirements promptly.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI Master Circular, issued on 25 July 2025 as Ref. IRDAI/NL/CIR/RSS/85/07/2025, consolidates and updates the insurer obligations relating to rural sector, social sector, and motor third-party business under the Insurance Act framework and the IRDAI (Obligations of Insurers to Rural and Social Sectors) Regulations, 2024. It applies to Indian insurance companies and uses two annexures/schedules: Schedule-1 and Schedule-2, which are referenced as the operative bases for compliance reporting and targets. The circular expressly ties the obligations to the 2024-25 base year and then sets revised compliance expectations for 2025-26 and 2026-27.

For rural-sector obligations, the circular sets minimum thresholds by insurer category and product type. For one category of insurers, the rural business requirement is 15% for 2025-26 and rises to 25% for 2026-27, with minimum numbers of 25,000 policies in 2025-26 and 50,000 policies in 2026-27. For another category, the obligation is 15% in 2025-26 and 25% in 2026-27, again with 25,000 and 50,000 policy minimums, and the circular also refers to split requirements of 25% and 10% for sub-components of the obligation. For certain other classes, the rural business requirement is 10% for 2025-26 and 12% for 2026-27. The document also provides a rate table for another rural-sector compliance measure by business size bands, with rates increasing from 2025-26 to 2026-27: for 2% business size, the rate moves from 12.50% to 13.75%; for 2%–5%, from 10.00% to 11.00%; for 5%–10%, from 7.50% to 8.25%; and for above 10%, from 5.00% to 5.50%.

For social-sector obligations, the circular preserves the requirement framework under the 2024 regulations and indicates that social-sector targets are to be complied with for the relevant 2025-26 and 2026-27 periods, with the operative provisions linked to the earlier schedule/annexure structure. The document also appears to require reporting and compliance with identified categories of social-sector persons/beneficiaries, with the detailed operational definitions and counts captured in the referenced schedules rather than fully restated in the visible excerpt. Compliance officers should therefore treat the annexed schedules as mandatory for determining exact population coverage, reporting format, and fulfillment calculations.

For motor third-party obligations, the circular updates the premium-based contribution structure, with a specific requirement that the “motor third-party” related obligation be met in line with the schedule, and the excerpt shows a percentage increase for 2025-26 and 2026-27. A highlighted obligation is 2% under one measure, and the schedule also indicates the insurer categories and sub-bands used to determine the required contribution level. The visible text also references the need to ensure policy issuance/reporting and accounting alignment by 30 days and includes a compliance date of 31 March 2025/31 March 2026 in the context of annual reporting and calculation windows, meaning companies should confirm their year-end compliance extraction, reconciliation, and filing processes against those deadlines.

Operationally, the circular requires insurers to maintain the records and filings needed to prove compliance with rural, social, and motor third-party obligations, and to use the updated schedules/annexures for measurement rather than legacy internal assumptions. It also contemplates category-specific classification of business and insurer type, so compliance teams should verify which of the insurer classes they fall into for each obligation before applying the percentage targets and minimum policy counts. The practical effect is that insurers must update their planning, underwriting, distribution, and reporting controls for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 to ensure they can meet the higher rural thresholds and the revised motor-third-party/social-sector calculations, with any shortfall likely to create regulatory non-compliance under the IRDAI obligations regime.

This IRDAI guideline, dated **11 February 2026** and issued under reference **IRDAI/F&I/GDL/MISC/27/02/2026**, replaces/updates the earlier framework referenced in the document (including the prior **17 October 2022** guidance) and sets out the rules for **insurance companies registered outside India** that want to **establish or close a liaison office in India**. It is aimed at foreign insurers, and it ties the liaison-office process to Indian regulatory oversight rather than treating it as a purely corporate-filings matter.

On **establishment**, the document requires the foreign insurance company to make an application to IRDAI in the prescribed format and with the supporting information listed in the annexures. The application package is structured to cover the applicant’s identity and regulatory status, details of the parent/foreign insurer, proposed India liaison-office activity, and the required declarations/undertakings. The guideline indicates that the liaison office is limited to permitted liaison-type functions and is not a full operating insurance business presence; the office is subject to conditions and oversight, and the document’s annexures specify the reporting, declarations, and compliance documentation that must accompany the request.

The guidance also imposes **ongoing compliance and reporting obligations** on the liaison office after approval, including maintaining the office only for the purposes allowed under the framework and complying with the regulator’s information requests and procedural requirements. The document points to defined annexures for the detailed contents of the application, the declarations to be furnished, and the requirements for closure, which means compliance teams need to treat the annexures as operative parts of the rule, not just explanatory notes. If the office ceases to be needed or the insurer wants to terminate it, closure is not automatic: the foreign insurer must follow the prescribed closure process, submit the required closure request/documents, and ensure that the office’s activities are wound down in accordance with IRDAI’s instructions.

The guideline is therefore relevant to any **non-Indian registered insurer** considering a liaison presence in India or already operating one. The practical compliance takeaway is that both **entry** and **exit** are regulated events requiring prior/structured regulatory filings, prescribed declarations, and adherence to the conditions attached by IRDAI; firms should review the annexures closely to confirm the exact form, supporting documents, and any office-specific obligations before making changes.

The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework Guidelines, 2025** under **Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** and **Section 14(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999** to create a regulatory framework for how insurers and distribution channels must identify, monitor, and manage insurance fraud risk. The guidelines apply broadly to **all insurers and distribution channels**, unless a specific exemption is stated elsewhere in the document, and they are intended to cover fraud risk arising across the insurance business and its external intermediaries. The document is titled and effective as the **IRDAI (Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework) Guidelines, 2025**, with the reference date shown as **09.10.2025** and an applicability/commencement date indicated in the text as **1 January 2026**.

A key requirement is that insurers must implement a formal fraud monitoring framework, with governance and controls designed to detect, prevent, report, and respond to fraud. The document defines terms relevant to the framework, including “fraud,” “distribution channels,” and other operational concepts, and then sets out obligations for insurers and distribution channels to maintain appropriate systems, records, controls, and escalation processes. The framework is meant to cover both **internal fraud** and **external fraud** affecting the insurer’s operations, policy servicing, claims, procurement, and distribution-related activities.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has amended Clause 15(a) of the “Revised Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and Electronic Issuance of Insurance Policies” (originally issued 29 May 2015). The substantive change is to the annual review requirement for an insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards: instead of requiring the review to be conducted by an “external system audit firm approved by the Authority” on a yearly basis, the clause now requires that the review of the controls, systems, procedures and safeguards established under Clause 14 be conducted **at least once a year**, **at the repository’s own cost**, by an **external auditor** who is **either** a **Certified Information System Auditor (CISA)**, a **Chartered Accountant with DISA (ICAI) qualification**, or a **CERT-In certified expert**.

For compliance purposes, this means insurance repositories must ensure their annual audit/review program is performed by a suitably qualified individual auditor meeting one of those three credentials, rather than by a generic external system audit firm, and must budget for the review themselves. The amendment applies specifically to entities operating as insurance repositories under the referenced IRDAI guidelines and to the review of the controls/systems/procedures/safeguards described in Clause 14. The circular is stated to come into force **with immediate effect**; no transition period, later effective date, or numerical threshold beyond the “at least once a year” frequency is provided.
