rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered an April 22, 2025 disciplinary order against registered public accounting firm Adeptus Partners LLC and partner Howard S. Krant, CPA, based on violations tied to supervision, audit review, and quality control in connection with the audits of two issuers. The Board censured both Adeptus and Krant; suspended Krant from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm for one year starting on the date of the Order; imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty on Krant; imposed a $75,000 civil money penalty on Adeptus; and required Adeptus to retain an independent consultant to review its quality-control system and make recommendations as specified in Section IV of the Order. The PCAOB’s findings state that Krant violated PCAOB rules and standards in the two issuer audits, and that Adeptus violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards, indicating deficiencies not only in individual audit performance but also in the firm’s supervisory and system-level controls.

For compliance purposes, the key immediate obligations are the monetary sanctions, the one-year association ban on Krant effective from April 22, 2025, and the firm’s duty to engage an independent consultant and implement the consultant-review process required by the Order. The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the matter was resolved through offers of settlement accepted by the Board under PCAOB Rule 5205. The order is relevant to any registered public accounting firm, particularly those auditing issuers, because it underscores PCAOB enforcement exposure for failures in supervision, audit review, and quality control systems.

rows.title: The PCAOB has sanctioned James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner for audit failures.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, imposes significant disciplinary sanctions for audit-related violations involving two audits of one issuer client. The Board found that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in performing those audits, and that the firm specifically failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR). The order also states that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with those engagements, which is a separate reporting/compliance failure.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured both the firm and Pai, revoked the firm’s registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. In addition, the firm is required to undertake remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, on top of any CPE required for licensing, before he may file a petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm.

The order provides that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may file a petition for Board consent to associate only after three years from the same date. For compliance teams, the key takeaways are that the PCAOB treated the audit failures, missing EQR, and inaccurate Form AP filings as serious violations warranting revocation, a personal bar, monetary penalty, and mandatory remediation/CPE conditions tied to any future re-entry into the PCAOB-regulated practice environment.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 11, 2025 Order against Jaslyn Sellers, CPA imposes three sanctions: a censure, a bar from associating with any registered public accounting firm, and a $15,000 civil money penalty. The Board based these sanctions on findings that Sellers violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards in connection with two issuer audits and also violated auditor independence requirements in one of those audits. The Order was issued under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), following Sellers’ settlement offer under Rule 5205, which the Board accepted.

For compliance purposes, the key practical consequence is that Sellers is immediately barred from acting as an associated person of a registered public accounting firm, which means she cannot perform work for or hold an associated-person role with such a firm unless she later obtains Board consent. The Order states she may file a petition for Board consent to associate only after two years from the date of the Order, so the earliest petition date would be March 11, 2027. Although the penalty imposed was $15,000, the Order notes that the civil money penalty would have been $75,000 based on the conduct, but PCAOB reduced it after considering Sellers’ financial resources.

The document does not describe the underlying audit failures in detail, but it makes clear that the misconduct involved two issuer audits and included at least one independence violation, which is especially significant because independence requirements apply to the audit engagement and the firm’s ability to issue an informative, accurate, and independent audit report. The proceeding was instituted to protect investors and the public interest, indicating that the PCAOB treated these violations as serious professional conduct failures rather than isolated technical errors.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB sanctioned PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC Singapore) on March 11, 2025 in PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-018 for violations tied to the firm’s administration of Personal Independence Compliance Testing (PICT) over an approximately two-year period. The Board found that, in connection with that testing program, the firm violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards, and it treated the matter as significant enough to warrant disciplinary proceedings under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) to protect investors and the public interest in accurate, independent audit reports.

As a result, the PCAOB issued an order that does three things: it censures PwC Singapore, imposes a civil money penalty of $1,500,000, and requires the firm to undertake remedial actions described later in the Order. The document states that PwC Singapore submitted an Offer of Settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205, which the Board accepted; for purposes of these proceedings, the firm consented to entry of the Order without admitting or denying the findings, except that it admitted the PCAOB’s jurisdiction over the firm and the subject matter.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the sanction is specifically linked to independence compliance testing and the firm’s internal quality control over that process, not merely a technical filing issue. The Order is effective as of its issuance on March 11, 2025, and the monetary penalty is immediate unless otherwise specified in the later remedial section. Because the document expressly references further remedial actions in Section IV, compliance staff should review the full Order for any mandated process changes, monitoring, reporting, or governance enhancements beyond the censure and penalty.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 11, 2025 settled order against KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. (KPMG Brazil) censures the firm, imposes a $700,000 civil money penalty, and requires remedial actions described in the order. The sanctions are based on conduct occurring between 2020 and 2023 and concern 38 issuer audits in which the firm failed to make required communications to the applicable audit committee or audit committee equivalent, in violation of PCAOB Auditing Standard AS 1301.10d on communications with audit committees. The PCAOB also found that KPMG Brazil failed to report certain audit reports or consents on PCAOB Form 2 for six issuer audits, violating PCAOB Rule 2200’s annual reporting requirement, and filed two inaccurate Form APs, violating PCAOB Rule 3211(a), which governs reporting of certain audit participants.

In addition to the monetary penalty and censure, the order requires the firm to implement specific remedial measures under Section V of the order, reflecting the PCAOB’s view that quality control deficiencies were also present. The matter was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the proceedings were resolved through a settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated failures in audit committee communications, issuer reporting filings, and Form AP accuracy as enforcement-level violations, and the order applies specifically to KPMG Brazil’s issuer-audit work during the 2020–2023 period.

The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that Murphy: (1) failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) (“Heaton & Co.” or the “Firm”) by providing misleading information to PCAOB inspectors in connection with two issuer audits; (2) failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two issuer audits; and (3) failed to timely assemble for retention a complete and final set of audit documentation in a total of five issuer audits. 1 Murphy may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm after five years from the date of this Order. Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Natalie Murphy, CPA, Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-006 February 25, 2025 2 I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted pursu
rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a disciplinary order against former engagement partner Natalie Murphy, CPA, based on misconduct tied to issuer audit work and her cooperation with a PCAOB inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah). The Board censured Murphy, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before she can even petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm; any such petition cannot be filed until five years after the date of the Order, February 25, 2025.

The conduct leading to the sanctions was that Murphy failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection by providing misleading information to inspectors regarding two issuer audits, failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two audits, and failed to timely assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation for retention in a total of five issuer audits. For compliance purposes, the order underscores that engagement partners and other personnel at registered public accounting firms must provide truthful, complete, and timely responses during PCAOB inspections, and must properly document post-completion changes to audit workpapers and finalize audit files within the required retention timeline.

The practical effect is that Murphy is prohibited from working in any capacity that would constitute being “associated with” a registered public accounting firm unless and until the PCAOB grants consent after the five-year period and she satisfies the additional 40-hour CPE شرط. The report does **not** announce a new rule or deadline for issuers; rather, it documents inspection findings from audits RSM performed, and it distinguishes among three types of issues: **Part I.A deficiencies**, where the PCAOB believed RSM had **not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence** to support its audit opinion(s) on issuer financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR); **Part I.B deficiencies**, which are other instances of noncompliance with PCAOB standards or rules that do not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions; and **Part I.C deficiencies**, which are apparent noncompliance with independence rules. The report expressly cautions that the presence of Part I.A or Part I.B findings does **not automatically mean** an issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated or that a material weakness in ICFR exists, and a Part I.C finding is a separate independence matter rather than an audit-evidence issue. Because the provided excerpt stops in the middle of the executive summary, it does not include the specific engagement names, counts of deficiencies, affected audit areas, remediation requirements, or any firm-specific sanctions or deadlines. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the excerpt is that RSM was subject to PCAOB inspection and the report flags possible audit-quality and independence deficiencies in certain issuer audits, which may warrant heightened attention to audit documentation, evidence sufficiency, and independence controls if your company is an RSM audit client.
